topics.t: What makes something living, and how diverse is life?
topics.h: A crystal of salt grows in brine and a mule cannot reproduce. So which of them is alive? Biology starts by answering exactly this.
p: Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response to surroundings (consciousness). Metabolism and cellular organisation are the defining features.
Growth alone cannot define life: non-living mountains, sand mounds and crystals also grow, by accumulation of material on the outer surface. Living organisms grow from inside.
Reproduction alone cannot define life: mules, sterile worker bees and infertile couples do not reproduce, yet they are alive.
Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in the body. No non-living object shows metabolism, so it is a defining property of life.
Biodiversity means the number and variety of organisms on Earth. About 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described so far, and many more are still unknown.

ex.q: Explain why a sterile worker honeybee is classed as living even though it never reproduces.
st: Reproduction is not shown by every living individual, so it cannot be a defining feature.
The worker bee shows metabolism: it digests nectar, respires and builds wax.
It also shows cellular organisation and responds to stimuli such as light and smell.
Metabolism and cellular organisation are defining features of life.
ex.a: It is living because it has cellular organisation and metabolism; reproduction is not a defining property.

topics.rl: India is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries. The Western Ghats and the north-east alone hold thousands of plant and animal species, many found nowhere else.

rv.summary: Living things show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response, but only metabolism and cellular organisation define life. Biodiversity is the number and variety of organisms; about 1.7–1.8 million species are described.
focus: Why growth and reproduction are not defining features of life
Metabolism and cellular organisation as the defining features
Difference between growth from inside and growth by surface accumulation
Meaning of biodiversity and the number of described species
remember: Defining features of life: metabolism and cellular organisation
Metabolism = sum of all chemical reactions in the body
Described species: about 1.7 to 1.8 million
traps: Don't call growth a defining feature: crystals and mountains also grow
Don't say non-reproducing organisms (mule, worker bee) are non-living

topics.t: Why scientific names? Identification and nomenclature
topics.h: Brinjal, baingan, vankaya, kathirikai, aubergine, eggplant: six names for one vegetable. A scientist in Chennai and one in Berlin need one name they both trust.
p: Local names of the same organism differ from place to place, even within one country, so a standard name is needed worldwide.
Identification: describing an organism correctly so that we know exactly which organism it is. It comes before naming.
Nomenclature: giving a correct scientific name to an organism that has been identified.
Scientific names follow international codes: ICBN (International Code for Botanical Nomenclature) for plants and ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature) for animals.
These codes make sure each organism has only one correct name, and that no name is used for two different organisms.

ex.q: Put the steps in order: a new plant found in Meghalaya must be given a scientific name.
st: First describe its features accurately (identification).
Check it against known plants to confirm it is new.
Name it following the rules of ICBN (nomenclature).
ex.a: Identification first, then nomenclature under ICBN.

topics.rl: When AIIMS doctors report a fungal infection, or the Botanical Survey of India lists a new orchid from Arunachal Pradesh, they use scientific names so labs anywhere can understand them.

rv.summary: Local names of an organism differ from place to place, so biologists identify an organism first and then give it one standard scientific name under international codes: ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals.
focus: Why scientific names are needed instead of local names
Identification versus nomenclature, and their order
Full forms and scope of ICBN and ICZN
remember: Identification = correct description of an organism; it comes first
Nomenclature = giving a correct scientific name
ICBN: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (plants); ICZN: International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (animals)
traps: Don't confuse nomenclature (naming) with classification (grouping)
Don't mix up ICBN (plants) and ICZN (animals)

topics.t: Binomial nomenclature: writing scientific names right
topics.h: A board examiner can cut marks for writing 'Mangifera Indica'. One wrong capital letter, and the name is wrong. Let's get it right forever.
p: Binomial nomenclature was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus. Every scientific name has two parts: the generic name (genus) and the specific epithet (species).
Names are in Latin or are latinised, whatever their origin.
When printed, the name is in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately to show their Latin origin.
The genus name begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter. Example: Mangifera indica.
The name of the author who first described the species appears after the epithet in abbreviated form, e.g. Mangifera indica Linn. (Linn. = Linnaeus).

ex.q: A student writes the human scientific name as 'Homo Sapiens' in her answer sheet with no underline. Correct it.
st: Genus Homo starts with a capital: correct.
Specific epithet must start with a small letter: sapiens.
Handwritten names must be underlined, each word separately.
ex.a: Homo sapiens, with 'Homo' and 'sapiens' each underlined separately.

topics.rl: The mango, India's national fruit, is Mangifera indica, and the peacock, the national bird, is Pavo cristatus. 'indica' itself honours India.

rv.summary: Linnaeus's binomial nomenclature gives every organism a two-part Latin name: genus (capital letter) and specific epithet (small letter), italicised in print or underlined separately by hand, with the author's name abbreviated after it.
focus: The two parts of a scientific name and how to identify each
Rules for capitals, italics and underlining
Meaning of the author abbreviation such as Linn.
remember: Proposed by Carolus Linnaeus
Genus: capital first letter; specific epithet: small first letter
Printed in italics; handwritten with each word underlined separately
Example: Mangifera indica Linn.
traps: Don't capitalise the specific epithet (Panthera leo, not Panthera Leo)
Don't draw one line under both words when handwriting; underline each separately

topics.t: Classification, taxon, taxonomy and systematics
topics.h: Supermarkets put all dals in one aisle and all spices in another so you find things fast. Biologists do the same with 1.7 million species.
p: Classification: grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters.
Taxon: a group at any level of classification. 'Plants', 'animals', 'mammals' and 'dogs' are all taxa.
Taxonomy includes characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature of organisms.
Bases of modern taxonomic studies: external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information.
Systematics (from Latin 'systema', systematic arrangement) studies the kinds and diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships. It is broader than taxonomy.

ex.q: Is 'mammals' a taxon? Is 'wheat'? Explain.
st: A taxon is any group at any level of classification.
Mammals form a group at class level, so they are a taxon.
Wheat refers to a group at species level, which is also a taxon.
ex.a: Yes, both are taxa; one at class level, the other at species level.

topics.rl: Seed banks of the ICAR and the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi store lakhs of crop samples. Without careful classification, finding the right rice variety would be impossible.

rv.summary: Classification groups organisms by observable characters; any group at any rank is a taxon. Taxonomy covers characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature, while systematics also studies evolutionary relationships.
focus: Definitions of classification, taxon, taxonomy and systematics
Why systematics is broader than taxonomy
remember: Taxon = a group at any level of classification
Taxonomy = characterisation + identification + classification + nomenclature
Systematics (Latin 'systema') adds evolutionary relationships
traps: Don't say taxonomy is broader than systematics; it is the other way round
Don't think a taxon means only a species; it can be any rank

topics.t: Taxonomic hierarchy: species and genus
topics.h: Your address goes Country → State → City → Street → House. Each organism has a 'biological address' too, and species is the house number.
p: Taxonomic hierarchy: categories arranged in a step-like order, kingdom at the top and species at the bottom.
Each category (rank) is a unit of classification and represents a taxon at that level.
Species: a group of individuals with fundamental similarities. It is the basic unit of classification. Examples: leo (lion), tigris (tiger), pardus (leopard) in Panthera.
Genus: a group of related species with more characters in common than species of other genera. Panthera has lion, tiger and leopard; Solanum has potato (S. tuberosum) and brinjal (S. melongena).
Lion, tiger and leopard share many features, so they are placed in one genus, Panthera; the cat is in a different genus, Felis.

ex.q: Why are potato and brinjal in the same genus but given different species names?
st: Both share many fundamental features, so they belong to the genus Solanum.
They differ in key characters, so each is a separate species.
Hence potato is Solanum tuberosum and brinjal is Solanum melongena.
ex.a: Same genus Solanum, different species: tuberosum and melongena.

topics.rl: The Bengal tiger in Sundarbans, the Asiatic lion in Gir and the leopards of Mumbai's Sanjay Gandhi National Park are all members of one genus: Panthera.

rv.summary: The taxonomic hierarchy arranges ranks from kingdom down to species. Species, a group of individuals with fundamental similarities, is the basic unit; a genus groups related species, e.g. Panthera (lion, tiger, leopard) and Solanum (potato, brinjal).
focus: Meaning of taxonomic hierarchy and category (rank)
Species as the basic unit of classification
Examples of genus: Panthera and Solanum
remember: Species = group of individuals with fundamental similarities
Genus = group of related species
Panthera leo, P. tigris, P. pardus; Solanum tuberosum (potato), S. melongena (brinjal)
traps: Don't say lion, tiger and leopard are the same species; they share only the genus
Don't place the cat in Panthera; it is in genus Felis

topics.t: Family, order, class, phylum and kingdom
topics.h: Going up the hierarchy is like zooming out on Google Maps: you see more and more places, but each one shows fewer shared details.
p: Family: a group of related genera. Felidae (Panthera, Felis), Canidae (dogs) and Solanaceae (Solanum, Petunia, Datura) are families.
Order: an assemblage of families with a few similar characters. Carnivora includes Felidae and Canidae; Polymoniales includes Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae.
Class: related orders. Mammalia includes orders such as Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog). Dicotyledonae is a plant class.
Phylum (animals) or Division (plants): related classes. Chordata includes Mammalia, Aves, Reptilia and Amphibia. Kingdom is the highest category (Animalia, Plantae).
As we go up from species to kingdom, the number of common characters decreases, and the number of organisms in the group increases.

ex.q: Arrange in ascending order (lowest first): Order, Species, Kingdom, Family, Class, Genus, Phylum.
st: Ascending means from the lowest rank to the highest.
Lowest rank is species, then genus, family, order, class, phylum, and kingdom on top.
ex.a: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom

topics.rl: Indian Railways groups its trains into zones, divisions and routes. Bigger units hold more trains but those trains share fewer specific features, just like higher taxa.

rv.summary: Related genera form a family, families an order, orders a class, classes a phylum (division in plants), and phyla a kingdom. Going up, groups hold more organisms but share fewer characters.
focus: Correct order of the seven obligate categories
Examples: Felidae, Canidae in Carnivora; Solanaceae, Convolvulaceae in Polymoniales
How the number of common characters changes up the hierarchy
remember: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom
Division in plants = phylum in animals
Up the hierarchy: common characters decrease, number of organisms increases
traps: Don't say higher categories share more characters; they share fewer
Don't call Primata a family or class; it is an order in class Mammalia

topics.t: Classifying common organisms: man, housefly, mango, wheat
topics.h: Your breakfast roti (wheat) and the fly hovering over it have full biological addresses. Can you read them?
p: Man: Homo sapiens; family Hominidae; order Primata; class Mammalia; phylum Chordata; kingdom Animalia.
Housefly: Musca domestica; family Muscidae; order Diptera; class Insecta; phylum Arthropoda; kingdom Animalia.
Mango: Mangifera indica; family Anacardiaceae; order Sapindales; class Dicotyledonae; division Angiospermae; kingdom Plantae.
Wheat: Triticum aestivum; family Poaceae; order Poales; class Monocotyledonae; division Angiospermae; kingdom Plantae.
Mango and wheat share the division Angiospermae but differ from class downwards: mango is a dicot, wheat a monocot.

ex.q: At which level do mango and wheat stop sharing the same category?
st: Kingdom: both Plantae.
Division: both Angiospermae.
Class: mango is Dicotyledonae, wheat is Monocotyledonae.
ex.a: They separate at the class level.

topics.rl: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) from Punjab and Madhya Pradesh fills the FCI granaries, and Alphonso mangoes (Mangifera indica) from Ratnagiri are exported worldwide.

rv.summary: Man, housefly, mango and wheat show how the hierarchy is used: man and housefly share only kingdom Animalia, while mango (dicot) and wheat (monocot) share kingdom Plantae and division Angiospermae and separate at class.
focus: Full classification of man, housefly, mango and wheat
Finding the level at which two organisms stop sharing a category
Distinguishing order from family names (Primata vs Hominidae)
remember: Man: Hominidae, Primata, Mammalia, Chordata
Housefly: Muscidae, Diptera, Insecta, Arthropoda
Mango: Anacardiaceae, Sapindales, Dicotyledonae, Angiospermae
Wheat: Poaceae, Poales, Monocotyledonae, Angiospermae
traps: Don't call Primata the family of man; the family is Hominidae
Don't put mango in Poales or wheat in Dicotyledonae

topics.t: From two kingdoms to five: history of classification
topics.h: Linnaeus put mushrooms and mango trees in the same kingdom. It took two centuries and a microscope to fix that.
p: Aristotle made the earliest attempt: plants as trees, shrubs and herbs; animals as those with red blood and those without.
Linnaeus used two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia. It did not separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, or photosynthetic green algae from non-photosynthetic fungi.
R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Whittaker's criteria: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
A three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) has also been proposed, which splits Monera into two domains and keeps all eukaryotes in the third.

ex.q: Use the five-kingdom table to place an organism: eukaryotic, cell wall of chitin (no cellulose), heterotrophic by absorption.
st: Eukaryotic rules out Monera.
A cell wall without cellulose rules out Plantae and Animalia (no wall).
Chitin walls and absorptive heterotrophy are features of Fungi.
ex.a: Kingdom Fungi

topics.rl: Mushroom farmers in Himachal Pradesh and spirulina startups in Tamil Nadu both deal with organisms that Linnaeus would have wrongly called 'plants'.

rv.summary: Classification moved from Aristotle and Linnaeus's two kingdoms (Plantae, Animalia) to Whittaker's five kingdoms (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia, based on cell structure, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction and phylogeny.
focus: Whittaker's five kingdoms and his five criteria
Placing an organism using cell type, wall and nutrition
remember: Whittaker (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia
Criteria: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, phylogenetic relationships
Three domains: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya
traps: Don't list size as one of Whittaker's criteria
Don't think the two-kingdom system separated prokaryotes from eukaryotes; it did not

topics.t: Kingdom Monera: bacterial shapes, nutrition and archaebacteria
topics.h: The gas cooking food in many Indian villages comes from cow dung. The real chefs are microbes living in the cow's stomach.
p: Bacteria are the most abundant microorganisms and live almost everywhere, from hot springs to deserts to the deep sea.
Shapes: coccus (spherical), bacillus (rod), vibrio (comma-shaped) and spirillum (spiral).
Nutrition: most are heterotrophs; some are autotrophs, either photosynthetic or chemosynthetic.

Archaebacteria live in extreme habitats: halophiles (very salty areas), thermoacidophiles (hot springs) and methanogens (marshy areas). Their cell wall structure is different from other bacteria, which helps them survive.
Methanogens live in the guts of ruminants such as cows and buffaloes and produce methane (biogas) from dung.

ex.q: A bacterium is found thriving in a hot acidic spring in Manikaran, Himachal Pradesh. Classify it.
st: Extreme habitat points to archaebacteria.
Hot and acidic conditions fit thermoacidophiles.
ex.a: An archaebacterium, a thermoacidophile.

topics.rl: Gobar gas plants promoted under India's biogas programmes rely on methanogens to turn cattle dung into cooking fuel and slurry manure.

rv.summary: Bacteria are the most abundant microbes, shaped as cocci, bacilli, vibrios or spirilla, and mostly heterotrophic. Archaebacteria (halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens) survive extreme habitats thanks to a different cell wall structure.
focus: Three groups of archaebacteria and their habitats
remember: Coccus = spherical, bacillus = rod, vibrio = comma, spirillum = spiral
Halophiles: salty areas; thermoacidophiles: hot springs; methanogens: marshes and ruminant guts
Methanogens produce methane (biogas) from dung
traps: Don't say all bacteria are heterotrophs; some are photosynthetic or chemosynthetic
Don't confuse halophiles (salt) with thermoacidophiles (hot acidic springs)

topics.t: Eubacteria: cyanobacteria and chemosynthetic bacteria
topics.h: Rice farmers in Odisha add 'blue-green algae' to their paddies for free nitrogen. But these 'algae' are actually bacteria!
p: Eubacteria ('true bacteria') have a rigid cell wall and, if motile, a flagellum.
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) have chlorophyll a like green plants and are photosynthetic autotrophs. They may be unicellular, colonial or filamentous, often with a gelatinous sheath.
Some cyanobacteria, such as Nostoc and Anabaena, fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts.
Cyanobacteria often form blooms in polluted water bodies.

Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites and ammonia and use the energy released to make ATP. They help recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur.

ex.q: A Nostoc filament shows a few larger, thick-walled cells. What are they and what do they do?
st: Nostoc is a filamentous cyanobacterium.
Its specialised thick-walled cells are heterocysts.
Heterocysts fix atmospheric nitrogen.
ex.a: Heterocysts, which fix nitrogen.

topics.rl: Many urban lakes in Indian cities turn green with cyanobacterial blooms when sewage adds excess nutrients.

rv.summary: Eubacteria have a rigid cell wall. Cyanobacteria have chlorophyll a and photosynthesise; Nostoc and Anabaena fix nitrogen in heterocysts. Chemosynthetic bacteria oxidise inorganic substances for ATP and recycle N, P, Fe and S.
focus: Features of cyanobacteria and why they are in Monera
How chemosynthetic bacteria get energy and their role in nutrient cycling
remember: Cyanobacteria have chlorophyll a
Heterocysts fix N₂ in Nostoc and Anabaena
Chemosynthetic bacteria oxidise nitrates, nitrites, ammonia to make ATP
traps: Don't place 'blue-green algae' in Protista or Plantae; they are prokaryotic Monera
Don't say chemosynthetic bacteria use sunlight

topics.t: Heterotrophic bacteria, reproduction and Mycoplasma
topics.h: The dahi setting in your kitchen tonight and the cholera outbreak in a flooded town are both bacterial stories.
p: Heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant in nature. Most are decomposers.
Helpful roles: making curd from milk, producing antibiotics and fixing nitrogen in legume roots.
Harmful roles: diseases such as cholera, typhoid and tetanus in humans, and citrus canker in plants.
Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission; under unfavourable conditions they form spores. A primitive DNA transfer from one bacterium to another is a sexual-like process.
Mycoplasma completely lack a cell wall. They are the smallest living cells known, can survive without oxygen, and many are pathogenic in plants and animals.

ex.q: Why are antibiotics that block cell wall formation useless against Mycoplasma?
st: Such antibiotics act on the bacterial cell wall.
Mycoplasma completely lack a cell wall.
So there is no target for the drug.
ex.a: Mycoplasma have no cell wall to attack.

topics.rl: Lactobacillus turns milk to curd in every Indian home, while clean water drives under Swachh Bharat cut cholera and typhoid risk.

rv.summary: Heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant; most are decomposers. They make curd and antibiotics and fix nitrogen, but also cause cholera, typhoid, tetanus and citrus canker. Bacteria reproduce by fission; Mycoplasma lack a cell wall.
focus: Useful and harmful roles of heterotrophic bacteria
remember: Main reproduction: fission; spores in bad conditions
Bacterial diseases: cholera, typhoid, tetanus, citrus canker
Mycoplasma: no cell wall, smallest living cells, survive without oxygen
traps: Don't call mumps a bacterial disease; it is viral
Don't say bacteria fuse gametes; they show only primitive DNA transfer

topics.t: Protista: chrysophytes, dinoflagellates and euglenoids
topics.h: Parts of India's coastline sometimes turn red and fish die off in large numbers. Tiny protists with armour plates are to blame.
p: Protista are single-celled eukaryotes, mostly aquatic. They have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles and form a link between plants, animals and fungi.

Chrysophytes include diatoms and desmids (golden algae). Diatom walls are two overlapping shells, like a soap box, embedded with silica. Deposits form diatomaceous earth, used in polishing and in filtering oils and syrups. Diatoms are the chief producers in the oceans.
Dinoflagellates are mostly marine and photosynthetic, with stiff cellulose plates on the outer wall and two flagella (one longitudinal, one transverse in a furrow).
Red dinoflagellates such as Gonyaulax multiply rapidly and cause red tides; their toxins can kill fishes.

Euglenoids (e.g. Euglena) live in stagnant fresh water, have no cell wall but a flexible, protein-rich pellicle and two flagella (one short, one long). They photosynthesise in light and behave as heterotrophs in the dark.

ex.q: A protist in a pond is green and photosynthetic in sunlight but catches small organisms when kept in darkness. It has a flexible body and no cell wall. Identify it.
st: No cell wall but a flexible body points to a pellicle.
Switching between photosynthesis and predation is mixotrophic behaviour.
These are features of euglenoids.
ex.a: Euglena, a euglenoid.

topics.rl: Diatomaceous earth is used in industry for filtering edible oils and in polishing; India's coastal fisheries suffer losses during red tides.

rv.summary: Protista are single-celled, mostly aquatic eukaryotes. Chrysophytes (diatoms) have silica walls and are chief ocean producers; dinoflagellates have cellulose plates and two flagella (Gonyaulax causes red tides); euglenoids have a pellicle and dual nutrition.
focus: Features of diatoms and diatomaceous earth
remember: Diatom walls: two overlapping silica shells, like a soap box
Gonyaulax causes red tides
Euglena: protein-rich pellicle, two flagella, photosynthetic in light, heterotrophic in dark
traps: Don't give Euglena a cell wall; it has a pellicle
Don't confuse silica walls (diatoms) with cellulose plates (dinoflagellates)

topics.t: Slime moulds and protozoans
topics.h: Malaria still affects many Indians each year. The culprit is a single-celled protist that hides in mosquito saliva.
p: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that creep over decaying twigs and leaves, engulfing organic matter.

In good conditions they form a plasmodium that can spread over several feet. In bad conditions the plasmodium forms fruiting bodies bearing spores with true walls; these spores are extremely resistant, survive for years and spread by air.
Protozoans are heterotrophs (predators or parasites), believed to be primitive relatives of animals.

Four groups: amoeboid (Amoeba; parasitic Entamoeba) with pseudopodia; flagellated (Trypanosoma, causes sleeping sickness); ciliated (Paramoecium, with a gullet and thousands of cilia); sporozoans (Plasmodium, causes malaria) with an infectious spore-like stage.

ex.q: A protozoan has rows of cilia whose coordinated beating pushes food-laden water into a cavity opening on the cell surface. Name the group, the cavity and an example.
st: Thousands of cilia: ciliated protozoan.
The cavity that receives food is the gullet.
Example: Paramoecium.
ex.a: Ciliated protozoan; gullet; Paramoecium.

topics.rl: India's National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control tracks Plasmodium-caused malaria, especially after the monsoon when mosquitoes breed.

rv.summary: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that form a plasmodium and resistant walled spores. Protozoans are heterotrophic relatives of animals in four groups: amoeboid, flagellated, ciliated and sporozoans.
focus: Life of slime moulds: plasmodium and spores
Four protozoan groups with an example each
Diseases caused by Trypanosoma and Plasmodium
remember: Amoeboid: Amoeba, Entamoeba (pseudopodia)
Flagellated: Trypanosoma (sleeping sickness)
Ciliated: Paramoecium (gullet, cilia)
Sporozoans: Plasmodium (malaria)
traps: Don't confuse the slime mould plasmodium with the malarial parasite Plasmodium
Don't call Trypanosoma a sporozoan; it is flagellated

topics.t: Kingdom Fungi: structure, nutrition and reproduction
topics.h: The bread in your tiffin, the penicillin in a hospital and the rust on a Punjab wheat field are all fungal stories.
p: Fungi are heterotrophs: saprophytes (absorb dead organic matter), parasites, or symbionts (with algae as lichens, with plant roots as mycorrhiza). Yeast makes bread and beer, Penicillium gives antibiotics, Puccinia causes wheat rust.

Except unicellular yeasts, fungi are filamentous. Thread-like hyphae form a network called mycelium. Coenocytic hyphae are continuous tubes with many nuclei; others have septa (cross walls). Cell walls contain chitin and polysaccharides.
Vegetative reproduction: fragmentation, fission, budding. Asexual spores: conidia, sporangiospores or zoospores. Sexual spores: oospores, ascospores, basidiospores, produced in fruiting bodies.
Sexual cycle: plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasms), karyogamy (fusion of nuclei) and meiosis in the zygote giving haploid spores.
In ascomycetes and basidiomycetes a dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell) comes between plasmogamy and karyogamy; this phase is the dikaryophase.

ex.q: Order the sexual cycle of a basidiomycete.
st: Two compatible haploid cells fuse their cytoplasm: plasmogamy.
Cells now have two separate nuclei: dikaryon (n + n).
The nuclei fuse: karyogamy, giving a diploid nucleus.
Meiosis produces haploid spores.
ex.a: Plasmogamy → dikaryon → karyogamy → meiosis

topics.rl: Fungal rusts are a major threat to Indian wheat, so ICAR scientists breed rust-resistant varieties; Penicillium-based antibiotics are made by Indian pharma firms.

rv.summary: Fungi are heterotrophs (saprophytes, parasites, symbionts) with chitin walls. Most are filamentous, with hyphae forming mycelium. They reproduce vegetatively, by asexual spores and by sexual spores via plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis.
focus: Modes of fungal nutrition, including lichens and mycorrhiza
Order of the sexual cycle, including dikaryophase
remember: Fungal wall: chitin and polysaccharides
Sexual cycle: plasmogamy → (dikaryon n + n) → karyogamy → meiosis
Sexual spores: oospores, ascospores, basidiospores
traps: Don't mix plasmogamy (cytoplasm fusion) and karyogamy (nucleus fusion)
Don't call conidia sexual spores

topics.t: Classes of fungi
topics.h: Truffles sell for lakhs of rupees a kilo, while a smut fungus ruins a maize cob. Both belong to the fungal family album.
p: Phycomycetes: aquatic or on decaying wood in damp places, or obligate plant parasites. Mycelium aseptate and coenocytic. Asexual zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile) formed inside sporangia. Zygospore from fusion of gametes. Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould), Albugo (parasite on mustard).

Ascomycetes (sac fungi): mostly multicellular (Penicillium), rarely unicellular (yeast, Saccharomyces). Septate, branched mycelium. Conidia formed exogenously on conidiophores; ascospores formed endogenously in asci, which are grouped in ascocarps. Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora (used in genetics); morels and truffles are edible.

Basidiomycetes: mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs. Septate mycelium; asexual spores generally absent; sex organs absent. Plasmogamy by fusion of two somatic cells, a dikaryon forms, karyogamy and meiosis in the basidium give four basidiospores borne exogenously. Basidia lie in basidiocarps. Agaricus, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust).

Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi): only asexual or vegetative phases known; reproduce by conidia; septate mycelium. Many are decomposers that help mineral cycling. Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma. When sexual stages are found, they are moved to ascomycetes or basidiomycetes.

ex.q: A fungus has septate mycelium and forms spores inside sac-like structures grouped in fruiting bodies. Identify the class and the fruiting body.
st: Septate mycelium rules out phycomycetes.
Spores formed endogenously in sacs are ascospores in asci.
Asci are grouped in ascocarps.
ex.a: Ascomycetes; the fruiting body is an ascocarp.

topics.rl: Button mushroom (Agaricus) farming is a big rural business in Haryana and Himachal, while Trichoderma is sold to Indian farmers as a bio-control agent.

rv.summary: Fungi are grouped into four classes: phycomycetes (aseptate, zygospores), ascomycetes (sac fungi, ascospores in asci), basidiomycetes (mushrooms, basidiospores on basidia) and deuteromycetes (imperfect, only asexual stages known).
focus: Distinguishing features of each fungal class
Where spores form: endogenous asci vs exogenous basidia
remember: Phycomycetes: Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo
Ascomycetes: yeast, Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora
Basidiomycetes: Agaricus, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust)
Deuteromycetes: Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma
traps: Don't say ascospores form on conidiophores; they form inside asci
Don't mix Puccinia (rust) with Ustilago (smut)

topics.t: Kingdoms Plantae and Animalia
topics.h: The amarbel (Cuscuta) draped over hedges in Indian towns is a plant that has given up making most of its own food.
p: Plantae: eukaryotic, chlorophyll-containing organisms with prominent chloroplasts and cell walls mainly of cellulose. Includes algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
A few plants are partially heterotrophic: insectivorous plants such as bladderwort and Venus fly trap, and parasites such as Cuscuta.
Plant life cycles alternate between a diploid sporophytic phase and a haploid gametophytic phase. This is alternation of generations.
Animalia: heterotrophic, multicellular eukaryotes whose cells lack cell walls. They depend directly or indirectly on plants, show holozoic nutrition (ingestion) and store food as glycogen or fat.

Animals follow a definite growth pattern to reach a definite shape and size; most can move; higher forms have elaborate sensory and neuromotor systems; sexual reproduction is followed by embryological development.

ex.q: Why is the Venus fly trap still placed in Plantae even though it traps insects?
st: It has chlorophyll and photosynthesises.
Its cells have cellulose walls.
Insects only supplement nitrogen; it is partially heterotrophic.
ex.a: It is a green, cellulose-walled photosynthetic plant that is only partially heterotrophic.

topics.rl: Bladderwort grows in Indian wetlands such as those of Kerala and Assam, trapping tiny animals in bladders, yet it is a true plant.

rv.summary: Plantae are eukaryotic, chlorophyll-bearing organisms with cellulose walls and alternation of generations. Animalia are multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls, with holozoic nutrition and glycogen or fat reserves.
focus: Defining features of Plantae and Animalia
Partially heterotrophic plants: insectivorous and parasitic
remember: Plant wall: cellulose
Alternation of generations: diploid sporophyte ↔ haploid gametophyte
Animals: no cell wall, holozoic, store glycogen or fat
traps: Don't call insectivorous plants parasites; Cuscuta is the parasite
Don't give animal cells a cell wall

topics.t: Viruses: discovery, structure and diseases
topics.h: COVID-19 showed the world how something that is not even a cell can bring cities to a halt.
p: Viruses are non-cellular. Outside a living cell they are inert, crystalline particles; inside a host they take over its machinery to multiply. They are obligate parasites.

Pasteur coined 'virus' (venom or poisonous fluid). D.J. Ivanowsky (1892) found the agent of tobacco mosaic disease passed through bacteria-proof filters. M.W. Beijerinek (1898) called the infectious extract 'Contagium vivum fluidum'. W.M. Stanley (1935) crystallised viruses and showed the crystals were mainly protein.
A virus is a nucleoprotein: genetic material (RNA or DNA, never both) inside a protein coat called a capsid made of capsomeres, arranged in helical or polyhedral forms.
Plant viruses usually have single-stranded RNA. Animal viruses have single- or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA. Bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA.
Human viral diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS. Plant symptoms: mosaic, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing and stunted growth.

ex.q: A tobacco leaf extract still infects healthy plants after passing through a filter that stops bacteria. What does this show?
st: The agent is smaller than bacteria.
It is not a bacterium.
This was Ivanowsky's 1892 observation, and Beijerinek later called it Contagium vivum fluidum.
ex.a: The agent is a filterable virus, smaller than bacteria.

topics.rl: The National Institute of Virology in Pune isolated India's first SARS-CoV-2 strain; India declared itself smallpox-free in 1977.

rv.summary: Viruses are non-cellular obligate parasites: inert crystals outside a cell, multiplying only inside a host. A virus is a nucleoprotein with RNA or DNA in a protein capsid. Ivanowsky, Beijerinek and Stanley shaped their discovery.
focus: Genetic material of plant viruses, animal viruses and bacteriophages
Viral diseases of humans and symptoms in plants
remember: Ivanowsky 1892; Beijerinek 1898 (Contagium vivum fluidum); Stanley 1935 (crystallised)
Capsid made of capsomeres
Plant viruses: ssRNA; bacteriophages: usually dsDNA
Human viral diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, AIDS
traps: Don't say a virus has both DNA and RNA
Don't say viruses multiply outside a host cell

topics.t: Viroids, prions and lichens
topics.h: Some infections are caused by naked RNA, some by misfolded protein, and some 'single organisms' on tree bark are really two partners living together.
p: Viroids: discovered by T.O. Diener (1971); cause potato spindle tuber disease. They are free RNA with no protein coat, of low molecular weight, smaller than viruses.

Prions: infectious agents made of abnormally folded protein, similar in size to viruses. They cause bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE, mad cow disease) in cattle and its human analogue Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD).

Lichens: symbiotic (mutually useful) associations of an alga (phycobiont, autotrophic) and a fungus (mycobiont, heterotrophic). The alga makes food; the fungus gives shelter and absorbs water and minerals.
Lichens are very good pollution indicators: they do not grow in polluted areas.
Comparison: a virus has nucleic acid plus a protein coat; a viroid is nucleic acid only; a prion is protein only.

ex.q: City A has lichens on its tree trunks; City B, beside a busy industrial belt, has none. What can you infer?
st: Lichens do not grow in polluted air.
Their absence suggests polluted air in City B.
ex.a: City B's air is likely more polluted; lichens act as pollution indicators.

topics.rl: Lichens are used to track air quality; some lichens are sold as the spice 'kalpasi' (stone flower) used in Chettinad cooking.

rv.summary: Viroids are free low-molecular-weight RNA without a protein coat (potato spindle tuber, Diener 1971); prions are abnormally folded proteins (BSE, CJD). Lichens are alga–fungus partnerships that act as pollution indicators.
focus: Diseases caused by viroids and prions
Roles of phycobiont and mycobiont in lichens
remember: Virus = nucleic acid + protein coat; viroid = RNA only; prion = protein only
Viroid: potato spindle tuber disease, T.O. Diener (1971)
Prions: BSE in cattle, CJD in humans
Phycobiont = alga (food); mycobiont = fungus (shelter, water, minerals)
traps: Don't say prions contain nucleic acid
Don't swap phycobiont and mycobiont

topics.t: Systems of plant classification
topics.h: Imagine sorting your class only by height. Tall friends would be 'related'. Early plant classification made a similar mistake.
p: Artificial systems (e.g. Linnaeus) used only a few characters such as habit, colour, number and shape of leaves, or the androecium. They gave equal weight to vegetative and sexual characters, which is unacceptable because vegetative characters are easily affected by the environment.
Natural systems (e.g. Bentham and Hooker) are based on natural affinities and use many characters: external features and internal ones such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry.
Phylogenetic systems are based on evolutionary relationships; they assume members of a taxon share a common ancestor.
Numerical taxonomy uses computers: all observable characters are coded as numbers and given equal importance, so hundreds of characters can be handled.
Cytotaxonomy uses chromosome number, structure and behaviour; chemotaxonomy uses the plant's chemical constituents.

ex.q: Two plant groups look alike, but one has 2n = 14 and the other 2n = 24, and their alkaloids differ. Which branches of taxonomy use these clues?
st: Chromosome number is cytological information: cytotaxonomy.
Chemical constituents such as alkaloids: chemotaxonomy.
ex.a: Cytotaxonomy (chromosomes) and chemotaxonomy (chemicals).

topics.rl: Indian scientists at institutes such as the Botanical Survey of India now combine DNA, chromosome and chemical data to classify medicinal plants used in Ayurveda.

rv.summary: Plant classification moved from artificial systems (few characters, e.g. Linnaeus) to natural systems (many characters, Bentham and Hooker) and phylogenetic systems (evolutionary relationships). Numerical, cyto- and chemotaxonomy add computer, chromosome and chemical data.
focus: Difference between artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems
What numerical taxonomy, cytotaxonomy and chemotaxonomy use
remember: Artificial: Linnaeus, few characters, equal weight to vegetative and sexual
Natural: Bentham and Hooker, natural affinities
Numerical taxonomy: characters coded as numbers, equal importance, computers
Cytotaxonomy: chromosomes; chemotaxonomy: chemical constituents
traps: Don't credit the natural system to Linnaeus; his was artificial
Don't confuse cytotaxonomy (chromosomes) with chemotaxonomy (chemicals)

topics.t: Algae: forms, reproduction and importance
topics.h: The agar in your school lab petri dish and in some ice creams comes from red seaweed off the coast. Algae are quietly everywhere.
p: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and mostly aquatic. Forms range from unicellular (Chlamydomonas) and colonial (Volvox) to filamentous (Ulothrix, Spirogyra) and massive marine kelps.
Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation; asexual reproduction is by spores, most commonly flagellated zoospores.

Sexual reproduction: isogamy (gametes similar in size; flagellated in Chlamydomonas, non-flagellated in Spirogyra), anisogamy (gametes dissimilar in size, e.g. species of Eudorina), oogamy (large non-motile female and small motile male gamete, e.g. Volvox, Fucus).
Algae carry out at least half of the total CO₂ fixation on Earth and are primary producers in aquatic food chains.

Uses: about 70 marine species are eaten, e.g. Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum. Algin (brown algae) and carrageen (red algae) are used commercially; agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria) is used to grow microbes and in jellies and ice creams; Chlorella, rich in protein, is a food supplement even for space travellers.

ex.q: In an alga, a large non-motile egg is fertilised by a small motile male gamete. Name the type of sexual reproduction and give two examples.
st: Gametes differ in size and motility.
Large non-motile female with small motile male is oogamy.
ex.a: Oogamy, e.g. Volvox and Fucus.

topics.rl: Seaweed farming of Gracilaria and Kappaphycus along Tamil Nadu's Ramanathapuram coast gives coastal women's groups an income from agar and carrageenan.

rv.summary: Algae are simple, thalloid, autotrophic, mostly aquatic plants, from unicellular to kelps. They reproduce by fragmentation, zoospores and isogamy, anisogamy or oogamy, fix at least half of Earth's CO₂ and give food, algin, carrageen and agar.
focus: Types of sexual reproduction: isogamy, anisogamy, oogamy
remember: Isogamy: Chlamydomonas (flagellated), Spirogyra (non-flagellated); anisogamy: Eudorina; oogamy: Volvox, Fucus
Agar: Gelidium, Gracilaria; algin: brown algae; carrageen: red algae
Chlorella: protein-rich supplement
traps: Don't call Spirogyra gametes flagellated
Don't say agar comes from brown algae; it is from red algae

topics.t: Classes of algae: green, brown and red
topics.h: Why are some seaweeds red even when they live deep under the sea? The answer lies in a pigment that catches the light that reaches the depths.
p: Chlorophyceae (green algae): chlorophyll a and b; chloroplasts of many shapes; pyrenoids store protein and starch; food stored as starch (and oil); cell wall of inner cellulose and outer pectose; 2 to 8 equal apical flagella. Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara.

Phaeophyceae (brown algae): mainly marine; chlorophyll a and c, carotenoids and xanthophylls (fucoxanthin); food as laminarin or mannitol; cellulose wall covered by gelatinous algin; body has holdfast, stipe and frond; 2 unequal lateral flagella. Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus.

Rhodophyceae (red algae): pigment r-phycoerythrin with chlorophyll a and d; mostly marine, near the surface and at great depths; food as floridean starch (like amylopectin and glycogen); wall of cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters; no flagella. Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium.
Red algae reproduce sexually by oogamy with complex post-fertilisation development; asexual spores are non-motile.

ex.q: An alga has chlorophyll a and c, stores mannitol, and has a holdfast and frond. Classify it.
st: Chlorophyll c and mannitol are brown-algal features.
Holdfast, stipe and frond describe brown algae.
ex.a: Phaeophyceae (brown algae).

topics.rl: Sargassum washes up on the Gulf of Mannar beaches, and Porphyra is a sea vegetable widely eaten in East Asia.

rv.summary: Algae are classed by pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella: green algae (chlorophyll a, b; starch), brown algae (chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin, mannitol) and red algae (r-phycoerythrin; floridean starch; no flagella).
focus: Cell wall and flagella of each class
remember: Chlorophyceae: chl a, b; starch; pyrenoids; 2–8 equal apical flagella
Phaeophyceae: chl a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin/mannitol; algin; 2 unequal lateral flagella
Rhodophyceae: r-phycoerythrin, chl a, d; floridean starch; no flagella
traps: Don't mix laminarin (brown) with floridean starch (red)
Don't give red algae flagella

topics.t: Bryophytes: amphibians of the plant kingdom
topics.h: After the monsoon, a green velvet covers old walls in Kerala. These mosses need land to live on but water to have babies, just like frogs.
p: Bryophytes live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom. They grow in damp, humid, shaded places and help plant succession on bare rocks and soil.
The plant body is thallus-like, prostrate or erect, attached by rhizoids. It has no true roots, stems or leaves. The main plant body is the haploid gametophyte.
Sex organs are multicellular. The antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids; the flask-shaped archegonium has a single egg. Antherozoids swim through water to reach the egg.

The zygote forms a multicellular sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) that stays attached to the gametophyte and depends on it for food. Some sporophyte cells undergo meiosis to form haploid spores, which grow into new gametophytes.

Uses: food for herbivorous mammals and birds; Sphagnum gives peat, used as fuel and as packing material for living material because it holds water. Mosses with lichens are first colonisers of rocks, and moss mats reduce soil erosion.

ex.q: Why does a moss plant fail to produce a sporophyte in a long dry spell?
st: Antherozoids are flagellated and must swim to the archegonium.
Without water, they cannot reach the egg.
No fertilisation means no zygote, so no sporophyte.
ex.a: Fertilisation needs water; without it no zygote or sporophyte forms.

topics.rl: Sphagnum peat moss is used by plant nurseries to pack and transport living saplings because it holds water so well.

rv.summary: Bryophytes are the amphibians of the plant kingdom: they live on land but need water for fertilisation. The haploid gametophyte is dominant; the sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) stays attached and dependent, and makes spores by meiosis.
focus: Why bryophytes are amphibians of the plant kingdom
Sex organs and need for water
remember: Main plant body: haploid gametophyte with rhizoids, no true roots, stems, leaves
Antheridium → biflagellate antherozoids; archegonium → one egg
Sporophyte: foot, seta, capsule; spores by meiosis
Sphagnum: peat; holds water
traps: Don't say the moss sporophyte is free-living
Don't give bryophytes true roots; they have rhizoids

topics.t: Liverworts and mosses
topics.h: Marchantia carries tiny 'cups' full of green buds that splash away in rain drops to start new plants.
p: Liverworts grow in moist shady places such as stream banks, marshy ground, damp soil, tree bark and deep woods. The thalloid body of Marchantia is dorsiventral and closely pressed to the ground; leafy liverworts have tiny leaf-like parts in two rows.
Liverworts reproduce asexually by fragmentation or by gemmae: green, multicellular asexual buds formed in gemma cups on the thallus. Gemmae detach and grow into new plants.
In liverworts, male and female sex organs may be on the same or different thalli; the sporophyte has foot, seta and capsule, and spores form after meiosis.

Mosses: the gametophyte has two stages. The protonema grows directly from a spore and is creeping, green, branched and often filamentous. The leafy stage grows from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud, with upright axes bearing spirally arranged leaves and multicellular branched rhizoids; it bears the sex organs.

Mosses reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation and budding of the secondary protonema. Their sporophyte is more elaborate than in liverworts, with an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal. Examples: Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum.

ex.q: A student sees a green filament growing from a moss spore. What is it and what will it give rise to?
st: A creeping green filament growing directly from a spore is the protonema.
Lateral buds on it grow into the leafy stage that bears sex organs.
ex.a: Protonema; it gives rise to the leafy gametophyte stage.

topics.rl: Polytrichum and Funaria carpet Himalayan slopes in Darjeeling and Sikkim, holding soil during heavy rains.

rv.summary: Liverworts like Marchantia have a flat dorsiventral thallus and reproduce asexually by gemmae. Mosses have a protonema and a leafy stage bearing sex organs, multicellular branched rhizoids and a more elaborate sporophyte.
focus: Structure of Marchantia and role of gemmae
Two stages of the moss gametophyte
remember: Gemmae: green multicellular asexual buds in gemma cups
Protonema grows from spore; leafy stage from secondary protonema as lateral bud
Mosses: Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum; liverwort: Marchantia
traps: Don't call gemmae sexual spores
Don't confuse protonema (moss) with prothallus (fern)

topics.t: Pteridophytes: the first vascular land plants
topics.h: The lacy ferns in Ooty's gardens were the first plants to build 'plumbing pipes'. That's why they could stand taller than mosses.
p: Pteridophytes (horsetails and ferns) are the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissues, xylem and phloem. They mostly grow in cool, damp, shady places.
The main plant body is the diploid sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves. Leaves may be small (microphylls, as in Selaginella) or large (macrophylls, as in ferns).
Sporangia are borne on leaf-like sporophylls. In some, sporophylls form compact strobili or cones (Selaginella, Equisetum). Spore mother cells undergo meiosis to form spores.
Spores grow into a small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophyte called the prothallus, which needs cool, damp, shady places.
The prothallus bears antheridia and archegonia; water is needed for antherozoids to reach the egg. The zygote grows into the well-differentiated sporophyte.

ex.q: Fern spores on a dry concrete wall do not produce new ferns, but on wet soil near a stream they do. Explain.
st: Spores grow into the prothallus, which needs cool, damp, shady places.
Fertilisation on the prothallus also needs water for antherozoids to swim.
ex.a: The prothallus and fertilisation both need moist conditions.

topics.rl: Ferns like Adiantum (maidenhair fern) are popular ornamental plants in Indian homes and hill-station gardens.

rv.summary: Pteridophytes are the first vascular land plants. The diploid sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves is dominant; spores grow into a free-living prothallus, and fertilisation needs water, so they favour cool, damp, shady places.
focus: Microphylls vs macrophylls; sporophylls and strobili
The prothallus and why pteridophytes need moist places
remember: First terrestrial plants with xylem and phloem
Gametophyte = prothallus (free-living, photosynthetic)
Selaginella: microphylls; ferns: macrophylls; strobili in Selaginella, Equisetum
traps: Don't say pteridophytes produce seeds; they reproduce by spores
Don't call the prothallus diploid; it is the haploid gametophyte

topics.t: Heterospory and classes of pteridophytes
topics.h: Selaginella makes two sizes of spores. That small step, keeping the female spore at home, set plants on the road to seeds.
p: Most pteridophytes are homosporous: they produce one kind of spore.
Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous: they produce large megaspores and small microspores, which grow into female and male gametophytes.
In heterosporous forms, the female gametophyte stays on the parent sporophyte for some time and the embryo develops inside it. This is a precursor to the seed habit, an important step in evolution.
Classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum) and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).
Uses: medicinal purposes, as soil binders, and as ornamentals.

ex.q: Why is heterospory in Selaginella considered a step towards the seed habit?
st: Megaspores and microspores form female and male gametophytes.
The female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte.
The zygote develops into an embryo within it, as happens inside a seed.
ex.a: Retention of the female gametophyte and development of the embryo on the parent is a precursor to seeds.

topics.rl: Pteris and Adiantum ferns grow on the walls of old forts in Rajasthan and the Western Ghats, and many ferns help bind soil on slopes.

rv.summary: Most pteridophytes are homosporous, but Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous, and retaining the female gametophyte with the embryo on the parent is a precursor to seeds. Classes: Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida, Pteropsida.
focus: Why heterospory leads towards the seed habit
Four classes of pteridophytes with examples
remember: Heterosporous: Selaginella, Salvinia
Microspore → male gametophyte; megaspore → female gametophyte
Psilopsida: Psilotum; Lycopsida: Selaginella, Lycopodium; Sphenopsida: Equisetum; Pteropsida: Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum
traps: Don't call most ferns heterosporous; most pteridophytes are homosporous
Don't place Equisetum in Lycopsida

topics.t: Gymnosperms: naked seeds, roots and leaves
topics.h: The tallest trees on Earth, the redwoods, are gymnosperms. So is the pine whose resin makes turpentine, and the cycad in your local park.
p: Gymnosperms (gymnos = naked, sperma = seeds) have ovules not enclosed by an ovary wall, before or after fertilisation.
They include medium to tall trees and shrubs. Sequoia, the giant redwood, is one of the tallest tree species.
Roots are generally tap roots. Pinus has mycorrhizal roots (fungal association); Cycas has small coralloid roots associated with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.
Stems may be unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus). Leaves may be simple or compound; Cycas has pinnate leaves that last a few years.

Conifer needle-like leaves reduce surface area, and a thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss, helping them survive extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. Economic uses include timber, and products such as resin and turpentine from pines.

ex.q: How do needle leaves help a Himalayan pine survive cold, dry winds?
st: Needles have a small surface area, so less water is lost.
A thick cuticle cuts evaporation.
Sunken stomata lose less water.
ex.a: Small area, thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss.

topics.rl: Deodar (Cedrus deodara) and chir pine forests of Himachal and Uttarakhand supply timber and resin; Cycas is a common ornamental in Indian gardens.

rv.summary: Gymnosperms bear naked ovules not enclosed by an ovary wall. They are trees and shrubs (Sequoia is among the tallest) with tap roots, mycorrhizal roots in Pinus, coralloid roots in Cycas, and needle leaves adapted to cut water loss.
focus: Meaning of gymnosperm and naked ovules
Special roots of Pinus and Cycas
Stem and leaf features; conifer adaptations
remember: Gymnos = naked, sperma = seed
Pinus: mycorrhizal roots; Cycas: coralloid roots with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria
Needles: small area, thick cuticle, sunken stomata
Uses: timber, resin, turpentine
traps: Don't swap the roots: coralloid is Cycas, mycorrhizal is Pinus
Don't say gymnosperm ovules are inside an ovary

topics.t: Reproduction in gymnosperms
topics.h: In spring, pine forests release clouds of yellow pollen. The wind carries it to female cones, and no water is needed at all.
p: Gymnosperms are heterosporous: haploid microspores and megaspores form in sporangia on sporophylls arranged spirally in strobili (cones).
Male strobili carry microsporophylls with microsporangia. Microspores develop into a highly reduced male gametophyte, the pollen grain, inside the microsporangium.

Female strobili carry megasporophylls with ovules. The ovule is the nucellus (megasporangium) protected by envelopes (integuments). A megaspore mother cell in the nucellus divides by meiosis into four megaspores; one forms the multicellular female gametophyte with two or more archegonia.

In Pinus, male and female cones are on the same tree; in Cycas, male cones and megasporophylls are on different trees. Male and female gametophytes are not free-living; they stay within sporangia on the sporophyte.

Pollen is carried by air to the ovule opening. A pollen tube carries male gametes to the archegonia. After fertilisation the zygote forms the embryo and the ovule becomes a seed, which is not covered.

ex.q: Trace the path from microspore to seed in Pinus.
st: Microspore develops into a pollen grain in the microsporangium.
Air carries pollen to an ovule on the female cone.
A pollen tube carries male gametes to the archegonia.
Fertilisation forms a zygote, which becomes the embryo.
The ovule develops into a naked seed.
ex.a: Microspore → pollen → pollination by air → pollen tube → fertilisation → embryo → naked seed.

topics.rl: Pine pollen can coat cars yellow in Shimla in spring, a sign of wind pollination at work.

rv.summary: Gymnosperms are heterosporous, with spores in cones. The pollen grain is the reduced male gametophyte; the female gametophyte inside the ovule bears archegonia. Air carries pollen, a pollen tube delivers male gametes, and the ovule becomes a naked seed.
focus: Male and female strobili and their spores
Structure of the ovule and formation of the female gametophyte
Pollination by air and the role of the pollen tube
remember: Male gametophyte = pollen grain
Ovule = nucellus + integuments; megaspore mother cell → 4 megaspores by meiosis
Pinus: both cones on one tree; Cycas: on different trees
Gametophytes not free-living
traps: Don't say gymnosperms need water for fertilisation; the pollen tube carries gametes
Don't say all four megaspores form gametophytes; only one does

topics.t: Comparing plant groups: from algae to gymnosperms
topics.h: Imagine plants climbing a ladder out of the water: algae in the sea, mosses at the shore, ferns with pipes, pines with seeds, and flowering plants at the top.
p: Increasing complexity: algae → bryophytes → pteridophytes → gymnosperms → angiosperms. Angiosperms have ovules inside an ovary and seeds inside fruits.
Dominant phase: haploid gametophyte in bryophytes; diploid sporophyte in pteridophytes and gymnosperms.
Vascular tissue is absent in algae and bryophytes, present in pteridophytes and gymnosperms. Seeds appear first in gymnosperms (naked); angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruits.
Water is needed for fertilisation in bryophytes and pteridophytes; gymnosperms use pollen tubes.

Ploidy check: moss protonema, leafy gametophyte, gemma cell, fern prothallus, spores and gametes are haploid (n); zygotes and sporophytes are diploid (2n). Algae are classified mainly by pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella.

ex.q: Give the ploidy of: moss protonema cell, fern prothallus cell, zygote of fern, gemma cell of Marchantia.
st: Protonema is part of the gametophyte: n.
Prothallus is the fern gametophyte: n.
Zygote forms by fusion of gametes: 2n.
Gemma is an asexual bud of the haploid thallus: n.
ex.a: n, n, 2n, n

topics.rl: In a typical Indian forest walk in the Western Ghats you can see the whole ladder in a day: algae in streams, mosses on rocks, ferns on banks, and cycads or pines planted nearby.

rv.summary: From algae to angiosperms, plants grow more complex: bryophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte; pteridophytes and gymnosperms a dominant diploid sporophyte with vascular tissue; seeds start in gymnosperms, and pollen tubes free them from water.
focus: Dominant phase in each plant group
Which groups have vascular tissue, seeds and fruits
Which groups need water for fertilisation
Ploidy of protonema, prothallus, gemma, spores, zygote
remember: Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant; pteridophytes, gymnosperms: sporophyte dominant
Vascular tissue: from pteridophytes on; seeds: from gymnosperms
Gametophyte parts, spores, gametes = n; zygote, sporophyte = 2n
traps: Don't call the prothallus or protonema diploid
Don't say pteridophytes have seeds

topics.t: Basis of classification: levels of organisation, gut and circulation
topics.h: A sponge and a cheetah are both animals, yet one is a loose bag of cells and the other a high-speed machine. How do we compare them fairly?
p: Animals differ hugely in structure, but share fundamental features (arrangement of cells, body symmetry, coelom, digestive, circulatory and reproductive patterns) that are used for classification.

Levels of organisation: cellular level in sponges (loose cell aggregates); tissue level in coelenterates; organ level in Platyhelminthes; organ-system level in annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates.
Incomplete digestive system: a single opening serves as both mouth and anus (e.g. Platyhelminthes). Complete digestive system: two openings, mouth and anus.

Open circulatory system: blood is pumped out of the heart and cells and tissues are directly bathed in it (e.g. arthropods, molluscs). Closed circulatory system: blood flows through a series of vessels of varying diameters (e.g. annelids, chordates).

ex.q: A flatworm takes food in and throws undigested waste out through the same opening. What type of digestive system is this?
st: Only one opening to the gut.
One opening working as both mouth and anus means an incomplete digestive system.
ex.a: Incomplete digestive system.

topics.rl: Indian Railways uses a 'closed' system of pipes for train brakes; a garden sprinkler is 'open'. Animal circulation follows the same two designs.

rv.summary: Animals are classified using fundamental features. Levels of organisation run from cellular (sponges) to tissue (coelenterates), organ (flatworms) and organ-system (annelids onwards). Guts are incomplete or complete; circulation is open or closed.
focus: Level of organisation of each major group
Open vs closed circulatory system with examples
remember: Cellular: Porifera; tissue: Coelenterata; organ: Platyhelminthes; organ-system: annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms, chordates
Incomplete gut: one opening; complete: mouth and anus
Open: arthropods, molluscs; closed: annelids, chordates
traps: Don't give molluscs or arthropods closed circulation
Don't put flatworms at organ-system level; they are at organ level

topics.t: Symmetry and germ layers
topics.h: Cut a starfish like a pizza and every slice looks alike. Cut yourself (only in imagination!) and only one cut gives two mirror halves.
p: Asymmetrical: no plane divides the body into equal halves (most sponges).
Radial symmetry: any plane through the central axis gives two identical halves (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms).
Bilateral symmetry: only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves (annelids, arthropods and others).
Diploblastic animals have two germ layers, external ectoderm and internal endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea in between (coelenterates).
Triploblastic animals have a third germ layer, mesoderm, between ectoderm and endoderm (Platyhelminthes to chordates).

ex.q: A Hydra has ectoderm and endoderm with a jelly-like layer in between. Classify its germ-layer organisation and symmetry.
st: Two germ layers with mesoglea between them: diploblastic.
Coelenterates are radially symmetrical.
ex.a: Diploblastic and radially symmetrical.

topics.rl: Starfish found in tide pools along the Gujarat and Goa coasts are bilaterally symmetrical as larvae but become radially symmetrical as adults.

rv.summary: Animals may be asymmetrical (most sponges), radially symmetrical (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms) or bilaterally symmetrical. Diploblastic animals have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea; triploblastic animals add mesoderm.
focus: Asymmetry, radial and bilateral symmetry with examples
remember: Radial: any plane through central axis gives identical halves
Bilateral: only one plane gives identical left and right halves
Diploblastic: coelenterates, ctenophores; triploblastic: Platyhelminthes to chordates
traps: Don't call mesoglea a germ layer
Don't forget echinoderm larvae are bilateral though adults are radial

topics.t: Coelom, segmentation and notochord
topics.h: A body cavity is like a padded room inside you where organs can move and grow. Not every animal has one, and some have a 'fake' one.
p: Coelom: a body cavity lined by mesoderm. Coelomates: annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates.
Pseudocoelom: the cavity is not lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm (Aschelminthes). Acoelomates have no body cavity (Platyhelminthes).
Metameric segmentation (metamerism): the body is divided externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of some organs, as in the earthworm.

Notochord: a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development. Animals with it are chordates; those without are non-chordates (Porifera to Echinodermata).

Broad flowchart: cellular level (Porifera) → tissue level, diploblastic, radial (Coelenterata, Ctenophora) → triploblastic acoelomate (Platyhelminthes), pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes), coelomate (annelids onwards) → notochord (Chordata).

ex.q: An animal is triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, with a body cavity not lined by mesoderm. Name its phylum.
st: Triploblastic and bilateral rules out sponges and coelenterates.
A cavity with scattered mesoderm pouches is a pseudocoelom.
Pseudocoelomates are Aschelminthes.
ex.a: Aschelminthes (roundworms).

topics.rl: Farmers in Punjab value earthworms as 'friends of farmers'; their segmented body is a textbook example of metamerism.

rv.summary: A coelom is a body cavity lined by mesoderm; a pseudocoelom has scattered mesoderm pouches (Aschelminthes); acoelomates (flatworms) have none. Earthworms show metameric segmentation, and a dorsal mesodermal notochord marks chordates.
focus: Coelomate, pseudocoelomate and acoelomate with examples
Notochord: origin, position, and chordates vs non-chordates
remember: Coelom: lined by mesoderm
Pseudocoelomate: Aschelminthes; acoelomate: Platyhelminthes
Notochord: mesodermal, dorsal, formed in embryo
Non-chordates: Porifera to Echinodermata
traps: Don't call Aschelminthes acoelomate; they are pseudocoelomate
Don't say the notochord is ectodermal or ventral

topics.t: Porifera, Coelenterata and Ctenophora
topics.h: Swimmers in the Andaman Sea learn to respect jellyfish tentacles. Each one is loaded with thousands of tiny harpoons.
p: Porifera (sponges): mostly marine, asymmetrical, cellular level. A water canal system: water enters through ostia into the spongocoel and leaves by the osculum; it helps in food gathering, gas exchange and waste removal. Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and canals. Digestion is intracellular. Skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres. Hermaphrodite; asexual reproduction by fragmentation; fertilisation internal; development indirect. Sycon, Spongilla (freshwater), Euspongia (bath sponge).

Coelenterata (Cnidaria): aquatic, mostly marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) with nematocysts on tentacles are used for anchorage, defence and prey capture. Gastrovascular cavity with a single opening, the mouth on the hypostome; digestion extracellular and intracellular. Corals have a calcium carbonate skeleton.

Two body forms: polyp (sessile, cylindrical; Hydra, Adamsia) and medusa (umbrella-shaped, free-swimming; Aurelia). In Obelia, polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually: metagenesis (alternation of generation). Examples: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (sea anemone), Pennatula (sea-pen), Gorgonia (sea-fan), Meandrina (brain coral).

Ctenophora (sea walnuts or comb jellies): exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates help locomotion. Bioluminescence is well marked. Sexes not separate; only sexual reproduction; external fertilisation; indirect development. Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana.

ex.q: Trace the path of water through a sponge.
st: Water enters through tiny pores, the ostia.
It passes into the central cavity, the spongocoel, lined by choanocytes.
It exits through the osculum.
ex.a: Ostia → spongocoel → osculum

topics.rl: Coral reefs of the Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep and the Andamans are built by coelenterates and are protected marine areas in India.

rv.summary: Sponges are cellular-level animals with a water canal system (ostia → spongocoel → osculum) and choanocytes. Coelenterates are diploblastic with cnidoblasts, polyp and medusa forms and metagenesis. Ctenophores move by eight rows of comb plates.
focus: Water canal system and choanocytes in sponges
Comb plates and bioluminescence in ctenophores
remember: Porifera: Sycon, Spongilla (freshwater), Euspongia; hermaphrodite, intracellular digestion
Coelenterata: Hydra, Adamsia, Aurelia, Obelia, Physalia, Meandrina
Ctenophora: Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana; 8 rows of comb plates
traps: Don't swap ostia (water in) and osculum (water out)
Don't confuse metagenesis with metamerism

topics.t: Flatworms, roundworms and annelids
topics.h: Deworming tablets are given to crores of Indian children on National Deworming Day. The targets are flatworms and roundworms.
p: Platyhelminthes (flatworms): dorsoventrally flattened, mostly endoparasites; bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level. Hooks and suckers in parasites; some absorb nutrients through the body surface. Flame cells help osmoregulation and excretion. Sexes not separate; fertilisation internal; many larval stages. Planaria has high regeneration capacity. Taenia (tapeworm), Fasciola (liver fluke).

Aschelminthes (roundworms): circular in cross-section; free-living or parasitic; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate. Complete alimentary canal with a muscular pharynx; an excretory tube opens by an excretory pore. Dioecious, with females often longer than males (sexual dimorphism). Fertilisation internal; development direct or indirect. Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filarial worm), Ancylostoma (hookworm).

Annelida: aquatic or terrestrial; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, metamerically segmented. Longitudinal and circular muscles help locomotion; Nereis has parapodia for swimming.

Annelids have a closed circulatory system and nephridia for osmoregulation and excretion; the nervous system has paired ganglia joined to a double ventral nerve cord. Nereis is dioecious; earthworms and leeches are monoecious. Pheretima (earthworm), Hirudinaria (blood-sucking leech).

ex.q: A worm is circular in cross-section, has separate sexes with a longer female and a complete gut. Name its phylum and one example.
st: Circular cross-section suggests roundworm.
Separate sexes with sexual dimorphism and a complete gut fit Aschelminthes.
ex.a: Aschelminthes, e.g. Ascaris.

topics.rl: Wuchereria causes lymphatic filariasis, which India aims to eliminate through mass drug administration campaigns.

rv.summary: Flatworms are flattened, acoelomate, mostly parasitic, with flame cells. Roundworms are pseudocoelomate, dioecious with a complete gut. Annelids are segmented coelomates with closed circulation, nephridia and a double ventral nerve cord.
focus: Key features of Platyhelminthes, Aschelminthes and Annelida
Excretory organs: flame cells, excretory pore, nephridia
Examples and monoecious vs dioecious annelids
remember: Platyhelminthes: Taenia, Fasciola, Planaria; flame cells
Aschelminthes: Ascaris, Wuchereria (filarial), Ancylostoma (hookworm)
Annelida: Nereis (parapodia, dioecious), Pheretima, Hirudinaria (monoecious)
traps: Don't call annelids acoelomate
Don't say earthworms are dioecious; Nereis is

topics.t: Arthropoda and Mollusca
topics.h: More than two out of every three named species on Earth are arthropods. Honeybees, silkworms, mosquitoes and crabs all wear armour.
p: Arthropoda: the largest phylum (over two-thirds of named species). Organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, segmented, coelomate. Chitinous exoskeleton; body of head, thorax and abdomen; jointed appendages (arthros = joint, poda = appendages).

Arthropods breathe by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae; circulation is open; excretion by Malpighian tubules; senses include antennae, compound and simple eyes and statocysts. Mostly dioecious, fertilisation usually internal, mostly oviparous.

Arthropod examples: Apis (honeybee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect) are useful; Anopheles, Culex and Aedes (mosquitoes) are vectors; Locusta (locust) is a gregarious pest; Limulus (king crab) is a living fossil.

Mollusca: the second largest phylum; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate. Unsegmented soft body with a calcareous shell, distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump. The mantle covers the hump; feather-like gills in the mantle cavity do respiration and excretion. Head has sensory tentacles; the mouth has a rasping, file-like radula.

Molluscs are usually dioecious and oviparous with indirect development. Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia (cuttlefish), Loligo (squid), Octopus (devil fish), Aplysia (sea-hare), Dentalium (tusk shell), Chaetopleura (chiton).

ex.q: An animal has a soft unsegmented body, a muscular foot, a mantle and a rasping tongue-like organ. Identify the phylum and the organ.
st: Soft unsegmented body with foot and mantle points to molluscs.
The rasping feeding organ is the radula.
ex.a: Mollusca; the organ is the radula.

topics.rl: Jharkhand is a major lac producer from Laccifer, and Karnataka's mulberry silk comes from Bombyx; Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue after the monsoon.

rv.summary: Arthropoda, the largest phylum, have a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, open circulation and Malpighian tubules. Mollusca, the second largest, have an unsegmented soft body with shell, foot, visceral hump, mantle and radula.
focus: Features of arthropods: exoskeleton, jointed legs, respiration, excretion
Features of molluscs: mantle, foot, radula, gills
Examples of each and their importance
remember: Arthropoda: over two-thirds of named species; arthros = joint, poda = appendages
Arthropods: Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer, Anopheles, Locusta, Limulus (living fossil)
Molluscs: Pila, Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia, Loligo, Octopus; radula
traps: Don't say molluscs are segmented
Don't list nephridia as arthropod organs

topics.t: Echinodermata and Hemichordata
topics.h: A starfish walks on hundreds of tiny water-filled feet and has no excretory system at all. Strange, but true.
p: Echinodermata (spiny-skinned): endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles; all marine; organ-system level; triploblastic, coelomate. Adults are radially symmetrical, larvae bilaterally symmetrical.

Complete gut with mouth on the lower (ventral) side and anus on the upper (dorsal) side. The water vascular system, their most distinctive feature, helps locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration. There is no excretory system. Sexes separate; fertilisation usually external; development indirect with a free-swimming larva.
Examples: Asterias (starfish), Echinus (sea urchin), Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Ophiura (brittle star).

Hemichordata: small group of worm-like marine animals, once a sub-phylum of Chordata, now a separate non-chordate phylum. Body of proboscis, collar and trunk. A rudimentary stomochord in the collar is similar to a notochord. Open circulation; respiration by gills; excretion by a proboscis gland; sexes separate; external fertilisation; indirect development. Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus.

Signature features to remember: water canal system (Porifera), cnidoblasts (Coelenterata), comb plates (Ctenophora), flame cells (Platyhelminthes), parapodia (Nereis), Malpighian tubules (insects), radula (Mollusca), water vascular system (Echinodermata).

ex.q: Why are Balanoglossus and its relatives no longer placed in Chordata?
st: They have only a stomochord in the collar, a rudimentary structure similar to a notochord, not a true notochord.
So they are placed in a separate phylum, Hemichordata, under non-chordates.
ex.a: They lack a true notochord; the stomochord is only notochord-like.

topics.rl: Sea cucumbers along India's coasts are protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act because overharvesting threatened them.

rv.summary: Echinoderms are spiny-skinned marine animals with calcareous ossicles, radial adults, bilateral larvae, a water vascular system and no excretory system. Hemichordates are worm-like, with proboscis, collar and trunk and only a stomochord, so they are non-chordates.
focus: Water vascular system and other echinoderm features
Hemichordate body plan and why it is a non-chordate
remember: Echinoderms: Asterias, Echinus, Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria, Ophiura (brittle star)
Hemichordata: Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus; proboscis gland excretion
Stomochord is notochord-like, not a true notochord
traps: Don't confuse the water vascular system (echinoderms) with the water canal system (sponges)
Don't place Hemichordata in Chordata

topics.t: Phylum Chordata: key features and subphyla
topics.h: A tiny sea squirt larva has a notochord in its tail, then loses it as an adult. Yet both it and you are chordates.
p: Fundamental chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail. Chordates are bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, at organ-system level, with a closed circulatory system.

Chordates vs non-chordates: notochord present vs absent; nerve cord dorsal, hollow, single vs ventral, solid, double; pharynx with gill slits vs no gill slits; heart ventral vs dorsal (if present); post-anal tail present vs absent.

Subphyla: Urochordata (Tunicata), notochord only in the larval tail (Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum); Cephalochordata, notochord from head to tail throughout life (Branchiostoma, also called Amphioxus or lancelet); Vertebrata.

Vertebrates have a notochord only in the embryo; it is replaced by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column. They have a ventral muscular heart (2, 3 or 4 chambers), kidneys and paired appendages (fins or limbs). All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates.

Vertebrata: Agnatha (no jaws; class Cyclostomata) and Gnathostomata (jaws; superclass Pisces with fins: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes; superclass Tetrapoda with limbs: Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia).

ex.q: Why is Branchiostoma a chordate but not a vertebrate?
st: It has a notochord from head to tail throughout life.
It never develops a vertebral column.
So it is a cephalochordate, not a vertebrate.
