ex.a: It keeps a notochord all its life and has no vertebral column.

topics.rl: The soft jelly-like core of each disc in your spine is a remnant of your embryonic notochord, which is why spine surgeons treating slipped discs care about it.

rv.summary: Chordates have a notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits and post-anal tail. Subphyla: Urochordata (notochord in larval tail), Cephalochordata (notochord throughout life) and Vertebrata (notochord replaced by a vertebral column).
focus: The three subphyla and where the notochord is
remember: Chordate nerve cord: dorsal, hollow, single; heart ventral
Urochordata: Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum; Cephalochordata: Branchiostoma (Amphioxus)
All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates
traps: Don't call Ascidia a non-chordate just because the adult lacks a notochord
Don't say all chordates have a vertebral column

topics.t: Cyclostomes and fishes
topics.h: Sharks must keep swimming or they sink, while a rohu in a Bengal pond can hover still. The secret is an air bladder.
p: Cyclostomata: jawless ectoparasites on fishes; elongated body with 6–15 pairs of gill slits; sucking circular mouth without jaws; no scales or paired fins; cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column; closed circulation. Marine, but migrate to fresh water to spawn, and die within a few days; larvae return to the ocean. Petromyzon (lamprey), Myxine (hagfish).

Chondrichthyes: marine, streamlined, cartilaginous endoskeleton; ventral mouth; notochord persists throughout life; gill slits separate, no operculum; tough skin with minute placoid scales; teeth are modified placoid scales directed backwards. No air bladder, so they swim constantly to avoid sinking. Two-chambered heart; cold-blooded.

Chondrichthyes contd.: some have electric organs (Torpedo) or a poison sting (Trygon); males have claspers on pelvic fins; internal fertilisation; many viviparous. Scoliodon (dogfish), Pristis (sawfish), Carcharodon (great white shark), Trygon (stingray).

Osteichthyes: marine and freshwater, bony endoskeleton; mouth mostly terminal; four pairs of gills covered by an operculum on each side; cycloid or ctenoid scales; air bladder regulates buoyancy; two-chambered heart; cold-blooded; fertilisation usually external; mostly oviparous, development direct.
Osteichthyes examples: Exocoetus (flying fish), Hippocampus (sea horse), Labeo (rohu), Catla (katla), Clarias (magur), Betta (fighting fish), Pterophyllum (angel fish).

ex.q: A fish has a ventral mouth, placoid scales, no operculum and claspers on its pelvic fins. Classify it and say why it must keep swimming.
st: Ventral mouth, placoid scales and no operculum indicate cartilaginous fish.
Claspers are in males of Chondrichthyes.
They lack an air bladder, so they would sink if they stopped.
ex.a: Chondrichthyes; no air bladder.

topics.rl: Rohu, katla and magur are the backbone of inland fish farming in West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh.

rv.summary: Cyclostomes are jawless ectoparasites with 6–15 pairs of gill slits that migrate to fresh water to spawn. Cartilaginous fishes have placoid scales, no operculum and no air bladder; bony fishes have an operculum, cycloid or ctenoid scales and an air bladder.
focus: Chondrichthyes vs Osteichthyes: skeleton, mouth, scales, operculum, air bladder
remember: Cyclostomata: Petromyzon (lamprey), Myxine (hagfish)
Chondrichthyes: Scoliodon, Pristis, Carcharodon, Trygon, Torpedo; claspers in males
Osteichthyes: Exocoetus, Hippocampus, Labeo, Catla, Clarias, Betta, Pterophyllum
Fish heart: 2 chambers
traps: Don't give sharks a bony skeleton or an air bladder
Don't mix placoid scales (cartilaginous) with cycloid/ctenoid (bony)

topics.t: Amphibians and reptiles
topics.h: A frog breathes through its skin, and a crocodile has a four-chambered heart like ours. Tetrapods start getting interesting.
p: Amphibia: live in water and on land; most have two pairs of limbs; body of head and trunk; moist skin without scales; eyelids; a tympanum represents the ear.

Amphibians: the gut, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common cloaca; respiration by gills, lungs and skin; three-chambered heart (two auricles, one ventricle); cold-blooded; sexes separate; external fertilisation; oviparous; development indirect. Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra (salamander), Ichthyophis (limbless amphibian).
Reptilia (Latin repere, to creep): mostly terrestrial; dry, cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes; no external ear openings, a tympanum represents the ear; limbs, when present, two pairs.

Reptiles: heart usually three-chambered but four-chambered in crocodiles; poikilotherms; snakes and lizards shed scales as skin cast; internal fertilisation; oviparous; development direct. Chelone (turtle), Testudo (tortoise), Chameleon (tree lizard), Calotes (garden lizard), Crocodilus (crocodile), Alligator, Hemidactylus (wall lizard), and poisonous snakes Naja (cobra), Bangarus (krait), Vipera (viper).

ex.q: Compare fertilisation and development in a frog and a garden lizard.
st: Frog: external fertilisation, eggs hatch into tadpoles, so development is indirect.
Garden lizard: internal fertilisation; young hatch looking like adults, so development is direct.
ex.a: Frog: external fertilisation, indirect development. Lizard: internal fertilisation, direct development.

topics.rl: India's 'big four' venomous snakes, the cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper, cause most snakebite cases, which is why hospitals stock polyvalent antivenom.

rv.summary: Amphibians live on land and in water, have moist scaleless skin, a cloaca, a three-chambered heart, external fertilisation and indirect development. Reptiles have dry cornified skin with scales, are cold-blooded, fertilise internally and develop directly.
focus: Amphibian features: skin, cloaca, heart, respiration, development
Reptile features: skin, heart (crocodile exception), skin cast, development
Examples of amphibians and reptiles, including poisonous snakes
remember: Amphibian heart: 2 auricles + 1 ventricle
Crocodile: four-chambered heart
Amphibians: Bufo, Rana, Hyla, Salamandra, Ichthyophis (limbless)
Poisonous snakes: Naja, Bangarus, Vipera
traps: Don't call reptiles warm-blooded
Don't call Ichthyophis a snake; it is a limbless amphibian

topics.t: Birds and mammals
topics.h: A peacock's bones are hollow like bamboo, and a platypus lays eggs yet feeds its young milk. Nature loves exceptions.
p: Aves: feathers; most fly (flightless: ostrich); beak; forelimbs modified into wings; hind limbs scaly, adapted for walking, swimming or perching. Dry skin with only an oil gland at the base of the tail.

Birds: fully ossified endoskeleton with hollow, air-filled (pneumatic) long bones; crop and gizzard in the gut; completely four-chambered heart; warm-blooded (homoiothermous); lungs with air sacs; internal fertilisation; oviparous; direct development. Corvus (crow), Columba (pigeon), Psittacula (parrot), Struthio (ostrich), Pavo (peacock), Aptenodytes (penguin), Neophron (vulture).

Mammalia: mammary glands (milk-producing) are the most unique feature. Two pairs of limbs adapted for walking, running, climbing, burrowing, swimming or flying. Hair on the skin; external ears (pinnae); different types of teeth; four-chambered heart; homoiothermous; lungs.

Mammals: sexes separate, internal fertilisation; viviparous with few exceptions; development direct. Oviparous: Ornithorhynchus (platypus). Viviparous: Macropus (kangaroo), Pteropus (flying fox), Camelus, Macaca (monkey), Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Equus, Delphinus (dolphin), Balaenoptera (blue whale), Panthera tigris, Panthera leo.

ex.q: A dolphin lives in water and has flippers. Give two features that show it is a mammal, not a fish.
st: It has mammary glands and feeds its young on milk.
It breathes with lungs and is warm-blooded, with a four-chambered heart.
ex.a: Mammary glands and lung breathing (also warm-blooded, viviparous).

topics.rl: The Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus) is India's national bird, the Bengal tiger the national animal, and the Ganges river dolphin the national aquatic animal.

rv.summary: Birds have feathers, wings, beaks, pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard, a four-chambered heart and are warm-blooded and oviparous. Mammals have mammary glands, hair, pinnae, different teeth and a four-chambered heart, and are mostly viviparous.
focus: Bird features and adaptations for flight
remember: Birds: pneumatic bones, oil gland only, crop and gizzard, air sacs
Mammals' most unique feature: mammary glands
Ornithorhynchus: oviparous mammal; Pteropus: flying fox
traps: Don't say a four-chambered heart is unique to mammals; birds have it too
Don't call all mammals viviparous; the platypus lays eggs

topics.t: Salient features of the phyla: putting it together
topics.h: Board exams love a 'which phylum is this?' question. Master the summary table and you can crack any of them.
p: Porifera: cellular level, asymmetrical, canal system. Coelenterata and Ctenophora: tissue level, radial, diploblastic.
Platyhelminthes: organ level, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, incomplete gut. Aschelminthes: pseudocoelomate, complete gut. Annelida: coelomate, segmented, closed circulation.

Arthropoda: segmented, jointed appendages, open circulation. Mollusca: unsegmented, open circulation. Echinodermata: adult radial, coelomate, water vascular system, complete gut. Hemichordata: open circulation. Chordata: notochord, closed circulation.
Direct development: young resemble adults (e.g. reptiles, birds, mammals, bony fish). Indirect development: a larval stage different from the adult (e.g. sponges, echinoderms, amphibians).
Open circulation in arthropods, molluscs and hemichordates; closed in annelids and chordates.

ex.q: Identify the phylum: triploblastic, coelomate, segmented, jointed appendages, open circulation.
st: Segmented coelomates: annelids or arthropods.
Jointed appendages and open circulation point to arthropods.
ex.a: Arthropoda

topics.rl: A visit to the Zoological Survey of India's museum in Kolkata shows specimens arranged phylum by phylum, much like this summary table.

rv.summary: Each phylum has a signature set of features: level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation, gut, circulation and development. Combining these lets you identify any phylum from a description.
focus: Identifying a phylum from a set of features
Which phyla have open vs closed circulation
Direct vs indirect development with examples
remember: Open circulation: Arthropoda, Mollusca, Hemichordata; closed: Annelida, Chordata
Acoelomate: Platyhelminthes; pseudocoelomate: Aschelminthes
Direct development: reptiles, birds, mammals; indirect: sponges, echinoderms, amphibians
traps: Don't call molluscs segmented
Don't call coelenterates or ctenophores coelomate just because they are radial

topics.t: Morphology and root systems
topics.h: Pull out a mustard seedling and a wheat seedling from a Punjab field. One has a single deep anchor; the other has a bushy beard of roots.
p: Morphology is the study of the external form and features of organisms. A flowering plant has a root, stem, leaves, flowers and fruits.
Tap root system: in most dicots the radicle elongates into a primary root that bears secondary and tertiary lateral roots, e.g. mustard.
Fibrous root system: in monocots the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by many roots arising from the base of the stem, e.g. wheat.
Adventitious roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle, e.g. grass, Monstera and the banyan tree.
Functions of roots: absorption of water and minerals, anchorage, storage of reserve food, and synthesis of plant growth regulators.

ex.q: A banyan's hanging roots grow down from its branches. Classify these roots and explain.
st: Tap and fibrous roots develop from the radicle or stem base of a seedling.
These roots arise from branches, a part other than the radicle.
ex.a: They are adventitious roots.

topics.rl: The banyan, India's national tree, spreads using adventitious roots that become pillar-like; the Great Banyan in Howrah's botanical garden covers several acres.

rv.summary: Morphology studies external form. Dicots usually have a tap root system from the radicle (mustard); monocots have fibrous roots from the stem base (wheat); adventitious roots arise from other parts (banyan). Roots absorb, anchor, store and make growth regulators.
focus: Tap, fibrous and adventitious roots with examples
remember: Tap root: from radicle, dicots (mustard)
Fibrous root: from stem base, monocots (wheat)
Adventitious: from parts other than radicle (grass, Monstera, banyan)
traps: Don't call photosynthesis a main root function
Don't say fibrous roots develop from the radicle

topics.t: Regions of the root, and the stem
topics.h: A root tip pushes through hard soil every day without getting hurt. It wears a helmet, just like a cricketer facing a fast bowler.
p: The root apex is covered by a thimble-like root cap that protects it as it pushes through soil.
Region of meristematic activity, a few millimetres above the root cap: small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly.

Region of elongation: cells elongate and enlarge rapidly, making the root grow in length. Region of maturation: cells differentiate; some epidermal cells form fine root hairs that absorb water and minerals.

The stem is the ascending part of the axis that develops from the plumule. It bears nodes (where leaves arise), internodes (between nodes), and terminal or axillary buds. It is green when young, often woody and dark brown later.
Stem functions: spreading out branches with leaves, flowers and fruits; conducting water, minerals and photosynthates; and in some plants storage, support, protection and vegetative propagation.

ex.q: List the regions of a root from the tip upwards.
st: Tip is covered by the root cap.
Next is the region of meristematic activity.
Then the region of elongation.
Then the region of maturation, which bears root hairs.
ex.a: Root cap → meristematic region → elongation region → maturation region

topics.rl: Sugarcane growers in Uttar Pradesh plant stem cuttings with nodes to raise new plants, using the stem's power of vegetative propagation.

rv.summary: A root tip has a protective root cap, then regions of meristematic activity, elongation and maturation (with root hairs). The stem develops from the plumule, bears nodes, internodes and buds, and conducts water, minerals and food.
focus: Order and role of the root regions
Which region produces root hairs and which causes elongation
Parts and functions of the stem
remember: Root cap → meristematic region → elongation region → maturation region
Root hairs form in the maturation region
Stem from plumule; nodes bear leaves; internodes lie between nodes
traps: Don't credit root growth in length to the root cap
Don't say the stem develops from the radicle

topics.t: The leaf: parts and venation
topics.h: Watch a peepal leaf flutter in the slightest breeze. Its long, flexible petiole is cooling the leaf, a design trick worth learning.
p: A leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem at a node, with a bud in its axil. Leaves arise from the shoot apical meristem in acropetal order.

A typical leaf has a leaf base, petiole and lamina. The leaf base may bear two small leaf-like stipules. In monocots the leaf base forms a sheath around the stem; in some legumes it is swollen into a pulvinus.
The petiole holds the blade to the light. Long, thin, flexible petioles let blades flutter, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface.
The lamina is the green expanded part with veins and veinlets; the prominent middle vein is the midrib. Veins give rigidity and carry water, minerals and food.
Venation: reticulate (veinlets form a network), generally in dicots; parallel (veins run parallel), generally in monocots.

ex.q: A leaf has parallel veins and a sheathing leaf base. What group does the plant probably belong to?
st: Parallel venation is typical of monocots.
A sheathing leaf base is also a monocot feature.
ex.a: A monocot.

topics.rl: Banana and maize leaves show parallel venation, while the mango and peepal leaves used in Indian festive decorations show reticulate venation.

rv.summary: A leaf is a lateral flattened structure at a node with a bud in its axil. It has a leaf base (stipules, sheath or pulvinus), a petiole and a lamina with veins. Venation is reticulate in dicots and parallel in monocots.
focus: Leaf base modifications: stipules, sheath, pulvinus
remember: Leaf parts: leaf base, petiole, lamina
Pulvinus: swollen leaf base in some legumes; sheath in monocots
Reticulate: dicots; parallel: monocots
traps: Don't confuse stipules with leaflets
Don't call parallel venation a dicot feature

topics.t: Simple and compound leaves, and phyllotaxy
topics.h: Is a neem 'leaf' one leaf or many? The answer depends on where you find a bud.
p: Simple leaf: the lamina is entire, or its incisions do not reach the midrib.
Compound leaf: incisions reach the midrib, breaking the lamina into leaflets. A bud is present in the axil of the petiole, but never in the axil of a leaflet.

Pinnately compound: leaflets on a common axis, the rachis (which represents the midrib), e.g. neem. Palmately compound: leaflets attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole, e.g. silk cotton.
Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem.
Alternate: one leaf per node (china rose, mustard, sunflower). Opposite: a pair of leaves per node, facing each other (Calotropis, guava). Whorled: more than two leaves per node (Alstonia).

ex.q: How can you tell a leaflet of neem from a simple leaf?
st: A simple leaf has a bud in its axil.
In a compound leaf, the bud is only in the axil of the petiole, not of each leaflet.
So a leaflet has no axillary bud.
ex.a: A leaflet has no bud in its axil; a simple leaf does.

topics.rl: Neem twigs used as datun in Indian villages carry pinnately compound leaves; the silk cotton (semal) tree that lights up in red in spring has palmately compound leaves.

rv.summary: A simple leaf has an entire lamina or incisions not reaching the midrib; a compound leaf has leaflets, pinnate (neem) or palmate (silk cotton), with a bud only in the petiole's axil. Phyllotaxy may be alternate, opposite or whorled.
focus: Simple vs compound leaves and how to tell a leaflet from a leaf
Three types of phyllotaxy with examples
remember: Pinnate: neem (rachis); palmate: silk cotton
Alternate: china rose, mustard, sunflower
Opposite: Calotropis, guava; whorled: Alstonia
Axillary bud only at the petiole, never at a leaflet
traps: Don't confuse phyllotaxy (leaf arrangement) with venation
Don't expect a bud in the axil of a leaflet

topics.t: Inflorescence: racemose and cymose
topics.h: On a mustard spike in a Rajasthan field, the youngest buds are at the top. On some other plants, the oldest flower sits at the tip. The axis decides.
p: A flower is a modified shoot: the shoot apical meristem becomes a floral meristem, internodes do not elongate, the axis condenses, and floral appendages form at successive nodes instead of leaves.
When the shoot tip itself becomes a flower, the flower is solitary. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is the inflorescence.
Racemose: the main axis continues to grow, and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (older flowers at the base, younger towards the tip).
Cymose: the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited; flowers are borne in basipetal order (older at the tip, younger below).
Quick test: if the apex keeps growing, it is racemose; if the apex has become a flower, it is cymose.

ex.q: On an inflorescence, the topmost flower opened first and the lower ones later. Which type is it?
st: The terminal flower is the oldest, so the axis ended in a flower.
Older flowers above, younger below means basipetal order.
ex.a: Cymose inflorescence.

topics.rl: Mustard fields of Punjab and Rajasthan in winter show racemose inflorescences, with buds still opening near the tip as the axis grows.

rv.summary: A flower is a modified shoot with a condensed axis. In racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing and flowers form in acropetal succession; in cymose inflorescence the axis ends in a flower and flowers form in basipetal order.
focus: Why a flower is a modified shoot
remember: Racemose: axis keeps growing; acropetal (older at base)
Cymose: axis ends in a flower; basipetal (older at top)
Inflorescence = arrangement of flowers on the floral axis
traps: Don't say racemose axes have limited growth
Don't swap acropetal and basipetal

topics.t: The flower: whorls, sex and symmetry
topics.h: Cut a datura flower in any direction through the centre and you get two equal halves. Try that with a pea flower and only one cut works.
p: The flower is the reproductive unit of angiosperms. Its four whorls sit on the swollen end of the pedicel, the thalamus (receptacle): calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx and corolla are accessory organs; androecium and gynoecium are reproductive organs. When calyx and corolla are not distinct, as in lily, they are called perianth.
Bisexual flower: has both androecium and gynoecium. Unisexual flower: has only stamens or only carpels.

Symmetry: actinomorphic (radial) if any radial plane through the centre gives two equal halves (mustard, datura, chilli); zygomorphic (bilateral) if only one vertical plane does (pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia); asymmetric if none does (canna).

Trimerous, tetramerous and pentamerous flowers have floral parts in multiples of 3, 4 and 5. Flowers with bracts (reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel) are bracteate; those without are ebracteate.

ex.q: A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 5 stamens and can be cut into two equal halves along any radial plane. Describe it.
st: Parts in multiples of five: pentamerous.
Equal halves in any radial plane: actinomorphic.
ex.a: Pentamerous and actinomorphic.

topics.rl: Chilli flowers in Andhra Pradesh's Guntur district, India's chilli capital, are small, white and actinomorphic.

rv.summary: A flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx and corolla (accessory) and androecium and gynoecium (reproductive). Flowers may be bisexual or unisexual; actinomorphic, zygomorphic or asymmetric; trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous; bracteate or ebracteate.
focus: The four floral whorls and their roles
Actinomorphic, zygomorphic and asymmetric with examples
remember: Thalamus = swollen end of pedicel
Perianth: undifferentiated calyx and corolla (lily)
Actinomorphic: mustard, datura, chilli; zygomorphic: pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia; asymmetric: canna
traps: Don't say unisexual flowers lack sepals and petals
Don't call a pea flower actinomorphic

topics.t: Position of ovary, calyx and corolla aestivation
topics.h: Look at a guava fruit: the dried flower parts sit on its top. That tells you the ovary was 'inferior', sunk inside the thalamus.
p: Hypogynous: gynoecium highest, other parts below it; ovary superior (mustard, china rose, brinjal). Perigynous: gynoecium in the centre, other parts on the rim of the thalamus at about the same level; ovary half-inferior (plum, rose, peach). Epigynous: thalamus grows up and fuses with the ovary, other parts arise above it; ovary inferior (guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower).
Calyx: outermost whorl of sepals, usually green and leaf-like, protecting the bud. Gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (free).
Corolla: petals, usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination; gamopetalous or polypetalous. Shapes include tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped and wheel-shaped.

Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud relative to others in the same whorl. Valvate: margins just touch, no overlap (Calotropis). Twisted: each margin overlaps the next in one direction (china rose, lady's finger, cotton). Imbricate: margins overlap in no particular direction (Cassia, gulmohur).
Vexillary (papilionaceous) in pea and bean: the largest petal (standard) overlaps two lateral wings, which overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel).

ex.q: In a pea flower, which petal is outermost in the bud and which is innermost?
st: Vexillary aestivation has five petals.
The large standard overlaps the two wings.
The wings overlap the two keel petals.
ex.a: Standard is outermost; keel is innermost.

topics.rl: Cotton and bhindi (lady's finger), both major crops in Gujarat and Maharashtra, show twisted aestivation in their petals.

rv.summary: By ovary position, flowers are hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior) or epigynous (inferior). Sepals and petals may be free or united, and their arrangement in bud (aestivation) is valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary.
focus: Hypogynous, perigynous and epigynous with examples
Calyx and corolla: gamo- vs poly-
remember: Hypogynous: mustard, china rose, brinjal; perigynous: plum, rose, peach; epigynous: guava, cucumber
Valvate: Calotropis; twisted: china rose, lady's finger, cotton; imbricate: Cassia, gulmohur
Vexillary: standard → wings → keel
traps: Don't call guava's ovary superior
Don't confuse twisted (one direction) with imbricate (no particular direction)

topics.t: Androecium: stamens and their unions
topics.h: In a hibiscus flower, the stamens form a single tube around the style. In a pea, nine join and one stays apart. Stamens love teamwork in different ways.
p: The androecium is made of stamens, the male reproductive organs. Each stamen has a stalk (filament) and an anther.
An anther is usually bilobed, and each lobe has two chambers, the pollen sacs, where pollen grains form. A sterile stamen is a staminode.
Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals (brinjal). Epiphyllous stamens are attached to the perianth (lily).
Stamens may be free (polyandrous) or united: monoadelphous (one bundle, china rose), diadelphous (two bundles, pea), polyadelphous (more than two bundles, citrus).
Filament length may vary within a flower, as in Salvia and mustard.

ex.q: How many pollen sacs does a typical stamen have?
st: A typical anther is bilobed: 2 lobes.
Each lobe has 2 chambers (pollen sacs).
Total = 2 × 2 = 4.
ex.a: 4 pollen sacs

topics.rl: Lemon and orange orchards of Nagpur grow citrus flowers with polyadelphous stamens in several bundles.

rv.summary: The androecium is made of stamens, each a filament and a usually bilobed anther with four pollen sacs. Stamens may be epipetalous or epiphyllous, free or united into one, two or many bundles; a sterile stamen is a staminode.
focus: Structure of a stamen and number of pollen sacs
Monoadelphous, diadelphous and polyadelphous with examples
remember: Anther: 2 lobes × 2 pollen sacs = 4
Epipetalous: brinjal; epiphyllous: lily
Monoadelphous: china rose; diadelphous: pea; polyadelphous: citrus
Staminode = sterile stamen
traps: Don't mix epipetalous (on petals) with epiphyllous (on perianth)
Don't call pea stamens monoadelphous

topics.t: Gynoecium and placentation
topics.h: Slice a tomato across and you see seeds attached to a central axis in separate chambers. Slice a pea pod and they sit along one edge. That's placentation.
p: The gynoecium is the female reproductive part, made of one or more carpels. Each carpel has a stigma (receptive surface for pollen), style (connects stigma to ovary) and ovary (enlarged base).
Ovules are attached to a flattened, cushion-like placenta in the ovary. After fertilisation ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Apocarpous: carpels free (lotus, rose). Syncarpous: carpels fused (mustard, tomato).

Placentation types: marginal (ridge along the ventral suture, two rows of ovules; pea), axile (central axis in a multilocular ovary; china rose, tomato, lemon), parietal (ovules on the inner wall; one-chambered ovary made two-chambered by a false septum; mustard, Argemone).
Free central: ovules on a central axis with no septa (Dianthus, Primrose). Basal: placenta at the base with a single ovule (sunflower, marigold).

ex.q: A lemon cut crosswise shows several chambers with seeds attached at the centre. Name the placentation.
st: Multilocular ovary.
Ovules attached to a central axis.
This is axile placentation.
ex.a: Axile placentation.

topics.rl: Marigold flowers, used in lakhs of garlands during Diwali, have basal placentation with a single ovule.

rv.summary: The gynoecium is made of carpels, each with stigma, style and ovary; it may be apocarpous or syncarpous. Ovules sit on placentae in marginal, axile, parietal, free central or basal placentation. After fertilisation ovules form seeds and the ovary forms the fruit.
focus: Five types of placentation with examples
remember: Marginal: pea; axile: china rose, tomato, lemon
Parietal: mustard, Argemone (false septum)
Free central: Dianthus, Primrose; basal: sunflower, marigold
traps: Don't confuse parietal (on wall) with axile (central axis with septa)
Don't call free central placentation axile; it has no septa

topics.t: Fruit and the parts of a seed
topics.h: In a mango, you eat the middle layer and throw away the hard inner one. In a coconut, the middle layer becomes coir ropes.
p: A fruit is a mature or ripened ovary that develops after fertilisation; it is a characteristic feature of flowering plants. A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic.
A fruit has a wall (pericarp) and seeds. A thick, fleshy pericarp is differentiated into an outer epicarp, middle mesocarp and inner endocarp.
Mango and coconut fruits are drupes: they develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded.
In mango, the epicarp is thin, the mesocarp is fleshy and edible, and the endocarp is stony and hard. In coconut, the mesocarp is fibrous.
A seed develops from a fertilised ovule. It has a seed coat and an embryo; the embryo has a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (wheat, maize) or two (gram, pea) cotyledons.

ex.q: Which layer of a mango do we eat, and which forms the hard 'guthli' shell?
st: Mango is a drupe with epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp.
The fleshy edible part is the mesocarp.
The stony layer around the seed is the endocarp.
ex.a: We eat the mesocarp; the hard shell is the endocarp.

topics.rl: Kerala's coir industry turns the fibrous mesocarp of coconut into ropes and mats; seedless banana and grapes are parthenocarpic varieties sold in Indian markets.

rv.summary: A fruit is a ripened ovary with a pericarp (epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp) and seeds; parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilisation. Mango and coconut are one-seeded drupes. A seed has a seed coat and an embryo with one or two cotyledons.
remember: Pericarp: epicarp (outer), mesocarp (middle), endocarp (inner)
Mango: edible mesocarp, stony endocarp; coconut: fibrous mesocarp
Drupe: monocarpellary superior ovary, one-seeded
traps: Don't call the hard mango stone the mesocarp; it is the endocarp
Don't put wheat and maize among two-cotyledon seeds

topics.t: Structure of dicot and monocot seeds
topics.h: Soak a gram seed overnight and it splits into two fat halves. A maize grain refuses to split. Their insides are built differently.
p: Dicot seed: the seed coat has an outer testa and inner tegmen. The hilum is the scar where the seed was attached to the fruit; the micropyle is a small pore above the hilum.
The dicot embryo has an embryonal axis with a radicle and plumule at its ends, and two cotyledons that are often fleshy and full of food.
Endospermic seeds keep the endosperm (formed by double fertilisation) as food-storing tissue, e.g. castor. Non-endospermic seeds have no endosperm in the mature seed, e.g. bean, gram, pea.

Monocot seeds are generally endospermic (orchids are non-endospermic). In maize, the seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall; the bulky endosperm is separated from the embryo by a proteinous aleurone layer.

The maize embryo lies in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum, and a short axis with plumule and radicle enclosed in sheaths, the coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.

ex.q: Name the sheaths that cover the plumule and the radicle in a maize embryo.
st: The plumule is the future shoot; its sheath is the coleoptile.
The radicle is the future root; its sheath is the coleorhiza.
ex.a: Coleoptile covers the plumule; coleorhiza covers the radicle.

topics.rl: India's maize belt in Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh grows corn whose grains are endospermic; soaked chana (gram) sprouts show two cotyledons and no endosperm.

rv.summary: A dicot seed has a seed coat (testa, tegmen), hilum, micropyle and an embryo with two cotyledons; it may be endospermic (castor) or not (bean, gram, pea). Maize has a fused seed coat, an aleurone-covered endosperm and an embryo with scutellum, coleoptile and coleorhiza.
focus: Structure of the maize grain and embryo
remember: Testa outer, tegmen inner; hilum = attachment scar
Endospermic: castor; non-endospermic: bean, gram, pea; orchids non-endospermic monocots
Maize: scutellum (cotyledon), coleoptile (plumule), coleorhiza (radicle), aleurone layer
traps: Don't swap coleoptile (plumule) and coleorhiza (radicle)
Don't call gram or pea endospermic

topics.t: Semi-technical description, floral formula and floral diagram
topics.h: A floral formula is like a cricket scorecard: a single line tells you everything about a flower if you know the symbols.
p: A semi-technical description uses brief, scientific language in a set sequence: habit, then vegetative characters (root, stem, leaves), then floral characters (inflorescence and flower parts), followed by the floral diagram and floral formula.
Symbols: Br bracteate, K calyx, C corolla, P perianth, A androecium, G gynoecium; ♂ male, ♀ female, ⚥ bisexual; ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic.
A line below G (G̲) shows a superior ovary; a line above G (Ḡ) shows an inferior ovary. Numbers give the count of parts.

Fusion (cohesion) of members of a whorl is shown by putting the number in brackets, e.g. C(5) means five united petals. Adhesion between whorls is shown by a line drawn above the symbols of those whorls, e.g. joining C and A for epipetalous stamens.

Floral diagram: a dot at the top shows the position of the mother axis. Calyx (outermost), corolla, androecium and gynoecium (centre) are drawn as successive whorls, showing number, aestivation, cohesion, adhesion and placentation. The NCERT example is mustard (family Brassicaceae).

ex.q: Decode: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with a line joining C and A, and G(2) underlined.
st: ⊕ actinomorphic, ⚥ bisexual.
K(5): five united sepals; C(5): five united petals.
A5 joined to C by a line: five epipetalous stamens.
G(2) underlined: bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary.
ex.a: An actinomorphic bisexual flower with 5 united sepals, 5 united petals, 5 epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary.

topics.rl: Botanists at the Botanical Survey of India write floral formulae in field notebooks to record new plants quickly, much like a scorer's shorthand at a Ranji Trophy match.

rv.summary: A semi-technical description runs habit → vegetative → floral characters → floral diagram and formula. In floral formulas, brackets show cohesion, a line above symbols shows adhesion, and a line below or above G shows a superior or inferior ovary.
focus: Reading and writing a floral formula
remember: Br, K, C, P, A, G; ♂, ♀, ⚥; ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic
Number in brackets = fused parts, e.g. C(5)
G underlined = superior ovary; line above G = inferior
Dot at top of floral diagram = mother axis
traps: Don't read brackets as adhesion; they show cohesion within one whorl
Don't swap the superior and inferior ovary signs

topics.t: Family Solanaceae: the potato family
topics.h: Your aloo paratha, tomato chutney, baingan bharta and green chilli all come from one plant family. Meet Solanaceae.
p: Solanaceae (potato family) is a large family spread across tropics, subtropics and temperate zones. Plants are mostly herbs and shrubs, rarely small trees.

Stem: herbaceous, rarely woody; erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous; underground stem in potato (Solanum tuberosum). Leaves: alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate, reticulate venation.

Floral characters: inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose (as in Solanum); flowers bisexual and actinomorphic. Calyx: five united sepals, persistent, valvate. Corolla: five united petals, valvate. Androecium: five epipetalous stamens.

Gynoecium: bicarpellary, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules; axile placentation. Fruit: berry or capsule. Seeds: many, endospermous. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with C and A joined (epipetalous) and G underlined (superior).
Uses: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamental (petunia).

ex.q: A brinjal flower has 5 united persistent sepals, 5 united petals, 5 stamens attached to petals, and a 2-carpelled fused superior ovary. Write its floral formula.
st: Actinomorphic and bisexual: ⊕ ⚥.
Sepals united: K(5). Petals united: C(5).
Stamens epipetalous: A5 joined to C(5) by a line.
Two fused carpels, superior: G(2) underlined.
ex.a: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) (C and A joined by a line, G underlined)

topics.rl: India is among the world's largest producers of potato, tomato and brinjal, and ashwagandha is a major medicinal crop grown in Madhya Pradesh's Mandsaur and Neemuch districts.

rv.summary: Solanaceae (potato family) are mostly herbs and shrubs with alternate exstipulate leaves. Flowers are bisexual and actinomorphic: K(5) valvate persistent, C(5) valvate, A5 epipetalous, G(2) superior with axile placentation; fruit a berry or capsule.
focus: Vegetative and floral features of Solanaceae
remember: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2): C and A joined, G underlined
Axile placentation, bilocular ovary, many ovules
Uses: tomato, brinjal, potato (food); chilli (spice); belladonna, ashwagandha (medicine); tobacco (fumigatory); petunia (ornamental)
traps: Don't call Solanaceae stamens free; they are epipetalous
Don't give an inferior ovary; it is superior

topics.t: Anatomy, tissues and the three tissue systems
topics.h: Slice a bhindi or a sugarcane and look closely: inside are neat layers and bundles, like cables in an underground metro tunnel.
p: Anatomy is the study of internal structure. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and monocots and dicots differ in their internal structure.
Meristematic tissues divide (apical, intercalary, lateral). Permanent tissues are simple (one cell type: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or complex (many cell types: xylem and phloem).

Parenchyma: living, thin-walled, with spaces, for storage and photosynthesis. Collenchyma: living, thickened at corners, gives mechanical support to young stems. Sclerenchyma: dead, lignified fibres and sclereids for strength.
Xylem conducts water and minerals (tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma). Phloem transports food (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres).
Based on location, tissues form three systems: epidermal tissue system, ground (fundamental) tissue system and vascular (conducting) tissue system.

ex.q: Classify xylem and collenchyma as simple or complex tissues.
st: Collenchyma is made of one type of cell: simple.
Xylem has tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma: complex.
ex.a: Collenchyma is simple; xylem is complex.

topics.rl: Jute fibres from West Bengal and Assam, used for gunny bags, are sclerenchyma fibres from the plant's phloem region.

rv.summary: Anatomy studies internal structure. Meristematic tissues divide; permanent tissues are simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or complex (xylem, phloem). By location, plant tissues form epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems.
focus: Simple vs complex tissues with examples
Features of parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma
remember: Simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem, phloem
Xylem: water and minerals; phloem: food
Tissue systems: epidermal, ground, vascular
traps: Don't call sclerenchyma living; it is dead and lignified
Don't call xylem a simple tissue

topics.t: Epidermal tissue system: epidermis, stomata and hairs
topics.h: A single mango leaf has thousands of tiny 'mouths' that open and close all day. Each is guarded by two kidney-bean cells.
p: The epidermis is the outermost layer: elongated, compactly arranged cells forming a continuous, usually single layer of parenchyma with little cytoplasm and a large vacuole.
A waxy cuticle often covers the epidermis to prevent water loss; it is absent in roots.

Stomata in the leaf epidermis regulate transpiration and gas exchange. Each stoma has two guard cells around a pore: bean-shaped in dicots, dumb-bell shaped in grasses. Their outer walls (away from the pore) are thin and inner walls (towards the pore) are highly thickened; guard cells have chloroplasts.
Subsidiary cells are specialised epidermal cells near the guard cells. The stomatal aperture, guard cells and subsidiary cells together form the stomatal apparatus.

Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epidermal cells that absorb water and minerals. Trichomes on the shoot are usually multicellular, branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, sometimes secretory, and help prevent water loss.

ex.q: Name the parts of the stomatal apparatus.
st: The pore itself: stomatal aperture.
Two cells enclosing the pore: guard cells.
Specialised epidermal cells around them: subsidiary cells.
ex.a: Stomatal aperture + guard cells + subsidiary cells

topics.rl: Wheat and rice leaves in Indian paddy and wheat fields have dumb-bell shaped guard cells, typical of grasses.

rv.summary: The epidermis is a compact single layer, often covered by a waxy cuticle (absent in roots). Stomata, with bean-shaped (dicot) or dumb-bell shaped (grass) guard cells, regulate transpiration and gas exchange. Root hairs are unicellular; trichomes are usually multicellular.
focus: Structure of the epidermis and cuticle
Guard cell shape and wall thickening
remember: Stomatal apparatus = aperture + guard cells + subsidiary cells
Guard cells: thick inner wall, thin outer wall, have chloroplasts
Root hairs unicellular; trichomes usually multicellular
traps: Don't say roots have a cuticle
Don't give grasses bean-shaped guard cells

topics.t: Ground tissue and vascular bundles
topics.h: Why can a neem trunk grow thicker every year but a coconut trunk can't? The answer is a thin strip of cambium in the vascular bundles.
p: Ground tissue system: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles, made of parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. Parenchyma is found in the cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays of primary stems and roots. In leaves, ground tissue is the chloroplast-rich mesophyll.
The vascular tissue system has xylem and phloem, which together form vascular bundles.
Open vascular bundles have cambium between phloem and xylem and can form secondary tissues (dicot stems). Closed vascular bundles lack cambium and form no secondary tissues (monocots).

Radial bundles: xylem and phloem alternate on different radii (roots). Conjoint bundles: xylem and phloem lie on the same radius (stems and leaves), usually with phloem on the outer side (collateral).
Exarch xylem: protoxylem towards the periphery, metaxylem towards the centre (roots). Endarch xylem: protoxylem towards the centre (pith), metaxylem towards the periphery (stems).

ex.q: A section shows xylem and phloem on the same radius with cambium between them and protoxylem towards the pith. Describe the bundle.
st: Same radius: conjoint.
Cambium present: open.
Protoxylem towards centre: endarch.
ex.a: Conjoint, open, endarch: typical of a dicot stem.

topics.rl: Coconut palms of Kerala have closed bundles and no true secondary growth, so their trunks stay nearly the same width; neem and teak keep thickening.

rv.summary: The ground tissue system is everything except epidermis and vascular bundles (mesophyll in leaves). Vascular bundles may be open (with cambium) or closed, radial (roots) or conjoint (stems, leaves), with exarch (roots) or endarch (stems) xylem.
focus: What the ground tissue system includes
remember: Open: cambium present (dicot stems); closed: no cambium (monocots)
Radial: roots; conjoint collateral: stems and leaves
Exarch: protoxylem outside (roots); endarch: protoxylem inside (stems)
traps: Don't swap exarch and endarch
Don't call root bundles conjoint

topics.t: Anatomy of dicot and monocot roots
topics.h: Inside a sunflower root sits a ring of cells with waxy belts, the Casparian strips, acting like a security checkpoint for water.
p: Dicot root (sunflower): outermost epiblema, many cells forming unicellular root hairs; cortex of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces.
Endodermis is the innermost cortical layer: one layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces; their tangential and radial walls have water-impermeable, waxy suberin as Casparian strips.
Pericycle: a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma next to the endodermis; lateral roots and the vascular cambium (during secondary growth) arise here.

Dicot root has 2 to 4 xylem and phloem patches, parenchymatous conjunctive tissue between them, and a small or inconspicuous pith. Everything inside the endodermis (pericycle, vascular bundles, pith) is the stele.
Monocot root: same basic layers but usually more than six xylem bundles (polyarch), a large well-developed pith, and no secondary growth.

ex.q: A root T.S. shows 12 xylem patches and a large pith. Is it dicot or monocot? Will it show secondary growth?
st: More than six xylem bundles is polyarch, typical of monocot roots.
A large pith also fits monocot root.
Monocot roots do not undergo secondary growth.
ex.a: Monocot root; no secondary growth.

topics.rl: Maize roots in Bihar's fields are polyarch monocot roots, while sunflower roots in Karnataka are the classic dicot example.

rv.summary: A dicot root has epiblema with root hairs, a parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with suberin Casparian strips, pericycle, 2–4 xylem and phloem patches with conjunctive tissue and a small pith. Monocot roots are polyarch with a large pith and no secondary growth.
focus: Layers of a root from outside in
remember: Casparian strips: suberin on tangential and radial walls
Lateral roots and vascular cambium arise from pericycle
Stele = everything inside endodermis
Dicot root: 2–4 xylem patches; monocot: more than six (polyarch)
traps: Don't say Casparian strips are lignin or cellulose
Don't credit lateral roots to the endodermis

topics.t: Anatomy of dicot and monocot stems
topics.h: Cut a sunflower stem and the bundles form a neat ring. Cut a maize stalk and they are sprinkled everywhere like masala on chaat.
p: Dicot stem: epidermis with a thin cuticle, may bear trichomes and a few stomata. The cortex has three zones: hypodermis (a few layers of collenchyma for mechanical strength), parenchymatous cortex with intercellular spaces, and endodermis rich in starch grains (starch sheath).
Pericycle lies inside the endodermis and above the phloem as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma. Radially placed parenchyma cells between bundles form medullary rays.

Many vascular bundles are arranged in a ring, characteristic of dicot stems. Each bundle is conjoint, open, with endarch protoxylem. A large central pith of rounded parenchyma cells with large spaces.
Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis; many scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue.
Monocot bundles are conjoint and closed; peripheral ones are smaller than central ones; phloem parenchyma is absent; water-containing cavities are present within the bundles.

ex.q: A stem T.S. shows scattered bundles, each with a bundle sheath and a water-containing cavity. Identify it.
st: Scattered bundles: monocot stem.
Bundle sheath of sclerenchyma and water cavities confirm a monocot stem.
ex.a: Monocot stem.

topics.rl: Sugarcane and maize stalks, key crops in Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka, are monocot stems with scattered bundles.

rv.summary: A dicot stem has a collenchymatous hypodermis, starch sheath, sclerenchymatous pericycle patches, a ring of conjoint open endarch bundles and a large pith. A monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and scattered closed bundles with bundle sheaths and water cavities.
focus: Arrangement and type of vascular bundles
Distinguishing features of the monocot stem
remember: Dicot stem: collenchyma hypodermis, starch sheath, bundles in a ring, open, endarch
Monocot stem: sclerenchyma hypodermis, scattered closed bundles, bundle sheath, water cavities, no phloem parenchyma
Monocot peripheral bundles smaller than central ones
traps: Don't swap the hypodermis types of dicot and monocot stems
Don't call monocot stem bundles open

topics.t: Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves
topics.h: In a hot afternoon in Rajasthan, wheat and grass leaves roll into tubes. Special 'hinge' cells are saving water.
p: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: epidermis on the upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) surfaces with a conspicuous cuticle. The abaxial epidermis generally has more stomata; the adaxial may even lack them.

Mesophyll is parenchyma with chloroplasts, for photosynthesis. Palisade parenchyma (adaxial) has elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel. Spongy parenchyma (below it) has oval or round, loosely arranged cells with large spaces and air cavities.
Vascular bundles in veins and midrib vary in size with reticulate venation and are surrounded by thick-walled bundle sheath cells.
Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: stomata on both surfaces, and mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy layers.

In grasses, some adaxial epidermal cells along veins become large, empty, colourless bulliform cells. When turgid, the leaf stays open; when flaccid under water stress, the leaf curls inwards to reduce water loss. Parallel venation shows as bundles of nearly similar size.

ex.q: Why do maize leaves roll up on a very hot, dry day?
st: Water stress makes bulliform cells lose water and become flaccid.
Flaccid bulliform cells make the leaf curl inwards.
Curling reduces the exposed surface and water loss.
ex.a: Bulliform cells become flaccid and the leaf rolls to cut water loss.

topics.rl: During heat waves in north India, farmers notice maize and sugarcane leaves rolling at noon, a sign of bulliform cells at work and of water stress in the crop.

rv.summary: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has more stomata below and mesophyll of palisade and spongy parenchyma. An isobilateral (monocot) leaf has stomata on both sides and undifferentiated mesophyll; grasses have bulliform cells that roll the leaf under water stress.
remember: Palisade: adaxial, elongated, parallel; spongy: loose, air spaces
Dicot leaf: more stomata on abaxial side
Monocot leaf: stomata both sides, no palisade/spongy distinction
Flaccid bulliform cells → leaf curls inwards
traps: Don't say bulliform cells open the leaf when flaccid; they make it curl
Don't put palisade on the lower side

topics.t: Comparing dicot and monocot anatomy and identifying sections
topics.h: In the practical exam, the examiner hands you an unlabelled slide. Two minutes, one question: root or stem, dicot or monocot?
p: Root or stem? Roots have radial bundles with exarch xylem, an epiblema with root hairs and no cuticle. Stems have conjoint bundles with endarch xylem and a cuticle-covered epidermis.
Dicot root: 2 to 4 xylem patches, small pith, secondary growth possible. Monocot root: more than six xylem bundles (polyarch), large pith, no secondary growth.

Dicot stem: collenchymatous hypodermis, bundles in a ring, open, starch sheath, medullary rays, distinct pith. Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered closed bundles with bundle sheath and water cavities, no distinct pith.
Dicot leaf: dorsiventral, palisade and spongy mesophyll, more stomata on the lower side. Monocot leaf: isobilateral, stomata on both sides, undifferentiated mesophyll, bulliform cells.

In T.S. diagrams, label: epidermis or epiblema, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, xylem (protoxylem and metaxylem), phloem, cambium where present, pith; for leaves: cuticle, epidermis, palisade, spongy cells, stomata, bundle sheath, xylem and phloem.

ex.q: A T.S. shows radial bundles, exarch xylem with 4 patches, and a small pith. Identify it.
st: Radial bundles and exarch xylem: root.
Only 4 xylem patches and small pith: dicot.
ex.a: Dicot root.

topics.rl: Practical exams across CBSE schools include slide identification of exactly these sections, so spotting features fast earns easy marks.

rv.summary: Sections are identified by a few clues: radial exarch bundles mean root, conjoint endarch bundles mean stem; xylem patch number and pith size separate dicot and monocot roots; bundle arrangement separates stems; stomata and mesophyll separate leaves.
focus: Telling a root from a stem in T.S.
Distinguishing dicot and monocot roots, stems and leaves
What to label in each T.S. diagram
remember: Root: radial, exarch, epiblema, no cuticle; stem: conjoint, endarch, cuticle
Dicot root 2–4 xylem, small pith; monocot root polyarch, large pith
Dicot stem: ring, open; monocot stem: scattered, closed
Dicot leaf dorsiventral; monocot leaf isobilateral with bulliform cells
traps: Don't say stems have radial exarch bundles
Don't call a polyarch root dicot

topics.t: Tissues, organs and organ systems
topics.h: A cricket team works because the bowler, keeper and batters each do one job well. Your body runs on the same idea: division of labour.
p: In multicellular animals, similar cells with their intercellular material form tissues that perform a common function.
Animals have four basic tissue types: epithelial (covering and lining), connective (linking and supporting), muscular (movement) and neural (control and coordination).

Tissues are organised in specific proportions and patterns to form organs such as the stomach, lungs, heart and kidney. Organs working together form organ systems, such as the digestive and respiratory systems.
Division of labour among cells, tissues, organs and organ systems helps the whole body survive. The complexity of organs and organ systems shows a discernible evolutionary trend.
Morphology studies the externally visible form and features; in animals, anatomy refers to the study of the morphology of internal organs.

ex.q: Arrange from simplest to most complex: organ system, cell, organ, tissue.
st: The cell is the basic unit.
Similar cells form a tissue.
Tissues form an organ.
Organs work together as an organ system.
ex.a: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system

topics.rl: At AIIMS, different departments (cardiology, nephrology, pulmonology) mirror organ systems: each specialises, and the hospital works only when all cooperate.

rv.summary: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs and organs form organ systems. Animals have four basic tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular and neural. Division of labour among these levels keeps the body alive, and their complexity shows an evolutionary trend.
focus: Four basic animal tissues and their roles
remember: Tissue = similar cells + intercellular material doing a common function
Four tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, neural
Anatomy (animals) = morphology of internal organs
traps: Don't call the heart a tissue; it is an organ
Don't say all animals have the same organ systems

topics.t: The frog: habits and external features
topics.h: When the monsoon arrives, frogs suddenly croak everywhere. Where were they all summer? Sleeping underground.
p: The common Indian frog is Rana tigrina (class Amphibia, phylum Chordata). Frogs are poikilotherms: their body temperature changes with the surroundings. They change colour to hide from enemies (camouflage); this protective colouration is called mimicry.
In peak summer and winter, frogs shelter in deep burrows: summer sleep is aestivation and winter sleep is hibernation.

Skin is smooth, slippery with mucus, and always moist. The dorsal side is olive green with dark irregular spots; the ventral side is uniformly pale yellow. A frog never drinks water; it absorbs water through its skin.

Body is divided into head and trunk; there is no neck or tail. A pair of nostrils lies above the mouth; bulging eyes are covered by a nictitating membrane that protects them in water; a membranous tympanum (ear) on each side receives sound.

Forelimbs end in four digits; hind limbs are larger and more muscular and end in five webbed digits for swimming. Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb, absent in females (sexual dimorphism).

ex.q: How can you tell a male frog from a female by external features?
st: Look for sound-producing vocal sacs: present only in males.
Check the first digit of the forelimb for a copulatory pad: present only in males.
ex.a: Males have vocal sacs and copulatory pads on the forelimbs.

topics.rl: Frogs vanish from Indian fields in the dry summer and reappear with the first monsoon showers, after aestivating in moist burrows. (Dissection of frogs has been discontinued in many Indian institutions; models, charts and virtual dissections are used instead, and wild frogs should never be harmed.)

rv.summary: Rana tigrina, the common Indian frog, is a poikilotherm that changes colour for camouflage, aestivates and hibernates, and absorbs water through moist skin. Its body is head and trunk; males have vocal sacs and copulatory pads.
focus: External features: skin, eyes, tympanum, limbs
remember: Aestivation = summer sleep; hibernation = winter sleep
Frog never drinks; absorbs water through skin
Forelimb 4 digits; hind limb 5 webbed digits
Male only: vocal sacs, copulatory pad on first forelimb digit
traps: Don't swap aestivation and hibernation
Don't say frogs have a neck or tail

topics.t: Frog digestive and respiratory systems
topics.h: A frog can breathe through its skin while sitting at the bottom of a pond. Humans cannot: we depend entirely on our lungs.
p: The body cavity holds the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, excretory and reproductive systems.
Digestive system: the alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores. Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → cloaca. Food is caught by a bilobed tongue.

Stomach walls secrete HCl and gastric juices; partly digested food (chyme) passes to the duodenum, which receives bile (from liver via gall bladder) and pancreatic juice through a common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Villi and microvilli in the intestine absorb digested food.

Respiration in water: through the skin by diffusion (cutaneous respiration). On land: buccal cavity, skin and lungs (pulmonary respiration through elongated pink sac-like lungs in the thorax). During aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange is through the skin.
Adaptations to amphibious life: moist skin for breathing, webbed hind feet for swimming, nictitating membrane for eyes, lungs for air, and the ability to aestivate or hibernate.

ex.q: Order the path of food in a frog from mouth to exit.
st: Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx
→ oesophagus → stomach
→ intestine (duodenum first) → rectum
→ cloaca, which opens outside
ex.a: Mouth, buccal cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, intestine, rectum, cloaca

topics.rl: Frogs in paddy fields of Assam and Bengal stay submerged for long periods, relying on cutaneous respiration through their moist skin.

rv.summary: Frogs have a short carnivore gut: mouth to cloaca, with bile from the liver and pancreatic juice entering the duodenum. They breathe through the skin in water and with the buccal cavity, skin and lungs on land; skin alone during aestivation and hibernation.
focus: Path of food through the frog gut
Roles of bile and pancreatic juice
remember: Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → cloaca
Liver secretes bile; gall bladder stores it
In water: cutaneous respiration; on land: buccal, skin, lungs
traps: Don't say the gall bladder secretes bile
Don't confuse chyme with bile

topics.t: Frog circulatory and excretory systems
topics.h: A frog's heart has three chambers, but its red blood cells keep their nuclei, unlike ours. Small differences, big stories.
p: Circulation is closed, with a well-developed lymphatic system (lymph, lymph channels, lymph nodes). The heart is in the upper body cavity, covered by the pericardium, with three chambers: two atria and one ventricle.
The sinus venosus, a triangular structure, joins the right atrium and receives blood through the venae cavae. The ventricle opens into the sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side.
Arteries carry blood from the heart; veins bring it back. Special venous connections: hepatic portal system (between intestine and liver) and renal portal system (between lower body and kidney).
Blood has plasma and cells: RBCs (erythrocytes) that are nucleated and have haemoglobin, WBCs (leucocytes) and platelets. Lymph lacks some proteins and RBCs.

Excretory system: a pair of compact, dark red, bean-like kidneys made of uriniferous tubules (nephrons), ureters, cloaca and a thin-walled urinary bladder. In males the ureters act as urinogenital ducts; in females ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca. Frogs excrete urea, so they are ureotelic.

ex.q: Trace the path of blood entering a frog's heart from the body.
st: Body blood returns through the venae cavae.
It enters the sinus venosus.
The sinus venosus joins the right atrium.
From the atria blood goes to the single ventricle, then into the conus arteriosus.
ex.a: Venae cavae → sinus venosus → right atrium → ventricle → conus arteriosus

topics.rl: Doctors in India explain portal circulation to medical students using the human hepatic portal system; the frog shows both hepatic and renal portal systems.

rv.summary: Frogs have closed circulation with a lymphatic system and a three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) plus sinus venosus and conus arteriosus, and hepatic and renal portal systems. Kidneys of uriniferous tubules excrete urea.
focus: Structure of the frog heart and path of blood
remember: Venae cavae → sinus venosus → right atrium → ventricle → conus arteriosus
Frog RBCs nucleated with haemoglobin
Frogs are ureotelic
Male ureters = urinogenital ducts
traps: Don't give the frog heart two ventricles
Don't say frog RBCs lack a nucleus

topics.t: Frog control, coordination and sense organs
topics.h: A frog's brain is tiny, but it still has three parts and ten pairs of cranial nerves, enough to snap a fly mid-air.
p: Control and coordination use both the neural system and endocrine glands. Endocrine glands of the frog: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads.
Nervous system: central (brain and spinal cord), peripheral (cranial and spinal nerves) and autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic). Ten pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain.

The brain, in a bony brain box (cranium), has fore-brain (olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon), mid-brain (pair of optic lobes) and hind-brain (cerebellum and medulla oblongata).
The medulla oblongata passes out through the foramen magnum and continues as the spinal cord inside the vertebral column.

Sense organs: touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes) and hearing (tympanum with internal ears). Eyes and internal ears are well organised; the others are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. Frog eyes are simple; the ear is for hearing and balance; there is no external ear.

ex.q: Name the parts of the frog's hind-brain and the opening through which it continues as the spinal cord.
st: Hind-brain: cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
The medulla passes out through the foramen magnum.
ex.a: Cerebellum and medulla oblongata; foramen magnum.

topics.rl: Frogs in Indian fields are early warning signs of pollution: their thin skin and sensitive nervous and endocrine systems are easily affected by pesticides.

rv.summary: Frogs coordinate by nerves and endocrine glands. The nervous system is central, peripheral (10 pairs of cranial nerves) and autonomic. The brain has fore-, mid- (optic lobes) and hind-brain (cerebellum, medulla). Eyes and internal ears are the well-organised sense organs.
focus: Divisions of the frog nervous system
remember: 10 pairs of cranial nerves
Mid-brain: optic lobes; hind-brain: cerebellum, medulla oblongata
Medulla exits through foramen magnum
No external ear; tympanum only
traps: Don't list the gall bladder as an endocrine gland
Don't say frogs have a pinna

topics.t: Frog reproduction and usefulness
topics.h: One female frog can lay up to 3000 eggs at a time. From each, a tadpole may swim out and transform into a frog.
p: Male organs: a pair of yellowish, ovoid testes attached to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum (mesorchium). 10 to 12 vasa efferentia enter the kidneys and open into Bidder's canal, which joins the urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca.
The cloaca is a small median chamber that passes faecal matter, urine and sperms to the exterior.
Female organs: a pair of ovaries near the kidneys with no functional connection to them; a pair of oviducts opens separately into the cloaca. A mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time.
Fertilisation is external, in water. Development includes a larval stage, the tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis into the adult.
Usefulness: frogs eat insects and protect crops; they keep ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs; in some countries frog legs are eaten.

ex.q: Trace the path of sperms from the testis to the outside in a male frog.
st: Testis → vasa efferentia.
Vasa efferentia enter the kidney and open into Bidder's canal.
Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca → outside.
ex.a: Testis → vasa efferentia → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca

topics.rl: Farmers benefit from frogs in rice fields because they eat crop pests; declining frog numbers can mean more pest attacks.

rv.summary: Male frogs have testes attached by the mesorchium; sperms pass via 10–12 vasa efferentia, Bidder's canal and the urinogenital duct to the cloaca. Females lay 2500–3000 ova; fertilisation is external and development is indirect via a tadpole. Frogs protect crops and balance food webs.
focus: Male reproductive path in the frog
remember: Testis → vasa efferentia (10–12) → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct → cloaca
Female lays 2500–3000 ova at a time
External fertilisation; tadpole; metamorphosis
traps: Don't say frogs have internal fertilisation
Don't say ovaries connect functionally to the kidneys

topics.t: What is a cell? The cell theory
topics.h: Every living thing, from the bacteria in your dahi to a blue whale, is made of cells. It took three scientists and two centuries to say this clearly.
p: The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms. Unicellular organisms are a single cell that lives independently; multicellular organisms have many cells.
Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus.

Matthias Schleiden (1838, botanist) showed that all plants are made of different kinds of cells forming tissues. Theodor Schwann (1839, zoologist) studied animal cells, reported the thin outer layer now called the plasma membrane, and concluded that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. Together they formulated the cell theory.
Their theory did not explain how new cells form. Rudolf Virchow (1855) explained that cells divide and new cells arise from pre-existing cells: Omnis cellula-e cellula.
Modern cell theory: (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells; (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

ex.q: What did Virchow add to the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann?
st: Schleiden and Schwann said organisms are made of cells and cell products.
They could not explain where new cells come from.
Virchow showed new cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.
ex.a: That all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula).

topics.rl: Every pathology lab in India, from AIIMS to a district hospital, diagnoses disease by examining cells, a direct use of the cell theory.

rv.summary: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed the cell theory; Virchow added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Modern cell theory combines both ideas.
focus: Contributions of Leeuwenhoek, Brown, Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow
The two statements of modern cell theory
Gap in the original cell theory
remember: Leeuwenhoek: first saw a live cell; Robert Brown: nucleus
Schleiden 1838 (plants), Schwann 1839 (animals, cell wall unique to plants)
Virchow 1855: Omnis cellula-e cellula
Modern theory: organisms are cells and cell products; cells arise from pre-existing cells
traps: Don't credit 'Omnis cellula-e cellula' to Schleiden or Schwann
Don't say cells can arise from non-living matter

topics.t: An overview of the cell: size, shape and parts
topics.h: The smallest known cell is about 0.3 micrometre long; the largest single cell is an ostrich egg. That is a size range of about five lakh times.
p: Cytoplasm, a semi-fluid matrix, fills the cell and is the main arena of cellular activities. Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus with chromosomes carrying DNA; prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies and vacuoles. Prokaryotic cells lack these.

Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound organelles found in all cells: in the cytoplasm, on rough ER, and inside chloroplasts and mitochondria. Animal cells also have a non-membrane-bound centrosome that helps in cell division.
Size: Mycoplasma about 0.3 µm long; bacteria 3 to 5 µm; human red blood cells about 7.0 µm in diameter; the ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell; nerve cells are among the longest cells.
Shape varies with function: disc-like, polygonal, columnar, cuboid, thread-like or irregular.

ex.q: How many times longer is a 3 µm bacterium than a 0.3 µm Mycoplasma cell?
st: Divide the bacterium's length by the Mycoplasma's length.
ex.a: 10 times

topics.rl: When blood is tested at a diagnostic lab, technicians check that RBCs are about 7 µm across; abnormal sizes can point to anaemia.

rv.summary: The cytoplasm is the main arena of cell activity. Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; prokaryotic cells lack them. Ribosomes occur in all cells. Cells range from Mycoplasma (0.3 µm) to the ostrich egg, and their shape suits their function.
focus: Cell sizes: Mycoplasma, bacteria, RBC, ostrich egg, nerve cell
remember: Mycoplasma ~0.3 µm; bacteria 3–5 µm; human RBC ~7.0 µm
Ostrich egg: largest isolated single cell
Ribosomes and centrosome are not membrane-bound
traps: Don't call ribosomes membrane-bound
Don't say prokaryotes lack ribosomes

topics.t: Prokaryotic cells: DNA, plasmids and the cell envelope
topics.h: Antibiotic resistance, one of India's biggest health worries, often travels on tiny rings of extra DNA in bacteria called plasmids.
p: Prokaryotic cells include bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO (pleuro-pneumonia-like organisms). They are generally smaller and multiply faster than eukaryotic cells. Shapes: bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum.
All prokaryotes except mycoplasma have a cell wall around the cell membrane. The genetic material is naked, not enclosed by a nuclear membrane: a single circular genomic DNA in the nucleoid.
Many bacteria also have small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA, called plasmids, which give special traits such as resistance to antibiotics.

Cell envelope: a tightly bound three-layered structure: outer glycocalyx, then cell wall, then plasma membrane, working together as one protective unit. The glycocalyx may be a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule. The cell wall gives shape and prevents bursting or collapsing; the plasma membrane is semi-permeable.
Based on their cell envelopes and response to Gram's staining, bacteria are Gram-positive (take up the stain) or Gram-negative (do not).

ex.q: List the layers of a bacterial cell envelope from outside to inside.
st: Outermost is the glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule).
Next is the cell wall.
Innermost is the plasma membrane.
ex.a: Glycocalyx → cell wall → plasma membrane

topics.rl: ICMR monitors antimicrobial resistance across Indian hospitals; resistance genes often spread between bacteria on plasmids.

rv.summary: Prokaryotes (bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma, PPLO) have naked circular genomic DNA in a nucleoid, often with plasmids. Except mycoplasma they have a three-layered envelope: glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule), cell wall and plasma membrane. Gram staining separates bacteria by envelope.
focus: Layers of the cell envelope and their roles
remember: Envelope: glycocalyx → cell wall → plasma membrane
Plasmids: small circular DNA; e.g. antibiotic resistance
Mycoplasma lack a cell wall
traps: Don't say the bacterial cell wall is semi-permeable; the plasma membrane is
Don't enclose bacterial DNA in a nuclear membrane

topics.t: Mesosomes, flagella, pili, ribosomes and inclusions
topics.h: A bacterial flagellum spins like a ship's propeller. It has a 'motor' (basal body), a 'joint' (hook) and a long 'blade' (filament).
p: Mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane (vesicles, tubules, lamellae). They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion, and increase membrane surface area and enzyme content. Cyanobacteria have pigment-containing chromatophores.
Motile bacteria have thin filamentous flagella extending from the cell wall. A bacterial flagellum has three parts: filament (longest, outside), hook and basal body.
Pili (elongated tubular structures of a special protein) and fimbriae (small bristle-like fibres) do not help in motility. Fimbriae help some bacteria attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are associated with the plasma membrane, about 15 nm by 20 nm, made of 50S and 30S subunits forming 70S ribosomes. Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a polyribosome (polysome).

Inclusion bodies store reserve material free in the cytoplasm without membranes: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules. Gas vacuoles occur in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

ex.q: Name the subunits of a prokaryotic ribosome and its total S value.
st: Prokaryotic ribosomes have a larger 50S and a smaller 30S subunit.
Together they form the 70S ribosome. (S values are not simply added; 50S + 30S gives 70S.)
ex.a: 50S and 30S subunits; 70S ribosome.

topics.rl: Pathogenic bacteria such as those causing cholera use fimbriae-like structures to cling to the gut lining; this is one reason why clean-water and hygiene drives in India focus on stopping infection before it starts.

rv.summary: Bacterial mesosomes are plasma membrane infoldings that aid wall formation, DNA replication, respiration and secretion. Flagella (filament, hook, basal body) give motility; pili and fimbriae do not. Ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S); inclusion bodies store reserves without membranes.
focus: Parts of a bacterial flagellum; pili and fimbriae
remember: Flagellum: filament, hook, basal body
70S ribosome = 50S + 30S
Inclusions: phosphate, cyanophycean, glycogen granules; gas vacuoles in some
traps: Don't add S values: 50S + 30S gives 70S, not 80S
Don't say pili and fimbriae help in motility

topics.t: Eukaryotic cells: plant cell versus animal cell
topics.h: An onion peel cell and a cheek cell are both eukaryotic, yet one has a wall and a big vacuole, and the other has centrioles. Spot the difference!
p: Eukaryotes include all protists, plants, animals and fungi. Their cytoplasm is extensively compartmentalised by membrane-bound organelles; they have an organised nucleus with a nuclear envelope, complex locomotory and cytoskeletal structures, and genetic material organised into chromosomes.
Plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole, which are absent in animal cells.
Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells.
Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic: no nuclear membrane vs true nucleus; no membrane-bound organelles vs many; 70S vs 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes; circular naked DNA vs linear DNA in chromosomes with proteins.

Key labels in diagrams: plant cell (cell wall, plasma membrane, chloroplast, large vacuole, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, ER); animal cell (plasma membrane, centrioles, lysosome, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, ER).

ex.q: A cell has a nuclear envelope, mitochondria, a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, but no centrioles. What is it?
st: Nuclear envelope and mitochondria: eukaryotic.
Cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole: plant cell.
No centrioles also fits a plant cell.
ex.a: A eukaryotic plant cell.

topics.rl: When school students in India first look at onion peel and cheek cells under the microscope, they see the cell wall and vacuole in the onion and their absence in the cheek cell.

rv.summary: Eukaryotes (protists, plants, animals, fungi) have a nuclear envelope, membrane-bound organelles and 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole; animal cells have centrioles.
focus: Plant cell vs animal cell differences
Labels in plant and animal cell diagrams
remember: Plant only: cell wall, plastids, large central vacuole
Animal only: centrioles
Prokaryotes 70S; eukaryotic cytoplasm 80S ribosomes
traps: Don't call fungi prokaryotes
Don't say only plant cells have mitochondria

topics.t: The cell membrane: structure and transport
topics.h: Your RBC membrane is about half protein and half fat, and the proteins drift around like boats on a lake. That's the fluid mosaic model.
p: The membrane is mainly lipids and proteins. Phospholipids form a bilayer with polar heads facing outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards; cholesterol is also present, along with carbohydrates.
The protein-lipid ratio varies; the human RBC membrane has about 52% protein and 40% lipids. Peripheral proteins lie on the surface; integral proteins are partly or totally buried in the membrane.

Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): the quasi-fluid lipid lets proteins move laterally. This fluidity is important for cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

Passive transport needs no energy: simple diffusion of neutral solutes from higher to lower concentration; osmosis is diffusion of water. Polar molecules need carrier proteins to cross the non-polar bilayer.
Active transport moves ions or molecules against the concentration gradient (low to high) using ATP, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

ex.q: In a human RBC membrane, protein is 52% and lipid 40%. What percentage is left for other components such as carbohydrates?
st: Total = 100%.
Protein + lipid = 52 + 40 = 92%.
Remaining = 100 - 92 = 8%.

topics.rl: ORS (oral rehydration solution), promoted in India for diarrhoea, works because glucose and sodium are carried into gut cells together by membrane transport proteins, pulling water in by osmosis.
