rv.summary: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer (polar heads out, tails in) with cholesterol, proteins and carbohydrates. In the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) proteins move laterally. Transport is passive (diffusion, osmosis) or active against the gradient using ATP.
focus: Fluid mosaic model and importance of fluidity
remember: Fluid mosaic model: Singer and Nicolson, 1972
Human RBC membrane: ~52% protein, ~40% lipid
Active transport uses ATP against gradient, e.g. Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Osmosis = diffusion of water
traps: Don't say membrane proteins are fixed
Don't call active transport energy-free

topics.t: The cell wall
topics.h: Your cotton T-shirt is made of almost pure plant cell wall material: cellulose. Cell walls literally clothe India.
p: The cell wall is a non-living rigid outer covering of the plasma membrane in fungi and plants. It gives shape, protects from mechanical damage and infection, helps cell-to-cell interaction and blocks undesirable macromolecules.
Algal cell walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals such as calcium carbonate. In other plants, the wall has cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins.
The primary wall of a young plant cell can grow; this capacity diminishes as the cell matures, and a secondary wall is laid on the inner side (towards the membrane).
The middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, glues neighbouring cells together.
Plasmodesmata traverse the cell wall and middle lamella and connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

ex.q: Place these in order from the plasma membrane of one cell to the plasma membrane of its neighbour: middle lamella, primary wall, secondary wall.
st: The secondary wall is laid on the inner side, next to the membrane.
Outside it is the primary wall.
The middle lamella glues the two cells.
Then the neighbour's primary wall and secondary wall.
ex.a: Membrane → secondary wall → primary wall → middle lamella → primary wall → secondary wall → membrane

topics.rl: India is one of the world's largest cotton producers; each cotton fibre is a single plant cell whose wall is mostly cellulose.

rv.summary: The cell wall is a non-living rigid covering in plants and fungi that gives shape and protection. Young cells have a growing primary wall; mature cells add a secondary wall inside it. The middle lamella (calcium pectate) glues cells, and plasmodesmata connect them.
focus: Composition of algal and plant walls
Primary wall, secondary wall and middle lamella
remember: Middle lamella: mainly calcium pectate
Secondary wall forms inside the primary wall, towards the membrane
Plasmodesmata connect cytoplasm of neighbouring cells
traps: Don't say the secondary wall forms outside the primary wall
Don't make the middle lamella of cellulose

topics.t: Endomembrane system: ER and Golgi apparatus
topics.h: Insulin made in your pancreas is built on the rough ER, polished in the Golgi and shipped out in vesicles, like a factory with a packing department.
p: The endomembrane system includes the ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, whose functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of it.

The ER is a network of tubules dividing the cell into luminal (inside ER) and extra-luminal (cytoplasm) compartments. Rough ER (RER) has ribosomes, is common in cells making and secreting proteins, and is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane.
Smooth ER (SER) lacks ribosomes and is the major site of lipid synthesis; in animal cells, steroidal hormones are made in the SER.
Golgi apparatus (Camillo Golgi, 1898): stacks of flat disc-shaped cisternae (0.5 to 1.0 µm across) near the nucleus, with a convex cis (forming) face and a concave trans (maturing) face.

Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face and move to the trans face. The Golgi packages materials for targets inside the cell or for secretion, modifies proteins, and is an important site for forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

ex.q: Trace a secretory protein from synthesis to release.
st: Ribosomes on the RER make the protein.
It is carried in vesicles to the cis face of the Golgi.
It is modified in the cisternae and moves to the trans face.
It is packaged into vesicles and secreted.
ex.a: RER → vesicle → cis Golgi → trans Golgi → secretory vesicle → outside

topics.rl: Cells of the adrenal gland make steroid hormones like cortisol in smooth ER; Indian biotech firms producing insulin harness the same RER-Golgi route in engineered cells.

rv.summary: The endomembrane system (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles) works as a coordinated unit. RER with ribosomes makes proteins; SER makes lipids and steroids. The Golgi (cis forming face, trans maturing face) receives ER vesicles, modifies, packages and forms glycoproteins and glycolipids.
focus: Which organelles belong to the endomembrane system
remember: Not endomembrane: mitochondria, chloroplasts, peroxisomes
SER: lipids, steroidal hormones
Golgi: Camillo Golgi 1898; cis = convex forming, trans = concave maturing
RER → vesicle → cis Golgi → trans Golgi → secretion
traps: Don't include mitochondria in the endomembrane system
Don't swap cis and trans faces

topics.t: Lysosomes, vacuoles and microbodies
topics.h: Amoeba lives in fresh water that keeps flooding in. It survives by pumping water out with a contractile vacuole, like bailing a leaking boat.
p: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles formed by packaging in the Golgi. They are rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that are optimally active at acidic pH and can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

A vacuole is a membrane-bound space containing water, sap, excretory products and materials not useful to the cell. Its single membrane is the tonoplast. In plant cells, vacuoles can occupy up to 90% of cell volume.
In plants the tonoplast moves ions and other materials into the vacuole against their concentration gradients, so their concentration in the vacuole is much higher than in the cytoplasm.
In Amoeba, the contractile vacuole is important for osmoregulation and excretion. In many protists, food vacuoles form by engulfing food particles.
Microbodies are many minute membrane-bound vesicles containing various enzymes, found in both plant and animal cells.

ex.q: Why do lysosomal enzymes not digest the cytoplasm under normal conditions?
st: Lysosomal enzymes are enclosed by a membrane.
They work best at acidic pH, which is maintained inside the lysosome, not in the cytoplasm.
ex.a: They are kept inside a membrane and work best at acidic pH.

topics.rl: Rare inherited conditions called lysosomal storage disorders, such as Gaucher disease, occur when one lysosomal enzyme is missing, so undigested material piles up inside cells.

rv.summary: Lysosomes are Golgi-formed vesicles of hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH that digest all major biomolecules. Vacuoles, bounded by the tonoplast, can fill up to 90% of a plant cell and concentrate ions. Contractile and food vacuoles occur in protists; microbodies are enzyme-filled vesicles.
focus: Contractile and food vacuoles in protists
remember: Lysosomal enzymes: optimally active at acidic pH
Tonoplast = vacuole membrane; plant vacuole up to 90% of volume
Contractile vacuole (Amoeba): osmoregulation and excretion
traps: Don't say lysosomal enzymes work at alkaline pH
Don't say the tonoplast moves ions only along the gradient

topics.t: Mitochondria and plastids
topics.h: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own DNA and ribosomes, almost like tiny tenants with their own furniture inside your cells.
p: Mitochondria: usually sausage-shaped or cylindrical, about 0.2 to 1.0 µm wide (average 0.5 µm) and 1.0 to 4.1 µm long; number depends on activity. Double membrane: the outer is a continuous boundary; the inner folds into cristae that increase surface area, enclosing the matrix.

Mitochondria are sites of aerobic respiration and make ATP, so they are the 'power houses' of the cell. The matrix has a single circular DNA, a few RNAs, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis. Mitochondria divide by fission.

Plastids occur in all plant cells and in euglenoids. Chloroplasts have chlorophyll and carotenoids for photosynthesis. Chromoplasts have fat-soluble carotenoids (carotene, xanthophylls) giving yellow, orange or red colours. Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts (starch, e.g. potato), elaioplasts (oils and fats), aleuroplasts (proteins).

Chloroplasts are found mostly in leaf mesophyll; they are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5 to 10 µm long and 2 to 4 µm wide. Numbers range from 1 per cell in Chlamydomonas to 20 to 40 per mesophyll cell.

Chloroplast: double membrane (inner less permeable); stroma inside; flattened sacs called thylakoids stacked as grana; stroma lamellae connect grana; thylakoids enclose a lumen and carry chlorophyll. The stroma has enzymes for making carbohydrates and proteins, double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.

ex.q: Which plastid stores starch in a potato tuber, and which colours a ripe tomato red?
st: Starch-storing colourless plastids are amyloplasts, a type of leucoplast.
Red, orange and yellow colours come from carotenoids in chromoplasts.
ex.a: Amyloplasts in potato; chromoplasts in tomato.

topics.rl: The red of Kashmiri chillies and the orange of carrots in winter come from carotenoids stored in chromoplasts.

rv.summary: Mitochondria are double-membraned power houses with cristae and a matrix holding circular DNA and 70S ribosomes; they divide by fission. Plastids are chloroplasts, chromoplasts or leucoplasts; chloroplasts have thylakoids stacked as grana in the stroma, with their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.
focus: Types of plastids and what each stores
Why mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes
remember: Cristae: infoldings of inner mitochondrial membrane
Amyloplasts: starch; elaioplasts: oils, fats; aleuroplasts: proteins
Thylakoids stacked into grana; chlorophyll in thylakoids
Mitochondria and chloroplasts: circular DNA, 70S ribosomes
traps: Don't give mitochondria 80S ribosomes
Don't confuse cristae (mitochondria) with grana (chloroplasts)

topics.t: Ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella and centrioles
topics.h: Cilia lining your windpipe beat like oars hundreds of times a minute to sweep out dust from Delhi's winter smog.
p: Ribosomes were first observed by George Palade (1953). They are made of RNA and proteins, not surrounded by a membrane. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S); prokaryotic are 70S (50S + 30S). S (Svedberg unit) is the sedimentation coefficient, an indirect measure of density and size.
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments) for mechanical support, motility and maintaining cell shape.

Cilia are small and work like oars to move the cell or surrounding fluid; flagella are longer and move the cell. Their core, the axoneme, has nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a central pair: the 9+2 array. A central sheath joins each peripheral doublet by a radial spoke (nine spokes); doublets are joined by linkers. Both arise from basal bodies. Bacterial flagella are structurally different.

The centrosome usually has two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation of nine evenly spaced peripheral triplet fibrils of tubulin; the central proteinaceous hub is joined to the triplets by radial spokes.
Centrioles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella, and the spindle fibres that make the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.

ex.q: How many microtubules are there in the axoneme of a cilium with the 9+2 arrangement?
st: Nine peripheral doublets = 9 × 2 = 18 microtubules.
Central pair = 2 microtubules.
ex.a: 20 microtubules

topics.rl: Sperm motility tests at IVF clinics in Indian cities check how well the sperm flagellum, with its 9+2 axoneme, can beat.

rv.summary: Ribosomes (Palade, 1953) are RNA–protein particles: 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes, 70S (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes. The cytoskeleton gives support, motility and shape. Cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme from basal bodies; centrioles have nine triplets and form spindle fibres.
focus: Ribosome subunits and the S unit
remember: S = Svedberg unit (sedimentation coefficient)
Axoneme: 9 doublets + central pair (9+2) = 20 microtubules
Centriole: 9 triplets of tubulin, cartwheel
traps: Don't give centrioles a 9+2 arrangement; they have 9 triplets
Don't treat S values as simply additive

topics.t: The nucleus and chromosomes
topics.h: Each of your cells packs about two metres of DNA into a nucleus a few micrometres wide. That's like stuffing about 20 km of thread into a tennis ball.
p: The nucleus was first described by Robert Brown (1831); Flemming named its stainable material chromatin. The interphase nucleus has chromatin, a nuclear matrix (nucleoplasm) and one or more nucleoli.

The nuclear envelope has two parallel membranes with a perinuclear space (10 to 50 nm). The outer membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. Nuclear pores let RNA and proteins move both ways. Mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.

The nucleolus is a spherical, non-membrane-bound body, the site of active rRNA synthesis; it is larger and more numerous in cells actively making proteins. Chromatin has DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA. A human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 (23 pairs) chromosomes.

Each chromosome has a primary constriction, the centromere, with disc-shaped kinetochores on its sides. By centromere position: metacentric (middle, equal arms), sub-metacentric (slightly away from middle, one shorter and one longer arm), acrocentric (close to the end, one very short and one very long arm), telocentric (terminal).
Some chromosomes have a non-staining secondary constriction at a constant location, giving a small fragment called a satellite.

ex.q: A chromosome has arms of 2 µm and 8 µm. Where is the centromere and how would you classify it?
st: The arms are very unequal: one very short, one very long.
So the centromere is close to one end.
This is an acrocentric chromosome.
ex.a: Acrocentric (centromere near one end).

topics.rl: Karyotyping labs at AIIMS and other genetic centres look at centromere position and satellites to identify each human chromosome and diagnose disorders.

rv.summary: The nucleus (Robert Brown) has chromatin, nucleoplasm, nucleoli and a double nuclear envelope with pores; the outer membrane is continuous with the ER. Chromosomes have a centromere with kinetochores and are metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric or telocentric.
focus: Classification of chromosomes by centromere position
remember: Nucleolus: site of rRNA synthesis
Perinuclear space: 10–50 nm
Metacentric: middle; sub-metacentric: slightly off-middle; acrocentric: near end; telocentric: at end
Enucleate: mature mammalian RBCs, sieve tube cells
traps: Don't call the nucleolus membrane-bound
Don't confuse acrocentric (near end) with telocentric (at end)

topics.t: How do we analyse the chemicals in living tissue?
topics.h: Carbon is a tiny 0.03% of the Earth's crust, but about 18.5% of your body. Life is a carbon-hungry chemist.
p: Grind a living tissue in trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) with a mortar and pestle to get a slurry. Strain it through cheesecloth or cotton to get two fractions: the filtrate (acid-soluble pool) and the retentate (acid-insoluble fraction).
Analytical techniques applied to separated compounds give their molecular formula and probable structure. All carbon compounds obtained from living tissues are called biomolecules.

Ash analysis: weigh the tissue (wet weight), dry it to remove water (dry weight), then burn it completely. Carbon compounds are oxidised to gases (CO₂, water vapour) and removed; the remaining ash contains inorganic elements such as calcium and magnesium.
Inorganic compounds such as sulphate and phosphate are also seen in the acid-soluble fraction.

Living matter is far richer in carbon (18.5% vs 0.03%), hydrogen (0.5% vs 0.14%), oxygen (65.0% vs 46.6%) and nitrogen (3.3% vs very little) than the Earth's crust, but much poorer in silicon (negligible vs 27.7%).

ex.q: Order the steps of ash analysis.
st: Weigh the fresh tissue: wet weight.
Dry it to evaporate water: dry weight.
Burn it completely: carbon compounds leave as CO₂ and water vapour.
Weigh and analyse the remaining ash for inorganic elements.
ex.a: Wet weight → dry weight → burning → ash with inorganic elements

topics.rl: Food testing labs under FSSAI measure ash content in spices and flours to check for adulteration with sand or chalk.

rv.summary: To analyse living tissue, grind it in trichloroacetic acid and strain it into an acid-soluble filtrate and an acid-insoluble retentate. Burning tissue removes carbon compounds as gases, leaving ash of inorganic elements. Living matter is richer in C, H, O and N than the Earth's crust.
focus: Steps of chemical analysis with trichloroacetic acid
Elemental composition of living matter vs Earth's crust
remember: Filtrate = acid-soluble pool; retentate = acid-insoluble fraction
Biomolecules = all carbon compounds from living tissues
Carbon: 18.5% body vs 0.03% crust; silicon: negligible body vs 27.7% crust
traps: Don't say carbon compounds stay in the ash; they leave as gases
Don't swap filtrate and retentate

topics.t: Amino acids, sugars and nucleotides: the small building blocks
topics.h: Only 20 kinds of amino acids build every protein in your body, from hair keratin to the enzymes in your saliva.
p: Amino acids have an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, the α-carbon; they are substituted methanes with four groups: hydrogen, carboxyl, amino and a variable R group. Twenty types occur in proteins.

R group: hydrogen in glycine, methyl in alanine, hydroxymethyl in serine. Amino acids may be acidic (glutamic acid), basic (lysine) or neutral (valine); aromatic ones are tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan.
The –NH₂ and –COOH groups ionise, so the structure of an amino acid changes with pH; at a particular pH it exists as a zwitterion carrying both a positive and a negative charge.
Simple sugars (monosaccharides) such as glucose and ribose are carbohydrate units.

Nitrogen bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine. Base + sugar = nucleoside (adenosine, guanosine, thymidine, uridine, cytidine). Base + sugar + phosphate = nucleotide (adenylic, guanylic, thymidylic, uridylic, cytidylic acids).

ex.q: Adenine is joined to a sugar, and a phosphate is then esterified to the sugar. Name the compound at each stage.
st: Adenine + sugar = nucleoside: adenosine.
Adding a phosphate gives a nucleotide: adenylic acid.
ex.a: Adenosine (nucleoside), then adenylic acid (nucleotide).

topics.rl: Dal and paneer in an Indian thali are rich sources of amino acids, the building blocks your body uses to make its own proteins.

rv.summary: Amino acids are substituted methanes with H, –COOH, –NH₂ and an R group on the α-carbon; 20 types occur in proteins and they ionise with pH. Sugars like glucose and ribose are carbohydrate units. Base + sugar = nucleoside; + phosphate = nucleotide.
focus: Structure of an amino acid and R groups
Acidic, basic, neutral and aromatic amino acids
remember: Glycine R = H; alanine = methyl; serine = hydroxymethyl
Acidic: glutamic acid; basic: lysine; neutral: valine; aromatic: tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan
Nucleoside = base + sugar (adenosine); nucleotide = + phosphate (adenylic acid)
traps: Don't call adenosine a nucleotide; it is a nucleoside
Don't call glutamic acid basic

topics.t: Lipids: fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids
topics.h: Why does coconut oil turn solid on a cold Delhi winter morning, but gingelly (til) oil stays liquid? Melting points tell the story.
p: Lipids are generally water-insoluble. A fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group, which may be methyl, ethyl or a chain of –CH₂ groups (1 to 19 carbons).
Palmitic acid has 16 carbons and arachidonic acid has 20 carbons, including the carboxyl carbon. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bond; unsaturated ones have one or more.

Glycerol is trihydroxy propane. Fatty acids esterified with glycerol give monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides. These are called fats or oils by melting point; oils (e.g. gingelly oil) have lower melting points and stay liquid in winter.
Phospholipids contain phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound; they are found in cell membranes, e.g. lecithin. Neural tissues have more complex lipids.
Lipids are small (below 800 Da) and are not true macromolecules. They appear in the acid-insoluble fraction because grinding breaks membranes into water-insoluble vesicles.

ex.q: How many fatty acid molecules are esterified to one glycerol in a triglyceride?
st: Glycerol has three –OH groups.
In a triglyceride, all three are esterified with fatty acids.

topics.rl: India's National Institute of Nutrition advises using a mix of oils because different oils provide different proportions of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.

rv.summary: Lipids are water-insoluble. Fatty acids have a –COOH on an R chain (palmitic 16 C, arachidonic 20 C) and are saturated or unsaturated. Glycerol (trihydroxy propane) with fatty acids gives glycerides (fats or oils). Phospholipids like lecithin are in membranes. Lipids are below 800 Da.
focus: Structure of fatty acids, saturated vs unsaturated
Why lipids appear in the acid-insoluble fraction
remember: Palmitic acid 16 C; arachidonic acid 20 C
Glycerol = trihydroxy propane
Lecithin is a phospholipid
Lipids < 800 Da, not true macromolecules
traps: Don't call lipids true macromolecules
Don't say oils have higher melting points than fats

topics.t: Primary and secondary metabolites
topics.h: The yellow of haldi, the bitterness of neem and the latex of rubber trees in Kerala are all 'extra' chemicals that plants did not need just to stay alive.
p: Primary metabolites, such as amino acids and sugars, have identifiable functions and known roles in normal physiological processes.
Secondary metabolites are found in plants, fungi and microbes. We do not yet understand the role of all of them in their hosts, but many are useful to humans and some have ecological importance.
Pigments: carotenoids, anthocyanins. Alkaloids: morphine, codeine. Terpenoids: monoterpenes, diterpenes. Essential oils: lemon grass oil.
Toxins: abrin, ricin. Lectins: concanavalin A. Drugs: vinblastine, curcumin. Polymeric substances: rubber, gums, cellulose.
Human uses include rubber, drugs, spices, scents and pigments.

ex.q: Classify curcumin and ricin as secondary metabolites.
st: Curcumin from turmeric is used as a drug: drug category.
Ricin from castor is poisonous: toxin category.
ex.a: Curcumin is a drug; ricin is a toxin.

topics.rl: Kerala's rubber plantations, Assam's lemon grass and the turmeric of Erode in Tamil Nadu all trade in secondary metabolites.

rv.summary: Primary metabolites (amino acids, sugars) have known roles in normal physiology. Secondary metabolites in plants, fungi and microbes include pigments, alkaloids, terpenoids, essential oils, toxins, lectins, drugs and polymers; many are useful to humans.
focus: Categories of secondary metabolites with examples
remember: Pigments: carotenoids, anthocyanins; alkaloids: morphine, codeine
Terpenoids: monoterpenes, diterpenes; essential oil: lemon grass oil
Toxins: abrin, ricin; lectin: concanavalin A; drugs: vinblastine, curcumin
Polymers: rubber, gums, cellulose
traps: Don't call amino acids secondary metabolites
Don't call concanavalin A a toxin; it is a lectin

topics.t: Biomacromolecules and the composition of a cell
topics.h: If you dried out a typical cell, most of what's left would be protein. But first, you'd have to remove a lot of water.
p: The acid-soluble pool contains molecules with molecular weights from about 18 to around 800 daltons (Da).

The acid-insoluble fraction contains four types of organic compounds: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. Except lipids, they have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
Biomolecules are micromolecules (molecular weight below 1000 Da) or macromolecules (biomacromolecules). Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are true macromolecules.
Average composition of cells: water 70 to 90%, proteins 10 to 15%, nucleic acids 5 to 7%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2%, ions 1%.
So water is the most abundant chemical in living organisms, followed by proteins.

ex.q: Which is the second most abundant component of a cell after water?
st: Water is 70 to 90%.
Proteins are 10 to 15%, higher than nucleic acids (5 to 7%), carbohydrates (3%) and lipids (2%).
ex.a: Proteins

topics.rl: The water in your body is why doctors in Indian hospitals watch for dehydration so closely during summer heat waves.

rv.summary: The acid-soluble pool holds molecules of about 18 to 800 Da; the acid-insoluble fraction holds proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides (≥10,000 Da) and lipids. A cell is on average 70–90% water, 10–15% protein, 5–7% nucleic acids, 3% carbohydrate, 2% lipid, 1% ions.
focus: Contents of acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions
Average chemical composition of a cell
remember: Acid-soluble: ~18 to 800 Da
Macromolecules: ≥10,000 Da; micromolecules: <1000 Da
Water 70–90%, proteins 10–15%, nucleic acids 5–7%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2%, ions 1%
traps: Don't put proteins or nucleic acids in the acid-soluble pool
Don't count lipids as true macromolecules

topics.t: Proteins: heteropolymers with many jobs
topics.h: The most abundant protein on the whole planet is not in animals at all. It sits in every green leaf, fixing CO₂.
p: Proteins are polypeptides: linear chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
With 20 types of amino acids, a protein is a heteropolymer, not a homopolymer (which repeats a single type of monomer).
Essential amino acids must come from the diet; non-essential amino acids can be made by the body.

Functions: collagen (intercellular ground substance), trypsin (enzyme), insulin (hormone), antibody (fights infectious agents), receptor (sensory reception: smell, taste, hormone), GLUT-4 (glucose transport into cells). Some proteins transport nutrients across membranes.
Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world; RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.

ex.q: Why is a protein called a heteropolymer while cellulose is a homopolymer?
st: A protein is built from up to 20 different amino acids.
Cellulose is built from only one monomer, glucose.
ex.a: Protein has many kinds of monomers; cellulose has only glucose.

topics.rl: Pulses (dal) and milk are important in Indian diets partly because they supply essential amino acids the body cannot make.

rv.summary: Proteins are polypeptides of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; with 20 kinds of monomers they are heteropolymers. They act as structural material, enzymes, hormones, antibodies, receptors and transporters. Collagen is the commonest animal protein, RuBisCO the commonest in the biosphere.
remember: Collagen: most abundant in animals; RuBisCO: most abundant in biosphere
Trypsin: enzyme; insulin: hormone; GLUT-4: glucose transport
Essential amino acids must come from diet
traps: Don't call RuBisCO the most abundant animal protein
Don't call proteins homopolymers

topics.t: Polysaccharides
topics.h: Drop iodine on a slice of potato and it turns blue-black. Drop it on cotton wool and nothing happens. Both are chains of glucose. Why the difference?
p: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugars (monosaccharides) as building blocks.
Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose. Starch (plant energy store) and glycogen (animal store) are other variants; inulin is a polymer of fructose.
In a chain such as glycogen, the right end is the reducing end and the left end the non-reducing end; glycogen is branched.
Starch forms helical secondary structures that can hold I₂ molecules, giving a blue colour. Cellulose has no complex helices, cannot hold iodine and gives no colour.

Plant cell walls are made of cellulose; paper and cotton fibre are cellulosic. Complex polysaccharides with amino sugars and modified sugars (e.g. glucosamine, N-acetyl galactosamine) include chitin in arthropod exoskeletons.

ex.q: Why does iodine solution turn blue with starch but not with cellulose?
st: Starch forms helices that can hold iodine molecules; starch-I₂ is blue.
Cellulose lacks complex helices and cannot hold iodine.
ex.a: Only starch's helices trap iodine to form a blue complex.

topics.rl: School and FSSAI-style kitchen tests use iodine to detect starch added as an adulterant to milk or paneer: a blue colour gives it away.

rv.summary: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugars. Cellulose (plant walls, paper, cotton), starch (plant store) and glycogen (animal store) are glucose polymers; inulin is a fructose polymer. Starch helices hold iodine and turn blue; cellulose does not. Chitin contains amino sugars.
focus: Monomers of cellulose, starch, glycogen and inulin
remember: Cellulose: homopolymer of glucose; inulin: fructose polymer
Glycogen: animal store, branched; starch: plant store
Starch + I₂ = blue; cellulose gives no colour
Right end reducing, left end non-reducing
traps: Don't call starch a fructose polymer
Don't expect cellulose to turn blue with iodine

topics.t: Nucleic acids
topics.h: Your entire genetic instruction book is written with just four letters, A, T, G and C, strung on a sugar-phosphate thread.
p: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polynucleotides. With polysaccharides and polypeptides, they form the true macromolecular fraction of tissues.
A nucleotide has three chemically distinct parts: a heterocyclic nitrogen base, a monosaccharide (pentose sugar) and phosphoric acid (phosphate).
Bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine. Adenine and guanine are substituted purines; cytosine, uracil and thymine are substituted pyrimidines.
The sugar is ribose in RNA and 2'-deoxyribose in DNA.
Thymine occurs in DNA and uracil in RNA; adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both.

ex.q: Which of these bases are purines: adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine, uracil?
st: Purines have the purine double-ring skeleton.
Adenine and guanine are substituted purines; the rest are pyrimidines.
ex.a: Adenine and guanine.

topics.rl: DNA fingerprinting labs, such as the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics in Hyderabad, read the sequence of these bases to identify people.

rv.summary: Nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) are polynucleotides. Each nucleotide has a nitrogen base, a pentose sugar and phosphate. Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, uracil and thymine are pyrimidines. DNA has deoxyribose and thymine; RNA has ribose and uracil.
focus: Differences between DNA and RNA in sugar and base
remember: Purines: A, G; pyrimidines: C, T, U
DNA: 2'-deoxyribose, thymine; RNA: ribose, uracil
Five bases in all
traps: Don't call cytosine a purine
Don't put uracil in DNA

topics.t: Structure of proteins: four levels
topics.h: A protein is like a phone charger cable: first a sequence of wires, then twisted, then coiled into a ball, and sometimes several bundled together.
p: Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids, i.e. the positional information. The first amino acid is the N-terminal amino acid; the last is the C-terminal amino acid.
Secondary structure: the chain is not a rigid rod; some portions fold into a helix (only right-handed helices occur in proteins), and other regions fold into other forms.
Tertiary structure: the long chain folds upon itself like a hollow woollen ball, giving a 3-D shape. It is absolutely necessary for many biological activities of proteins.
Quaternary structure: the arrangement of two or more folded polypeptides (subunits) with respect to each other.
Adult human haemoglobin has 4 subunits: two α and two β.

ex.q: Which structural level is shown by haemoglobin but not by a single-chain protein?
st: A single chain can have primary, secondary and tertiary structure.
Haemoglobin has four subunits (2 α + 2 β) arranged together.
Arrangement of subunits is quaternary structure.
ex.a: Quaternary structure.

topics.rl: Thalassaemia, common in parts of India, is linked to defects in the α or β chains of haemoglobin, a protein with quaternary structure.

rv.summary: Proteins have four levels of structure: primary (amino acid sequence, N- to C-terminal), secondary (right-handed helices and other folds), tertiary (3-D folding like a woollen ball, needed for activity) and quaternary (arrangement of subunits, e.g. haemoglobin's 2 α + 2 β).
remember: Primary = sequence; secondary = helices; tertiary = 3-D fold; quaternary = subunit arrangement
Only right-handed helices in proteins
Adult Hb: 2 α + 2 β
traps: Don't say proteins have left-handed helices
Don't give a single-chain protein quaternary structure

topics.t: Enzymes and the speed of chemical reactions
topics.h: Without an enzyme, about 200 molecules of carbonic acid form in an hour. With carbonic anhydrase, about 600,000 form every second.
p: Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids act as enzymes, called ribozymes. In the tertiary structure, a crevice or pocket called the active site holds the substrate.

Inorganic catalysts work well at high temperature and pressure, but enzymes are damaged at high temperatures (say above 40°C). Enzymes from thermophilic organisms in hot vents and sulphur springs stay stable even at 80 to 90°C.
A physical change alters shape or state without breaking bonds (ice melting). A chemical reaction breaks and forms bonds, e.g. Ba(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2H₂O, or hydrolysis of starch to glucose.
Rate of reaction = amount of product formed per unit time. As a rule of thumb, the rate doubles or halves for every 10°C change. Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ about 10 million times.

A metabolic pathway is a series of enzyme-catalysed steps. Glucose becomes pyruvic acid through ten enzyme-catalysed reactions; in skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions lactic acid forms, and in yeast during fermentation ethanol forms.

ex.q: A reaction at 25°C gives 100 units of product per minute. Using the 10°C rule of thumb, estimate the rate at 35°C.
st: A 10°C rise roughly doubles the rate.
100 × 2 = 200 units per minute.
ex.a: About 200 units per minute

topics.rl: Enzymes from heat-loving microbes are used in PCR machines in Indian diagnostic labs, which cycle up to about 95°C to test for infections.

rv.summary: Almost all enzymes are proteins (some RNAs are ribozymes) with an active site. Enzymes are damaged by high heat, except those of thermophiles. Rate of reaction is product per unit time and roughly doubles per 10°C. Metabolic pathways are chains of enzyme steps, e.g. glucose to pyruvate.
focus: Rate of reaction and the 10°C rule
remember: Ribozymes: nucleic acids acting as enzymes
Rate doubles or halves for each 10°C change (rule of thumb)
Carbonic anhydrase: ~10 million-fold speed-up
Glucose → pyruvate (10 steps) → lactic acid (muscle) or ethanol (yeast)
traps: Don't call ice melting a chemical reaction
Don't say yeast makes lactic acid in fermentation

topics.t: How enzymes work: ES complex, activation energy and the catalytic cycle
topics.h: Rolling a heavy boulder over a hill takes a big push even if the other side is downhill. Enzymes dig a tunnel through that hill.
p: The substrate (S) binds the enzyme's active site to form a short-lived enzyme-substrate complex (ES), which is essential for catalysis: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P.
The substrate is converted to product through an unstable, high-energy transition state.

If the product is at a lower energy level than the substrate, the reaction is exothermic and needs no heating; if higher, it is endothermic. Either way, the substrate must pass through the transition state.
Activation energy is the difference in energy between the substrate and the transition state. Enzymes lower this energy barrier, making S → P easier.

Catalytic cycle: (i) substrate binds the active site; (ii) binding induces the enzyme to change shape and fit more tightly (induced fit); (iii) the active site breaks bonds of the substrate and an enzyme-product complex forms; (iv) products are released, and the free enzyme is ready for another substrate.

ex.q: In an energy diagram, the substrate is at 40 units, the transition state without enzyme at 100 units and with enzyme at 70 units. Find the activation energy with and without the enzyme.
st: Without enzyme: 100 - 40 = 60 units.
With enzyme: 70 - 40 = 30 units.
The enzyme halves the barrier here.
ex.a: Without enzyme 60 units; with enzyme 30 units.

topics.rl: Biological washing powders sold in India contain enzymes that lower activation energy so stains break down in cold water, saving electricity.

rv.summary: An enzyme binds its substrate at the active site to form a short-lived ES complex; the substrate passes through a high-energy transition state to product: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P. Enzymes lower the activation energy and are released unchanged after each catalytic cycle.
focus: ES complex and the reaction sequence
Steps of the catalytic cycle and induced fit
remember: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P
Activation energy = transition state − substrate energy
Induced fit: enzyme changes shape to fit substrate tightly
traps: Don't say enzymes raise or supply energy; they lower the barrier
Don't say enzymes are used up

topics.t: Factors affecting enzyme activity and inhibition
topics.h: Why do we keep curd in the fridge and boil milk to stop it spoiling? Temperature controls enzymes.
p: Enzymes work in a narrow range of temperature and pH. Each has an optimum temperature and optimum pH where activity is highest; activity falls above and below the optimum.
Low temperature keeps an enzyme temporarily inactive; high temperature destroys activity because the protein is denatured by heat.
As substrate concentration rises, the reaction velocity first rises and then reaches a maximum, Vmax, which is not exceeded by adding more substrate, because all enzyme molecules are saturated.

A chemical that binds an enzyme and shuts off its activity is an inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor closely resembles the substrate and competes for the substrate-binding site, so the substrate cannot bind.
Example: malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it resembles succinate. Competitive inhibitors are often used to control bacterial pathogens.

ex.q: An enzyme gives a velocity of 50 units at 2 mM substrate, 80 at 4 mM, 100 at 8 mM and 100 at 16 mM. What is Vmax and why does the curve level off?
st: Velocity stops rising at 100 units.
All enzyme molecules are busy (saturated); extra substrate finds no free enzyme.
ex.a: Vmax = 100 units; the enzyme is saturated.

topics.rl: Many antibiotics used in Indian hospitals work as enzyme inhibitors in bacteria; for example, sulpha drugs compete with a substrate bacteria need to make folic acid.

rv.summary: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; low temperature inactivates it temporarily and high temperature denatures it. Velocity rises with substrate concentration to Vmax when enzymes are saturated. Competitive inhibitors like malonate resemble the substrate and block the active site.
focus: Competitive inhibition and the malonate example
remember: High temperature denatures; low temperature temporarily inactivates
Vmax: velocity cannot exceed it once enzymes are saturated
Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase (resembles succinate)
traps: Don't say cold permanently destroys enzymes
Don't say adding more substrate raises velocity beyond Vmax

topics.t: Classification of enzymes and co-factors
topics.h: Some enzymes can't work alone. They need a 'sidekick' such as zinc, haem or a vitamin-derived NAD.
p: Six classes: oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases (oxidation-reduction between two substrates), transferases (transfer of a group other than hydrogen, S–G + S' → S + S'–G), hydrolases (hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds).

Lyases remove groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds. Isomerases interconvert optical, geometric or positional isomers. Ligases link two compounds, joining C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds and so on.
Many enzymes need non-protein co-factors to be active; the protein part is the apoenzyme. Removing the co-factor destroys catalytic activity.

Prosthetic groups are organic and tightly bound, e.g. haem in peroxidase and catalase (which break down H₂O₂ into water and oxygen). Co-enzymes are organic but bind only transiently and serve many enzymes; many contain vitamins, e.g. NAD and NADP contain niacin.
Metal ions form coordination bonds with the active site and substrate, e.g. zinc for carboxypeptidase.

ex.q: An enzyme joins two molecules to form a C–N bond using energy. Which class is it?
st: Joining two compounds by forming a bond is ligation.
So the enzyme is a ligase.
ex.a: Ligase

topics.rl: Niacin (vitamin B3), present in groundnuts and whole grains common in Indian diets, is needed to make the co-enzymes NAD and NADP.

rv.summary: Enzymes form six classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases. Many need co-factors: prosthetic groups (tightly bound, e.g. haem), coenzymes (transient, often vitamin-based, e.g. NAD with niacin) and metal ions (e.g. zinc in carboxypeptidase).
focus: What each of the six enzyme classes does
Prosthetic groups vs coenzymes vs metal ions
remember: Transferase: S–G + S' → S + S'–G; lyase: removes groups leaving double bonds; ligase: joins two compounds
Haem: prosthetic group of peroxidase and catalase
NAD, NADP contain niacin; zinc for carboxypeptidase
traps: Don't call haem a coenzyme; it is a prosthetic group
Don't confuse lyases (remove groups) with ligases (join compounds)

topics.t: The cell cycle and its two phases
topics.h: A human cell in culture takes about 24 hours to divide, but spends only about one hour actually dividing. What is it doing the other 23?
p: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and finally divides into two daughter cells. Cell growth is continuous, but DNA synthesis occurs in only one specific stage.
Human cells in culture divide about once every 24 hours; yeast can complete a cycle in only about 90 minutes. Duration varies between organisms and cell types.
Two basic phases: interphase (between two M phases) and M phase (mitosis phase, when actual division occurs). In a 24-hour human cycle, M phase lasts only about an hour.
M phase starts with nuclear division (karyokinesis, separation of daughter chromosomes) and usually ends with division of cytoplasm (cytokinesis).
Interphase, often called the resting phase, takes more than 95% of the cycle. It is not idle: the cell grows and replicates DNA in an orderly way. It has three sub-phases: G1, S and G2.

ex.q: In a 24-hour human cell cycle with M phase lasting 1 hour, what percentage of the cycle is interphase?
st: Interphase = 24 - 1 = 23 hours.
ex.a: About 95.8%, which is more than 95%

topics.rl: Cancer drugs used at the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai often target dividing cells in specific phases of the cell cycle.

rv.summary: The cell cycle is the series of events by which a cell duplicates its genome and divides into two. It has interphase (over 95% of the cycle; G1, S, G2) and a short M phase of karyokinesis and cytokinesis. A human cell cycle takes about 24 hours.
focus: The two phases of the cell cycle and their durations
Why interphase is not a resting phase
remember: Human cells ~24 h per cycle; yeast ~90 min; M phase ~1 h
Interphase > 95% of the cycle: G1, S, G2
DNA synthesis only in S phase
traps: Don't call interphase an inactive phase
Don't confuse karyokinesis (nucleus) with cytokinesis (cytoplasm)

topics.t: G1, S, G2 and G0: inside interphase
topics.h: Heart muscle cells mostly stop dividing in adults. They park in a special 'waiting room' of the cell cycle called G0.
p: G1 (Gap 1): between mitosis and the start of DNA replication. The cell is metabolically active and grows but does not replicate its DNA.

S phase (synthesis): DNA replicates and the DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C, but the chromosome number stays the same (2n stays 2n). In animal cells, DNA replication begins in the nucleus and the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
G2 (Gap 2): proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues.
Quiescent stage (G0): cells that stop dividing (e.g. heart cells) exit G1 into G0. They remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless needed.
In animals, mitosis occurs only in diploid somatic cells. Plants can show mitosis in both haploid and diploid cells.

ex.q: A diploid cell has 2n = 8 and DNA content 2C in G1. Give the chromosome number and DNA content after S phase.
st: S phase doubles DNA: 2C → 4C.
Each chromosome now has two chromatids, but the number of chromosomes is unchanged: 2n = 8.
ex.a: 8 chromosomes, 4C DNA

topics.rl: Liver cells usually sit in G0 but can re-enter the cycle after injury, which is why living-donor liver transplants at Indian hospitals work: the donated part regrows.

rv.summary: G1: the cell grows without replicating DNA. S: DNA doubles from 2C to 4C while chromosome number stays 2n, and centrioles duplicate. G2: proteins for mitosis are made. Non-dividing cells such as heart cells enter G0.
focus: Events in G1, S and G2
DNA content vs chromosome number through S phase
Mitosis in haploid and diploid cells
remember: S phase: 2C → 4C; chromosome number unchanged
Centriole duplicates in S phase
G0: metabolically active, not dividing (e.g. heart cells)
traps: Don't double the chromosome number in S phase; only DNA doubles
Don't say G0 cells are metabolically inactive

topics.t: Mitosis: prophase and metaphase
topics.h: Cytogenetics labs make karyotypes from cells stopped at metaphase, because chromosomes are then at their most compact and clearest.
p: M phase is also called equational division because parent and daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes. Mitosis is described in four stages of karyokinesis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), though it is a continuous process.

Prophase: chromatin condenses into compact mitotic chromosomes, each with two chromatids joined at the centromere. The centrosome (duplicated in S phase) moves to opposite poles; each radiates microtubules called asters; asters and spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.
At the end of prophase, the Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope are no longer visible.

Metaphase begins with complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope. Chromosomes are fully condensed, so morphology is best studied now. Each has two sister chromatids held at the centromere, with disc-shaped kinetochores where spindle fibres attach.
Chromosomes align at the equator; each chromatid's kinetochore is connected to spindle fibres from one pole and its sister's to the opposite pole. The plane of alignment is the metaphase plate.

ex.q: At which stage of mitosis would you count chromosomes, and why?
st: Chromosome condensation is complete at metaphase.
Chromosomes are aligned at the metaphase plate and clearly separate.
ex.a: Metaphase, when chromosomes are most condensed and clearly visible.

topics.rl: Prenatal genetic testing in Indian hospitals uses karyotypes from metaphase cells to check chromosome number.

rv.summary: Mitosis is equational: daughter cells keep the parent's chromosome number. In prophase chromatin condenses, centrosomes move apart and the nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER vanish. In metaphase condensed chromosomes align on the metaphase plate, attached by kinetochores.
focus: Events of metaphase and the metaphase plate
remember: Metaphase: best stage to study chromosome morphology
Metaphase starts with complete breakdown of the nuclear envelope
Asters + spindle fibres = mitotic apparatus
traps: Don't say the nuclear envelope reforms in metaphase
Don't say metaphase chromosomes have one chromatid

topics.t: Mitosis: anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis
topics.h: Tender coconut water is liquid endosperm with many free nuclei and no cell walls between them. The nuclei divided, but the cytoplasm never did.
p: Anaphase: each chromosome at the metaphase plate splits simultaneously; centromeres split and the two daughter chromatids (now chromosomes) move to opposite poles, centromere leading and arms trailing.
Telophase: chromosomes at the poles decondense and lose their individuality; a nuclear envelope forms around each cluster, giving two daughter nuclei; the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform.
Cytokinesis in animal cells: a furrow appears in the plasma membrane, deepens and joins at the centre, dividing the cytoplasm.

Cytokinesis in plant cells: wall formation starts at the centre and grows outward to meet the lateral walls. It begins with a cell plate, which becomes the middle lamella between the walls of the two cells. Organelles such as mitochondria and plastids are distributed to the daughters.
If karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate condition called a syncytium forms, e.g. the liquid endosperm of coconut.

ex.q: Why do plant cells form a cell plate instead of a furrow during cytokinesis?
st: Plant cells are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall.
A furrow cannot pinch a rigid wall inwards.
So a new wall is built from the centre outwards, starting as a cell plate.
ex.a: Their rigid cell wall prevents furrowing, so a cell plate forms from the centre.

topics.rl: Kerala's tender coconuts sold by the roadside contain liquid endosperm, a natural example of a syncytium.

rv.summary: In anaphase centromeres split and chromatids move to opposite poles, centromere first. In telophase chromosomes decondense and two nuclei reform. Animal cells divide cytoplasm by a furrow; plant cells build a cell plate (future middle lamella). Nuclear division without cytokinesis gives a syncytium.
focus: Cytokinesis in animal vs plant cells
remember: Anaphase: centromeres split, centromere leads
Telophase: nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi, ER reform
Cell plate → middle lamella
Syncytium: coconut liquid endosperm
traps: Don't say plant cells divide by furrowing
Don't place nuclear envelope reformation in anaphase

topics.t: Significance of mitosis
topics.h: When you scrape your knee playing cricket, new skin cells form by mitosis to heal it. Mitosis is your built-in repair service.
p: Mitosis usually produces diploid daughter cells with an identical genetic complement.
Growth of multicellular organisms is due to mitosis.
As a cell grows, the ratio between nucleus and cytoplasm is disturbed; division restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.
Cell repair and replacement: cells of the upper epidermis, the lining of the gut and blood cells are constantly replaced by mitosis.
Mitosis in meristems (apical meristem and lateral cambium) gives continuous growth of plants throughout their life.

ex.q: A single cell divides by mitosis 5 times, with every cell dividing each time. How many cells result?
st: Each division doubles the number of cells.
After 5 divisions: 2⁵ = 32.
ex.a: 32 cells

topics.rl: Banyan and neem trees across India keep growing taller and thicker for decades because their apical meristems and cambium keep dividing by mitosis.

rv.summary: Mitosis gives genetically identical diploid daughter cells. It drives growth of multicellular organisms, restores the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio, replaces cells such as epidermis, gut lining and blood cells, and keeps plants growing through meristems.
remember: Mitosis: diploid, identical daughter cells
Restores nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio
Meristems: apical meristem, lateral cambium
n divisions of one cell give 2ⁿ cells
traps: Don't credit wound healing to meiosis
Don't say mitosis only happens in diploid cells

topics.t: Meiosis and the early stages of prophase I
topics.h: Why are you not an exact copy of your elder sibling? Part of the answer is a gene swap that happens in pachytene.
p: Meiosis is a reductional division that halves the chromosome number to form haploid cells. It produces the haploid phase in sexually reproducing organisms; fertilisation restores the diploid phase. It occurs during gametogenesis in plants and animals.

Key features: two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division (meiosis I and II) but only one cycle of DNA replication; pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids; four haploid cells at the end of meiosis II.
Prophase I is longer and more complex than mitotic prophase and has five sub-stages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.

Leptotene: chromosomes become gradually visible and keep compacting. Zygotene: homologous chromosomes start pairing (synapsis), with formation of a synaptonemal complex; a pair of synapsed homologues is a bivalent or tetrad.

Pachytene (longer than the first two stages): the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct as tetrads. Recombination nodules appear, where crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Crossing over is enzyme-mediated (recombinase) and leads to recombination.

ex.q: A human primary spermatocyte has 46 chromosomes. How many bivalents form in zygotene?
st: Each bivalent is a pair of homologous chromosomes.
46 ÷ 2 = 23 bivalents.
ex.a: 23 bivalents

topics.rl: Recombination during pachytene is one reason children of the same parents look different; plant breeders at ICAR rely on it to combine useful traits in new crop varieties.

rv.summary: Meiosis halves the chromosome number by two divisions after one DNA replication, giving four haploid cells. Prophase I has five sub-stages: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis, synaptonemal complex, bivalents), pachytene (crossing over by recombinase), diplotene and diakinesis.
focus: Order of the prophase I sub-stages
Events of leptotene, zygotene and pachytene
Crossing over: where, between what, which enzyme
remember: One DNA replication, two divisions, four haploid cells
Leptotene → zygotene → pachytene → diplotene → diakinesis
Zygotene: synapsis; pachytene: crossing over
Crossing over: non-sister chromatids of homologues; recombinase
traps: Don't put crossing over in zygotene; it is in pachytene
Don't say crossing over is between sister chromatids

topics.t: Diplotene to telophase I
topics.h: In human females, oocytes pause in diplotene before birth and may stay paused for over a decade until puberty. Patience at the cellular level!
p: Diplotene: the synaptonemal complex dissolves and recombined homologues tend to separate except at crossover sites, which appear as X-shaped chiasmata. In oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene can last for months or years (this arrested stage is often called dictyotene).

Diakinesis: terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle assembles. By the end, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down. It is the transition to metaphase.
Metaphase I: bivalents align on the equatorial plate; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the pair of homologous chromosomes.
Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain together at their centromeres.

Telophase I: the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear, cytokinesis follows, giving a dyad of cells. Interkinesis, the stage between the two meiotic divisions, is generally short and has no DNA replication.

ex.q: A cell with 2n = 8 completes meiosis I. How many chromosomes, and how many chromatids per chromosome, does each daughter cell have?
st: Anaphase I separates homologues, so each cell gets one of each pair: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes.
Sister chromatids are still joined, so each chromosome has 2 chromatids.
ex.a: 4 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids

topics.rl: In human females, oocytes arrested in diplotene before birth resume meiosis only at puberty, a fact gynaecologists use to explain the age-related risk of chromosomal errors.

rv.summary: In diplotene the synaptonemal complex dissolves and chiasmata appear; diakinesis terminalises chiasmata. In metaphase I bivalents align; in anaphase I homologues separate while sister chromatids stay joined; telophase I gives a dyad. Interkinesis has no DNA replication.
remember: Diplotene: chiasmata; can last months or years in some vertebrate oocytes
Diakinesis: terminalisation of chiasmata
Anaphase I: homologues separate, centromeres do not split
Interkinesis: no DNA replication
traps: Don't call meiosis I equational
Don't say centromeres split in anaphase I

topics.t: Meiosis II and the significance of meiosis
topics.h: If gametes were not haploid, chromosome number would double every generation. Meiosis keeps the count steady, generation after generation.
p: Meiosis II starts right after cytokinesis of meiosis I, usually before chromosomes have fully elongated, and resembles normal mitosis. Prophase II: nuclear membrane disappears by its end and chromosomes compact again.

Metaphase II: chromosomes align at the equator; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. Anaphase II: the centromere of each chromosome splits and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
Telophase II: the two groups of chromosomes are enclosed by nuclear envelopes; cytokinesis follows, giving a tetrad of four haploid daughter cells.
Meiosis I is reductional (homologues separate, halving chromosome number); meiosis II is equational (sister chromatids separate, number stays the same as at the start of meiosis II).

Significance: meiosis conserves the chromosome number of each species across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, although it halves the number in gametes. It increases genetic variability (crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes), which is very important for evolution.

ex.q: Why is meiosis II called equational even though it is part of meiosis?
st: At the start of meiosis II each cell is already haploid (n), each chromosome with two chromatids.
In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate.
Each daughter cell still has n chromosomes, the same as the cell entering meiosis II.
ex.a: Because chromosome number does not change during meiosis II; only sister chromatids separate.

topics.rl: Variation produced by meiosis is the raw material that let farmers and ICAR scientists select drought-tolerant and disease-resistant crop varieties.

rv.summary: Meiosis II follows meiosis I without DNA replication and resembles mitosis: centromeres split in anaphase II and a tetrad of four haploid cells forms. Meiosis I is reductional, meiosis II equational. Meiosis conserves chromosome number across generations and creates variation for evolution.
focus: Events of prophase II to telophase II
remember: Anaphase II: centromeres split, sister chromatids separate
End result: four haploid cells
Meiosis I reductional; meiosis II equational
Variation from crossing over and independent assortment
traps: Don't say DNA replicates before meiosis II
Don't call meiosis II reductional

topics.t: Mitosis versus meiosis: comparing and identifying
topics.h: Exam favourite: 'Identify the stage from the diagram.' Learn the clues once and you'll never confuse anaphase I with anaphase II again.
p: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, identical to parent; no pairing or crossing over; occurs in somatic cells for growth and repair.
Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different; synapsis and crossing over in prophase I; occurs in gamete-forming cells.
Metaphase of mitosis and metaphase II: single chromosomes (two chromatids each) at the equator. Metaphase I: bivalents (paired homologues) at the equator.
Anaphase of mitosis and anaphase II: centromeres split, sister chromatids move apart. Anaphase I: centromeres do not split; homologous chromosomes move apart.
DNA tracking for a 2n cell: G1 2C → after S 4C → after mitosis 2C each; in meiosis, 4C → after meiosis I 2C (n chromosomes) → after meiosis II 1C (n chromosomes).

ex.q: A diagram shows chromosomes moving to poles with each chromosome still made of two chromatids, and the homologues separating. Name the stage.
st: Chromosomes moving to poles means anaphase.
Each still has two chromatids, so centromeres have not split.
Homologues separating means meiosis I.
ex.a: Anaphase I

topics.rl: Pathologists and genetic counsellors in India use these differences to explain chromosomal errors such as non-disjunction during meiosis.

rv.summary: Mitosis is one division giving two identical diploid cells, with no pairing or crossing over. Meiosis is two divisions giving four genetically different haploid cells, with synapsis and crossing over. Bivalents at metaphase I and intact centromeres at anaphase I identify meiosis I.
remember: Mitosis: 1 division, 2 cells, 2n, identical
Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 cells, n, varied
DNA: 2C → 4C (S) → 2C (meiosis I) → 1C (meiosis II)
Metaphase I: bivalents; metaphase II/mitosis: single chromosomes
traps: Don't say centromeres split in anaphase I
Don't confuse chromosome number with DNA content

topics.t: Photosynthesis: why it matters and simple experiments
topics.h: Every grain of rice, every roti and every breath of oxygen you take traces back to a green leaf trapping sunlight.
p: Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to synthesise organic compounds.
It is the primary source of all food on Earth and is responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere.
Variegated leaf experiment: a leaf with green and non-green patches, kept in light and tested for starch, shows starch only in green parts, so chlorophyll is needed.
Half-covered leaf experiment: a leaf partly covered with black paper and kept in light shows starch only in the exposed part, so light is needed.
KOH half-leaf experiment: part of a leaf is enclosed in a tube with KOH-soaked cotton (KOH absorbs CO₂); only the part exposed to air tests positive for starch, so CO₂ is needed.

ex.q: In the KOH half-leaf experiment, why does the enclosed half give a negative starch test?
st: KOH absorbs CO₂ from the air in the tube.
Without CO₂, that part cannot photosynthesise.
No photosynthesis means no starch.
ex.a: KOH removes CO₂, so no photosynthesis and no starch.

topics.rl: In school labs, the starch test uses iodine solution, and boiling the leaf in alcohol must be done in a water bath, never over a direct flame, because alcohol catches fire easily.

rv.summary: Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process in which green plants use light energy to make organic compounds; it is the primary source of food and releases oxygen. Simple experiments show it needs chlorophyll (variegated leaf), light (half-covered leaf) and CO₂ (KOH half-leaf).
focus: Variegated leaf, half-covered leaf and KOH experiments
remember: Variegated leaf → chlorophyll needed
Half-covered leaf → light needed
KOH absorbs CO₂ → CO₂ needed
Starch + iodine → blue-black
traps: Don't say KOH supplies CO₂; it absorbs it
Don't expect starch in the white parts of a variegated leaf

topics.t: Early experiments: from Priestley to van Niel
topics.h: A candle, a mouse, a mint plant and a glass jar: Joseph Priestley's 1770s experiments launched our understanding of photosynthesis.
p: Joseph Priestley (1770s): a candle in a closed bell jar went out and a mouse suffocated; with a mint plant inside, the candle kept burning and the mouse lived. He hypothesised that plants restore to the air what breathing animals and burning candles remove. He discovered oxygen in 1774.

Jan Ingenhousz: sunlight is essential for the plant to purify the air; an aquatic plant formed bubbles (later shown to be oxygen) around its green parts in bright sunlight, not in the dark. So only green parts release oxygen.
Julius von Sachs (1854): glucose is made in the green parts of plants and is usually stored as starch; chlorophyll is located in special bodies later called chloroplasts.

T.W. Engelmann: split light with a prism and lit the green alga Cladophora placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria. Bacteria gathered mainly in blue and red light, giving the first action spectrum of photosynthesis.

Cornelius van Niel, studying purple and green bacteria: photosynthesis is a light-dependent reaction where hydrogen from an oxidisable compound reduces CO₂ (2H₂A + CO₂ → 2A + CH₂O + H₂O). With H₂S, sulphur bacteria give sulphur, not O₂, so in green plants O₂ comes from water. Correct equation: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂ (in light).

ex.q: Using the equation 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂, how many oxygen atoms in the O₂ released come from water?
st: 6O₂ contains 12 oxygen atoms.
van Niel showed all released O₂ comes from water.
12 H₂O supply exactly 12 oxygen atoms.
ex.a: All 12 oxygen atoms come from water.

topics.rl: Engelmann's bacteria trick is similar to how scientists now use oxygen sensors to measure photosynthesis of crops in ICAR field trials.

rv.summary: Priestley showed plants restore air (discovering oxygen in 1774); Ingenhousz showed only green parts in light release O₂; von Sachs showed glucose forms in green parts and is stored as starch; Engelmann gave the first action spectrum; van Niel showed the O₂ comes from water.
focus: Engelmann's experiment and the action spectrum
Van Niel's reasoning that O₂ comes from water
remember: Priestley: bell jar, mint, mouse; oxygen 1774
Ingenhousz: sunlight and green parts
Von Sachs 1854: glucose, starch, chloroplasts; Engelmann: Cladophora, blue and red light
6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂
traps: Don't say released O₂ comes from CO₂
Don't credit the action spectrum to Priestley

topics.t: Where photosynthesis takes place
topics.h: The 'dark reaction' doesn't happen in the dark. That's one of the most misunderstood names in biology.
p: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in green leaves, but also in other green parts. Mesophyll cells have many chloroplasts.
Chloroplasts usually align along the walls of mesophyll cells so they receive optimum incident light.
Inside the chloroplast there is a division of labour. The membrane system (grana and stroma lamellae) traps light energy and makes ATP and NADPH: the light reactions (photochemical reactions).

In the stroma, enzymatic reactions synthesise sugar, which forms starch. These are not directly light-driven but depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so by convention they are called dark reactions (carbon reactions).
The term 'dark reaction' does not mean they occur in darkness or that they do not depend on light.

ex.q: Why does sugar synthesis in the stroma stop soon after the light is switched off?
st: Sugar synthesis needs ATP and NADPH.
These are made only by the light reactions in the thylakoid membranes.
Once light stops, ATP and NADPH run out, and the carbon reactions stop.
ex.a: Because the dark reactions depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

topics.rl: Paddy farmers in Punjab know rice plants grow best in full sun; shaded rice gives poorer yield because the light reactions slow down.

rv.summary: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in leaf mesophyll chloroplasts. Thylakoid membranes (grana, stroma lamellae) carry out the light reactions, making ATP and NADPH; the stroma carries out enzymatic carbon (dark) reactions that use them to make sugar.
focus: Division of labour inside the chloroplast
Why carbon reactions are called dark reactions
remember: Light reactions: thylakoid membranes → ATP, NADPH
Carbon (dark) reactions: stroma → sugar
Chloroplasts align along mesophyll walls for optimum light
traps: Don't say dark reactions happen only in darkness
Don't place sugar synthesis in the grana

topics.t: Photosynthetic pigments and spectra
topics.h: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light. The colours it actually uses are blue and red.
p: Paper chromatography of leaf pigments separates four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange).
Pigments absorb light at specific wavelengths. A graph of absorption at different wavelengths is the absorption spectrum; chlorophyll a absorbs most in the blue and red regions.

A graph of the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths is the action spectrum. It correlates closely with the absorption spectrum: most photosynthesis occurs in blue and red light, though some occurs at other wavelengths.
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment of photosynthesis.

Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) absorb light and transfer energy to chlorophyll a. They widen the range of wavelengths used and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

ex.q: A student runs a chromatogram of spinach pigments. Name the four bands and their colours.
st: Chlorophyll a: bright or blue-green.
Chlorophyll b: yellow-green.
Xanthophylls: yellow.
Carotenoids: yellow to yellow-orange.
ex.a: Chlorophyll a (blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow-orange).

topics.rl: Autumn leaves of Kashmir's chinar trees turn golden as chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow-orange carotenoids, hidden until then, show through.

rv.summary: Chromatography separates chlorophyll a (blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls and carotenoids. Chlorophyll a, the chief pigment, absorbs most in blue and red, and the action spectrum closely matches its absorption spectrum.
remember: Chlorophyll a: chief pigment, blue-green
Chlorophyll a absorbs most in blue and red
Accessory pigments: chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids
traps: Don't say chlorophyll absorbs green light most
Don't call accessory pigments reaction centres

topics.t: Light reaction: photosystems, Z scheme and splitting of water
topics.h: Photosystem II comes first in the chain but was discovered second. Its name is a history lesson, not a sequence.
p: The light reactions (photochemical phase) include light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release and formation of ATP and NADPH.

Pigments form light harvesting complexes (LHC) in Photosystem I (PS I) and Photosystem II (PS II), named in the order of discovery, not function. Each LHC has hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins forming the antennae; a single chlorophyll a molecule is the reaction centre.
The PS I reaction centre absorbs maximally at 700 nm (P700); the PS II reaction centre at 680 nm (P680).

Z scheme: PS II absorbs 680 nm light, electrons are excited and accepted by an acceptor, then pass downhill through an electron transport chain (cytochromes) to PS I. PS I electrons, excited by 700 nm light, go to another acceptor and then downhill to NADP⁺, reducing it to NADPH + H⁺.
Water splitting, associated with PS II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, replaces the electrons lost by PS II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻. Protons and O₂ are released into the thylakoid lumen.

ex.q: How many molecules of water must be split to release 3 molecules of O₂?
st: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻: 2 water molecules give 1 O₂.
For 3 O₂: 3 × 2 = 6 water molecules.
ex.a: 6 molecules of water

topics.rl: The oxygen in the air over India's forests, from the Sundarbans to the Western Ghats, is released by this water-splitting reaction.

rv.summary: Light reactions absorb light, split water, release O₂ and make ATP and NADPH. Pigments form light harvesting complexes in PS I (P700) and PS II (P680). In the Z scheme electrons pass from PS II through cytochromes to PS I and then to NADP⁺. Water splitting at PS II replaces lost electrons.
focus: PS I and PS II reaction centres
Path of electrons in the Z scheme
remember: PS I: P700; PS II: P680; named by order of discovery
2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻ (at PS II, lumen side)
Final electron acceptor: NADP⁺ → NADPH + H⁺
traps: Don't associate water splitting with PS I
Don't think PS I acts before PS II

topics.t: Photophosphorylation and the chemiosmotic hypothesis
topics.h: ATP synthase is a real molecular turbine: protons rush through it like water through a dam at Bhakra-Nangal, and that flow makes ATP.
p: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation: PS II and PS I work in series, connected by the electron transport chain; both ATP and NADPH + H⁺ are made.

Cyclic photophosphorylation: only PS I works; electrons cycle back to PS I through the electron transport chain. It occurs in stroma lamellae, which lack PS II and NADP reductase. Only ATP is made, not NADPH. It also occurs when only light beyond 680 nm is available.

Chemiosmotic hypothesis: ATP synthesis is linked to a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane. Protons build up in the lumen because (a) water is split on the inner side, (b) a carrier moves protons from the stroma into the lumen as electrons are transported, and (c) NADP reductase on the stroma side removes protons from the stroma. The lumen pH falls.

ATP synthase has two parts: F₀ (CF₀), a transmembrane channel for facilitated diffusion of protons, and F₁ (CF₁), protruding into the stroma. Protons flowing back through F₀ cause a conformational change in F₁ that makes ATP. Chemiosmosis needs a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase.

ex.q: Give two differences between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
st: Cyclic: only PS I; non-cyclic: PS II and PS I.
Cyclic makes only ATP; non-cyclic makes ATP and NADPH.
Cyclic occurs in stroma lamellae; non-cyclic in grana.
ex.a: Cyclic uses only PS I and makes only ATP (stroma lamellae); non-cyclic uses both photosystems and makes ATP and NADPH (grana).

topics.rl: Hydroelectric dams such as Bhakra-Nangal turn falling water into electricity; ATP synthase turns falling protons into ATP.

rv.summary: Photophosphorylation makes ATP from ADP and Pi in light. Non-cyclic uses PS II and PS I and makes ATP and NADPH; cyclic uses only PS I in stroma lamellae and makes only ATP. By chemiosmosis, a proton gradient in the lumen drives ATP synthase (F₀ channel, F₁ head).
focus: Why protons build up in the lumen
Structure and working of ATP synthase
remember: Cyclic: PS I only, ATP only, stroma lamellae, light beyond 680 nm
Non-cyclic: PS II + PS I, ATP + NADPH
F₀: proton channel; F₁: makes ATP
Chemiosmosis: membrane, proton pump, gradient, ATP synthase
traps: Don't say cyclic flow makes NADPH
Don't place NADP reductase on the lumen side

topics.t: The Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)
topics.h: Melvin Calvin fed radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ to algae and traced where the carbon went. The first stop was a 3-carbon acid, and a Nobel Prize followed.
p: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, with CO₂, are used in the biosynthetic phase to make sugars. O₂ diffuses out. Synthesis continues briefly after light stops, then halts.

Melvin Calvin used radioactive ¹⁴C in algal photosynthesis and found the first CO₂ fixation product is a 3-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA): the C3 pathway. In some plants the first product is oxaloacetic acid (OAA), a 4-carbon acid: the C4 pathway.
In C3 plants the primary CO₂ acceptor is ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), a 5-carbon ketose sugar.

The Calvin cycle occurs in all photosynthetic plants and has three stages: carboxylation (RuBisCO fixes CO₂ with RuBP to give two molecules of 3-PGA), reduction (2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed, leading to carbohydrate), and regeneration of RuBP (1 ATP per CO₂).
So each CO₂ needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. One glucose needs 6 CO₂ and 6 turns: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. The extra ATP need may be met by cyclic photophosphorylation.

ex.q: How much ATP and NADPH are needed to make 2 molecules of glucose by the Calvin cycle?
st: One glucose: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
Two glucose: 2 × 18 = 36 ATP and 2 × 12 = 24 NADPH.
ex.a: 36 ATP and 24 NADPH

topics.rl: Most Indian staples, including rice and wheat, are C3 plants that fix carbon directly through the Calvin cycle.

rv.summary: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into sugar. RuBP (5C) accepts CO₂ via RuBisCO giving two 3-PGA (C3 pathway). Its stages are carboxylation, reduction and regeneration; each CO₂ needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, so one glucose needs 6 turns, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
focus: Calvin's ¹⁴C work and the first product
Three stages of the Calvin cycle
ATP and NADPH cost per CO₂ and per glucose
remember: Acceptor: RuBP (5C); enzyme: RuBisCO; first product: 3-PGA (3C)
Per CO₂: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH
Per glucose: 6 turns, 18 ATP, 12 NADPH
traps: Don't say the Calvin cycle needs 2 ATP per CO₂; it needs 3
Don't call OAA the C3 first product

topics.t: The C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack pathway)
topics.h: Maize, sorghum and sugarcane thrive in hot Indian summers with super yields. Their leaves have a 'wreath' of special cells that act like CO₂ pumps.
p: C4 plants are adapted to dry tropical regions (e.g. maize, sorghum). Their first CO₂ fixation product is the 4-carbon OAA, but they still use the Calvin cycle as the main biosynthetic pathway. They tolerate higher temperatures, respond to high light, lack photorespiration and have greater biomass productivity.
Kranz anatomy ('Kranz' = wreath): large bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles, with many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gas exchange and no intercellular spaces.

In mesophyll cells, the primary CO₂ acceptor is the 3-carbon phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), fixed by PEP carboxylase (PEPcase) to OAA. OAA forms other 4-carbon acids such as malic acid or aspartic acid, which move to the bundle sheath cells.

In bundle sheath cells, the C4 acids are broken down to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule. The CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle; the 3-carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll and is converted back to PEP, completing the cycle.
Mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO; bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase.

ex.q: Trace one carbon from atmospheric CO₂ to sugar in a maize leaf.
st: In mesophyll, PEPcase fixes CO₂ with PEP to form OAA.
OAA becomes malate or aspartate and moves to the bundle sheath.
There it is decarboxylated, releasing CO₂.
RuBisCO fixes this CO₂ in the Calvin cycle to make sugar.
ex.a: Mesophyll (PEP → OAA → malate) → bundle sheath (CO₂ released) → Calvin cycle

topics.rl: Sugarcane in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra and maize in Karnataka are C4 crops that give high yields in hot, sunny conditions.

rv.summary: C4 plants (maize, sorghum) fix CO₂ in mesophyll by PEPcase onto PEP (3C), forming OAA (4C). C4 acids move to Kranz bundle sheath cells, where CO₂ is released and fixed by RuBisCO in the Calvin cycle; the 3C remnant returns to make PEP.
focus: Reactions in mesophyll vs bundle sheath
remember: Acceptor: PEP (3C); enzyme: PEPcase; first product: OAA (4C)
Kranz = wreath; bundle sheath: many chloroplasts, thick gas-tight walls, no air spaces
Mesophyll: PEPcase, no RuBisCO; bundle sheath: RuBisCO, no PEPcase
traps: Don't say C4 plants skip the Calvin cycle
Don't put RuBisCO in C4 mesophyll

topics.t: Photorespiration and C3 versus C4
topics.h: The world's most abundant enzyme sometimes grabs the wrong gas. When RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂, the plant wastes energy.
p: RuBisCO, the most abundant enzyme in the world, has an active site that can bind both CO₂ and O₂. It has a much greater affinity for CO₂, but the relative concentrations of O₂ and CO₂ decide which binds.
In C3 plants some O₂ binds RuBisCO, reducing CO₂ fixation. RuBP then combines with O₂ to form one molecule of PGA and one of phosphoglycolate: photorespiration.
