Photorespiration makes no sugar, no ATP and no NADPH; instead CO₂ is released and ATP is used. So it is a wasteful process.

C4 plants do not show photorespiration: breaking down C4 acids in bundle sheath cells raises the CO₂ concentration around RuBisCO, so it acts as a carboxylase and its oxygenase activity is minimised. This is one reason C4 plants have higher productivity and tolerate higher temperatures.

C3 vs C4: primary acceptor RuBP (5C) vs PEP (3C); first product PGA (3C) vs OAA (4C); fixing enzyme RuBisCO vs PEPcase (then RuBisCO); Kranz anatomy absent vs present; photorespiration present vs negligible; Calvin cycle in mesophyll vs bundle sheath.

ex.q: Why is photorespiration called wasteful?
st: RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂, forming PGA and phosphoglycolate.
No sugar, ATP or NADPH is made.
CO₂ that was fixed is released and ATP is consumed.
ex.a: Because it uses energy and releases CO₂ without making sugar, ATP or NADPH.

topics.rl: Scientists in India and abroad are trying to engineer rice (a C3 plant) to work more like a C4 plant to cut photorespiration and raise yields.

rv.summary: RuBisCO can bind CO₂ or O₂; when it binds O₂ in C3 plants, RuBP gives PGA and phosphoglycolate: wasteful photorespiration with no sugar, ATP or NADPH. C4 plants concentrate CO₂ in the bundle sheath, so they avoid photorespiration and are more productive.
remember: RuBP + O₂ → PGA + phosphoglycolate
Photorespiration: no sugar, ATP or NADPH; CO₂ released
C3: RuBP, PGA, mesophyll; C4: PEP, OAA, Kranz, bundle sheath
traps: Don't say C4 plants lack RuBisCO
Don't call photorespiration a source of ATP

topics.t: Factors affecting photosynthesis
topics.h: Greenhouse tomato growers pump extra CO₂ into their glasshouses. Why would anyone add a 'pollutant' to plants on purpose?
p: Internal (plant) factors: number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO₂ and amount of chlorophyll. External factors: light, CO₂, temperature and water.

Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905): if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value. E.g. a leaf with optimal light and CO₂ may not photosynthesise if the temperature is very low.

Light: rate rises linearly with light at low intensities, then levels off; light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting except in shade. Excess light breaks down chlorophyll and reduces photosynthesis.

CO₂: the major limiting factor (only about 0.03 to 0.04% in air). Up to about 0.05% it increases fixation; higher levels can be damaging over long periods. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µL L⁻¹; C3 plants respond up to beyond 450 µL L⁻¹, so present CO₂ levels limit C3 plants. Greenhouse tomatoes and bell peppers grown in CO₂-enriched air give higher yields.

Temperature: dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature-controlled; light reactions are much less affected. C4 plants have higher temperature optima than C3; tropical plants have higher optima than temperate ones. Water acts indirectly: water stress closes stomata (less CO₂) and makes leaves wilt (less surface area and activity).

ex.q: A C3 plant under bright light shows no increase in photosynthesis when light is doubled, but a large increase when CO₂ is raised. What is the limiting factor?
st: Increasing light has no effect, so light is not limiting.
Increasing CO₂ raises the rate, so CO₂ is nearest its minimum.
By Blackman's law, CO₂ is the limiting factor.
ex.a: CO₂ concentration.

topics.rl: Polyhouse farmers in Maharashtra and Karnataka grow capsicum and tomatoes under controlled conditions; CO₂ enrichment and shade nets help manage limiting factors.

rv.summary: Photosynthesis depends on internal factors (leaves, chloroplasts, chlorophyll) and external ones (light, CO₂, temperature, water). By Blackman's law (1905) the factor nearest its minimum limits the rate. Light saturates at about 10% of sunlight; CO₂ is the major limiting factor.
focus: Effect of CO₂: C3 vs C4 saturation
remember: Blackman 1905: factor nearest minimal value limits rate
Light saturation ≈ 10% of full sunlight
C4 saturate ≈ 360 µL L⁻¹ CO₂; C3 beyond 450 µL L⁻¹
Dark reactions are temperature-sensitive
traps: Don't say light is usually the limiting factor in open fields
Don't say temperature affects light reactions most

topics.t: Respiration, respiratory substrates and do plants breathe?
topics.h: A banyan tree can be hundreds of years old and enormous, yet it has no lungs. How does every cell in it get oxygen?
p: Cellular respiration is the breaking of C–C bonds of complex compounds by oxidation within cells, releasing energy. The compounds oxidised are respiratory substrates: usually carbohydrates, but also proteins, fats and even organic acids in some plants.
Energy is not released in one step but in a series of slow, enzyme-controlled steps, and trapped as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
Plants have no specialised respiratory organs; gas exchange occurs through stomata and lenticels.

Why plants manage without lungs: each part handles its own gas exchange; plants respire at far lower rates than animals; during photosynthesis O₂ is released inside the cells; living cells are close to the surface (in stems they lie in thin layers beneath the bark, with lenticels; interior cells are dead); loosely packed parenchyma gives a network of air spaces.

Complete combustion of glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (mostly heat). Cells instead oxidise glucose step by step. Some organisms are facultative or obligate anaerobes, and all organisms keep the machinery to partly oxidise glucose without O₂ (glycolysis), reflecting anaerobic ancestors.

ex.q: In the combustion equation of glucose, how many molecules of O₂ are used per molecule of CO₂ released?
st: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.
O₂ used = 6; CO₂ released = 6.
ex.a: 1 molecule of O₂ per CO₂

topics.rl: Old trees along Indian roads have lenticels, tiny raised pores on their bark, that let air reach the living cells beneath.

rv.summary: Respiration breaks C–C bonds of substrates (usually carbohydrates) by oxidation in cells, releasing energy step by step and trapping it as ATP. Plants have no respiratory organs: they exchange gases through stomata and lenticels because demand is low and living cells are near the surface.
focus: Meaning of respiration and respiratory substrates
Why plants manage without respiratory organs
remember: ATP is the energy currency of the cell
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy
Gas exchange in plants: stomata and lenticels
Glycolysis: partial oxidation without O₂ in all organisms
traps: Don't say plants do not respire
Don't say respiration releases all energy at once as heat

topics.t: Glycolysis: the steps
topics.h: Every organism on Earth, from bacteria to blue whales, runs glycolysis in its cytoplasm. It's the oldest energy app.
p: Glycolysis (Greek glycos = sugar, lysis = splitting) is the EMP pathway, worked out by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas. It occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms; in anaerobes it is the only respiratory process. It has ten enzyme-controlled reactions.
Glucose is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase (ATP used). This isomerises to fructose-6-phosphate, which is phosphorylated to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (second ATP used).
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
PGAL is oxidised (two redox equivalents to NAD⁺, forming NADH + H⁺) and, with inorganic phosphate, becomes 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA).
ATP is made directly (substrate-level phosphorylation) when BPGA becomes 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) and when phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) becomes pyruvic acid.

ex.q: At which two steps is ATP used in glycolysis?
st: Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase).
Fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.
ex.a: In the two phosphorylation steps before the sugar splits.

topics.rl: Sprinters at the Khelo India games rely heavily on glycolysis for quick bursts of energy before oxygen supply catches up.

rv.summary: Glycolysis (EMP pathway of Embden, Meyerhof and Parnas) is ten cytoplasmic reactions in all organisms. Glucose is phosphorylated twice using ATP, split into DHAP and PGAL, PGAL is oxidised to BPGA making NADH, and ATP forms directly at BPGA → PGA and PEP → pyruvate.
remember: Hexokinase: glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (ATP used)
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → DHAP + PGAL
PGAL → BPGA: NADH + H⁺ formed
ATP made at BPGA → PGA and PEP → pyruvic acid
traps: Don't place glycolysis in mitochondria
Don't say NADH forms at the hexokinase step

topics.t: Glycolysis: net yield and the fate of pyruvate
topics.h: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP and makes 4. Like a shopkeeper's ledger, the net profit is what counts.
p: In plants, glucose comes from sucrose (the end product of photosynthesis) or from storage carbohydrates. Invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose, which both enter glycolysis.
ATP used: 2 (hexokinase step and fructose-6-P step). ATP made: 4 (two at BPGA → PGA and two at PEP → pyruvate, since each glucose gives two 3-carbon molecules). Net gain: 2 ATP.
Per glucose, glycolysis also gives 2 NADH + H⁺ and 2 molecules of pyruvic acid.
Pyruvic acid is the key product of glycolysis. Its fate depends on the cell's need.

Three fates: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation (both anaerobic, in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes), and aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle, needs O₂) for complete oxidation to CO₂ and H₂O.

ex.q: Calculate the net ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule.
st: ATP used: 2.
ATP formed: 2 at BPGA → PGA + 2 at PEP → pyruvate = 4.
ex.a: Net 2 ATP

topics.rl: Sugarcane mills in Maharashtra ferment molasses (rich in sucrose) to ethanol for petrol blending under India's ethanol programme; the first step is splitting sucrose.

rv.summary: In plants, invertase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose for glycolysis. Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and makes 4, a net gain of 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH + H⁺ and 2 pyruvic acid per glucose. Pyruvate goes to lactic acid or alcoholic fermentation, or to aerobic respiration.
remember: ATP used 2, made 4, net 2
Per glucose: 2 NADH + H⁺, 2 pyruvic acid
Invertase: sucrose → glucose + fructose
traps: Don't give glycolysis a net gain of 4 ATP
Don't say aerobic oxidation of pyruvate can occur without O₂

topics.t: Fermentation
topics.h: Idli batter rises overnight and your legs ache after a long run. Both are fermentation stories.
p: Alcoholic fermentation (e.g. yeast): incomplete oxidation of glucose under anaerobic conditions; pyruvic acid is converted to CO₂ and ethanol by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase.

Lactic acid fermentation: some bacteria convert pyruvic acid to lactic acid. In animal cells such as muscles during exercise, when O₂ is inadequate, pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase.
In both, NADH + H⁺ is reoxidised to NAD⁺, so glycolysis can continue.
Fermentation releases less than 7% of the energy in glucose, and not all of it is trapped as ATP. The net gain is only the 2 ATP of glycolysis.
The products are hazardous: acid or alcohol. Yeasts poison themselves to death when alcohol reaches about 13%.

ex.q: Why does fermentation need to regenerate NAD⁺?
st: Glycolysis uses NAD⁺ when PGAL is oxidised.
If NAD⁺ runs out, glycolysis stops.
Converting pyruvate to lactic acid or ethanol reoxidises NADH to NAD⁺.
ex.a: So glycolysis can continue and keep making ATP.

topics.rl: Idli and dosa batters ferment with help from microbes that release CO₂, making them fluffy; curd forms by lactic acid fermentation.

rv.summary: In fermentation, glucose is partly oxidised without O₂: yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂; muscle and some bacteria make lactic acid. Both regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis continues. It releases under 7% of glucose's energy (net 2 ATP), and its products are hazardous.
focus: Alcoholic vs lactic acid fermentation and their enzymes
Energy yield and hazards of fermentation
remember: Yeast: pyruvic acid decarboxylase + alcohol dehydrogenase → ethanol + CO₂
Muscle: lactate dehydrogenase → lactic acid
Net 2 ATP; less than 7% energy released
Yeast dies at about 13% alcohol
traps: Don't say fermentation yields more ATP than aerobic respiration
Don't say muscles make ethanol

topics.t: Aerobic respiration: link reaction and Krebs cycle
topics.h: Hans Krebs worked out a cycle that turns one pyruvate into three CO₂ molecules and a stash of energy carriers. It runs nonstop in your mitochondria.
p: Aerobic respiration needs complete oxidation of pyruvate in mitochondria: stepwise removal of hydrogen leaving three CO₂ (in the matrix), and passing the electrons to O₂ with ATP synthesis (on the inner membrane).

Link reaction: in the matrix, pyruvate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase (needing NAD⁺, coenzyme A and Mg²⁺): pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺. Two NADH form per glucose.
Krebs cycle (TCA cycle): acetyl group condenses with oxaloacetic acid (OAA) and water to form citric acid, catalysed by citrate synthase, releasing CoA. Citrate isomerises to isocitrate.

Two successive decarboxylations give α-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl CoA. Succinyl CoA → succinic acid makes one GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation), which gives ATP. The remaining steps regenerate OAA.
Per pyruvate in the cycle: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (via GTP). Including the link reaction: pyruvic acid + 4NAD⁺ + FAD⁺ + 2H₂O + ADP + Pi → 3CO₂ + 4NADH + 4H⁺ + FADH₂ + ATP.

ex.q: How many NADH and FADH₂ are produced from one glucose in the link reaction plus Krebs cycle?
st: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate.
Per pyruvate: 1 NADH (link) + 3 NADH (cycle) = 4 NADH, and 1 FADH₂.
For 2 pyruvate: 8 NADH and 2 FADH₂.
ex.a: 8 NADH and 2 FADH₂ (plus 2 ATP)

topics.rl: Endurance athletes, like marathoners at the Mumbai Marathon, depend heavily on aerobic respiration through the Krebs cycle in their muscle mitochondria.

rv.summary: In mitochondria, the link reaction (pyruvic dehydrogenase) turns pyruvate into acetyl CoA, CO₂ and NADH. In the Krebs cycle acetyl CoA + OAA form citric acid; two decarboxylations and one GTP step follow and OAA is regenerated. Per pyruvate: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP in the cycle.
focus: Key steps of the Krebs cycle
Yield per pyruvate and per glucose
remember: Link reaction: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺
Citrate synthase: acetyl CoA + OAA → citric acid
Succinyl CoA → succinic acid: GTP (substrate-level)
Per pyruvate (cycle): 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP
traps: Don't place the Krebs cycle in the cytoplasm
Don't count the link reaction's NADH as part of the cycle's 3

topics.t: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation
topics.h: Cyanide is deadly because it blocks the last step of the electron transport chain. Without that step, oxygen can't do its job.
p: The electron transport system (ETS) is on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from NADH are oxidised by NADH dehydrogenase (complex I) and passed to ubiquinone.

FADH₂ (from succinate oxidation) passes its reducing equivalents to ubiquinone via complex II. Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) passes electrons to cytochrome c via the cytochrome bc₁ complex (complex III).

Cytochrome c is a small mobile protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane carrying electrons from complex III to complex IV. Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochromes a and a₃ and two copper centres.
Oxygen is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor, forming water. Its role is only at the terminal stage, but it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system.

Electron flow is coupled to ATP synthase (complex V: F₁ headpiece makes ATP; F₀ is the proton channel). Energy of oxidation-reduction builds a proton gradient (oxidative phosphorylation). 2H⁺ pass through F₀ from the intermembrane space to the matrix per ATP. One NADH gives 3 ATP; one FADH₂ gives 2 ATP.

ex.q: How many ATP are produced by oxidising 4 NADH and 1 FADH₂ in the ETS?
st: NADH: 4 × 3 = 12 ATP.
FADH₂: 1 × 2 = 2 ATP.
Total = 12 + 2 = 14 ATP.
ex.a: 14 ATP

topics.rl: Cyanide poisoning cases treated in Indian hospitals are emergencies because cyanide stops complex IV, halting ATP production.

rv.summary: The ETS on the inner mitochondrial membrane passes electrons from NADH (complex I) and FADH₂ (complex II) via ubiquinone, complex III, cytochrome c and complex IV to oxygen, forming water. The proton gradient drives ATP synthase (F₀ channel, F₁ head): oxidative phosphorylation.
focus: Order of ETS complexes and carriers
Role of oxygen as final acceptor
remember: Complex I NADH dehydrogenase; II via FADH₂; III cytochrome bc₁; IV cytochrome c oxidase; V ATP synthase
Cytochrome c: mobile carrier between III and IV
1 NADH → 3 ATP; 1 FADH₂ → 2 ATP
F₀ proton channel; F₁ makes ATP
traps: Don't call ubiquinone the final acceptor; oxygen is
Don't say FADH₂ gives 3 ATP

topics.t: The respiratory balance sheet: fermentation vs aerobic respiration
topics.h: Aerobic respiration can yield up to 38 ATP per glucose; fermentation only 2. That's like comparing a full salary to pocket money.
p: Balance sheet assumptions: a sequential, orderly pathway (glycolysis → TCA → ETS); NADH from glycolysis enters mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation; no intermediates are withdrawn to make other compounds; only glucose is respired. These are not fully valid in real cells, where pathways run simultaneously.
Under these assumptions there is a net gain of 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration.
Count: glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link reaction 2 NADH; Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂. NADH total 10 × 3 = 30 ATP; FADH₂ 2 × 2 = 4 ATP; direct ATP 4. Total 38.
Fermentation vs aerobic: partial vs complete breakdown of glucose; net 2 ATP vs many more; NADH oxidised slowly vs vigorously.

Glycolysis vs Krebs: cytoplasm vs mitochondrial matrix; anaerobic vs needs O₂ (via ETS); glucose → 2 pyruvate vs acetyl CoA → CO₂. Respiration differs from combustion: it is stepwise, enzyme-controlled and traps energy as ATP rather than releasing it all as heat.

ex.q: Use the balance sheet to verify 38 ATP per glucose.
st: Direct ATP: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (Krebs) = 4.
FADH₂: 2, giving 2 × 2 = 4.
ex.a: 38 ATP

topics.rl: Indian Railways keeps an energy balance sheet for every train; cells keep one for every glucose molecule.

rv.summary: Under simplifying assumptions (sequential pathway, glycolytic NADH enters mitochondria, no intermediates withdrawn, only glucose respired) aerobic respiration gives a net 38 ATP per glucose. Fermentation gives only 2. Respiration differs from combustion by being stepwise and trapping energy as ATP.
focus: Counting 38 ATP from NADH, FADH₂ and direct ATP
remember: Direct ATP 4; NADH 10 × 3 = 30; FADH₂ 2 × 2 = 4; total 38
Fermentation: net 2 ATP, partial breakdown
38 is theoretical: real pathways run simultaneously
traps: Don't forget the 2 NADH from the link reaction when counting
Don't treat 38 ATP as an exact real-cell figure

topics.t: The amphibolic pathway
topics.h: The respiratory pathway is not a one-way street to the dump yard. It's a busy junction where raw materials are also picked up to build new molecules.
p: Glucose is the favoured substrate, but others can be respired.
Fats are first broken into glycerol and fatty acids. Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA and enter the pathway; glycerol enters after conversion to PGAL.
Proteins are degraded by proteases; amino acids (after deamination) enter at various points: within the Krebs cycle, or as pyruvate or acetyl CoA.
The same intermediates are withdrawn when the organism needs to make fatty acids or proteins (e.g. acetyl CoA is withdrawn to make fatty acids).
Since the respiratory pathway is involved in both catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (synthesis), it is better called an amphibolic pathway than a catabolic one.

ex.q: Where do glycerol and fatty acids from a fat enter the respiratory pathway?
st: Glycerol is converted to PGAL, an intermediate of glycolysis.
Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.
ex.a: Glycerol enters as PGAL; fatty acids as acetyl CoA.

topics.rl: Groundnut and mustard seeds, rich in oil, germinate by respiring stored fats through acetyl CoA, the same molecule they later use to build new fatty acids.

rv.summary: Besides glucose, fats and proteins can be respired: fatty acids enter as acetyl CoA, glycerol as PGAL, and deaminated amino acids as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs intermediates. Since intermediates are also withdrawn for synthesis, the pathway is amphibolic.
focus: Entry points of fats and proteins
remember: Fatty acids → acetyl CoA; glycerol → PGAL
Amino acids: deaminated, enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs intermediates
Amphibolic = catabolic + anabolic
traps: Don't call the respiratory pathway purely catabolic
Don't say glycerol enters as acetyl CoA

topics.t: Respiratory quotient (RQ)
topics.h: By measuring just two gases, CO₂ out and O₂ in, you can guess whether a seed is burning starch, oil or protein.
p: Respiratory quotient (RQ) = volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed in respiration. It depends on the respiratory substrate.
Carbohydrates (completely oxidised): equal volumes of CO₂ and O₂, so RQ = 1. For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O gives RQ = 6/6 = 1.
Fats: RQ is less than 1. Tripalmitin: 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O; RQ = 102/145 ≈ 0.7.
Proteins: RQ is about 0.9.
In living organisms, substrates are usually a mixture; pure proteins or fats are never used alone.

ex.q: Calculate the RQ for malic acid: C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O.
st: CO₂ evolved = 4; O₂ consumed = 3.
ex.a: RQ ≈ 1.33 (more than 1)

topics.rl: Seed technologists at ICAR institutes use respirometers to study seed respiration; oil-rich mustard seeds show RQ below 1 while starchy wheat grains show about 1.

rv.summary: Respiratory quotient (RQ) = volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed and depends on the substrate: carbohydrates 1, fats less than 1 (tripalmitin about 0.7), proteins about 0.9. Real organisms usually respire a mixture.
focus: Calculating RQ from a balanced equation
RQ values for carbohydrates, fats and proteins
remember: RQ = CO₂ evolved ÷ O₂ consumed
Glucose: 6/6 = 1
Tripalmitin: 102/145 ≈ 0.7
Proteins ≈ 0.9
traps: Don't invert the ratio (O₂ ÷ CO₂)
Don't say fats have RQ above 1

topics.t: Growth and development: an open-ended story
topics.h: A neem tree can keep growing for centuries, but you stop growing taller by your early twenties. Plants have a superpower: meristems that never retire.
p: Development is the sum of growth and differentiation, from the zygote to senescence. A seed germinates under favourable conditions and develops into a seedling and a mature plant.
Development is controlled by intrinsic factors (genetic, and intracellular chemicals such as plant growth regulators) and extrinsic factors (light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition).

Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or even a single cell. It is generally accompanied by metabolic processes (anabolic and catabolic) that use energy. Example: expansion of a leaf.

Plant growth is generally indeterminate: plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout life because of meristems, whose cells divide and self-perpetuate. New cells are always being added: the open form of growth.

Root and shoot apical meristems cause primary growth (elongation along the axis). In dicots and gymnosperms, lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, appear later and cause secondary growth (increase in girth).

ex.q: Classify the growth caused by (a) the shoot apical meristem and (b) the vascular cambium.
st: Apical meristems increase length along the axis: primary growth.
Vascular cambium is a lateral meristem that increases girth: secondary growth.
ex.a: (a) Primary growth; (b) secondary growth.

topics.rl: Teak trees in Madhya Pradesh and Kerala thicken year after year because their vascular cambium keeps adding wood, which is why mature teak is valuable timber.

rv.summary: Development is growth plus differentiation, from germination to senescence, controlled by intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Growth is an irreversible increase in size. Plant growth is indeterminate (open) because of meristems: apical meristems give primary growth, lateral meristems secondary growth.
remember: Growth = irreversible permanent increase in size
Apical meristems → primary growth (length)
Vascular cambium, cork cambium → secondary growth (girth)
traps: Don't call a temporary or reversible change growth
Don't credit secondary growth to apical meristems

topics.t: Measuring growth and the phases of growth
topics.h: A single maize root tip can make more than 17,500 new cells every hour. A watermelon cell can swell up to 3,50,000 times. Both are growth, measured differently.
p: At the cellular level, growth is mainly an increase in protoplasm. Since this is hard to measure, we measure quantities proportional to it: fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number.
One maize root apical meristem can give more than 17,500 new cells per hour (growth as cell number). Watermelon cells may increase in size up to 3,50,000 times (growth as cell size).
Pollen tube growth is measured as length; growth of a dorsiventral leaf as increase in surface area.
Meristematic phase: constantly dividing cells at root and shoot apices, rich in protoplasm with large nuclei; thin, primary cellulose walls with abundant plasmodesmata.

Elongation phase (just behind the meristem): increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new wall deposition. Maturation phase (further from the apex): cells reach maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.

ex.q: A maize root apical meristem makes 17,500 cells per hour. How many cells does it make in 4 hours?
st: Cells per hour = 17,500.
ex.a: 70,000 cells

topics.rl: Crop scientists at ICAR measure wheat growth by plant height, leaf area and dry weight to compare varieties in field trials.

rv.summary: Growth is mainly an increase in protoplasm, so it is measured by proportional quantities: weight, length, area, volume or cell number. The growing region has a meristematic phase, an elongation phase (vacuolation, enlargement) and a maturation phase.
focus: Ways to measure growth with examples
Three phases of growth and their cell features
remember: Maize root apex: over 17,500 new cells per hour
Watermelon cells: up to 3,50,000 times larger
Pollen tube: length; leaf: surface area
Meristematic → elongation → maturation
traps: Don't place vacuolation in the meristematic phase
Don't measure pollen tube growth by area

topics.t: Growth rates: arithmetic and geometric
topics.h: A cricket score growing 6 runs every over is arithmetic. A WhatsApp forward doubling every hour is geometric. Plant growth can follow either pattern.
p: Growth rate is the increase in growth per unit time.

Arithmetic growth: after mitosis, only one daughter cell keeps dividing; the other differentiates. A root elongating at a constant rate gives a linear curve: Lt = L₀ + rt (Lt = length at time t, L₀ = length at time zero, r = growth rate).

Geometric growth: both daughter cells keep dividing. Growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid and exponential (log phase), then slows as nutrients become limited (stationary phase), giving a sigmoid (S) curve, typical of organisms in natural environments.

Exponential growth: W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ, where W₁ is final size, W₀ initial size, r the relative growth rate (efficiency index), t time and e the base of natural logarithms. Final size depends on initial size.

Absolute growth rate: total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate: growth per unit time per unit initial size. Example: leaf A grows from 5 to 10 cm² and leaf B from 50 to 55 cm²: same absolute growth (5 cm²), but A has a relative rate of 100% and B only 10%.

ex.q: A root is 4 cm long and grows arithmetically at 0.5 cm per day. Find its length after 6 days.
st: Use Lt = L₀ + rt.
L₀ = 4 cm, r = 0.5 cm/day, t = 6 days.
ex.a: 7 cm

topics.rl: Bacterial cultures in Indian biotech labs and populations of crop pests both show S-shaped growth: slow, then explosive, then levelling off.

rv.summary: Growth rate is growth per unit time. Arithmetic growth (one daughter cell keeps dividing) gives a straight line, Lt = L₀ + rt. Geometric growth (both divide) gives a sigmoid curve of lag, log and stationary phases, W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ. Absolute and relative growth rates differ.
focus: Using Lt = L₀ + rt and W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ
remember: Lt = L₀ + rt (arithmetic, linear)
W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ; r = relative growth rate (efficiency index)
Sigmoid: lag → log → stationary
Relative rate = growth per unit time per unit initial size
traps: Don't confuse absolute with relative growth rate
Don't say growth is fastest in the stationary phase

topics.t: Conditions for growth; differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
topics.h: A xylem cell sacrifices its own living contents to become a water pipe. Some mature cells can even 'turn back the clock' and divide again.
p: Conditions for growth: water (cell enlargement needs it; turgidity aids extension growth; it is the medium for enzymes), oxygen (releases metabolic energy), nutrients (macro and micro elements for protoplasm and energy), an optimum temperature range, and environmental signals such as light and gravity.

Differentiation: cells from apical meristems and cambium mature to perform specific functions, with changes in walls and protoplasm. E.g. tracheary elements lose their protoplasm and develop strong, elastic lignocellulosic secondary walls to carry water under tension.
Dedifferentiation: living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain it, e.g. formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma.
Redifferentiation: cells produced by dedifferentiated tissues lose the capacity to divide again and mature to perform specific functions (e.g. secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork).

Differentiation in plants is open: cells from the same meristem mature differently depending on location, e.g. cells pushed away from the root apical meristem become root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery become epidermis.

ex.q: Classify each: (a) parenchyma forming interfascicular cambium; (b) cambium-derived cells maturing into secondary xylem; (c) meristem cells becoming tracheids.
st: (a) A mature cell regaining division: dedifferentiation.
(b) Products of dedifferentiated tissue maturing: redifferentiation.
(c) Meristem cells maturing into specialised cells: differentiation.
ex.a: (a) Dedifferentiation, (b) redifferentiation, (c) differentiation

topics.rl: Plant tissue culture labs in India, such as those producing banana and sugarcane plantlets, make parenchyma cells dedifferentiate into callus and then redifferentiate into shoots and roots.

rv.summary: Growth needs water, oxygen, nutrients and a suitable temperature. Differentiation matures meristem cells; dedifferentiation lets mature cells divide again (e.g. cork cambium); redifferentiation matures their products (secondary xylem). Plant differentiation is open, depending on location.
focus: Differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation with examples
remember: Tracheary elements: lose protoplasm, form lignocellulosic secondary walls
Dedifferentiation: parenchyma → interfascicular cambium, cork cambium
Redifferentiation: secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork
traps: Don't mix up dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
Don't say cells from one meristem always become the same tissue

topics.t: Development and plasticity
topics.h: A coriander seedling's first leaves are broad and round, but later leaves are feathery. Same plant, different leaf designs.
p: Development includes all changes an organism goes through in its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence.
The sequence involves cell division, growth, differentiation and maturation of cells leading to mature tissues and organs, and finally senescence.
Plasticity is the ability of plants to follow different developmental pathways in response to the environment or phase of life, forming different kinds of structures.
Heterophylly due to life phase: juvenile and mature leaves differ in shape in cotton, coriander and larkspur. Heterophylly due to environment: buttercup forms different leaves in air and in water.

Development (growth plus differentiation) is controlled by intrinsic factors (genes, PGRs) and extrinsic factors (environment). (Photoperiodism, vernalisation and seed dormancy are not part of this rationalised chapter.)

ex.q: Buttercup leaves under water are finely divided, while those in air are broader. Is this developmental or environmental heterophylly?
st: Both leaf types can be on the same plant at the same stage.
The difference is caused by growing in water versus air.
So it is heterophylly due to environment.
ex.a: Environmental heterophylly, an example of plasticity.

topics.rl: Coriander (dhania) in every Indian kitchen garden shows heterophylly: the first leaves are rounded, later leaves are finely divided.

rv.summary: Development covers all changes from germination to senescence: division, growth, differentiation, maturation. Plasticity lets plants form different structures by environment or life phase, e.g. heterophylly in cotton, coriander, larkspur (life phase) and buttercup (environment).
remember: Development = growth + differentiation
Life-phase heterophylly: cotton, coriander, larkspur
Environmental heterophylly: buttercup (air vs water)
traps: Don't call buttercup heterophylly developmental
Don't list light or water as intrinsic factors

topics.t: Plant growth regulators: nature and discovery
topics.h: One discovery began with 'foolish' rice seedlings in Japan that grew absurdly tall. Another began with ripe oranges that made stored bananas ripen faster.
p: PGRs are small, simple molecules of diverse chemistry: indole compounds (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA), adenine derivatives (N⁶-furfurylamino purine, kinetin), carotenoid derivatives (abscisic acid, ABA), terpenes (gibberellic acid, GA₃) and gases (ethylene, C₂H₄).

Growth promoters (cell division, enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting, seed formation): auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins. Growth inhibitors (responses to wounds and stress, dormancy, abscission): abscisic acid. Ethylene can fit either group but is largely an inhibitor.

Auxin: Charles and Francis Darwin saw canary grass coleoptiles bend towards unilateral light (phototropism) and found the tip was the site of a transmittable influence. F.W. Went isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips.

Gibberellin: E. Kurosawa found that sterile filtrates of the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease of rice, produced the symptoms in uninfected rice seedlings; the active substance was gibberellic acid. Cytokinin: Skoog and co-workers found tobacco callus grew only with extra supplements; Skoog and Miller crystallised kinetin. Kinetin came from autoclaved herring sperm DNA; zeatin was later isolated from corn kernels and coconut milk.

ABA: in the mid-1960s, inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin were found to be chemically identical and named abscisic acid. Ethylene: Cousins confirmed that ripened oranges release a volatile substance that hastened ripening of stored unripe bananas; it was identified as ethylene.

ex.q: Classify these PGRs by chemical nature: IAA, kinetin, ABA, GA₃, ethylene.
st: IAA: indole compound.
Kinetin: adenine derivative.
ABA: carotenoid derivative.
GA₃: terpene.
Ethylene: gas.
ex.a: Indole, adenine derivative, carotenoid derivative, terpene, gas.

topics.rl: Indian fruit sellers often keep a ripe banana or mango with unripe fruit to speed ripening, the same ethylene effect Cousins observed with oranges and bananas.

rv.summary: PGRs are small molecules of varied chemistry: IAA (indole), kinetin (adenine derivative), ABA (carotenoid derivative), GA₃ (terpene) and ethylene (gas). Auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins promote growth; ABA inhibits; ethylene is largely an inhibitor. Each was discovered by key experiments.
focus: Discovery of auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, ABA and ethylene
remember: Darwins: canary grass coleoptile tip; Went: auxin from oat coleoptile
Kurosawa: Gibberella fujikuroi, bakanae disease → gibberellic acid
Skoog and Miller: kinetin from herring sperm DNA; zeatin from corn, coconut milk
Inhibitor-B, abscission II, dormin = ABA; Cousins: ethylene from oranges
traps: Don't say Went worked on canary grass; that was the Darwins
Don't say kinetin came from coconut milk; it came from autoclaved herring sperm DNA (zeatin came from corn and coconut milk)

topics.t: Auxins: physiological effects
topics.h: Tea gardens in Assam and Darjeeling are pruned regularly so the bushes grow sideways into flat 'plucking tables'. The trick works by removing the auxin source.
p: Auxins (Greek auxein, to grow) were first isolated from human urine. Natural auxins: IAA and IBA (indole butyric acid). Synthetic: NAA (naphthalene acetic acid) and 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid). They are produced at growing apices of stems and roots and migrate to regions of action.

Uses: initiate rooting in stem cuttings (plant propagation); promote flowering, e.g. in pineapple; prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits.
Apical dominance: the growing apical bud inhibits growth of lateral (axillary) buds. Decapitation (removing the shoot tip) lets lateral buds grow; used in tea plantations and hedge-making.
Auxins induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes.
Auxins are used as herbicides: 2,4-D kills dicot weeds but does not affect mature monocots, so it is used for weed-free lawns. Auxin also controls xylem differentiation and helps in cell division.

ex.q: Why does 2,4-D sprayed on a lawn kill broad-leaved weeds but not the grass?
st: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin used as a herbicide.
It kills dicotyledonous weeds.
It does not affect mature monocots such as lawn grasses.
ex.a: It is selective: it kills dicot weeds but spares mature monocot grass.

topics.rl: Nursery owners across India dip stem cuttings of roses and bougainvillea in auxin (IBA/NAA) rooting powder to make them root faster.

rv.summary: Auxins (IAA, IBA natural; NAA, 2,4-D synthetic) are made at growing apices. They root cuttings, promote flowering in pineapple, control abscission, cause apical dominance, induce parthenocarpy in tomato, and 2,4-D kills dicot weeds. They also control xylem differentiation.
focus: Uses: rooting, flowering, parthenocarpy, weed control
remember: Natural: IAA, IBA; synthetic: NAA, 2,4-D
Apical dominance: apical bud inhibits lateral buds; decapitation removes it
2,4-D kills dicot weeds, spares mature monocots
traps: Don't call NAA or 2,4-D natural auxins
Don't say 2,4-D kills lawn grass

topics.t: Gibberellins and cytokinins
topics.h: Spraying sugarcane with gibberellins can add as much as 20 tonnes per acre to the yield. Sweet results from a hormone.
p: More than 100 gibberellins (GA₁, GA₂, GA₃ ...) are reported from fungi and higher plants; GA₃ (gibberellic acid) was among the first discovered and is the most studied. All GAs are acidic.

Gibberellin uses: increase axis length (longer grape stalks); elongate and improve shape of fruits like apple; delay senescence so fruits stay on the tree longer; speed up malting in brewing; increase sugarcane stem length and yield (up to 20 tonnes per acre); hasten maturity and early seed production in juvenile conifers; promote bolting (internode elongation just before flowering) in beet, cabbage and other rosette plants.
Cytokinins promote cytokinesis. Kinetin, a modified adenine (purine), does not occur naturally in plants; zeatin is a natural cytokinin from corn kernels and coconut milk.
Natural cytokinins are made where rapid cell division occurs: root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits.

Cytokinin effects: production of new leaves and chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoot formation; overcoming apical dominance; promoting nutrient mobilisation, which delays leaf senescence.

ex.q: A farmer wants cabbage to bolt for seed production and wants a stored leaf to stay green longer. Which PGR suits each?
st: Bolting (internode elongation before flowering) is promoted by gibberellins.
Delay of leaf senescence through nutrient mobilisation is a cytokinin effect.
ex.a: Gibberellins for bolting; cytokinins to delay leaf senescence.

topics.rl: Sugarcane growers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra may use gibberellins to lengthen stems, and table-grape farmers in Nashik use GA₃ to lengthen bunches and enlarge berries.

rv.summary: Gibberellins (GA₃ best studied) lengthen axes (grape stalks, sugarcane), delay senescence, speed malting and cause bolting. Cytokinins (kinetin, natural zeatin) promote cell division, new leaves and chloroplasts, lateral shoots and delay leaf senescence.
focus: Natural vs synthetic cytokinins and where they are made
remember: GA₃: malting, bolting, grape stalks, sugarcane yield up to 20 t/acre
Kinetin: modified adenine, not natural; zeatin: natural
Cytokinins: overcome apical dominance, delay leaf senescence
traps: Don't credit bolting to cytokinins
Don't call kinetin a natural plant hormone

topics.t: Ethylene and abscisic acid
topics.h: One gas ripens mangoes and pineapples in Indian markets; another hormone tells plants to shut their stomata when drought hits. Meet ethylene and ABA.
p: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR made in large amounts by senescing tissues and ripening fruits. In dicot seedlings it causes horizontal growth, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation (the triple response).

Ethylene promotes senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers; is highly effective in fruit ripening, raising the respiration rate (respiratory climacteric); breaks seed and bud dormancy (germination of peanut, sprouting of potato tubers); promotes rapid internode and petiole elongation in deep-water rice; promotes root growth and root hairs; initiates flowering and synchronises fruit-set in pineapple; induces flowering in mango.

Ethephon is the most widely used source of ethylene; in water it is absorbed and releases ethylene slowly. It hastens ripening in tomatoes and apples, accelerates abscission (thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut) and promotes female flowers in cucumber.
Abscisic acid (ABA) regulates abscission and dormancy; it is a general inhibitor of growth and metabolism, and inhibits seed germination.

ABA stimulates stomatal closure and increases tolerance to stresses, so it is the stress hormone. It is important in seed development, maturation and dormancy, helping seeds withstand desiccation. In most situations ABA is an antagonist of GAs.

ex.q: Why do farmers use ethephon on cucumber crops?
st: Ethephon releases ethylene slowly inside the plant.
Ethylene promotes female flowers in cucumbers.
More female flowers mean more fruits.
ex.a: To increase female flowers and hence the yield.

topics.rl: Fruit traders in India are allowed to use ethylene gas (not calcium carbide, which is banned by FSSAI) in ripening chambers for mangoes and bananas.

rv.summary: Ethylene, a gas from ripening fruits, causes the triple response, promotes abscission and ripening (respiratory climacteric) and breaks dormancy; ethephon supplies it. ABA, the stress hormone, closes stomata, inhibits growth and germination, and induces seed dormancy.
focus: Effects of ABA and why it is the stress hormone
remember: Triple response: horizontal growth, axis swelling, apical hook
Ethylene: ripening, climacteric, flowering in pineapple and mango, deep-water rice elongation
Ethephon: ripening, thinning, female flowers in cucumber
ABA: stomatal closure, dormancy, antagonist of GAs
traps: Don't say ABA breaks seed dormancy
Don't say ethylene delays fruit ripening

topics.t: Interaction of PGRs and practical applications
topics.h: Plant hormones rarely act alone. Like players in a cricket team, they combine, compete or cover for each other.
p: Every phase of growth, differentiation and development is influenced by one PGR or another. Their roles may be complementary or antagonistic, individualistic or synergistic.
Many events involve interaction of more than one PGR: dormancy in seeds and buds, abscission, senescence and apical dominance.
Apical dominance: auxin from the apex maintains it, while cytokinins help overcome it. Dormancy: ABA maintains it, while GAs and ethylene can break it.
PGRs are only one kind of intrinsic control; along with genomic control and extrinsic factors they regulate growth and development.

Practical choices: rooting of cuttings (auxin, IBA/NAA); weed control in lawns (2,4-D); seedless tomato (auxin); longer grape stalks, malting, sugarcane yield, bolting (GAs); fruit ripening, female flowers in cucumber, flowering in pineapple and mango (ethylene/ethephon); stomatal closure under drought (ABA); delay leaf senescence (cytokinin).

ex.q: Pick a PGR for each: (a) speed up malting, (b) make stored tomatoes ripen evenly, (c) root a hibiscus cutting.
st: (a) Malting is speeded up by GA₃.
(b) Ripening is hastened by ethylene, released from ethephon.
(c) Rooting of cuttings is initiated by auxins such as IBA or NAA.
ex.a: (a) Gibberellin, (b) ethylene (ethephon), (c) auxin

topics.rl: Horticulture departments in states like Maharashtra and Himachal train farmers to use the right PGR at the right dose, because wrong use can damage crops or leave residues.

rv.summary: Every phase of plant growth is influenced by PGRs, which may act complementarily, antagonistically, individually or synergistically. Apical dominance (auxin vs cytokinin) and dormancy (ABA vs GA and ethylene) involve several PGRs. The right PGR is chosen for each practical task.
focus: Events controlled by more than one PGR
Choosing the right PGR for a practical use
remember: Rooting: IBA/NAA; lawn weeds: 2,4-D; seedless tomato: auxin
GAs: grape stalks, malting, sugarcane, bolting
Ethylene/ethephon: ripening, cucumber female flowers, pineapple and mango flowering
ABA: drought stomatal closure; cytokinin: delay leaf senescence
traps: Don't use ABA to break dormancy; GAs and ethylene break it
Don't think one PGR alone controls apical dominance

topics.t: Breathing and respiratory organs across animals
topics.h: A sponge breathes through its whole body, an insect through a network of air tubes, a fish through gills and you through lungs. Same goal, different plumbing.
p: Breathing is the exchange of O₂ from the atmosphere with CO₂ produced by the cells. It is different from cellular respiration, which is the use of O₂ in cells to break down food.
Lower invertebrates (sponges, coelenterates, flatworms) exchange gases by simple diffusion over the whole body surface.
Earthworms use their moist cuticle; insects have a network of tracheal tubes carrying air within the body.
Gills (branchial respiration) are used by most aquatic arthropods and molluscs and by fishes. Lungs (pulmonary respiration) are used by terrestrial forms: reptiles, birds and mammals.
Amphibians such as frogs can also respire through their moist skin (cutaneous respiration).

ex.q: Classify the respiratory surface: (a) cockroach, (b) rohu fish, (c) earthworm, (d) frog under water.
st: (a) Insects use tracheal tubes.
(b) Fishes use gills.
(c) Earthworms use the moist cuticle.
(d) Frogs under water use moist skin (cutaneous).
ex.a: Tracheae, gills, moist cuticle, skin.

topics.rl: Indian mountaineers acclimatise at base camps on Everest because thinner air at altitude makes breathing harder for the lungs.

rv.summary: Breathing exchanges atmospheric O₂ for CO₂ made by cells; cellular respiration uses O₂ to break down food. Simple animals use diffusion over the body surface, earthworms their moist cuticle, insects tracheae, aquatic animals gills and land vertebrates lungs; frogs also use skin.
focus: Respiratory surfaces in different animal groups
remember: Sponges, coelenterates, flatworms: simple diffusion
Earthworm: moist cuticle; insects: tracheal tubes
Gills (branchial): fishes, aquatic arthropods, molluscs; lungs (pulmonary): reptiles, birds, mammals
traps: Don't treat breathing and cellular respiration as the same
Don't say insects use lungs

topics.t: The human respiratory system
topics.h: Your lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny alveoli. Spread out, their surface area would be about the size of a badminton court.
p: Path of air: external nostrils (above the upper lip) → nasal passage → nasal chamber → pharynx (common passage for food and air) → larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary and tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → alveoli.

The larynx is a cartilaginous box for sound production (sound box). During swallowing the glottis is covered by a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, the epiglottis, preventing food from entering the larynx.

The trachea extends to the mid-thoracic cavity and divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi. The trachea, bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings.

Alveoli are very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures where gas exchange occurs. The lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between, which reduces friction.

Conducting part (nostrils to terminal bronchioles) transports, filters, humidifies and warms air; exchange (respiratory) part (alveoli and their ducts) is the site of diffusion. The lungs lie in an air-tight thoracic chamber formed by the vertebral column (dorsal), sternum (ventral), ribs (lateral) and dome-shaped diaphragm (below). Steps of respiration: pulmonary ventilation, alveolar diffusion, transport of gases by blood, diffusion between blood and tissues, and cellular respiration.

ex.q: Trace a breath of air from the nostrils to the site of gas exchange.
st: Nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx.
Larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary and tertiary bronchi.
Bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → alveoli (gas exchange).
ex.a: Nostrils → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli

topics.rl: Doctors at AIIMS and other hospitals advise N95 masks on high-AQI days in Delhi because fine particles can slip past the conducting part and reach the alveoli.

rv.summary: Air passes nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The epiglottis guards the larynx; cartilage rings support the airways; alveoli are the exchange sites; the pleura covers the lungs in an air-tight thoracic chamber floored by the diaphragm.
focus: Path of air to the alveoli
Roles of larynx, epiglottis and cartilage rings
remember: Trachea divides at 5th thoracic vertebra
Epiglottis covers glottis in swallowing
Pleura: double layer with pleural fluid
Steps: ventilation, alveolar diffusion, transport, tissue diffusion, cellular respiration
traps: Don't say gas exchange occurs in the bronchi
Don't confuse epiglottis with glottis

topics.t: Mechanism of breathing
topics.h: Your lungs have no muscles of their own. A dome-shaped muscle below them and small muscles between your ribs do all the pumping.
p: Breathing has two stages: inspiration (air drawn in) and expiration (alveolar air released). Air moves because of a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere.
Inspiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure (negative pressure); expiration when it is higher.

Inspiration: the diaphragm contracts, increasing thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis; the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs and sternum and increasing volume in the dorso-ventral axis. Pulmonary volume rises, pressure falls, and air rushes in.

Expiration: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, thoracic and pulmonary volume decrease, intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric, and air is expelled. Additional abdominal muscles can increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.
A healthy human breathes 12 to 16 times per minute. A spirometer measures volumes of air in breathing and helps clinical assessment of lung function.

ex.q: What happens to intra-pulmonary pressure when the diaphragm contracts, and why?
st: Diaphragm contraction increases thoracic volume.
Lung volume increases with it.
Greater volume means lower pressure (below atmospheric), so air flows in.
ex.a: It falls below atmospheric pressure, causing inspiration.

topics.rl: Yoga pranayama practised across India trains slow, deep breathing using the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.

rv.summary: Breathing moves air down a pressure gradient. In inspiration the diaphragm and external intercostals contract, enlarging the thorax and lowering lung pressure below atmospheric; in expiration they relax and pressure rises. Abdominal muscles aid forced breathing; we breathe 12–16 times a minute.
focus: Pressure changes in inspiration and expiration
Roles of diaphragm and external intercostals
remember: Inspiration: lung pressure < atmospheric
Diaphragm: antero-posterior axis; external intercostals: dorso-ventral axis
Normal rate 12–16 per minute; spirometer measures air volumes
traps: Don't say the lungs pump air by their own muscles
Don't say the diaphragm contracts in normal expiration

topics.t: Respiratory volumes and capacities
topics.h: Athletes and wind-instrument players often have large vital capacities. A spirometer can tell how much air you can move in one big breath.
p: Tidal volume (TV): air inspired or expired in normal breathing, about 500 mL. So a healthy person breathes about 6000 to 8000 mL per minute (minute ventilation = TV × breaths per minute).

Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV): extra air inspired by forcible inspiration, 2500 to 3000 mL. Expiratory reserve volume (ERV): extra air expired by forcible expiration, 1000 to 1100 mL. Residual volume (RV): air left after forcible expiration, 1100 to 1200 mL.
Inspiratory capacity (IC) = TV + IRV. Expiratory capacity (EC) = TV + ERV. Functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV.

Vital capacity (VC) = ERV + TV + IRV: the maximum air a person can breathe in after forced expiration (or out after forced inspiration). It indicates the strength of the lungs and respiratory muscles.
Total lung capacity (TLC) = VC + RV = RV + ERV + TV + IRV: total air in the lungs at the end of forced inspiration.

ex.q: TV = 500 mL, IRV = 2500 mL, ERV = 1000 mL, RV = 1200 mL. Find VC and TLC.
ex.a: VC = 4000 mL; TLC = 5200 mL

topics.rl: Spirometry tests at Indian hospitals help diagnose asthma and occupational lung disease by comparing measured volumes with expected values.

rv.summary: Tidal volume is about 500 mL; IRV 2500–3000 mL; ERV 1000–1100 mL; RV 1100–1200 mL. Capacities are sums: IC = TV + IRV, EC = TV + ERV, FRC = ERV + RV, VC = ERV + TV + IRV, TLC = VC + RV.
focus: Values of TV, IRV, ERV and RV
Formulae for IC, EC, FRC, VC and TLC
remember: TV ≈ 500 mL; minute ventilation 6000–8000 mL
VC = ERV + TV + IRV
TLC = VC + RV
FRC = ERV + RV
traps: Don't include RV in vital capacity
Don't confuse expiratory reserve volume with residual volume

topics.t: Exchange of gases at the alveoli and tissues
topics.h: Oxygen moves into your blood without any pump. It simply slides 'downhill' from high to low partial pressure.
p: Alveoli are the primary sites of gas exchange; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues. O₂ and CO₂ move by simple diffusion along pressure (concentration) gradients. Solubility and membrane thickness also matter.

Partial pressure is the pressure contributed by one gas in a mixture (pO₂, pCO₂). In mm Hg: atmosphere O₂ 159, CO₂ 0.3; alveoli O₂ 104, CO₂ 40; deoxygenated blood O₂ 40, CO₂ 45; oxygenated blood O₂ 95, CO₂ 40; tissues O₂ 40, CO₂ 45.
So O₂ diffuses from alveoli (104) to deoxygenated blood (40), and from oxygenated blood (95) to tissues (40). CO₂ diffuses from tissues (45) to blood and from deoxygenated blood (45) to alveoli (40).
CO₂ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than O₂, so more CO₂ diffuses per unit difference in partial pressure.

The diffusion membrane has three layers: thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and basement substance between them. Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre.

ex.q: Using the table, find the pO₂ gradient between alveoli and deoxygenated blood.
st: Alveolar pO₂ = 104 mm Hg.
Deoxygenated blood pO₂ = 40 mm Hg.
Gradient = 104 - 40 = 64 mm Hg.
ex.a: 64 mm Hg

topics.rl: At high-altitude places like Leh, atmospheric pO₂ is lower, the alveolar gradient shrinks, and visitors feel breathless until they acclimatise.

rv.summary: O₂ and CO₂ are exchanged by simple diffusion down partial pressure gradients at the alveoli and tissues. O₂ moves alveoli (104) → blood (40) and blood (95) → tissues (40); CO₂ moves the other way. CO₂ is 20–25 times more soluble than O₂, and the three-layer membrane is very thin.
focus: Partial pressures of O₂ and CO₂ at each site
Direction of diffusion of each gas
remember: pO₂: air 159, alveoli 104, deoxygenated blood 40, oxygenated blood 95, tissues 40
pCO₂: air 0.3, alveoli 40, deoxygenated blood 45, oxygenated blood 40, tissues 45
CO₂ 20–25 times more soluble than O₂
traps: Don't say CO₂ is actively pumped
Don't list the pleura as a layer of the diffusion membrane

topics.t: Transport of oxygen
topics.h: Haemoglobin is a smart carrier: it grabs oxygen in the lungs and lets it go in hard-working muscles, exactly where it's needed.
p: About 97% of O₂ is carried by RBCs (bound to haemoglobin); about 3% is dissolved in plasma.
Haemoglobin is a red, iron-containing pigment in RBCs. O₂ binds reversibly to form oxyhaemoglobin; each haemoglobin molecule can carry at most four O₂ molecules.
Binding depends mainly on pO₂; pCO₂, hydrogen ion concentration and temperature also affect it.

The oxygen dissociation curve (percentage saturation of haemoglobin vs pO₂) is sigmoid. In alveoli, high pO₂, low pCO₂, low H⁺ and lower temperature favour oxyhaemoglobin formation; in tissues, low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺ and higher temperature favour dissociation.
Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O₂ to the tissues under normal conditions.

ex.q: If cardiac output is 5000 mL of blood per minute, how much O₂ (mL) reaches the tissues per minute?
st: Each 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL O₂.
5000 mL blood = 50 × 100 mL.
O₂ delivered = 50 × 5 = 250 mL per minute.
ex.a: About 250 mL O₂ per minute

topics.rl: During a cricket match in Chennai's heat, a fast bowler's warm, CO₂-rich, acidic muscles pull more O₂ off haemoglobin, just as the dissociation curve predicts.

rv.summary: About 97% of O₂ travels bound to haemoglobin in RBCs and 3% dissolved in plasma. Each haemoglobin carries up to four O₂. Binding depends mainly on pO₂, giving a sigmoid dissociation curve; high pO₂ in alveoli loads O₂, low pO₂, high pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature in tissues unload it.
focus: How O₂ is carried in blood
remember: 97% via RBCs, 3% in plasma
Max 4 O₂ per haemoglobin
Dissociation curve: sigmoid
~5 mL O₂ delivered per 100 mL oxygenated blood
traps: Don't say most O₂ is carried dissolved in plasma
Don't say high pCO₂ favours O₂ binding

topics.t: Transport of carbon dioxide
topics.h: Most of the CO₂ you breathe out travelled from your cells disguised as bicarbonate ions, thanks to one super-fast enzyme.
p: CO₂ transport: about 20 to 25% by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 70% as bicarbonate, and about 7% dissolved in plasma.
Carbamino-haemoglobin formation depends on pCO₂, and pO₂ also affects it. In tissues (high pCO₂, low pO₂) more CO₂ binds; in alveoli (low pCO₂, high pO₂) CO₂ is released.
RBCs have a very high concentration of carbonic anhydrase (small amounts in plasma). It catalyses both directions: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺.

At tissues, high pCO₂ drives formation of HCO₃⁻ and H⁺; at alveoli, low pCO₂ reverses the reaction, releasing CO₂ and H₂O. So CO₂ is trapped as bicarbonate in tissues and released as CO₂ in the lungs.
Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂ to the alveoli.

ex.q: Why does carbonic anhydrase make CO₂ in the tissues but release CO₂ in the lungs?
st: The enzyme speeds the reaction in both directions.
In tissues, pCO₂ is high, so CO₂ + H₂O → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺.
In alveoli, pCO₂ is low, so HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O, and CO₂ is breathed out.
ex.a: The direction is set by pCO₂: high in tissues (forms bicarbonate), low in alveoli (releases CO₂).

topics.rl: Blood gas tests in Indian ICUs measure bicarbonate levels to check how well a patient's body is handling CO₂.

rv.summary: CO₂ travels about 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 70% as bicarbonate and about 7% dissolved. Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs converts CO₂ + H₂O to HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ in tissues (high pCO₂) and reverses it in alveoli (low pCO₂). 100 mL deoxygenated blood gives up about 4 mL CO₂.
focus: Direction of the reaction in tissues vs alveoli
remember: CO₂: 20–25% carbamino-Hb, ~70% bicarbonate, ~7% dissolved
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ (carbonic anhydrase)
~4 mL CO₂ delivered per 100 mL deoxygenated blood
traps: Don't say most CO₂ travels as carbamino-haemoglobin
Don't say bicarbonate forms in the alveoli

topics.t: Regulation of respiration
topics.h: Hold your breath and the urge to breathe grows stronger. Surprisingly, it's rising CO₂, not falling O₂, that sounds the alarm.
p: Humans can moderate their respiratory rhythm to suit the body's demands; this is done by the neural system.
The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla region of the brain is mainly responsible for regulation.
The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the rhythm centre; its signals can reduce the duration of inspiration and so alter the respiratory rate.

A chemosensitive area next to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺; a rise activates it, and it signals the rhythm centre to adjust breathing and eliminate them. Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also detect changes in CO₂ and H⁺.
The role of oxygen in regulating respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

ex.q: During a 400 m race, CO₂ and H⁺ rise in the blood. Trace how breathing speeds up.
st: The chemosensitive area (and aortic and carotid receptors) detect higher CO₂ and H⁺.
They signal the respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla.
The rhythm centre increases the rate and depth of breathing to remove CO₂.
ex.a: Chemoreceptors detect CO₂/H⁺ → rhythm centre in medulla → faster, deeper breathing.

topics.rl: Free divers and pearl divers, such as those once common in the Gulf of Mannar, learn to tolerate the CO₂ build-up that triggers the urge to breathe.

rv.summary: Breathing is regulated by the neural system. The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the rhythm; the pneumotaxic centre in the pons can shorten inspiration. A chemosensitive area and aortic and carotid receptors sense rising CO₂ and H⁺; O₂ plays an insignificant role.
focus: Locations and roles of the rhythm and pneumotaxic centres
Chemical regulation by CO₂ and H⁺
remember: Rhythm centre: medulla; pneumotaxic centre: pons
Chemosensitive area: sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺
Receptors: aortic arch, carotid artery
Role of O₂: quite insignificant
traps: Don't say O₂ level is the main regulator of breathing
Don't place the pneumotaxic centre in the medulla

topics.t: Disorders of the respiratory system
topics.h: Stone-crushing workers in parts of Rajasthan breathe dust all day. Without masks, their lungs slowly scar.
p: Asthma: difficulty in breathing causing wheezing, due to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
Emphysema: a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, so the respiratory surface decreases. Cigarette smoking is one of the major causes.

Occupational respiratory disorders: in industries involving grinding or stone-breaking, so much dust is produced that the body's defences cannot cope. Long exposure causes inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue) and serious lung damage.
Workers in such industries should wear protective masks.
Prevention: avoid smoking, reduce exposure to dust and polluted air, and seek early medical care for persistent breathlessness.

ex.q: Why does emphysema cause breathlessness?
st: Alveolar walls are damaged.
The total respiratory surface for gas exchange decreases.
Less O₂ can diffuse into the blood.
ex.a: Damaged alveoli reduce the surface for gas exchange.

topics.rl: Silicosis among stone-quarry and sandstone workers is recognised as an occupational disease in India, and masks and wet-drilling methods are promoted to prevent it.

rv.summary: Asthma is wheezing from inflamed bronchi and bronchioles. Emphysema is chronic damage to alveolar walls that reduces the respiratory surface; smoking is a major cause. Occupational dust exposure causes inflammation and fibrosis; masks, avoiding smoking and early care help prevent harm.
remember: Asthma: inflamed bronchi and bronchioles, wheezing
Emphysema: damaged alveolar walls; smoking a major cause
Fibrosis: proliferation of fibrous tissue from long dust exposure
traps: Don't confuse asthma (airway inflammation) with emphysema (alveolar damage)
Don't say dust exposure improves lung defences

topics.t: Body fluids, blood and plasma
topics.h: When you donate blood at a camp, the bag looks red, but more than half of it is a straw-coloured liquid called plasma.
p: All cells need a supply of nutrients and O₂ and removal of wastes, so organisms have circulating fluids. Simple organisms such as sponges and coelenterates circulate water from their surroundings through body cavities. Blood and lymph are the most common body fluids in higher animals.
Blood is a special connective tissue made of a fluid matrix (plasma) and formed elements.

Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid forming nearly 55% of blood. It is 90 to 92% water; proteins make up 6 to 8%. It also has minerals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻) and glucose, amino acids and lipids in transit.
Main plasma proteins: fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence mechanisms) and albumins (osmotic balance). Clotting factors are present in inactive form.
Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

ex.q: A blood sample is 5 L. About how much of it is plasma?
st: Plasma is nearly 55% of blood.
ex.a: About 2.75 L

topics.rl: Blood banks in India separate donated blood into components; plasma is used to treat burns, shock and clotting disorders.

rv.summary: Blood is a special connective tissue of plasma (about 55%) and formed elements. Plasma is 90–92% water and 6–8% proteins: fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence), albumins (osmotic balance). Serum is plasma without clotting factors. Simple animals circulate water instead.
focus: Roles of the three plasma proteins
remember: Plasma ≈ 55% of blood; 90–92% water, 6–8% proteins
Fibrinogen: clotting; globulins: defence; albumins: osmotic balance
Serum = plasma − clotting factors
traps: Don't credit clotting to globulins
Don't confuse serum with plasma

topics.t: Formed elements: RBCs, WBCs and platelets
topics.h: During dengue season in India, doctors anxiously watch one number on the blood report: the platelet count.
p: Formed elements (RBCs, WBCs and platelets) make up nearly 45% of blood. RBCs are the most abundant: 5 to 5.5 million per mm³ in a healthy adult man. They are formed in red bone marrow in adults, lack a nucleus in most mammals and are biconcave.

RBCs contain haemoglobin, a red, iron-containing protein; a healthy person has 12 to 16 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL of blood. RBCs live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen (graveyard of RBCs).

WBCs (leucocytes) are colourless, nucleated, short-lived, 6000 to 8000 per mm³. Granulocytes: neutrophils (60 to 65%, most abundant, phagocytic), eosinophils (2 to 3%, resist infections, allergic reactions), basophils (0.5 to 1%, least, secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin; inflammation).
Agranulocytes: lymphocytes (20 to 25%, B and T types, immune responses) and monocytes (6 to 8%, phagocytic).

Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments from megakaryocytes in bone marrow, 1,50,000 to 3,50,000 per mm³. They release substances involved in clotting; a fall in their number causes clotting disorders and excessive blood loss.

ex.q: A WBC count is 8000 per mm³. About how many of these are neutrophils if they form 60%?
st: Neutrophils = 60% of 8000.
ex.a: 4800 per mm³

topics.rl: In dengue, common after the monsoon in India, platelet counts can fall below 1,50,000 per mm³, raising the risk of bleeding.

rv.summary: Formed elements are about 45% of blood. RBCs (5–5.5 million/mm³, biconcave, mostly enucleate) carry haemoglobin and live about 120 days. WBCs (6000–8000/mm³) are granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) or agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes). Platelets from megakaryocytes aid clotting.
focus: RBC count, structure, haemoglobin and lifespan
Types of WBCs with percentages and roles
remember: RBC: 5–5.5 million/mm³; 120 days; destroyed in spleen; Hb 12–16 g/100 mL
Neutrophils 60–65%, eosinophils 2–3%, basophils 0.5–1%, lymphocytes 20–25%, monocytes 6–8%
Platelets: 1,50,000–3,50,000/mm³ from megakaryocytes
traps: Don't call lymphocytes the most abundant WBC
Don't say low platelets speed clotting

topics.t: Blood groups: ABO, Rh and erythroblastosis foetalis
topics.h: In an emergency, an O-negative donor's blood can save almost anyone. But mixing the wrong groups can be fatal. Blood groups decide.
p: ABO grouping is based on two surface antigens (A and B) on RBCs and two natural antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) in plasma.

Group A: antigen A, anti-B; can receive A, O. Group B: antigen B, anti-A; can receive B, O. Group AB: antigens A and B, no antibodies; can receive AB, A, B, O. Group O: no antigens, anti-A and anti-B; can receive only O.
Group O individuals are universal donors; group AB individuals are universal recipients.

The Rh antigen (similar to one in Rhesus monkeys) is present on RBCs of nearly 80% of humans (Rh+ve); those without it are Rh-ve. An Rh-ve person exposed to Rh+ve blood forms antibodies, so Rh should also be matched before transfusion.

Erythroblastosis foetalis: an Rh-ve mother with an Rh+ve foetus may be exposed to foetal blood during the first delivery and make anti-Rh antibodies. In later pregnancies these can leak into the Rh+ve foetus and destroy its RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice or even death. It is prevented by giving the mother anti-Rh antibodies immediately after the first delivery.

ex.q: A person of blood group B needs blood. Which groups can safely donate?
st: Group B has antigen B and anti-A antibodies.
Donor RBCs must not carry antigen A.
So donors of group B and O are safe.
ex.a: B and O

topics.rl: Hospitals and blood banks across India, linked through e-RaktKosh, cross-match ABO and Rh groups before every transfusion.

rv.summary: ABO groups depend on A and B antigens on RBCs and anti-A, anti-B antibodies in plasma; O is the universal donor and AB the universal recipient. About 80% of people are Rh+ve. An Rh-ve mother with an Rh+ve foetus risks erythroblastosis foetalis in later pregnancies.
focus: Antigens and antibodies of each ABO group
remember: A: antigen A, anti-B; B: antigen B, anti-A; AB: both antigens, no antibodies; O: no antigens, both antibodies
O = universal donor; AB = universal recipient
Rh+ve ≈ 80% of humans
traps: Don't call AB the universal donor
Don't say an Rh+ve mother with an Rh-ve foetus causes erythroblastosis

topics.t: Coagulation of blood and lymph
topics.h: Scrape your elbow in a game of kabaddi and within minutes a dark scab forms. That's a cascade of enzymes building a net of fibrin threads.
p: Coagulation (clotting) in response to injury prevents excessive blood loss. A clot (coagulum) is mainly a network of fibrin threads in which dead and damaged formed elements are trapped.

Fibrin is formed from inactive fibrinogen by the enzyme thrombin; thrombin is formed from inactive prothrombin by the enzyme complex thrombokinase, produced by a cascade of linked enzyme reactions involving plasma factors.
Injury stimulates platelets to release factors that activate coagulation; factors released by injured tissues can also start it. Calcium ions play a very important role.

As blood passes through tissue capillaries, water and small soluble substances move into spaces between cells, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements in the vessels. This interstitial (tissue) fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma and is the medium of exchange between blood and cells.

The lymphatic system collects this fluid and drains it into major veins; the fluid inside it is lymph: colourless, containing lymphocytes for immunity, carrying nutrients and hormones, and absorbing fats through lacteals in intestinal villi. Unlike blood, lymph lacks RBCs and has fewer proteins.

ex.q: Write the clotting cascade in order from injury to clot.
st: Injury: platelets and tissues release factors.
A cascade forms thrombokinase.
Thrombokinase converts prothrombin to thrombin (Ca²⁺ needed).
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, whose threads trap cells to form a clot.
ex.a: Injury → thrombokinase → prothrombin to thrombin → fibrinogen to fibrin → clot

topics.rl: Blood banks add citrate (which binds calcium) to donated blood bags to stop the blood from clotting during storage.

rv.summary: Clotting: injury releases factors, a cascade makes thrombokinase, which turns prothrombin into thrombin; thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin threads that trap cells; Ca²⁺ is vital. Tissue fluid is drained as lymph, which has lymphocytes and no RBCs.
remember: Thrombokinase: prothrombin → thrombin
Thrombin: fibrinogen → fibrin
Ca²⁺ essential for clotting
Lacteals absorb fats; lymph has no RBCs
traps: Don't say thrombokinase acts on fibrinogen
Don't say lymph contains RBCs

topics.t: Circulatory pathways and evolution of the vertebrate heart
topics.h: A fish heart sends blood on one loop; your heart runs two separate loops at once. Evolution kept adding chambers.
p: Open circulatory system (arthropods, molluscs): blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or body cavities called sinuses.
Closed circulatory system (annelids, chordates): blood always circulates through a closed network of vessels; flow can be regulated more precisely, so it is more advantageous.
Fishes: 2-chambered heart (one atrium, one ventricle); the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills, oxygenated blood goes to the body and returns: single circulation.

Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles): 3-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle). The left atrium gets oxygenated blood and the right atrium deoxygenated blood, but they mix in the single ventricle: incomplete double circulation.
Crocodiles, birds and mammals: 4-chambered heart (two atria, two ventricles); oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate: double circulation.

ex.q: Why is circulation in a frog called incomplete double circulation?
st: Blood passes through the heart twice (from body and from lungs/skin).
But both atria empty into a single ventricle.
So oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix.
ex.a: Because the two kinds of blood mix in the single ventricle.

topics.rl: Doctors at AIIMS treat babies born with holes in the heart septum, where oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, much like in an amphibian heart.

rv.summary: Open circulation uses sinuses; closed circulation keeps blood in vessels. Fishes have a 2-chambered heart and single circulation; amphibians and most reptiles a 3-chambered heart with incomplete double circulation; crocodiles, birds and mammals a 4-chambered heart with double circulation.
focus: Heart chambers in each vertebrate group
Single, incomplete double and double circulation
remember: Fish: 1 atrium + 1 ventricle, single circulation
Amphibians, reptiles: 2 atria + 1 ventricle, incomplete double circulation
Crocodiles, birds, mammals: 4 chambers, double circulation
traps: Don't say fishes have double circulation
Don't forget crocodiles have a 4-chambered heart

topics.t: The human heart: structure, valves and nodal tissue
topics.h: Your heart has its own built-in electrician, the SA node, which fires about 72 times a minute without any instruction from the brain.
p: The human circulatory (blood vascular) system has a muscular chambered heart, a closed network of branching blood vessels, and blood.

The heart is mesodermal, lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left, about the size of a clenched fist. It is protected by a double-walled pericardium with pericardial fluid. It has two small upper atria and two larger lower ventricles; ventricle walls are much thicker than atrial walls.

A thin inter-atrial septum separates the atria; a thick inter-ventricular septum separates the ventricles; a thick fibrous atrio-ventricular septum separates atrium and ventricle of each side, with openings between them.

Valves: tricuspid valve (three cusps) between right atrium and right ventricle; bicuspid (mitral) valve between left atrium and left ventricle; semilunar valves at the openings of the pulmonary artery and aorta. Valves allow one-way flow and prevent backflow.

Nodal tissue: the sino-atrial node (SAN) in the right upper corner of the right atrium; the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) in the lower left corner of the right atrium near the AV septum; the AV bundle passes through the septa and divides into right and left bundles giving Purkinje fibres (the bundles with Purkinje fibres form the bundle of His). Nodal tissue is autoexcitable. The SAN generates the most action potentials (70 to 75 per minute) and is the pacemaker.

ex.q: Trace the impulse from the pacemaker to the ventricular muscles.
st: SAN (pacemaker) fires and the atria contract.
The impulse reaches the AVN.
It travels through the AV bundle, right and left bundles and Purkinje fibres.
The ventricular muscles contract.
ex.a: SAN → AVN → AV bundle → right and left bundles → Purkinje fibres → ventricles

topics.rl: Cardiologists at Indian hospitals implant artificial pacemakers when a patient's SA node or conduction system fails.

rv.summary: The human heart is a mesodermal, fist-sized organ in a double pericardium, with two atria and two thick-walled ventricles separated by septa. Tricuspid, bicuspid and semilunar valves keep flow one-way. Autoexcitable nodal tissue (SAN pacemaker, AVN, AV bundle, Purkinje fibres) starts each beat.
focus: Why the SAN is the pacemaker
remember: Tricuspid: right AV; bicuspid (mitral): left AV; semilunar: pulmonary artery and aorta
SAN: right upper corner of right atrium; 70–75 action potentials/min
SAN → AVN → AV bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
traps: Don't put the bicuspid valve on the right side
Don't call the AVN the pacemaker

topics.t: The cardiac cycle, cardiac output and heart sounds
topics.h: 'Lub-dub, lub-dub': each beat your doctor hears through a stethoscope is the sound of heart valves snapping shut.
p: Joint diastole: all four chambers relaxed; tricuspid and bicuspid valves open; blood flows from the pulmonary veins and vena cava through the atria into the ventricles; semilunar valves closed.
Atrial systole: the SAN fires, both atria contract, increasing ventricular filling by about 30%. The impulse passes via the AVN, AV bundle and bundle of His to the ventricles.
