Ventricular systole (atria relax): ventricular pressure rises, closing the tricuspid and bicuspid valves; further rise opens the semilunar valves and blood flows into the pulmonary artery and aorta. Ventricular diastole: pressure falls, semilunar valves close; AV valves open as atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; joint diastole again.

At 72 beats per minute, one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s. Each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (stroke volume). Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, about 5000 mL (5 L) per minute; it is much higher in athletes.
First heart sound (lub): closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves. Second heart sound (dub): closure of semilunar valves. These sounds have clinical diagnostic significance.

ex.q: Calculate cardiac output for a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 72 beats per minute.
st: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
70 × 72 = 5040 mL per minute.
That is about 5 L per minute.
ex.a: 5040 mL/min (about 5 L/min)

topics.rl: Cardiologists at Indian hospitals use a stethoscope to listen for abnormal 'murmurs' between lub and dub, which can signal faulty valves, such as after rheumatic heart disease.

rv.summary: The cardiac cycle runs joint diastole → atrial systole (adds about 30% filling) → ventricular systole (AV valves close, semilunar valves open) → ventricular diastole. Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ 5 L/min. Lub is AV valve closure; dub is semilunar valve closure.
focus: Events of each phase of the cardiac cycle
remember: Cycle ≈ 0.8 s at 72 beats/min
Stroke volume ≈ 70 mL; cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min
Lub: tricuspid + bicuspid close; dub: semilunar close
traps: Don't swap lub and dub
Don't divide stroke volume by heart rate for cardiac output

topics.t: ECG and double circulation
topics.h: An ECG strip in an emergency ward is a story in waves: P, QRS and T tell a doctor exactly what the heart's electrical system is doing.
p: An electrocardiograph records the electrical activity of the heart during the cardiac cycle as an ECG. A standard ECG uses three leads: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle; more chest leads give detail.

P wave: electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, leading to atrial contraction. QRS complex: depolarisation of the ventricles, initiating ventricular contraction; contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole. T wave: return of ventricles to normal (repolarisation); the end of T marks the end of systole.

Counting QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart rate. Since ECGs have roughly the same shape for a given lead setup, deviations indicate possible abnormality, so the ECG has great clinical significance.

Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → arteries, arterioles, capillaries → tissues → venules, veins, vena cava → right atrium.

The hepatic portal system carries blood from the intestine to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before it enters systemic circulation. The coronary system circulates blood to and from the heart muscle.

ex.q: An ECG strip shows 18 QRS complexes in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate?
st: Each QRS complex is one heartbeat.
Heart rate = 72 beats per minute.
ex.a: 72 beats per minute

topics.rl: Portable ECG machines are now used in rural health centres under India's health programmes to catch heart attacks early.

rv.summary: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity: P wave (atrial depolarisation), QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation) and T wave (ventricular repolarisation); counting QRS complexes gives heart rate. Double circulation has pulmonary and systemic circuits.
focus: Meaning of P, QRS and T
Standard ECG leads and heart rate from ECG
remember: P: atria depolarise; QRS: ventricles depolarise; T: ventricles repolarise
Leads: both wrists and left ankle
Pulmonary: RV → lungs → LA; systemic: LV → body → RA
traps: Don't call the T wave depolarisation
Don't start pulmonary circulation from the left ventricle

topics.t: Regulation of the heart and circulatory disorders
topics.h: India has one of the world's largest numbers of people with high blood pressure, and many don't know it. A simple BP check can save lives.
p: The heart is myogenic: its activity is auto-regulated by nodal tissue. A neural centre in the medulla oblongata moderates it through the autonomic nervous system: sympathetic signals increase heart rate, strength of ventricular contraction and cardiac output; parasympathetic signals decrease heart rate, conduction speed and cardiac output. Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output.

Hypertension: blood pressure higher than normal (120/80 mm Hg; 120 is systolic or pumping pressure, 80 is diastolic or resting pressure). Repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension, which leads to heart disease and affects the brain and kidneys.

Coronary artery disease (atherosclerosis): deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow the lumen of arteries supplying the heart muscle. Angina (angina pectoris): acute chest pain when not enough O₂ reaches the heart muscle; more common in middle-aged and elderly people.

Heart failure: the heart cannot pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs; also called congestive heart failure because lung congestion is a main symptom. It is not the same as cardiac arrest (heart stops beating) or heart attack (heart muscle suddenly damaged by inadequate blood supply).

Quick recap for exams: ABO compatibility depends on antigens and antibodies; the SAN is the pacemaker; open circulation uses sinuses while closed uses vessels; ECG waves P, QRS and T reflect atrial and ventricular electrical events.

ex.q: A person's BP readings over three visits are 142/92, 145/94 and 140/90. Interpret.
st: Normal BP is 120/80 mm Hg.
Repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension.
All three are at or above 140/90.
ex.a: The person has hypertension.

topics.rl: The India Hypertension Control Initiative screens adults at primary health centres, because uncontrolled BP damages the heart, brain and kidneys.

rv.summary: The heart is myogenic; a medulla centre moderates it through the ANS (sympathetic speeds it, parasympathetic slows it) and adrenal hormones raise output. Disorders: hypertension (repeated ≥140/90 mm Hg vs normal 120/80), coronary artery disease, angina and heart failure.
focus: Heart failure vs cardiac arrest vs heart attack
remember: Normal BP 120/80 mm Hg: systolic/diastolic
Hypertension: repeated ≥140/90 mm Hg
Atherosclerosis: calcium, fat, cholesterol, fibrous tissue in coronary arteries
Heart failure = ineffective pumping, lung congestion
traps: Don't call heart failure the same as cardiac arrest
Don't say parasympathetic signals raise heart rate

topics.t: Nitrogenous wastes and excretory structures in animals
topics.h: A pigeon's white droppings and a fish's invisible ammonia are both ways of getting rid of nitrogen. The choice depends on how much water an animal can spare.
p: The major nitrogenous wastes are ammonia, urea and uric acid. Ammonia is the most toxic and needs a large amount of water for removal; uric acid is the least toxic and can be removed with minimum water loss.

Ammonotelism (excreting ammonia): many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects. Ammonia, being readily soluble, diffuses out across body or gill surfaces as ammonium ions; kidneys play no significant role.

Ureotelism (excreting urea): mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes. Ammonia is converted to urea in the liver, released into blood and excreted by kidneys; some urea may be retained in the kidney matrix to maintain osmolarity.
Uricotelism (excreting uric acid as pellet or paste with minimum water loss): reptiles, birds, land snails and insects. Terrestrial life favoured less toxic wastes to conserve water.

Excretory structures: protonephridia or flame cells (Platyhelminthes such as Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, Amphioxus; mainly osmoregulation); nephridia (earthworm and other annelids); Malpighian tubules (most insects, including cockroaches); antennal or green glands (crustaceans such as prawns).

ex.q: Why do birds excrete uric acid instead of ammonia?
st: Ammonia is very toxic and needs a lot of water to remove.
Uric acid is the least toxic and can be removed as a paste with minimum water loss.
This conserves water on land and during flight.
ex.a: To conserve water; uric acid needs very little water.

topics.rl: White bird droppings on Mumbai's Marine Drive railings are mostly uric acid paste, a water-saving trick of uricotelic birds.

rv.summary: Animals excrete ammonia (most toxic, needs much water), urea or uric acid (least toxic, minimum water). Bony fishes are ammonotelic, mammals ureotelic, and reptiles and birds uricotelic. Excretory organs include flame cells, nephridia, Malpighian tubules and green glands.
focus: Toxicity and water need of ammonia, urea and uric acid
remember: Ammonia most toxic; uric acid least toxic
Urea is made in the liver
Flame cells: Planaria; nephridia: earthworm; Malpighian tubules: insects; green glands: prawn
traps: Don't say kidneys make urea; the liver does
Don't call birds ureotelic

topics.t: The human excretory system and the kidney
topics.h: Your two kidneys are each about the size of your fist and weigh only 120 to 170 g, yet they filter about 180 litres of fluid a day.
p: The human excretory system has a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.

Kidneys are reddish-brown, bean-shaped, between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity. Each adult kidney is 10 to 12 cm long, 5 to 7 cm wide, 2 to 3 cm thick and weighs 120 to 170 g.
The hilum is a notch on the inner concave surface through which the ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter. Inner to it is the funnel-shaped renal pelvis with projections called calyces.
The outer layer is a tough capsule. Inside are the outer cortex and inner medulla; the medulla forms conical medullary pyramids projecting into the calyces.
The cortex extends between medullary pyramids as renal columns, the columns of Bertini.

ex.q: List the path of urine from the kidney to the outside.
st: Urine collects in the calyces and renal pelvis.
It passes down the ureter.
It is stored in the urinary bladder.
It leaves through the urethra.
ex.a: Renal pelvis → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra

topics.rl: Ultrasound scans at Indian hospitals measure kidney length; a normal adult kidney of about 10 to 12 cm is reassuring.

rv.summary: The human excretory system has two kidneys, two ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. Bean-shaped kidneys lie between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae. Each has a hilum, renal pelvis with calyces, an outer cortex and inner medulla with pyramids, and columns of Bertini.
focus: Organs of the human excretory system
Position, size and weight of the kidney
Internal structure: hilum, pelvis, calyces, cortex, medulla, columns of Bertini
remember: Location: last thoracic to third lumbar vertebrae
Columns of Bertini: cortex between medullary pyramids
traps: Don't confuse renal pelvis with calyces; calyces are projections of the pelvis
Don't place medullary pyramids in the cortex

topics.t: The nephron: the kidney's working unit
topics.h: Each of your kidneys has about a million nephrons. Laid end to end, the tubules would stretch for kilometres.
p: Each kidney has nearly one million nephrons, the functional units. Each nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule.
The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole (a branch of the renal artery); blood leaves it by the efferent arteriole.

The renal tubule begins as the double-walled, cup-like Bowman's capsule enclosing the glomerulus; together they form the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle). Then come the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), the hairpin-shaped Henle's loop (descending and ascending limbs), the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), and collecting ducts into which many DCTs open; collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids.

The Malpighian corpuscle, PCT and DCT lie in the cortex; Henle's loop dips into the medulla. Cortical nephrons have a short loop barely reaching the medulla; juxtamedullary nephrons have a very long loop running deep into the medulla.

The efferent arteriole forms peritubular capillaries around the tubule; a minute vessel running parallel to Henle's loop forms the U-shaped vasa recta, which is absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons.

ex.q: Trace the path of filtrate through a nephron.
st: Filtrate forms in Bowman's capsule.
It flows through the PCT.
Then through the descending and ascending limbs of Henle's loop.
Then the DCT, and into the collecting duct.
ex.a: Bowman's capsule → PCT → Henle's loop → DCT → collecting duct

topics.rl: Doctors use kidney biopsies at AIIMS to see nephron damage under the microscope in diseases such as glomerulonephritis.

rv.summary: Each kidney has about one million nephrons. A nephron has a glomerulus (from the afferent arteriole) inside Bowman's capsule, then PCT, Henle's loop, DCT and collecting duct. Cortical nephrons have short loops and little vasa recta; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops.
focus: Parts of a nephron in order
Blood supply: afferent, efferent arterioles, peritubular capillaries, vasa recta
Which parts lie in cortex and medulla
remember: Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule = Malpighian body
Bowman's capsule → PCT → Henle's loop → DCT → collecting duct
Cortex: Malpighian corpuscle, PCT, DCT; medulla: Henle's loop
traps: Don't say the efferent arteriole forms the glomerulus
Don't say cortical nephrons have long loops

topics.t: Urine formation: glomerular filtration and GFR
topics.h: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid every day, enough to fill nine 20-litre water cans, yet you pass only about 1.5 litres of urine.
p: Urine forms by three processes: glomerular filtration, reabsorption and secretion, in different parts of the nephron.
About 1100 to 1200 mL of blood is filtered by the kidneys per minute, roughly one-fifth of the blood pumped by each ventricle per minute.

Glomerular capillary blood pressure filters blood through three layers: endothelium of glomerular vessels, epithelium of Bowman's capsule (podocytes with filtration slits or slit pores), and the basement membrane between them. Almost everything in plasma except proteins passes through, so it is ultrafiltration.
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR), the filtrate formed per minute, is about 125 mL/min, i.e. 180 litres per day.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), formed by cellular modifications in the DCT and afferent arteriole where they touch, regulates GFR. A fall in GFR activates JG cells to release renin, which restores glomerular blood flow and GFR.

ex.q: Show that a GFR of 125 mL/min equals 180 L per day.
st: Minutes in a day = 60 × 24 = 1440.
ex.a: 180 L per day

topics.rl: Nephrologists in India estimate GFR from blood creatinine to grade chronic kidney disease, which is common among people with diabetes and hypertension.

rv.summary: Urine forms by glomerular filtration, reabsorption and secretion. Kidneys filter 1100–1200 mL blood per minute through endothelium, basement membrane and podocyte epithelium; this ultrafiltration gives a GFR of about 125 mL/min (180 L/day). The JGA releases renin when GFR falls.
remember: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min = 180 L/day
Filtration membrane: endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes
Low GFR → JG cells release renin
traps: Don't say proteins pass into the filtrate
Don't confuse renal blood flow (1100–1200 mL/min) with GFR (125 mL/min)

topics.t: Reabsorption, secretion, and the PCT and Henle's loop
topics.h: Of 180 litres filtered daily, only about 1.5 litres leave as urine. Your tubules recover about 99% of the filtrate.
p: Comparing 180 L of filtrate per day with about 1.5 L of urine shows that nearly 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.
Reabsorption is active for glucose, amino acids, Na⁺ etc., and passive for nitrogenous wastes; water is reabsorbed passively in the initial segments.
Tubular secretion of H⁺, K⁺ and ammonia into the filtrate helps maintain ionic and acid-base balance.

PCT: simple cuboidal brush-border epithelium increases surface area. It reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients and 70 to 80% of electrolytes and water, maintains pH and ionic balance by secreting H⁺, NH₃ and K⁺ and absorbing HCO₃⁻.

Henle's loop: minimal reabsorption, but it maintains high osmolarity of the medullary interstitium. The descending limb is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes (filtrate becomes concentrated). The ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes (filtrate becomes dilute).

ex.q: What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed if 180 L is filtered and 1.8 L of urine is produced?
st: Reabsorbed = 180 - 1.8 = 178.2 L.

topics.rl: Diabetic patients in India sometimes show sugar in urine because blood glucose exceeds what the PCT can actively reabsorb.

rv.summary: About 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed: actively for glucose, amino acids and Na⁺, passively for nitrogenous wastes and early water. Secretion of H⁺, K⁺ and NH₃ keeps ionic and acid-base balance. The PCT reabsorbs most nutrients and 70–80% of electrolytes and water.
focus: Permeability of the two limbs of Henle's loop
remember: ~99% of filtrate reabsorbed
PCT: brush-border cuboidal epithelium; 70–80% electrolytes and water
Descending limb: water-permeable; ascending limb: water-impermeable, transports electrolytes
traps: Don't swap the permeabilities of the descending and ascending limbs
Don't say nitrogenous wastes are reabsorbed actively

topics.t: DCT, collecting duct and the counter-current mechanism
topics.h: Camels and kangaroo rats make very concentrated urine. Humans can make urine about four times as concentrated as the filtrate, thanks to a clever counter-current design.
p: DCT: conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water; reabsorbs HCO₃⁻; selectively secretes H⁺, K⁺ and NH₃ to maintain pH and sodium-potassium balance.

Collecting duct: runs from cortex to inner medulla; large amounts of water can be reabsorbed to make concentrated urine; lets small amounts of urea into the medullary interstitium to keep up osmolarity; secretes H⁺ and K⁺ for pH and ionic balance.

Counter-current: filtrate flows in opposite directions in the two limbs of Henle's loop, and blood flows in opposite directions in the two limbs of the vasa recta. Their closeness maintains increasing osmolarity of the medullary interstitium from 300 mOsmol L⁻¹ (cortex) to about 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹ (inner medulla).

The gradient is mainly due to NaCl and urea. NaCl from the ascending limb is exchanged with the descending limb of the vasa recta and returned to the interstitium by its ascending limb. Small amounts of urea enter the thin ascending limb and are returned to the interstitium by the collecting tubule.
This interstitial gradient lets water pass easily out of the collecting tubule, concentrating urine. Human kidneys can make urine nearly four times as concentrated as the initial filtrate.

ex.q: If the medullary interstitium rises from 300 to 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹, by what factor does osmolarity increase?
st: This matches urine about four times as concentrated as the filtrate.
ex.a: 4 times

topics.rl: During summer in Rajasthan, ADH and the counter-current system together help people conserve water by producing small volumes of concentrated urine.

rv.summary: The DCT conditionally reabsorbs Na⁺ and water; the collecting duct reabsorbs much water. Counter-current flow in Henle's loop and vasa recta builds a medullary gradient from 300 to about 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹ using NaCl and urea, so urine can be about four times as concentrated as filtrate.
focus: Functions of the DCT and collecting duct
Medullary osmotic gradient and its solutes
remember: Gradient: 300 (cortex) → 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹ (inner medulla)
Gradient solutes: NaCl and urea
Urine up to ~4 times as concentrated as filtrate
traps: Don't say glucose builds the medullary gradient
Don't place conditional Na⁺ reabsorption in the PCT

topics.t: Regulation of kidney function
topics.h: After a long, sweaty cricket match you pass very little, dark urine. A hormone called ADH has quietly told your kidneys to save water.
p: Kidney function is regulated by hormonal feedback involving the hypothalamus, the JGA and, to some extent, the heart. Osmoreceptors respond to changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration.

Excess fluid loss activates osmoreceptors, which stimulate the hypothalamus to release ADH (vasopressin) from the neurohypophysis. ADH increases water reabsorption from the later parts of the tubule, preventing diuresis. An increase in body fluid switches off osmoreceptors and suppresses ADH. ADH also constricts blood vessels, raising BP and GFR.

Renin-angiotensin mechanism: a fall in glomerular blood flow, pressure or GFR activates JG cells to release renin, which converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I and then angiotensin II. Angiotensin II, a powerful vasoconstrictor, raises glomerular blood pressure and GFR.
Angiotensin II also activates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which causes reabsorption of Na⁺ and water from distal parts of the tubule, raising BP and GFR.
A rise in blood flow to the atria causes release of atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which causes vasodilation and lowers BP. ANF acts as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.

ex.q: Order the renin-angiotensin steps after a fall in GFR.
st: JG cells release renin.
Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
Angiotensin I becomes angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone release, raising BP and GFR.
ex.a: Renin → angiotensin I → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone

topics.rl: Many BP medicines prescribed in India (ACE inhibitors such as enalapril) work by blocking the formation of angiotensin II.

rv.summary: Fluid loss triggers ADH (from the neurohypophysis) to increase water reabsorption. Low GFR triggers renin → angiotensin I → angiotensin II, which constricts vessels and releases aldosterone. ANF from the atria dilates vessels and checks this system.
remember: ADH (vasopressin) from neurohypophysis: more water reabsorbed
Renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → angiotensin II
Angiotensin II: vasoconstriction + aldosterone from adrenal cortex
ANF from atria: vasodilation, lowers BP
traps: Don't say extra water intake raises ADH
Don't say ANF raises blood pressure

topics.t: Micturition, urine composition and other excretory organs
topics.h: Your lungs breathe out about 200 mL of CO₂ every minute, and your sweat carries a little urea. Kidneys are not the only exit doors for waste.
p: Urine is stored in the urinary bladder until the CNS gives a voluntary signal. As the bladder fills and stretches, stretch receptors send signals to the CNS; the CNS sends motor messages to contract the bladder's smooth muscles and relax the urethral sphincter. Release of urine is micturition; its neural mechanism is the micturition reflex.
An adult excretes 1 to 1.5 L of urine per day: a light yellow, watery, slightly acidic (pH 6.0) fluid with a characteristic odour; about 25 to 30 g of urea is excreted daily.
Urine analysis helps diagnose disease: glucose (glycosuria) and ketone bodies (ketonuria) in urine indicate diabetes mellitus.

Lungs remove large amounts of CO₂ (about 200 mL/min) and water. The liver, the largest gland, secretes bile containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs, which mostly pass out with faeces.

Skin: sweat (watery fluid with NaCl, small amounts of urea, lactic acid) mainly cools the body but also removes some wastes; sebaceous glands remove sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through sebum, which gives an oily protective covering. Small amounts of nitrogenous wastes are also lost through saliva.

ex.q: If an adult excretes 27 g of urea per day, how much is that over a week?
st: Urea per day = 27 g.
Per week = 27 × 7 = 189 g.

topics.rl: Routine urine tests in Indian health check-ups look for sugar and ketones, early signs of diabetes, a fast-growing health problem in India.

rv.summary: Urine is stored in the bladder and released by the micturition reflex. Adults pass 1–1.5 L/day of slightly acidic urine (pH 6.0) with 25–30 g urea; glucose or ketones in it suggest diabetes. Lungs, liver (bile), skin (sweat, sebum) and saliva also remove wastes.
focus: Excretory roles of lungs, liver and skin
remember: Urine: 1–1.5 L/day, pH 6.0, 25–30 g urea/day
Glycosuria, ketonuria → diabetes mellitus
Lungs remove ~200 mL CO₂/min
Sebum: sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes
traps: Don't say the bladder relaxes during micturition
Don't call normal urine alkaline

topics.t: Disorders of the excretory system
topics.h: Thousands of Indians with kidney failure stay alive thanks to a machine that cleans their blood several times a week: the artificial kidney.
p: Uremia: malfunctioning kidneys lead to accumulation of urea in the blood; it is highly harmful and may lead to kidney failure.

Haemodialysis: blood from an artery is mixed with an anticoagulant (heparin) and pumped through a coiled cellophane tube in dialysing fluid that has the same composition as plasma except nitrogenous wastes. Wastes move out down their concentration gradient; cleared blood gets anti-heparin and returns through a vein.
Kidney transplantation is the ultimate method to correct acute renal failure. The donor kidney is preferably from a close relative to minimise the chance of rejection by the immune system.
Renal calculi: stones or insoluble masses of crystallised salts (oxalates etc.) formed in the kidney.
Glomerulonephritis: inflammation of the glomeruli of the kidney.

ex.q: Why does dialysing fluid contain no nitrogenous wastes but the same salts as plasma?
st: Substances diffuse across the cellophane down their concentration gradient.
With no urea in the fluid, urea moves out of the blood.
With the same salts as plasma, useful ions do not leave the blood.
ex.a: So wastes diffuse out while useful salts stay in balance.

topics.rl: The Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme supports dialysis services at district hospitals in India, free for poor patients with kidney failure.

rv.summary: Uremia is urea build-up in blood from kidney malfunction. Haemodialysis pumps heparinised arterial blood through cellophane tubing in fluid like plasma but without nitrogenous wastes, then adds anti-heparin. Kidney transplant from a close relative is the ultimate cure.
remember: Haemodialysis: heparin in, anti-heparin before return
Dialysing fluid = plasma minus nitrogenous wastes
Donor preferably a close relative to reduce rejection
traps: Don't say dialysing fluid is pure water
Don't confuse renal calculi with glomerulonephritis

topics.t: Movement, locomotion and types of movement
topics.h: When you blink, you move but stay in place. When you run a 100 m dash, you move and change location. Only one of them is locomotion.
p: Movement is a significant feature of living beings: streaming of protoplasm in Amoeba, movement of cilia, flagella and tentacles, and in humans movement of limbs, jaws, eyelids and tongue.
Locomotion is voluntary movement that results in a change of place or location (walking, running, climbing, flying, swimming). All locomotions are movements, but all movements are not locomotions.

The same structures can serve both: Paramoecium uses cilia to move food through the cytopharynx and for locomotion; Hydra uses tentacles to capture prey and to move; we use limbs for posture changes and locomotion.

Human cells show three main movements. Amoeboid movement: macrophages and leucocytes move by pseudopodia formed by protoplasmic streaming; cytoskeletal microfilaments are involved. Ciliary movement: in tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium, e.g. cilia in the trachea remove dust, and cilia help ova pass through the female reproductive tract.
Muscular movement: movement of limbs, jaws and tongue uses the contractile property of muscles. Locomotion needs perfectly coordinated activity of the muscular, skeletal and neural systems.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a WBC squeezing through a capillary, (b) dust being swept up the trachea, (c) chewing food.
st: (a) Pseudopodia by protoplasmic streaming: amoeboid movement.
(b) Coordinated beating of cilia: ciliary movement.
(c) Jaw muscles contracting: muscular movement.
ex.a: (a) Amoeboid, (b) ciliary, (c) muscular

topics.rl: Neeraj Chopra's javelin throw is a perfect example of muscular, skeletal and neural systems working in precise coordination.

rv.summary: Movement is a key feature of life; locomotion is voluntary movement that changes location, so all locomotions are movements but not all movements are locomotions. Human cells show amoeboid (leucocytes, macrophages), ciliary (trachea, oviducts) and muscular movement.
focus: Three types of movement in human cells with examples
remember: All locomotions are movements, not all movements are locomotions
Amoeboid: macrophages, leucocytes (pseudopodia)
Ciliary: trachea, female reproductive tract
Locomotion needs muscular, skeletal and neural systems
traps: Don't call blinking or chewing locomotion
Don't say leucocytes move by cilia

topics.t: Muscle: properties and types
topics.h: About 40 to 50% of your body weight is muscle. That's like a 60 kg student carrying 24 to 30 kg of muscle everywhere.
p: Muscle is a specialised tissue of mesodermal origin, contributing about 40 to 50% of an adult human's body weight.
Special properties of muscle: excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.
Skeletal muscles: closely associated with skeletal components; striped (striated) under the microscope; under voluntary control (voluntary muscles); mainly for locomotion and posture changes.

Visceral muscles: in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs such as the alimentary canal and reproductive tract; no striations (smooth or non-striated); involuntary; help move food through the gut and gametes through the genital tract.
Cardiac muscles: muscles of the heart; many cells assemble in a branching pattern; striated but involuntary, since the nervous system does not control them directly.

ex.q: A 60 kg adult has muscles making up 45% of body weight. What is the mass of muscle?
st: Muscle mass = 45% of 60 kg.
ex.a: 27 kg

topics.rl: Gym trainers in Indian cities train skeletal (voluntary) muscles, but no amount of willpower can directly speed up your cardiac or gut muscles.

rv.summary: Muscle is a mesodermal tissue making up 40–50% of body weight, with excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity. Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary; visceral muscle is smooth and involuntary; cardiac muscle is striated, branched and involuntary.
focus: Three types of muscle and where they occur
remember: Muscle: mesodermal, 40–50% of body weight
Skeletal: striated, voluntary
Visceral: non-striated, involuntary
Cardiac: striated, involuntary
traps: Don't call skeletal muscle non-striated
Don't call cardiac muscle voluntary

topics.t: Structure of skeletal muscle and the sarcomere
topics.h: Under a microscope, a muscle fibre looks like a barcode of light and dark stripes. Each stripe pattern repeats in tiny units called sarcomeres.
p: A skeletal muscle is made of bundles called fascicles held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer, the fascia. Each fascicle contains many muscle fibres.

Each muscle fibre is lined by the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) enclosing the sarcoplasm; it has many nuclei, so it is a syncytium. Its sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions. The sarcoplasm has many parallel myofibrils (myofilaments).
Myofibrils show alternate light and dark bands due to actin and myosin. The light I band (isotropic) contains actin (thin filaments); the dark A band (anisotropic) contains myosin (thick filaments).
An elastic fibre, the Z line, bisects each I band; thin filaments are attached to it. Thick filaments are held together in the middle of the A band by the M line.

The sarcomere, the portion between two successive Z lines, is the functional unit of contraction. At rest, thin filaments partially overlap the ends of thick filaments; the central part of the thick filaments not overlapped is the H zone.

ex.q: Label the bands and lines from one Z line to the next in a resting sarcomere.
st: Z line, then half an I band (actin only).
The A band (myosin) begins; at its centre is the H zone, bisected by the M line.
The A band ends, then half an I band, then the next Z line.
ex.a: Z line → ½ I band → A band (with H zone and M line) → ½ I band → Z line

topics.rl: Sports physiologists at the National Institute of Sports, Patiala, study muscle biopsies to understand how training changes muscle fibres.

rv.summary: Skeletal muscle has fascicles of multinucleate fibres whose myofibrils carry the bands. Myofibrils show light I bands (actin) bisected by Z lines and dark A bands (myosin) with H zone and M line. The sarcomere, Z line to Z line, is the unit of contraction.
focus: A band, I band, Z line, M line, H zone
remember: I band: actin, light, isotropic; A band: myosin, dark, anisotropic
Z line bisects I band; M line bisects A band
Sarcomere = Z line to Z line
Sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca²⁺
traps: Don't put myosin in the I band
Don't call the H zone the region of overlap; it is the non-overlapped centre

topics.t: Contractile proteins: actin and myosin
topics.h: Myosin heads are tiny motors that grab actin, pull and let go, hundreds of times a second, powered by ATP.
p: Each actin (thin) filament has two F (filamentous) actins helically wound around each other; each F actin is a polymer of G (globular) actin monomers.
Two filaments of tropomyosin run close to the F actins along their length.
The complex protein troponin is distributed at regular intervals on tropomyosin. At rest, a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on actin.

Each myosin (thick) filament is a polymer of many monomers called meromyosins. Each meromyosin has a globular head with a short arm, the heavy meromyosin (HMM), and a tail, the light meromyosin (LMM).

The HMM (head and short arm) projects outwards at regular distances and angles from the thick filament as a cross arm. The globular head is an active ATPase enzyme with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.

ex.q: Why can a resting muscle not contract even if ATP is present?
st: Myosin heads need to bind actin to form cross bridges.
At rest, a troponin subunit masks the myosin-binding sites on actin.
Until Ca²⁺ removes this masking, cross bridges cannot form.
ex.a: Troponin masks the actin sites until Ca²⁺ arrives.

topics.rl: Muscle cramps after heavy training at Indian sports academies are linked to problems in this actin-myosin cycle and in calcium and energy supply.

rv.summary: A thin filament has two helically wound F actins (polymers of G actin), two tropomyosin strands and troponin, which masks myosin-binding sites at rest. A thick filament is a polymer of meromyosins, each with a heavy meromyosin head and arm (cross arm, an ATPase) and a light meromyosin tail.
focus: Structure of meromyosin: HMM and LMM
remember: F actin = polymer of G actin; two F actins per thin filament
Troponin masks actin sites at rest
HMM: head + short arm (cross arm); LMM: tail
Myosin head: ATPase with ATP and actin sites
traps: Don't say tropomyosin is made of meromyosin
Don't call LMM the head

topics.t: Mechanism of muscle contraction: the sliding filament theory
topics.h: When you lift your school bag, millions of thin filaments slide over thick ones. The filaments themselves don't get shorter at all.
p: Sliding filament theory: a muscle fibre contracts by the sliding of thin filaments over thick filaments.

A signal from the CNS travels via a motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction (motor end plate), releasing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, which generates an action potential in the sarcolemma. It spreads through the fibre and causes release of Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasm.

Ca²⁺ binds a subunit of troponin, unmasking the active sites on actin. Using energy from ATP hydrolysis, the myosin head binds actin to form a cross bridge and pulls the actin towards the centre of the A band. The Z lines are pulled inward, shortening the sarcomere.

During contraction, the I bands shorten (and the H zone narrows), while the A bands keep their length. Myosin releases ADP and Pi and goes back to its relaxed state; a new ATP binds, breaking the cross bridge; the cycle repeats.
When Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic cisternae, actin sites are masked again and the Z lines return to their original positions: relaxation.

ex.q: Put the events of muscle contraction in order, from the nerve signal to sarcomere shortening.
st: Motor neuron signal reaches the neuromuscular junction; acetylcholine is released.
Action potential spreads in the sarcolemma; Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing actin sites.
Myosin heads form cross bridges using ATP energy and pull actin inward; the sarcomere shortens.
ex.a: Signal → acetylcholine → action potential → Ca²⁺ release → troponin binding → cross bridges → sliding

topics.rl: Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu's lifts depend on rapid, repeated cross-bridge cycles in her muscles, each powered by ATP.

rv.summary: In the sliding filament theory, acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction triggers Ca²⁺ release; Ca²⁺ binds troponin to expose actin sites, and myosin heads use ATP to form cross bridges and pull actin inward. I bands shorten; A bands do not. Ca²⁺ pumped back causes relaxation.
focus: Sequence of events from nerve signal to contraction
Roles of acetylcholine, Ca²⁺, troponin and ATP
remember: Neurotransmitter: acetylcholine
Ca²⁺ + troponin → actin sites exposed
New ATP breaks the cross bridge
A band constant; I band shortens; Z lines pulled inward
traps: Don't say actin or myosin filaments shorten
Don't say the A band shortens

topics.t: Motor units, fatigue, and red versus white fibres
topics.h: Marathon runners and sprinters train very different muscles. One relies on oxygen-loving red fibres, the other on quick white fibres.
p: A motor neuron together with the muscle fibres connected to it forms a motor unit.
Reaction time of fibres varies in different muscles.
Repeated activation of muscles can cause accumulation of lactic acid from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, causing fatigue.
Red fibres: high content of the red, oxygen-storing pigment myoglobin; plenty of mitochondria using stored O₂ for ATP; called aerobic muscles.
White fibres: very little myoglobin, so pale; few mitochondria but a large amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum; depend on anaerobic processes for energy.

ex.q: A muscle fibre has lots of myoglobin and mitochondria. Classify it and say how it gets energy.
st: High myoglobin gives a red colour.
Many mitochondria use stored oxygen.
So it is a red, aerobic fibre.
ex.a: Red fibre; aerobic ATP production.

topics.rl: Marathon runners at events like the Mumbai Marathon rely on red, aerobic fibres for endurance, while 100 m sprinters rely more on white fibres for short bursts.

rv.summary: A motor neuron and its muscle fibres form a motor unit. Lactic acid build-up causes fatigue. Red fibres have much myoglobin and many mitochondria (aerobic); white fibres have little myoglobin, few mitochondria and much sarcoplasmic reticulum (anaerobic).
remember: Fatigue: lactic acid from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen
Red fibres: high myoglobin, many mitochondria, aerobic
White fibres: little myoglobin, few mitochondria, much sarcoplasmic reticulum, anaerobic
traps: Don't say white fibres have more myoglobin
Don't call red fibres anaerobic

topics.t: The skeleton: axial skeleton, skull and vertebral column
topics.h: A newborn has about 300 bones, but many fuse, leaving an adult with 206. Eighty of them run along your body's central axis.
p: The skeletal system is a framework of bones and a few cartilages. Bone has a very hard matrix due to calcium salts; cartilage has a slightly pliable matrix due to chondroitin salts. Adults have 206 bones, grouped into axial and appendicular skeletons.
The axial skeleton has 80 bones along the main axis: skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs.

Skull: 22 bones: 8 cranial bones forming the cranium that protects the brain, and 14 facial bones. A U-shaped hyoid bone at the base of the buccal cavity and three ear ossicles in each middle ear (malleus, incus, stapes) are also included. The skull joins the vertebral column by two occipital condyles (dicondylic skull).

Vertebral column: 26 serially arranged vertebrae, dorsally placed. Each vertebra has a central neural canal for the spinal cord. The first vertebra, the atlas, articulates with the occipital condyles.

Regions: cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1 (fused), coccygeal 1 (fused). Almost all mammals, including humans, have 7 cervical vertebrae. The column protects the spinal cord, supports the head and anchors the ribs and back muscles.

ex.q: Show that the axial skeleton has 80 bones.
st: Skull 22 + hyoid 1 + ear ossicles 6 (3 × 2) = 29.
Vertebrae 26 + sternum 1 + ribs 24 (12 pairs) = 51.
ex.a: 80 bones

topics.rl: A giraffe's long neck and your neck have the same number of cervical vertebrae: seven. Orthopaedic surgeons in India often treat cervical spondylosis in desk workers.

rv.summary: Adults have 206 bones: 80 axial and 126 appendicular. The axial skeleton has the skull (8 cranial + 14 facial), hyoid, ear ossicles, 26 vertebrae, sternum and ribs. The dicondylic skull joins the atlas; vertebrae are cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1, coccygeal 1.
focus: Bones of the skull, hyoid and ear ossicles
remember: 206 bones = 80 axial + 126 appendicular
Skull 22 (8 + 14); ossicles: malleus, incus, stapes
Vertebrae 26: C7, T12, L5, S1, Co1
Atlas articulates with occipital condyles
traps: Don't count the fused sacrum or coccyx as several bones; each counts as one, giving 26 vertebrae
Don't confuse atlas with axis

topics.t: Ribs, limbs and girdles: the appendicular skeleton
topics.h: Each of your hands and feet holds 14 phalanges. Count your finger joints and you'll see why.
p: The sternum is a flat bone on the ventral midline of the thorax. There are 12 pairs of ribs; each is a thin flat bone joined dorsally to the vertebral column and ventrally to the sternum, with two articulation surfaces at its dorsal end (bicephalic).

Ribs 1 to 7 (true ribs) attach dorsally to thoracic vertebrae and ventrally to the sternum by hyaline cartilage. Ribs 8, 9, 10 (vertebrochondral or false ribs) join the 7th rib by hyaline cartilage. Ribs 11 and 12 (floating ribs) are not connected ventrally. Thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum form the rib cage.

Appendicular skeleton (126 bones): limbs and girdles. Each limb has 30 bones. Forelimb: humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges. Hind limb: femur (longest bone), tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges and the patella (knee cap).

Pectoral girdle: each half has a clavicle (collar bone) and a scapula. The scapula is a large triangular flat bone on the dorsal thorax between the 2nd and 7th ribs; its spine projects as the acromion, with which the clavicle articulates. Below the acromion, the glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint.

Pelvic girdle: two coxal bones, each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis. At their fusion is the acetabulum, where the thigh bone articulates. The two halves meet ventrally at the pubic symphysis, containing fibrous cartilage.

ex.q: Show that one forelimb has 30 bones.
st: Humerus 1 + radius 1 + ulna 1 = 3.
Carpals 8 + metacarpals 5 + phalanges 14 = 27.
ex.a: 30 bones

topics.rl: Cricketers often fracture phalanges or metacarpals while fielding; orthopaedic doctors in India read X-rays using exactly these bone names.

rv.summary: There are 12 pairs of bicephalic ribs: 7 true, 3 vertebrochondral (false) and 2 floating. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) has limbs of 30 bones each and girdles. Each coxal bone is fused ilium, ischium and pubis.
focus: Bones of the forelimb and hind limb
remember: True ribs 1–7; false 8–10; floating 11–12
Forelimb: humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges
Hind limb: femur (longest), tibia, fibula, patella, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges
Coxal bone = ilium + ischium + pubis
traps: Don't call ribs 8–10 floating
Don't confuse glenoid cavity (shoulder) with acetabulum (hip)

topics.t: Joints
topics.h: Your shoulder can swing a cricket bat in a full circle, but your knee only bends one way. Different joints, different jobs.
p: Joints are points of contact between bones, or between bones and cartilages. They are essential for all movements of bony parts. The force from muscles acts through the joint, which works as a fulcrum.
Fibrous joints do not allow any movement, e.g. flat skull bones fused end to end by dense fibrous connective tissue as sutures, forming the cranium.
Cartilaginous joints join bones with cartilage and allow limited movement, e.g. the joints between adjacent vertebrae.
Synovial joints have a fluid-filled synovial cavity between the articulating surfaces, allowing considerable movement; they help in locomotion and many other movements.
Types of synovial joints: ball and socket (humerus and pectoral girdle), hinge (knee), pivot (atlas and axis), gliding (between carpals), saddle (between carpal and metacarpal of the thumb).

ex.q: Which joint lets you turn your head to say 'no', and which type is it?
st: Turning the head is rotation around the neck's axis.
This happens between the atlas and the axis.
It is a pivot joint, a type of synovial joint.
ex.a: The atlas-axis joint, a pivot (synovial) joint.

topics.rl: Bharatanatyam dancers use the full range of ball and socket joints at the shoulders and hips, while the knees act as hinges.

rv.summary: Joints are contacts between bones or bone and cartilage and act as fulcrums. Fibrous joints (skull sutures) allow no movement; cartilaginous joints (between vertebrae) limited movement; synovial joints, with a fluid-filled cavity, much movement: ball and socket, hinge, pivot, gliding and saddle.
focus: Three structural types of joints with examples
Five types of synovial joints with examples
remember: Fibrous: skull sutures; cartilaginous: between vertebrae
Ball and socket: humerus–pectoral girdle; hinge: knee
Pivot: atlas–axis; gliding: between carpals; saddle: thumb carpal–metacarpal
traps: Don't call the knee a ball and socket joint
Don't call vertebral joints synovial

topics.t: Disorders of the muscular and skeletal system
topics.h: Many elderly women in India break a wrist or hip from a minor fall. A silent bone disease called osteoporosis is often the cause.
p: Myasthenia gravis: an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle.
Muscular dystrophy: progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder.
Tetany: rapid spasms (wild contractions) in muscle due to low Ca²⁺ in body fluid.
Arthritis: inflammation of joints. Gout: inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals.
Osteoporosis: an age-related disorder with decreased bone mass and higher chances of fractures; decreased levels of oestrogen are a common cause.

ex.q: A patient has painful swollen joints, and tests show uric acid crystals in them. Name the disorder.
st: Joint inflammation suggests arthritis-type disorders.
Uric acid crystals in joints specifically indicate gout.
ex.a: Gout

topics.rl: Calcium and vitamin D intake and weight-bearing exercise are promoted in India to reduce osteoporosis, especially after menopause.

rv.summary: Disorders: myasthenia gravis (autoimmune, neuromuscular junction), muscular dystrophy (genetic muscle degeneration), tetany (spasms from low Ca²⁺), arthritis (joint inflammation), gout (uric acid crystals in joints) and osteoporosis (low bone mass, often from low oestrogen).
focus: Cause and effect of each disorder
Distinguishing gout from arthritis and tetany
remember: Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune, neuromuscular junction
Tetany: low Ca²⁺
Gout: uric acid crystals in joints
Osteoporosis: decreased oestrogen, fractures
traps: Don't link gout to low calcium
Don't call muscular dystrophy autoimmune

topics.t: Coordination and the organisation of the neural system
topics.h: When you sprint for a bus, your muscles, heart and lungs all speed up together. Who is the conductor of this orchestra?
p: Coordination is the process by which two or more organs interact and complement each other's functions, e.g. during exercise, muscle activity, breathing and heart rate all increase together. The neural system gives quick point-to-point coordination; the endocrine system gives chemical integration through hormones.

Neurons are highly specialised cells that detect, receive and transmit stimuli. Neural organisation is simple in lower invertebrates (a network of neurons in Hydra), better organised in insects (a brain and many ganglia), and most developed in vertebrates.

The human neural system has the central neural system (CNS: brain and spinal cord), the site of information processing and control, and the peripheral neural system (PNS: all nerves associated with the CNS, i.e. cranial and spinal nerves).

Afferent fibres carry impulses from tissues and organs to the CNS; efferent fibres carry regulatory impulses from the CNS to peripheral tissues and organs. The PNS has a somatic neural system (CNS to skeletal muscles) and an autonomic neural system (CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles).

The autonomic system has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. The visceral nervous system is the part of the PNS (nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses) carrying impulses between the CNS and the viscera.

ex.q: A signal from your fingertip about a hot cup travels to the spinal cord, and a signal comes back to move your arm muscles. Name the fibre types and the division involved.
st: Fingertip to CNS: afferent fibres.
CNS to arm (skeletal) muscles: efferent fibres.
Skeletal muscles are served by the somatic neural system.
ex.a: Afferent then efferent fibres, via the somatic neural system.

topics.rl: Neurologists at NIMHANS in Bengaluru diagnose disorders by testing which division of the neural system is affected.

rv.summary: Coordination lets organs work together: the neural system gives quick point-to-point control, the endocrine system chemical integration. The human neural system has the CNS (brain, spinal cord) and the PNS (cranial and spinal nerves) with somatic and autonomic parts.
focus: Neural organisation in Hydra, insects and vertebrates
remember: CNS: brain + spinal cord; PNS: cranial + spinal nerves
Afferent → towards CNS; efferent → away from CNS
Somatic: skeletal muscles; autonomic: involuntary organs, smooth muscles
traps: Don't swap afferent and efferent
Don't put cranial nerves in the CNS

topics.t: The neuron: structure and types
topics.h: Some neurons in your body run from the base of your spine to your toes, about a metre long. They're among the longest cells you have.
p: A neuron has three major parts: cell body, dendrites and axon. The cell body has cytoplasm with typical organelles and granular Nissl's granules.
Dendrites are short, repeatedly branched fibres (also with Nissl's granules) that transmit impulses towards the cell body.

The axon is a long fibre whose distal end is branched; each branch ends in a bulb-like synaptic knob containing synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters. Axons carry impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or neuromuscular junction.

Types by processes: multipolar (one axon, two or more dendrites; cerebral cortex), bipolar (one axon, one dendrite; retina of the eye), unipolar (cell body with one axon only; usually in the embryonic stage).

Myelinated fibres are enveloped by Schwann cells forming a myelin sheath; gaps between adjacent sheaths are nodes of Ranvier; found in spinal and cranial nerves. Non-myelinated fibres are enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath; common in autonomous and somatic neural systems.

ex.q: A neuron has one axon and one dendrite. Name the type and where it is found.
st: One axon + one dendrite = bipolar.
Bipolar neurons are found in the retina of the eye.
ex.a: Bipolar neuron; retina.

topics.rl: In diseases like multiple sclerosis, treated at Indian neurology centres, the myelin sheath is damaged and nerve signals slow down.

rv.summary: A neuron has a cell body with Nissl's granules, dendrites carrying impulses towards it and an axon carrying them away to synaptic knobs. Neurons are multipolar, bipolar or unipolar. Schwann cells form myelin sheaths with nodes of Ranvier.
focus: Parts of a neuron and direction of impulse
Multipolar, bipolar and unipolar neurons with locations
remember: Nissl's granules: cell body and dendrites
Multipolar: cerebral cortex; bipolar: retina; unipolar: embryonic stage
Myelin by Schwann cells; gaps = nodes of Ranvier
traps: Don't say dendrites carry impulses away from the cell body
Don't place bipolar neurons in the cerebral cortex

topics.t: Generation and conduction of a nerve impulse
topics.h: A nerve impulse is not electricity flowing like in a wire. It's a wave of sodium ions rushing in and potassium ions rushing out, travelling along the axon.
p: Neuron membranes are polarised. Ion channels are selectively permeable. At rest, the axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ and nearly impermeable to Na⁺ and to the negatively charged proteins in the axoplasm.

So the axoplasm has high K⁺ and negatively charged proteins and low Na⁺; the outside fluid has low K⁺ and high Na⁺. The sodium-potassium pump maintains these gradients by actively transporting 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in.
The outer surface becomes positive and the inner surface negative: the membrane is polarised. The potential difference across the resting membrane is the resting potential.

A stimulus at a site makes the membrane freely permeable to Na⁺; rapid Na⁺ influx reverses polarity (outside negative, inside positive): depolarisation. This potential difference is the action potential, i.e. the nerve impulse.

Local currents flow on the inner surface from the excited site A to the next site B (and on the outer surface from B to A), depolarising B; this repeats along the axon. The rise in Na⁺ permeability is very short-lived and is followed by a rise in K⁺ permeability; K⁺ diffuses out and restores the resting potential (repolarisation), so the fibre can respond again.

ex.q: If the Na⁺/K⁺ pump runs 100 cycles, how many Na⁺ ions are pumped out and K⁺ ions pumped in?
st: Each cycle: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in.
ex.a: 300 Na⁺ out and 200 K⁺ in

topics.rl: Local anaesthetics used by Indian dentists before a filling block Na⁺ channels, so action potentials cannot travel and you feel no pain.

rv.summary: At rest the axon membrane is more permeable to K⁺; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in, so the outside is positive and the inside negative (resting potential). A stimulus lets Na⁺ rush in, reversing polarity (action potential), which spreads by local currents; K⁺ outflow repolarises.
focus: Ion distribution and permeability at rest
remember: Pump: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in
Resting: outside positive, inside negative
Depolarisation: Na⁺ influx; repolarisation: K⁺ efflux
traps: Don't reverse the pump ratio (it is 3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in)
Don't say K⁺ influx causes depolarisation

topics.t: Transmission of impulses: synapses
topics.h: Between two neurons there is often a gap only a few tens of nanometres wide. Chemicals ferry the message across in a fraction of a millisecond.
p: A nerve impulse passes from one neuron to another through a synapse, formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the synaptic cleft.

Electrical synapses: the membranes of the two neurons are very close; current flows directly from one neuron to the other, similar to conduction along an axon. Transmission is always faster than at chemical synapses, but electrical synapses are rare in our system.
Chemical synapses: the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft. Axon terminals have vesicles filled with neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine).
When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, synaptic vesicles move to and fuse with the membrane, releasing neurotransmitters into the cleft (exocytosis).

Neurotransmitters bind specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, opening ion channels; the ions entering generate a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron, which may be excitatory or inhibitory. Myelinated fibres conduct faster than non-myelinated ones.

ex.q: Order the events at a chemical synapse.
st: Action potential reaches the axon terminal.
Synaptic vesicles fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft.
Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the post-synaptic membrane.
Ion channels open, producing an excitatory or inhibitory potential.
ex.a: Impulse arrives → vesicles release transmitter → binding to receptors → ion channels open → new potential

topics.rl: Many medicines prescribed by psychiatrists in India, such as some antidepressants, work by changing how neurotransmitters act at chemical synapses.

rv.summary: Impulses pass between neurons at synapses. Electrical synapses pass current directly and are faster but rare. At chemical synapses, neurotransmitter released into the synaptic cleft binds post-synaptic receptors and opens ion channels.
focus: Sequence of events at a chemical synapse
remember: Electrical synapse: direct current, faster, rare
Chemical synapse: synaptic cleft, neurotransmitter in vesicles
Example neurotransmitter: acetylcholine
traps: Don't say chemical synapses are faster
Don't say neurotransmitters enter the pre-synaptic nucleus

topics.t: The brain: protection and forebrain
topics.h: Your brain controls breathing, heartbeat, hunger, memory and emotions, all at once. Its largest part, the cerebrum, is folded so tightly it fits inside your skull.
p: The brain is the central information processing organ, the 'command and control system'. It controls voluntary movements, balance, vital involuntary organs (lungs, heart, kidneys), thermoregulation, hunger and thirst, circadian (24-hour) rhythms, several endocrine glands and behaviour; it processes vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.

It is protected by the skull and covered by cranial meninges: outer dura mater, very thin middle arachnoid and inner pia mater (in contact with brain tissue). The brain has forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

Forebrain: cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. A deep cleft divides the cerebrum into left and right cerebral hemispheres, connected by the corpus callosum. The cerebral cortex, folded, is grey matter (concentrated cell bodies) with motor areas, sensory areas and association areas (intersensory associations, memory, communication). The inner part, of myelinated fibre tracts, is white matter.

The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus, a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling. The hypothalamus, at the base of the thalamus, has centres controlling body temperature and the urge to eat and drink, and neurosecretory cells that secrete hypothalamic hormones.

The limbic system (limbic lobe): inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres with deep structures such as the amygdala and hippocampus. With the hypothalamus, it regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions (excitement, pleasure, rage, fear) and motivation.

ex.q: A patient has lost control of body temperature and has abnormal hunger and thirst. Which brain part is probably affected?
st: Centres for body temperature, eating and drinking are in the hypothalamus.
So damage there would affect all three.
ex.a: The hypothalamus.

topics.rl: Helmets for two-wheeler riders, compulsory in Indian cities, protect the brain, which even with three meninges and a skull can be badly injured in accidents.

rv.summary: The brain, protected by the skull and three meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia), has forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain. The forebrain has the cerebrum (two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum; grey cortex, white interior), thalamus, hypothalamus and the limbic system.
focus: Parts of the forebrain and their roles
Grey vs white matter; limbic system
remember: Meninges: dura mater (outer), arachnoid, pia mater (inner)
Corpus callosum joins hemispheres
Thalamus: sensory and motor coordination; hypothalamus: temperature, hunger, thirst, hormones
Limbic system: amygdala, hippocampus; emotions, motivation
traps: Don't call the cortex white matter
Don't place temperature control in the thalamus

topics.t: Midbrain, hindbrain and the brain stem
topics.h: Breathing, heartbeat and digestion keep running even when you are fast asleep. A small region at the base of the brain is on night duty.
p: The midbrain lies between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain. A canal, the cerebral aqueduct, passes through it.
The dorsal portion of the midbrain has four round swellings (lobes) called corpora quadrigemina.

The hindbrain has the pons, cerebellum and medulla (medulla oblongata). The pons has fibre tracts interconnecting different regions of the brain. The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface to give extra space for many more neurons.
The medulla is connected to the spinal cord and has centres controlling respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.
The brain stem (midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata) connects the brain and the spinal cord. (Reflex action and the sense organs eye and ear are not part of this rationalised chapter.)

ex.q: Which three regions make up the brain stem, and what does it connect?
st: Midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata form the brain stem.
It connects the brain with the spinal cord.
ex.a: Midbrain, pons and medulla; it connects the brain to the spinal cord.

topics.rl: Doctors in Indian ICUs test brain stem reflexes to assess patients after severe head injury, because the brain stem keeps breathing and heartbeat going.

rv.summary: The midbrain has the cerebral aqueduct and corpora quadrigemina. The hindbrain has the pons (fibre tracts), cerebellum (convoluted for more neurons) and medulla (respiration, cardiovascular and gastric centres). The brain stem is midbrain, pons and medulla.
focus: Parts and roles of the hindbrain
remember: Corpora quadrigemina: dorsal midbrain; cerebral aqueduct passes through it
Hindbrain: pons, cerebellum, medulla
Medulla: respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, gastric secretions
Brain stem: midbrain + pons + medulla
traps: Don't include the cerebellum in the brain stem
Don't place the medulla in the forebrain

topics.t: Endocrine glands, hormones and the human endocrine system
topics.h: A few micrograms of a hormone can change your heart rate, mood or growth. Tiny messengers, giant effects.
p: Endocrine glands lack ducts, so they are called ductless glands; their secretions are hormones, released into the blood.

Classical definition: a hormone is a chemical produced by endocrine glands, released into blood and carried to a distant target organ. Current definition: hormones are non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts; this also covers molecules from non-gland tissues.
Invertebrates have very simple endocrine systems with few hormones; in vertebrates, a large number of chemicals act as hormones and provide coordination.
Organised endocrine bodies in humans: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus and gonads (testes in males, ovaries in females).
Other organs such as the gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney and heart also produce hormones.

ex.q: Why is the pancreas called both an exocrine and an endocrine gland while the thyroid is only endocrine?
st: The pancreas releases digestive juice through a duct (exocrine) and hormones into blood from the islets (endocrine).
The thyroid releases its hormones only into blood; it has no duct.
ex.a: The pancreas has both duct and ductless secretions; the thyroid only ductless.

topics.rl: India's iodised salt programme, one of the world's largest public health successes, targets a single endocrine gland: the thyroid.

rv.summary: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into blood; hormones are non-nutrient messengers made in trace amounts. Human glands: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus, gonads; the gut, liver, kidney and heart also make hormones.
focus: Classical vs current definition of hormones
remember: Hormones: non-nutrient chemical messengers in trace amounts
Glands: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus, gonads
Gut, liver, kidney, heart also produce hormones
traps: Don't call the liver an organised endocrine gland
Don't say hormones are released through ducts

topics.t: The hypothalamus and the pituitary gland
topics.h: The pituitary is called the 'master gland', but it takes orders from its boss just above it: the hypothalamus.
p: The hypothalamus, the basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain), has groups of neurosecretory cells called nuclei that produce hormones regulating pituitary secretion.

Hypothalamic hormones are releasing hormones (stimulate pituitary secretion, e.g. GnRH stimulates gonadotrophin release) and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin inhibits growth hormone release). They pass along axons, are released at nerve endings and reach the anterior pituitary through a portal circulatory system. The posterior pituitary is under direct neural regulation of the hypothalamus.
The pituitary sits in a bony cavity, the sella turcica, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It has an adenohypophysis (pars distalis and pars intermedia) and a neurohypophysis (pars nervosa).

Pars distalis (anterior pituitary) produces GH, prolactin (PRL), TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH. Pars intermedia secretes melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH); in humans it is almost merged with the pars distalis.
The neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, which are actually made in the hypothalamus and transported along axons.

ex.q: Which pituitary hormones are actually made in the hypothalamus, and how do they reach the pituitary?
st: Oxytocin and vasopressin are made by hypothalamic neurons.
They travel along axons to the neurohypophysis, where they are stored and released.
ex.a: Oxytocin and vasopressin; carried axonally to the posterior pituitary.

topics.rl: Endocrinologists at Indian hospitals treat pituitary tumours that can over-produce hormones such as growth hormone or prolactin.

rv.summary: Hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones reach the anterior pituitary by a portal system. The pituitary's pars distalis makes GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH and FSH; pars intermedia MSH; the neurohypophysis stores oxytocin and vasopressin made in the hypothalamus.
focus: Where oxytocin and vasopressin are made
remember: GnRH stimulates gonadotrophins; somatostatin inhibits GH
Pars distalis: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH
Pars intermedia: MSH
Neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin, vasopressin (made in hypothalamus)
traps: Don't say oxytocin is made in the posterior pituitary
Don't list oxytocin as a pars distalis hormone

topics.t: Functions and disorders of pituitary hormones
topics.h: Too much growth hormone in childhood can make a person over 7 feet tall; too little, and growth stays stunted.
p: Growth hormone (GH): over-secretion in children causes gigantism; low secretion causes pituitary dwarfism. Excess in adults, especially in middle age, causes acromegaly: severe disfigurement, especially of the face; it is hard to diagnose early and can lead to serious complications if unchecked.

Prolactin regulates growth of mammary glands and milk formation. TSH stimulates synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones. ACTH stimulates synthesis and secretion of glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex.

LH and FSH stimulate the gonads (gonadotrophins). In males, LH stimulates androgen secretion from the testis; FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis. In females, LH induces ovulation of mature Graafian follicles and maintains the corpus luteum; FSH stimulates growth and development of ovarian follicles. MSH regulates skin pigmentation.
Oxytocin stimulates contraction of smooth muscles: in females, vigorous uterine contraction at childbirth and milk ejection from mammary glands.

Vasopressin (ADH) acts on the kidney, stimulating reabsorption of water and electrolytes by distal tubules and reducing water loss (diuresis). Impaired ADH synthesis or release leads to water loss and dehydration: diabetes insipidus.

ex.q: A patient passes huge volumes of dilute urine and is always thirsty, but blood sugar is normal. Which hormone may be deficient?
st: Normal blood sugar rules out diabetes mellitus.
Large volumes of dilute urine mean the kidney cannot conserve water.
This happens when ADH (vasopressin) is lacking: diabetes insipidus.
ex.a: ADH (vasopressin); the condition is diabetes insipidus.

topics.rl: Doctors in Indian hospitals give synthetic oxytocin to help uterine contractions during childbirth and to reduce bleeding after delivery.

rv.summary: Excess GH causes gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults; too little causes dwarfism. PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH and MSH act on their targets. Oxytocin contracts the uterus and ejects milk; lack of ADH causes diabetes insipidus.
focus: Effects of GH excess and deficiency
Targets and actions of PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, MSH
remember: Gigantism (child), acromegaly (adult), pituitary dwarfism
LH: ovulation, corpus luteum; FSH: follicle growth; FSH + androgens: spermatogenesis
Oxytocin: uterine contraction, milk ejection
ADH lack → diabetes insipidus
traps: Don't say prolactin ejects milk; oxytocin does
Don't confuse diabetes insipidus (ADH) with diabetes mellitus (insulin)

topics.t: The pineal and thyroid glands
topics.h: Before iodised salt, goitre (a swollen neck) was common in the Himalayan foothills. A pinch of iodine changed that.
p: The pineal gland on the dorsal side of the forebrain secretes melatonin, which regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm: the sleep-wake cycle and body temperature. It also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle and defence capability.

The thyroid has two lobes on either side of the trachea joined by a thin flap of connective tissue, the isthmus. It is made of follicles and stromal tissue; follicular cells make tetraiodothyronine or thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃). Iodine is essential for normal hormone synthesis.

Iodine deficiency causes hypothyroidism and goitre (enlarged thyroid). Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development of the baby: stunted growth (cretinism), impaired mental development, low IQ, abnormal skin and deaf-mutism. In adult women it may make the menstrual cycle irregular.

Hyperthyroidism (from thyroid cancer or nodules) raises hormone levels abnormally. Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism with an enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, increased basal metabolic rate and weight loss.

Thyroid hormones regulate basal metabolic rate, support RBC formation, control metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and influence water and electrolyte balance. The thyroid also secretes thyrocalcitonin (TCT), a protein hormone regulating blood calcium.

ex.q: How many iodine atoms are in one molecule each of T₄ and T₃ together?
st: T₄ (tetraiodothyronine) has 4 iodine atoms.
T₃ (triiodothyronine) has 3 iodine atoms.
Total = 4 + 3 = 7.
ex.a: 7 iodine atoms

topics.rl: Under India's National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme, iodised salt is promoted nationwide to prevent goitre and cretinism.

rv.summary: The pineal gland secretes melatonin for the 24-hour rhythm. The thyroid (two lobes joined by the isthmus) makes T₄ and T₃, needing iodine, and TCT for calcium. Iodine lack causes goitre and hypothyroidism (cretinism in babies); Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism.
remember: Pineal: melatonin
Thyroid: T₄ (4 iodine), T₃ (3 iodine), TCT (blood calcium)
Iodine deficiency → goitre, hypothyroidism
Graves' disease: protruding eyes, high BMR, weight loss
traps: Don't link Graves' disease with hypothyroidism
Don't say TCT regulates blood glucose

topics.t: Parathyroid glands and thymus
topics.h: Four rice-grain-sized glands behind your thyroid decide whether your bones give up calcium to your blood. They work hand in hand with the thyroid's TCT.
p: There are four parathyroid glands on the back side of the thyroid, one pair in each of its two lobes. They secrete a peptide hormone, parathyroid hormone (PTH); its secretion is regulated by circulating Ca²⁺ levels.

PTH increases blood Ca²⁺: it stimulates bone resorption (dissolution or demineralisation), stimulates reabsorption of Ca²⁺ by renal tubules and increases Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food. So PTH is a hypercalcaemic hormone. With TCT, it plays a major role in calcium balance.
The thymus is a lobular structure on the dorsal side of the heart and the aorta. It plays a major role in development of the immune system.
It secretes peptide hormones called thymosins, which play a major role in differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and promote antibody production (humoral immunity).
The thymus degenerates in old individuals, decreasing thymosin production, so immune responses of old people become weak.

ex.q: Blood calcium falls. Name the gland that responds, the hormone, and three ways it raises calcium.
st: Parathyroid glands secrete PTH when Ca²⁺ falls.
PTH causes bone resorption.
It increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption in renal tubules.
It increases Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food.
ex.a: Parathyroid → PTH → bone resorption, renal reabsorption, intestinal absorption

topics.rl: Elderly people in India are more prone to infections partly because the thymus shrinks with age, weakening T-cell production.

rv.summary: Four parathyroid glands behind the thyroid secrete PTH when blood Ca²⁺ falls; PTH raises Ca²⁺ by bone resorption, renal reabsorption and intestinal absorption, and with TCT keeps calcium balance. The thymus, above the heart, secretes thymosins for T-cell differentiation; it shrinks in old age.
remember: 4 parathyroids; PTH is hypercalcaemic
PTH: bone resorption, renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, gut Ca²⁺ absorption
Thymosins: T-lymphocyte differentiation, antibody production
traps: Don't call PTH hypocalcaemic
Don't say PTH comes from the thymus

topics.t: The adrenal gland
topics.h: A dog barks suddenly at night and your heart pounds, your pupils widen and your hair stands up. That's adrenaline, the 'fight or flight' hormone.
p: A pair of adrenal glands sits one at the anterior part of each kidney. Each has a central adrenal medulla and an outer adrenal cortex.

The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), the catecholamines. They are secreted rapidly in stress and emergencies (emergency hormones, hormones of fight or flight): they increase alertness, pupil dilation, piloerection (raising of hairs) and sweating; increase heart rate, strength of heart contraction and breathing rate; and stimulate breakdown of glycogen (raising blood glucose), lipids and proteins.

The adrenal cortex has three layers: zona reticularis (inner), zona fasciculata (middle) and zona glomerulosa (outer). It secretes corticoids. Glucocorticoids (mainly cortisol) act on carbohydrate metabolism: they stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and proteolysis, inhibit cellular uptake and use of amino acids, help maintain cardiovascular and kidney functions, produce anti-inflammatory reactions, suppress the immune response and stimulate RBC production.

Mineralocorticoids (mainly aldosterone) regulate water and electrolytes: aldosterone acts on renal tubules to reabsorb Na⁺ and water and excrete K⁺ and phosphate, maintaining electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure.

Small amounts of androgenic steroids from the cortex help growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty. Underproduction of cortical hormones alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue: Addison's disease.

ex.q: List the layers of the adrenal cortex from outside inwards and the main hormone class of the outer layer.
st: Outer: zona glomerulosa.
Middle: zona fasciculata.
Inner: zona reticularis.
The zona glomerulosa is associated with mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone.
ex.a: Zona glomerulosa → zona fasciculata → zona reticularis

topics.rl: Adrenaline auto-injectors are carried by people with severe allergies, and doctors in Indian emergency rooms use adrenaline in cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis.

rv.summary: The adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline, the fight-or-flight hormones. The three-layered cortex secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) and some androgens. Low cortical output causes Addison's disease.
remember: Medulla: adrenaline, noradrenaline (emergency hormones)
Cortex outer → inner: glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis
Cortisol: gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive
Aldosterone: reabsorb Na⁺ and water, excrete K⁺ and phosphate
traps: Don't say adrenaline constricts pupils
Don't say aldosterone excretes Na⁺ and retains K⁺

topics.t: The pancreas: insulin and glucagon
topics.h: India has one of the largest numbers of people with diabetes in the world. At the heart of the disease are tiny islands of cells in the pancreas.
p: The pancreas is a composite gland, both exocrine and endocrine. The endocrine part is the islets of Langerhans: about 1 to 2 million islets, only 1 to 2% of pancreatic tissue.
Islets have α-cells (secrete glucagon) and β-cells (secrete insulin).

Glucagon, a peptide hormone, acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes): it stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces cellular glucose uptake, raising blood sugar (hyperglycaemia). So glucagon is a hyperglycaemic hormone.

Insulin, a peptide hormone, acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes: it enhances cellular glucose uptake and utilisation, lowering blood glucose (hypoglycaemia), and stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis). Insulin and glucagon together maintain glucose homeostasis.
Prolonged hyperglycaemia leads to diabetes mellitus, with loss of glucose in urine and formation of harmful ketone bodies. Diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy.

ex.q: After a sweet-heavy Diwali meal, blood glucose rises. Which islet cells respond, with which hormone, and what does it do?
st: High blood glucose stimulates β-cells.
β-cells release insulin.
Insulin increases glucose uptake by liver and fat cells and stimulates glycogenesis, lowering blood glucose.
ex.a: β-cells; insulin; increases glucose uptake and glycogenesis.

topics.rl: Indian pharma companies produce insulin at scale, and the national NCD screening programme checks adults for diabetes at health and wellness centres.

rv.summary: The pancreas is both exocrine and endocrine; its 1–2 million islets of Langerhans have α-cells (glucagon) and β-cells (insulin).
