Glucagon raises blood sugar by glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; insulin lowers it by glucose uptake and glycogenesis. Prolonged hyperglycaemia causes diabetes mellitus.
remember: α-cells: glucagon (hyperglycaemic); β-cells: insulin (hypoglycaemic)
Islets: 1–2 million, 1–2% of pancreas
Insulin targets hepatocytes and adipocytes
traps: Don't swap α- and β-cell hormones
Don't call insulin hyperglycaemic

topics.t: Gonads as endocrine glands: testis and ovary
topics.h: At puberty, a voice deepens or rises, and the body changes in many ways. The messengers behind these changes come from the testes and ovaries.
p: The testes, a pair in the scrotal sac, are primary sex organs and endocrine glands. They have seminiferous tubules and stromal (interstitial) tissue.

Leydig (interstitial) cells in the intertubular spaces produce androgens, mainly testosterone. Androgens regulate development, maturation and functions of male accessory sex organs (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, urethra); stimulate muscular growth, growth of facial and axillary hair, aggressiveness and low pitch of voice; play a major stimulatory role in spermatogenesis; influence male sexual behaviour (libido) through the CNS; and have anabolic effects on protein and carbohydrate metabolism.

The ovaries, a pair in the abdomen, are primary female sex organs producing one ovum in each menstrual cycle, and two groups of steroid hormones: oestrogen and progesterone. They have ovarian follicles and stromal tissue.

Oestrogen is mainly made by growing ovarian follicles. It stimulates growth and activities of female secondary sex organs, development of growing follicles, appearance of female secondary sex characters (e.g. high pitch of voice), and mammary gland development; it also regulates female sexual behaviour.

After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which mainly secretes progesterone. Progesterone supports pregnancy and acts on mammary glands to stimulate formation of alveoli (milk-storing sacs) and milk secretion.

ex.q: Which structure secretes progesterone, and where does it come from?
st: After ovulation, the ruptured Graafian follicle changes into the corpus luteum.
The corpus luteum mainly secretes progesterone.
ex.a: The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle after ovulation.

topics.rl: School health and life-skills programmes in India explain puberty changes clinically and respectfully, linking them to hormones from the testes and ovaries.

rv.summary: Leydig cells of the testes make androgens (mainly testosterone) for male sex organs, secondary characters and spermatogenesis. Ovaries make oestrogen from growing follicles and progesterone from the corpus luteum, which supports pregnancy.
remember: Leydig cells → testosterone
Growing follicles → oestrogen
Corpus luteum → progesterone
Progesterone: supports pregnancy, forms milk-storing alveoli
traps: Don't say progesterone ejects milk; oxytocin does
Don't credit androgens to the seminiferous tubule lumen

topics.t: Hormones of the heart, kidney and gut
topics.h: Your stomach, intestine, heart and kidney aren't classified as endocrine glands, yet each sends out hormones every day.
p: The atrial wall of the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), a peptide hormone. When BP rises, ANF causes dilation of blood vessels, reducing blood pressure.
Juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, a peptide hormone that stimulates erythropoiesis (RBC formation).

Endocrine cells of the gastrointestinal tract secrete four major peptide hormones. Gastrin acts on gastric glands to stimulate secretion of HCl and pepsinogen. Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas to stimulate secretion of water and bicarbonate ions.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on the pancreas and gall bladder to stimulate secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice. Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) inhibits gastric secretion and motility.
Several non-endocrine tissues secrete growth factors, essential for normal growth of tissues and their repair or regeneration.

ex.q: Fatty food enters the duodenum. Which gut hormone releases bile and pancreatic enzymes?
st: Bile comes from the gall bladder; enzymes from the pancreas.
Cholecystokinin acts on both.
ex.a: Cholecystokinin (CCK).

topics.rl: Patients with chronic kidney disease in India often become anaemic because damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin; synthetic erythropoietin injections help.

rv.summary: The atria secrete ANF, which dilates vessels and lowers BP; kidney JG cells make erythropoietin for RBC formation. Gut hormones are gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP. Non-endocrine tissues make growth factors.
focus: Four gut hormones and their actions
remember: ANF: atria, vasodilation, lowers BP
Erythropoietin: kidney JG cells, RBC formation
Gastrin: HCl, pepsinogen; secretin: water, HCO₃⁻; CCK: enzymes, bile; GIP: inhibits stomach
traps: Don't say secretin stimulates pancreatic enzymes; CCK does
Don't credit erythropoietin to the pancreas

topics.t: Mechanism of hormone action
topics.h: Insulin knocks on the cell's door and sends a message inside; steroid hormones walk right in and talk to the genes.
p: Hormones act by binding specific proteins called hormone receptors, present only in target tissues. Receptors on the cell membrane are membrane-bound receptors; those inside the cell are intracellular receptors, mostly nuclear receptors. Each receptor is specific to one hormone.
Binding forms a hormone-receptor complex, which causes biochemical changes in the target tissue and so regulates its metabolism and physiological functions.

By chemical nature: peptide, polypeptide and protein hormones (insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones); steroids (cortisol, testosterone, oestradiol, progesterone); iodothyronines (thyroid hormones); amino-acid derivatives (epinephrine).
Hormones acting on membrane-bound receptors normally do not enter the cell; they generate second messengers (e.g. cyclic AMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺) that regulate cellular metabolism.

Hormones acting on intracellular receptors (steroids, iodothyronines) mostly regulate gene expression or chromosome function through the hormone-receptor complex interacting with the genome, causing physiological and developmental effects. Hormone levels are kept in check by feedback: e.g. a rise in body fluid volume switches off osmoreceptors and suppresses ADH release.

ex.q: Classify insulin and cortisol by chemical nature and by type of receptor.
st: Insulin is a peptide hormone; it cannot cross the lipid membrane, so it binds membrane-bound receptors and uses second messengers.
Cortisol is a steroid; it enters the cell and binds intracellular (nuclear) receptors, regulating gene expression.
ex.a: Insulin: peptide, membrane receptor, second messengers. Cortisol: steroid, intracellular receptor, gene expression.

topics.rl: Many modern drugs developed and made in India are designed to block or mimic hormone receptors, such as drugs for diabetes and hormone-sensitive cancers.

rv.summary: Hormones act by binding specific receptors in target tissues, forming hormone-receptor complexes. Peptide hormones and epinephrine bind membrane receptors and act through second messengers (cAMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺); steroids and iodothyronines bind intracellular receptors and regulate gene expression.
focus: Chemical classes of hormones with examples
remember: Peptides: insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones
Steroids: cortisol, testosterone, oestradiol, progesterone
Iodothyronines: thyroid hormones; amino-acid derivative: epinephrine
Second messengers: cAMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺
traps: Don't say peptide hormones enter the nucleus
Don't call epinephrine a steroid

qa.q: Which property is regarded as a defining feature of living organisms?
qa.e: No non-living object shows metabolism, so it can be used to define life. Growth and reproduction fail this test.

qa.q: Why is growth NOT taken as a defining property of living things?
qa.a: Non-living objects such as crystals and mountains also grow
qa.e: Crystals and sand mounds increase in size by accumulation of material on the surface, so growth is not unique to life.

qa.q: A worker bee, a mule and an infertile human have one thing in common. What is it?
qa.a: They are living but do not reproduce
qa.e: All three are alive but cannot produce offspring, which shows reproduction is not a defining feature of life.

qa.q: How does growth in living organisms differ from growth in a salt crystal?
qa.a: Organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface
qa.e: Living organisms grow by cell division and increase in mass from within, while non-living things grow by external accumulation.

qa.q: About how many species have been described so far on Earth?
qa.e: Taxonomists have named and described roughly 1.7 to 1.8 million species; many more remain undiscovered.

qa.q: The term biodiversity refers to:
qa.a: The number and types of organisms present on Earth
qa.e: Biodiversity is the variety and number of living organisms in an area or on Earth as a whole.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Reproduction cannot be an all-inclusive defining feature of living organisms. Reason (R): Many living organisms, such as mules and sterile worker bees, do not reproduce.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the existence of living but non-reproducing organisms is exactly why reproduction cannot define life.

qa.q: A student says, 'A candle flame grows, uses oxygen and gives out CO₂, so it is alive.' What is the best reply?
qa.a: A flame has no cells and no metabolism; the features it shows are not defining features of life
qa.e: Life is defined by cellular organisation and metabolism inside cells. A flame shows neither, even if it looks like it grows and 'breathes'.

qa.q: Why do biologists need scientific names instead of local names?
qa.a: Local names differ from place to place and cause confusion
qa.e: The same organism has many local names, and the same local name may refer to different organisms. A standard name avoids confusion.

qa.q: Which process must come first before an organism can be named?
qa.e: You can only name an organism once you have described it correctly and know what it is.

qa.q: ICZN provides rules for naming:
qa.e: ICZN is the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature, used for animals.

qa.q: The full form of ICBN is:
qa.e: ICBN stands for International Code for Botanical Nomenclature, which governs plant names.

qa.q: Nomenclature means:
qa.a: Giving a correct scientific name to an organism
qa.e: Nomenclature is naming. Grouping is classification and relationships are part of systematics.

qa.q: A biologist correctly describes the features of a new beetle so that it can be told apart from all others. This step is:
qa.e: Correct description of an organism is identification; naming comes after it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Each organism can have only one correct scientific name. Reason (R): International codes such as ICBN and ICZN make sure a given name is used for only one organism.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and the codes are the reason a scientific name is unique and universal.

qa.q: Which statement about common names is correct?
qa.a: The same organism may have different common names in different regions
qa.e: Common names depend on local language and region, which is exactly why scientific names are needed.

qa.q: Who proposed binomial nomenclature?
qa.e: Carolus Linnaeus introduced the two-word naming system used for all organisms.

qa.q: A magazine prints the lion's name as 'Panthera Leo'. Which rule does this break?
qa.a: The specific epithet must begin with a small letter
qa.e: Genus takes a capital letter and the epithet a small letter, so it should be Panthera leo (in italics in print).

qa.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., the word 'indica' is the:
qa.e: The second word of a binomial is the specific epithet.

qa.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., what does 'Linn.' tell us?
qa.a: The scientist who first described the species
qa.e: The abbreviated author name follows the epithet; here it stands for Linnaeus.

qa.q: How should a scientific name be written in a handwritten answer?
qa.a: Each of the two words underlined separately
qa.e: Handwritten names are underlined, each word separately, to show their Latin origin.

qa.q: Scientific names are taken from which language, or are made to fit it?
qa.e: Biological names are Latin or latinised, whatever their source.

qa.q: A textbook prints 'Solanum tuberosum' in italics. What does 'Solanum' denote?
qa.e: The first word, beginning with a capital letter, is the genus.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The specific epithet in a binomial name begins with a small letter. Reason (R): The generic name always ends in '-ae'.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: The assertion is a correct rule. The reason is false: generic names such as Homo or Panthera do not end in '-ae'; the ending '-ae' is typical of plant family names.

qa.q: A group of organisms at any level of classification is called a:
qa.e: Taxon is the general word for a group at any rank, from kingdom down to species.

qa.q: Which word comes from the Latin 'systema'?
qa.e: Systematics comes from 'systema', meaning systematic arrangement of organisms.

qa.q: Systematics differs from taxonomy because it also includes:
qa.e: Systematics covers identification, nomenclature and classification and also takes account of evolutionary relationships.

qa.q: Which set lists the processes included in taxonomy?
qa.e: Taxonomy brings together characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a basis of modern taxonomic studies?
qa.a: The commercial price of the organism
qa.e: Taxonomy uses structure, cells, development and ecology. Market price has nothing to do with relationships.

qa.q: Grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters is:
qa.e: This is the definition of classification.

qa.q: 'Dogs', 'mammals' and 'plants' are examples of:
qa.e: Each is a group at some level of classification, so each is a taxon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Taxonomy is a broader study than systematics. Reason (R): Systematics also considers the evolutionary relationships between organisms.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: systematics is the broader study, not taxonomy. R is true: systematics adds evolutionary relationships to identification, naming and classification, which is exactly why it is broader.

qa.q: Which is the basic unit of classification?
qa.e: Species is the lowest category and the basic unit; all higher categories are built from species.

qa.q: Lion, tiger and leopard are placed in the same:
qa.e: All three belong to the genus Panthera but are different species.

qa.q: Solanum tuberosum and Solanum melongena belong to the same genus. What does this tell us?
qa.a: They share more characters with each other than with species of other genera
qa.e: A genus groups related species with many shared characters.

qa.q: Arranging taxonomic categories in a step-like order from kingdom to species is called:
qa.e: The ordered sequence of ranks is the taxonomic hierarchy.

qa.q: A taxonomic category, such as 'family', is best described as:
qa.a: A rank that represents a unit of classification
qa.e: Each category is a rank in the hierarchy and a unit of classification, and the group placed at that rank is a taxon.

qa.q: Which genus includes the potato?
qa.e: Potato is Solanum tuberosum.

qa.q: A 'species' is best defined as:
qa.a: A group of individuals with fundamental similarities
qa.e: Species is a group of individual organisms with fundamental similarities.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Species is considered the basic unit of classification. Reason (R): All higher categories such as genus and family are formed by grouping species on shared characters.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true and the reason explains why species is basic: everything above is built from species.

qa.q: Felidae and Canidae are placed in the same:
qa.e: Cat family (Felidae) and dog family (Canidae) are both in the order Carnivora.

qa.q: Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae are families placed in the order:
qa.e: Polymoniales includes Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae, based on floral characters.

qa.q: In plants, the category equivalent to 'phylum' in animals is:
qa.e: Plants use the term Division in place of Phylum.

qa.q: As we move from species to kingdom, the number of common characters among members:
qa.e: Higher categories are broader groups, so the members share fewer characters.

qa.q: Which is the highest taxonomic category?
qa.e: Kingdom is at the top of the hierarchy.

qa.q: Monkeys, gorillas and gibbons are placed in order Primata, which belongs to class:
qa.e: Primata and Carnivora are orders within the class Mammalia.

qa.q: How many obligate (main) categories are there from kingdom to species?
qa.e: Kingdom, phylum/division, class, order, family, genus and species: seven categories.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A family usually contains more organisms than a genus does. Reason (R): Members of a family share more characters than members of a genus.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A family is a group of genera, so it contains more organisms. But members of a family share fewer characters, not more, so R is false.

qa.q: The housefly belongs to the order:
qa.e: Musca domestica is placed in family Muscidae, order Diptera, class Insecta.

qa.q: The family of mango is:
qa.e: Mangifera indica belongs to the family Anacardiaceae.

qa.q: Wheat belongs to class:
qa.e: Wheat is a monocot: class Monocotyledonae, order Poales, family Poaceae.

qa.q: Human beings belong to the family:
qa.e: Homo sapiens is in family Hominidae; Primata is the order, not the family.

qa.q: Which category is shared by man and housefly?
qa.e: Man is a chordate and the housefly an arthropod, so they share only the kingdom.

qa.q: Which is the correct classification of mango?
qa.a: Plantae → Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera
qa.e: Mango: division Angiospermae, class Dicotyledonae, order Sapindales, family Anacardiaceae.

qa.q: The housefly's phylum is:
qa.e: Insects such as the housefly have jointed legs and belong to phylum Arthropoda.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mango and wheat are placed in the same division. Reason (R): Both are flowering plants with seeds enclosed in fruits.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both belong to division Angiospermae, the flowering plants whose seeds are enclosed in fruits, so R explains A.

qa.q: Who proposed the five-kingdom classification?
qa.e: Whittaker proposed it in 1969.

qa.q: Which was NOT one of Whittaker's criteria for the five kingdoms?
qa.e: His criteria were cell structure, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction and phylogeny. Size was not one.

qa.q: A major drawback of the two-kingdom system was that it:
qa.a: Did not distinguish prokaryotes from eukaryotes
qa.e: Bacteria, fungi, algae and plants were mixed because cell type and nutrition were ignored.

qa.q: In which kingdom is the cell wall made of chitin?
qa.e: Fungal cell walls contain chitin and polysaccharides; plant walls are mainly cellulose; animal cells have none.

qa.q: Which kingdom has members with no nuclear membrane?
qa.e: Monera are prokaryotes, so their genetic material is not enclosed in a nuclear membrane.

qa.q: Aristotle classified plants into:
qa.e: Aristotle used simple morphological characters: trees, shrubs and herbs.

qa.q: The three-domain system divides kingdom Monera into:
qa.e: Monera is split into the domains Archaea and Bacteria; eukaryotes form Eukarya.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chlamydomonas and Chlorella were placed with plants in the two-kingdom system. Reason (R): The two-kingdom system grouped organisms using cell type and body organisation.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: These green algae were put with plants because they photosynthesise. R is false: the two-kingdom system ignored cell type and body organisation, which was its weakness.

qa.q: Comma-shaped bacteria are called:
qa.e: Vibrio means comma-shaped.

qa.q: Methanogens are found in:
qa.a: The gut of ruminants such as cows
qa.e: Methanogens live in marshy places and in the guts of ruminants, where they make methane.

qa.q: What helps archaebacteria survive in extreme conditions?
qa.e: Archaebacteria have a distinct cell wall structure that helps them survive harsh habitats.

qa.q: Bacteria that live in extremely salty areas are called:
qa.e: 'Halo' refers to salt; halophiles love salty habitats.

qa.q: Which gas do methanogens produce from cattle dung?
qa.e: Methanogens release methane, the main fuel in biogas.

qa.q: Rod-shaped bacteria are known as:
qa.e: Bacillus (plural bacilli) is rod-shaped.

qa.q: Which statement about bacterial nutrition is correct?
qa.a: Most bacteria are heterotrophs, but some make their own food
qa.e: The majority are heterotrophic; some are photosynthetic or chemosynthetic autotrophs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Archaebacteria can live in hot springs and salt pans. Reason (R): Archaebacteria have a cell wall structure different from other bacteria.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and NCERT credits their distinct cell wall structure for their survival in extreme conditions.

qa.q: Specialised cells that fix nitrogen in cyanobacteria are:
qa.e: Heterocysts in Nostoc and Anabaena fix N₂.

qa.q: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic because they contain:
qa.e: Cyanobacteria have chlorophyll a, similar to green plants.

qa.q: Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria get energy by:
qa.a: Oxidising inorganic substances like ammonia and nitrites
qa.e: They oxidise inorganic compounds and use the released energy to make ATP.

qa.q: Which pair are nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria?
qa.e: Nostoc and Anabaena have heterocysts and fix nitrogen.

qa.q: Chemosynthetic bacteria are important in ecosystems because they:
qa.a: Recycle nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur
qa.e: By oxidising inorganic compounds they help cycle these nutrients.

qa.q: A key feature of eubacteria is:
qa.e: Eubacteria have a rigid cell wall, and a flagellum if motile.

qa.q: Why do cyanobacterial blooms appear in polluted lakes?
qa.a: Pollution adds nutrients that let them multiply rapidly
qa.e: Nutrient-rich polluted water supports explosive growth of cyanobacteria.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cyanobacteria are called blue-green algae, yet they are placed in Monera. Reason (R): Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes without a membrane-bound nucleus.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; being prokaryotic is why they go in Monera, despite the algal name.

qa.q: Which organisms completely lack a cell wall?
qa.e: Mycoplasma have no cell wall at all.

qa.q: Which is a bacterial disease of plants?
qa.e: Citrus canker is bacterial. Rust is fungal, mosaic is viral and white rust is caused by the fungus Albugo.

qa.q: The main mode of reproduction in bacteria is:
qa.e: Bacteria mainly divide by fission.

qa.q: Under unfavourable conditions, bacteria may:
qa.e: Spore formation helps bacteria survive harsh conditions.

qa.q: Which human disease is NOT caused by bacteria?
qa.e: Mumps is a viral disease. The others are bacterial.

qa.q: A sexual-like process in bacteria involves:
qa.a: A primitive transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another
qa.e: Bacteria show a primitive type of DNA transfer, not true gamete fusion.

qa.q: Which property describes Mycoplasma?
qa.e: Mycoplasma can live without oxygen, lack a wall and are often pathogenic.

qa.q: Which is a use of heterotrophic bacteria?
qa.e: Heterotrophic bacteria help make curd and antibiotics and fix nitrogen in legume roots. The other options belong to protists and red algae.

qa.q: Diatomaceous earth is formed from the cell walls of:
qa.e: Silica-rich diatom walls are indestructible and pile up as diatomaceous earth.

qa.q: Red tides are caused by:
qa.e: Rapid multiplication of the red dinoflagellate Gonyaulax makes the sea look red.

qa.q: Instead of a cell wall, euglenoids have:
qa.e: The pellicle makes Euglena's body flexible.

qa.q: Which group is called the chief 'producers' in the oceans?
qa.e: Diatoms carry out a huge share of ocean photosynthesis.

qa.q: The cell wall of diatoms is embedded with:
qa.e: Silica makes diatom walls hard and indestructible.

qa.q: Which is true of dinoflagellates?
qa.a: Most have two flagella, one longitudinal and one transverse
qa.e: The transverse flagellum lies in a furrow between the cellulose wall plates.

qa.q: All members of Protista are:
qa.e: Protista is the kingdom of unicellular eukaryotes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Euglena is often described as a link between plants and animals. Reason (R): Euglena photosynthesises in sunlight but behaves like a heterotroph when deprived of light.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, and its dual nutrition (plant-like and animal-like) is exactly why it is called a link.

qa.q: The malarial parasite belongs to which protozoan group?
qa.e: Plasmodium has an infectious spore-like stage, so it is a sporozoan.

qa.q: Sleeping sickness is caused by:
qa.e: The flagellated parasite Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness.

qa.q: Amoeboid protozoans capture prey using:
qa.e: Pseudopodia (false feet) are used for movement and catching prey.

qa.q: In Paramoecium, the cavity that receives food is the:
qa.e: Coordinated cilia beat food-laden water into the gullet.

qa.q: Slime moulds obtain their food as:
qa.e: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that engulf decaying organic matter.

qa.q: Why can slime mould spores survive for many years?
qa.a: They have true walls and are extremely resistant
qa.e: Walled, resistant spores withstand adverse conditions for years.

qa.q: Under favourable conditions, slime moulds form an aggregation called a:
qa.e: The plasmodium of slime moulds can spread over several feet. (Do not confuse it with the malarial parasite genus Plasmodium.)

qa.q: Entamoeba is best described as a:
qa.e: Entamoeba is an amoeboid protozoan that lives as a parasite.

qa.q: The fungal cell wall is made of:
qa.e: Chitin and polysaccharides form fungal walls; cellulose is typical of plants.

qa.q: Hyphae that are continuous tubes with many nuclei are called:
qa.e: Coenocytic hyphae lack cross walls and are multinucleate.

qa.q: Fusion of two nuclei during the sexual cycle of fungi is:
qa.e: Karyogamy is nuclear fusion; plasmogamy is cytoplasmic fusion.

qa.q: A dikaryotic cell has:
qa.e: Dikaryon means two nuclei per cell that have not yet fused.

qa.q: Fungi that live in association with roots of higher plants form:
qa.e: Fungus-root associations are mycorrhizae; fungus-alga associations are lichens.

qa.q: Which is a sexual spore in fungi?
qa.e: Ascospores, basidiospores and oospores are sexual spores.

qa.q: Which fungus is unicellular?
qa.e: Yeasts are the main unicellular fungi; most others are filamentous.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Food is kept in a refrigerator to stop it from spoiling quickly. Reason (R): Fungi prefer to grow in warm and humid places.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; cold, dry conditions slow fungal (and bacterial) growth, so R explains A.

qa.q: Rhizopus (bread mould) belongs to:
qa.e: Rhizopus has aseptate, coenocytic mycelium typical of phycomycetes.

qa.q: Albugo is a parasitic fungus found on:
qa.e: Albugo, a phycomycete, parasitises mustard.

qa.q: Which fungus is widely used in biochemical and genetic research?
qa.e: Neurospora, an ascomycete, is a classic tool in genetics.

qa.q: In basidiomycetes, basidiospores are produced:
qa.a: Exogenously on the basidium, usually four in number
qa.e: After karyogamy and meiosis in the basidium, four basidiospores form on its outside.

qa.q: Deuteromycetes are called imperfect fungi because:
qa.a: Only their asexual or vegetative phases are known
qa.e: 'Imperfect' means no sexual stage has been found.

qa.q: Conidia of ascomycetes are produced on special hyphae called:
qa.e: Conidia form exogenously on conidiophores.

qa.q: Which of the following is a rust fungus?
qa.e: Puccinia causes rust; Ustilago causes smut.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Morels and truffles belong to ascomycetes. Reason (R): Ascomycetes produce their ascospores exogenously on conidiophores.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Morels and truffles are edible ascomycetes, so A is true. R is false: ascospores form endogenously inside asci; conidiophores bear the asexual conidia.

qa.q: Which plant is a parasite?
qa.e: Cuscuta is a parasite. Venus fly trap and bladderwort are insectivorous, and mango is an ordinary photosynthetic plant.

qa.q: Animals store food reserves mainly as:
qa.e: Glycogen and fat are the animal reserves.

qa.q: Holozoic nutrition involves:
qa.e: Holozoic means taking in food and digesting it inside the body.

qa.q: Alternation of generations refers to alternation between:
qa.e: Plant life cycles alternate between 2n sporophyte and n gametophyte phases.

qa.q: The cell wall of plants is mainly made of:
qa.e: Plant cell walls are mainly cellulose.

qa.q: Which feature is NOT typical of kingdom Animalia?
qa.e: Animal cells have no cell walls.

qa.q: Insectivorous plants are described as:
qa.e: They make food by photosynthesis but also obtain nutrients from trapped insects.

qa.q: Fungi and animals are both heterotrophs. Which feature separates animals from fungi?
qa.a: Holozoic nutrition and no cell wall
qa.e: Animals ingest food and lack cell walls; fungi absorb food and have chitin walls.

qa.q: Who first discovered that the tobacco mosaic agent was smaller than bacteria?
qa.e: Ivanowsky (1892) found the agent passed through bacteria-proof filters.

qa.q: 'Contagium vivum fluidum' was the term used by:
qa.e: Beijerinek (1898) called the infectious fluid contagium vivum fluidum.

qa.q: The protein coat of a virus is called:
qa.e: The capsid is made of subunits called capsomeres.

qa.q: Bacteriophages usually contain:
qa.e: Most bacteriophages are dsDNA viruses.

qa.q: Which is a correct statement about viruses?
qa.a: No virus contains both RNA and DNA
qa.e: A virus has either RNA or DNA, never both.

qa.q: Which symptom is typical of a viral infection in plants?
qa.e: Mosaic, leaf curl, yellowing, vein clearing and stunting are viral symptoms.

qa.q: Who showed that viruses can be crystallised?
qa.e: Stanley (1935) crystallised viruses and found them to be largely protein.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Viruses can multiply on their own outside a host cell. Reason (R): Outside a living cell, viruses exist as inert crystalline particles.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: viruses multiply only inside a living host cell, using its machinery, which is why they are obligate parasites. R is true: outside a host they are inert crystalline particles.

qa.q: Viroids differ from viruses because viroids:
qa.e: A viroid is free RNA without a protein coat.

qa.q: Potato spindle tuber disease is caused by a:
qa.e: T.O. Diener (1971) found a viroid caused it.

qa.q: Prions are made of:
qa.e: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause infectious neurological diseases.

qa.q: Mad cow disease (BSE) is caused by:
qa.e: BSE is a prion disease; its human analogue is CJD.

qa.q: In a lichen, the fungal partner is called the:
qa.e: Myco- means fungus; phyco- means alga.

qa.q: Lichens are good indicators of:
qa.e: Lichens do not grow in polluted areas.

qa.q: In a lichen, the alga:
qa.e: The autotrophic alga makes food; the fungus provides shelter and absorbs water and minerals.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Viroids are smaller than viruses. Reason (R): Viroids are made of low-molecular-weight RNA with no protein coat.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true; having only a small RNA without a coat is why viroids are smaller than viruses.

qa.q: Why were artificial systems of classification found unsatisfactory?
qa.a: They gave equal weight to vegetative and sexual characters, and vegetative characters are easily affected by environment
qa.e: Using a few, environment-sensitive characters can group unrelated plants together.

qa.q: The natural system of classification was given by:
qa.e: Bentham and Hooker's system was based on natural affinities.

qa.q: Classification based on evolutionary relationships is called:
qa.e: Phylogenetic systems use evolutionary relationships among organisms.

qa.q: Numerical taxonomy is carried out using:
qa.a: Computers and characters coded as numbers
qa.e: Every observable character is coded and analysed with computers.

qa.q: Using the number and behaviour of chromosomes to classify plants is:
qa.e: Cyto- refers to cells; cytotaxonomy uses chromosome data.

qa.q: Which is NOT used by natural systems of classification?
qa.e: Natural systems use many characters; a single character like stamen number is typical of artificial systems.

qa.q: In numerical taxonomy, how are characters weighted?
qa.a: Every character is given equal importance
qa.e: All characters are given equal importance, so hundreds can be considered.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Vegetative characters alone are not reliable for classifying plants. Reason (R): Vegetative characters are easily affected by the environment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; environmental influence makes vegetative characters unreliable, which explains A.

qa.q: Volvox is an example of which algal form?
qa.e: Volvox is a colonial green alga.

qa.q: The most common asexual spores in algae are:
qa.e: Algae usually reproduce asexually by flagellated zoospores.

qa.q: Fusion of two gametes that are similar in size is called:
qa.e: Iso- means equal.

qa.q: Agar is obtained from:
qa.e: Agar comes from the red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria.

qa.q: Algae carry out roughly what share of Earth's total CO₂ fixation by photosynthesis?
qa.e: Algae fix at least half of all CO₂ fixed on Earth.

qa.q: Which alga is used as a protein-rich food supplement, even by space travellers?
qa.e: Chlorella is unicellular and rich in proteins.

qa.q: Spirogyra shows isogamy with gametes that are:
qa.e: Spirogyra's isogamous gametes are non-flagellated (non-motile).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Algae are called primary producers in aquatic ecosystems. Reason (R): Algae are photosynthetic and form the base of aquatic food chains.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; making food by photosynthesis for the food chain is what primary producer means.

qa.q: Floridean starch is the stored food of:
qa.e: Red algae store floridean starch, similar to amylopectin and glycogen.

qa.q: The main pigment that gives red algae their colour is:
qa.e: r-phycoerythrin gives red algae their colour.

qa.q: Brown algae store food as:
qa.e: Laminarin and mannitol are brown-algal reserves.

qa.q: Pyrenoids in green algae contain:
qa.e: Pyrenoids store protein besides starch.

qa.q: Which class has chlorophyll a and c along with fucoxanthin?
qa.e: Fucoxanthin and chlorophyll c are characteristic of brown algae.

qa.q: In brown algae, the leaf-like photosynthetic part of the body is the:
qa.e: Holdfast attaches, stipe is the stalk, and the frond photosynthesises.

qa.q: Which algal class lacks flagella altogether?
qa.e: Red algae have no flagella; green algae have 2–8 equal apical flagella and brown algae have 2 unequal lateral flagella.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Red algae can grow at great depths in the sea. Reason (R): Red algae have r-phycoerythrin, which absorbs the light that penetrates to those depths.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their pigment lets them use the light available deep down, explaining their depth range.

qa.q: Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because they:
qa.a: Live on land but need water for sexual reproduction
qa.e: Water is needed for antherozoids to reach the egg.

qa.q: The dominant, independent phase in bryophytes is the:
qa.e: The main plant body is the haploid gametophyte.

qa.q: The sporophyte of a bryophyte is differentiated into:
qa.e: Foot anchors, seta is a stalk, capsule bears spores.

qa.q: The female sex organ of a bryophyte is the:
qa.e: The flask-shaped archegonium holds a single egg.

qa.q: Bryophytes are important in plant succession because they:
qa.a: Colonise bare rocks along with lichens and help form soil
qa.e: Mosses and lichens are early colonisers that break down rock.

qa.q: Why is Sphagnum used to pack living plant material for transport?
qa.a: It has a high water-holding capacity
qa.e: Sphagnum holds lots of water, keeping material moist.

qa.q: In bryophytes, spores are produced by:
qa.e: Spore mother cells in the capsule undergo reduction division.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The sporophyte of a moss is free-living and independent of the gametophyte. Reason (R): The moss sporophyte stays attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and gets nourishment from it.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the moss sporophyte cannot live on its own. R is true: it stays attached to the gametophyte and depends on it for food, which is exactly why it is not free-living.

qa.q: Gemmae in Marchantia are:
qa.e: Gemmae form in gemma cups and grow into new thalli.

qa.q: The first stage of a moss gametophyte, developing directly from a spore, is the:
qa.e: The protonema is creeping, green, branched and filamentous.

qa.q: Rhizoids in mosses are:
qa.e: Moss rhizoids are multicellular and branched.

qa.q: In mosses, the sex organs are borne on the:
qa.e: Antheridia and archegonia form at the apex of the leafy shoots.

qa.q: Which is a liverwort?
qa.e: Marchantia is a thalloid liverwort; the others are mosses.

qa.q: Compared with liverworts, the sporophyte of mosses is:
qa.e: Moss sporophytes are more elaborate and have elaborate spore dispersal.

qa.q: The thallus of Marchantia is:
qa.a: Dorsiventral and closely appressed to the substrate
qa.e: Marchantia's thallus lies flat and is dorsiventral.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In mosses, the leafy stage develops from the secondary protonema. Reason (R): The leafy stage arises as a lateral bud on the protonema.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and R describes how the leafy stage arises from the protonema.

qa.q: Pteridophytes were the first terrestrial plants to have:
qa.e: Xylem and phloem first appear in pteridophytes.

qa.q: The gametophyte of a fern is called the:
qa.e: The fern gametophyte is the prothallus.

qa.q: In pteridophytes, the main plant body is:
qa.a: A diploid sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves
qa.e: The sporophyte is dominant and well differentiated.

qa.q: Selaginella has small leaves called:
qa.e: Selaginella has microphylls; ferns have macrophylls.

qa.q: Leaf-like structures that bear sporangia are called:
qa.e: Sporophylls subtend the sporangia; a cluster of sporophylls forms a strobilus.

qa.q: Which pteridophytes have sporophylls in compact strobili?
qa.e: Selaginella and Equisetum have compact cones.

qa.q: Why are pteridophytes mostly restricted to damp, shady places?
qa.a: The prothallus and fertilisation need moisture
qa.e: The free-living prothallus and water-dependent fertilisation limit them to moist places.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pteridophytes could grow taller than bryophytes. Reason (R): Pteridophytes were the first plants to produce seeds.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: xylem and phloem let pteridophytes carry water and food over longer distances and support a bigger body. R is false: pteridophytes reproduce by spores; seeds first appear in gymnosperms.

qa.q: Which pteridophyte is heterosporous?
qa.e: Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous; most ferns are homosporous.

qa.q: Equisetum belongs to class:
qa.e: Equisetum (horsetail) is a sphenopsid.

qa.q: Most pteridophytes are:
qa.e: The majority produce a single kind of spore.

qa.q: A microspore of Selaginella develops into a:
qa.e: Microspores give male gametophytes; megaspores give female gametophytes.

qa.q: Which event is regarded as a precursor to the seed habit?
qa.a: Retention of the female gametophyte and development of the embryo on the parent sporophyte
qa.e: In heterosporous forms the embryo develops within the retained female gametophyte, like in a seed.

qa.q: Dryopteris, Pteris and Adiantum belong to:
qa.e: These ferns are placed in Pteropsida.

qa.q: Which is a use of pteridophytes?
qa.e: Pteridophytes are used as soil binders, ornamentals and in medicine.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Salvinia is a heterosporous pteridophyte. Reason (R): Salvinia produces only one kind of spore.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Salvinia produces megaspores and microspores, so A is true and R is false.

qa.q: 'Gymnosperm' literally means:
qa.e: Gymnos = naked, sperma = seed.

qa.q: Coralloid roots are found in:
qa.e: Cycas has coralloid roots with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.

qa.q: Mycorrhizal roots are seen in:
qa.e: Pinus roots associate with fungi as mycorrhizae.

qa.q: Which adaptation of conifer leaves reduces water loss?
qa.e: Needles with thick cuticle and sunken stomata cut transpiration.

qa.q: In gymnosperms, the ovules are:
qa.a: Not enclosed by an ovary wall
qa.e: Ovules are exposed before and after fertilisation.

qa.q: Which gymnosperm is among the tallest tree species?
qa.e: Sequoia, the giant redwood, is one of the tallest trees.

qa.q: The leaves of Cycas are:
qa.a: Pinnate and persist for a few years
qa.e: Cycas has large pinnate compound leaves that last several years.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Conifers can withstand extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. Reason (R): Conifer leaves are needle-like with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these leaf adaptations cut water loss and explain their tolerance.

qa.q: Which of these is an economic use of gymnosperms such as pines and deodar?
qa.e: Conifers give timber, and pine resin is the source of turpentine. Agar and carrageen come from red algae; peat comes from the moss Sphagnum.

qa.q: In gymnosperms, the male gametophyte is the:
qa.e: The highly reduced male gametophyte is the pollen grain.

qa.q: Pollination in gymnosperms is mainly by:
qa.e: Pollen is carried by air currents to the ovules.

qa.q: The megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis to form how many megaspores?
qa.e: Meiosis of one megaspore mother cell gives four megaspores; one develops into the female gametophyte.

qa.q: In which gymnosperm are male cones and megasporophylls borne on different trees?
qa.e: Cycas is dioecious; in Pinus both cones are on the same tree.

qa.q: The female gametophyte of a gymnosperm bears:
qa.e: The multicellular female gametophyte bears two or more archegonia.

qa.q: Unlike bryophytes and pteridophytes, the gametophytes of gymnosperms:
qa.a: Do not have an independent free-living existence
qa.e: They remain within sporangia on the sporophyte.

qa.q: What carries male gametes to the archegonia in gymnosperms?
qa.e: The pollen tube carries male gametes, removing dependence on water.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gymnosperms do not need water for fertilisation. Reason (R): The pollen tube delivers male gametes directly to the archegonia.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the pollen tube removes the need for gametes to swim through water.

qa.q: Which group was the first to produce seeds?
qa.e: Gymnosperms have seeds, though they are naked.

qa.q: The dominant phase of a fern is the:
qa.e: In pteridophytes the sporophyte is dominant.

qa.q: What is the ploidy of a cell of a moss protonema?
qa.e: The protonema is a gametophytic stage, so haploid.

qa.q: Which feature distinguishes gymnosperms from angiosperms?
qa.a: Gymnosperm ovules are not enclosed in an ovary
qa.e: Angiosperm ovules lie inside an ovary and seeds inside fruits; gymnosperm ovules and seeds are exposed.

qa.q: Which plant group has vascular tissue but no seeds?
qa.e: Pteridophytes have xylem and phloem but reproduce by spores.

qa.q: Algae are classified into classes mainly on the basis of:
qa.a: Pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella
qa.e: The three algal classes differ in pigments, food reserves, walls and flagella.

qa.q: Which plant group needs water for fertilisation?
qa.e: Pteridophytes (and bryophytes) have swimming antherozoids.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The fern prothallus is haploid. Reason (R): The fern prothallus develops from a spore produced by meiosis.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the spore is haploid, so the prothallus that grows from it by mitosis is haploid.

qa.q: Sponges show which level of organisation?
qa.e: Sponge cells are loose aggregates without true tissues.

qa.q: In an open circulatory system:
qa.a: Blood is pumped out of the heart and bathes cells and tissues directly
qa.e: Open systems lack a continuous network of vessels; tissues are bathed in blood.

qa.q: A complete digestive system has:
qa.a: Two openings, a mouth and an anus
qa.e: Complete means separate entry (mouth) and exit (anus).

qa.q: Coelenterates show which level of organisation?
qa.e: Cells in coelenterates are arranged into tissues.

qa.q: Which animal has a closed circulatory system?
qa.e: Annelids such as the earthworm have closed circulation; arthropods and molluscs like Pila have open circulation.

qa.q: Members of Platyhelminthes show which level of organisation?
qa.e: Platyhelminthes are the first with tissues grouped into organs.

qa.q: Why are fundamental features used to classify animals?
qa.a: Animals differ in form, but common basic features like symmetry and coelom show relationships
qa.e: Shared fundamental features reveal relationships despite structural differences.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Flatworms have an incomplete digestive system. Reason (R): In flatworms the gut has only one opening to the outside.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; a single opening is what makes the system incomplete.

qa.q: Animals in which any plane through the central axis gives identical halves show:
qa.e: Radial symmetry: many planes through the axis divide the body equally.

qa.q: Which group is diploblastic?
qa.e: Coelenterates (and ctenophores) have only two germ layers.

qa.q: The undifferentiated layer between ectoderm and endoderm in diploblastic animals is the:
qa.e: Mesoglea is jelly-like and not a germ layer.

qa.q: Most sponges are:
qa.e: No plane divides most sponges into equal halves.

qa.q: Which group shows radial symmetry in adults but bilateral symmetry in larvae?
qa.e: Echinoderm larvae are bilateral; adults become radial.

qa.q: Triploblastic organisation first appears in:
qa.e: Platyhelminthes onwards have mesoderm.

qa.q: Bilateral symmetry means:
qa.a: Only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves
qa.e: Bilateral animals have a single plane of symmetry.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ctenophores are diploblastic. Reason (R): Ctenophores have ectoderm, endoderm and a well-formed mesoderm.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Ctenophores are diploblastic (ectoderm, endoderm and mesoglea). R is false because they lack mesoderm.

qa.q: A body cavity lined by mesoderm is called a:
qa.e: A true coelom is lined by mesoderm.

qa.q: Aschelminthes are:
qa.e: Their mesoderm is in scattered pouches, giving a pseudocoelom.

qa.q: Which phylum is acoelomate?
qa.e: Flatworms have no body cavity.

qa.q: Metameric segmentation is best seen in:
qa.e: Earthworm segments show serial repetition of organs.

qa.q: The notochord is derived from which germ layer?
qa.e: The notochord is mesodermally derived.

qa.q: The notochord forms on which side of the embryo?
qa.e: It forms on the dorsal side during embryonic development.

qa.q: Which group of phyla are all non-chordates?
qa.e: Animals from Porifera to Echinodermata lack a notochord.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ascaris has a pseudocoelom. Reason (R): In Ascaris, mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between the ectoderm and the endoderm.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; scattered mesoderm pouches (instead of a lining) is what makes the cavity a pseudocoelom.

qa.q: Water leaves a sponge through the:
qa.e: Water enters by ostia and exits through the osculum.

qa.q: Collar cells lining the spongocoel are called:
qa.e: Choanocytes line the spongocoel and canals.

qa.q: Cnidoblasts are used for:
qa.a: Anchorage, defence and capture of prey
qa.e: Stinging cnidoblasts with nematocysts help hold, defend and capture.

qa.q: Alternation between polyp and medusa forms is called:
qa.e: In Obelia, polyps make medusae asexually and medusae make polyps sexually.

qa.q: Comb plates of ctenophores help in:
qa.e: The eight rows of ciliated comb plates help the animal swim.

qa.q: Which is a freshwater sponge?
qa.e: Spongilla lives in fresh water.

qa.q: Digestion in coelenterates is:
qa.e: Food is partly digested in the gastrovascular cavity and finished inside cells.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sponges have separate male and female individuals. Reason (R): In sponges, eggs and sperms are produced by the same individual.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: sponges are hermaphrodites, not dioecious. R is true: one sponge produces both eggs and sperms, which is what hermaphrodite means.

qa.q: Flame cells in flatworms help in:
qa.e: Flame cells remove wastes and regulate water.

qa.q: Which flatworm shows high regeneration capacity?
qa.e: Planaria can regrow lost parts.

qa.q: Wuchereria is commonly known as the:
qa.e: Wuchereria causes filariasis.

qa.q: Lateral appendages that help Nereis swim are called:
qa.e: Parapodia are paddle-like appendages of Nereis.

qa.q: Excretion and osmoregulation in annelids are carried out by:
qa.e: Annelids use nephridia.

qa.q: Which annelid is dioecious?
qa.e: Nereis has separate sexes; earthworms and leeches are monoecious.

qa.q: Roundworms show sexual dimorphism, meaning:
qa.a: Males and females look different, females often longer
qa.e: Separate sexes that look different is sexual dimorphism.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Annelids have a closed circulatory system. Reason (R): Annelids are acoelomate.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Annelids do have closed circulation (A true), but they are true coelomates, so R is false.

qa.q: The largest phylum in the animal kingdom is:
qa.e: Arthropods make up over two-thirds of named species.

qa.q: Excretion in insects takes place through:
qa.e: Malpighian tubules are the arthropod excretory organs.

qa.q: Which arthropod is called a living fossil?
qa.e: Limulus, the king crab, has changed little over millions of years.

qa.q: The rasping feeding organ in molluscs is the:
qa.e: The file-like radula scrapes food.

qa.q: Pinctada is commonly known as the:
qa.e: Pinctada produces pearls.

qa.q: The respiratory organs of arthropods do NOT include:
qa.e: Nephridia are annelid excretory organs, not respiratory.

qa.q: In molluscs, the soft spongy skin covering the visceral hump is the:
qa.e: The mantle forms a mantle cavity with feather-like gills.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Arthropods have an open circulatory system. Reason (R): Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true facts about arthropods, but the exoskeleton does not explain open circulation.

qa.q: The most distinctive feature of echinoderms is the:
qa.e: The water vascular system aids movement, feeding and respiration.

qa.q: Which is the brittle star?
qa.e: Ophiura is the brittle star; Antedon is the sea lily.

qa.q: Echinoderm larvae are:
qa.e: Larvae are bilateral; adults become radial.

qa.q: The excretory organ of hemichordates is the:
qa.e: Hemichordates excrete through a proboscis gland.

qa.q: The body of Balanoglossus is divided into:
qa.e: Hemichordates have a proboscis, a collar and a long trunk.

qa.q: Which animal is matched with its distinctive feature correctly?
qa.e: Pleurobrachia is a ctenophore with comb plates.

qa.q: The endoskeleton of echinoderms is made of:
qa.e: Calcareous ossicles give them their spiny skin.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Hemichordata is now placed among non-chordates. Reason (R): Hemichordates have a stomochord, not a true notochord.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; lacking a true notochord is why they were moved out of Chordata.

qa.q: Which is NOT a fundamental feature of chordates?
qa.e: Chordates have a dorsal hollow nerve cord; a ventral solid double cord is non-chordate.

qa.q: In urochordates, the notochord is present:
qa.e: Tunicates have a notochord only in the larval tail.

qa.q: Branchiostoma is also called:
qa.e: Branchiostoma is Amphioxus, the lancelet.

qa.q: In vertebrates, the notochord is replaced by:
qa.a: A cartilaginous or bony vertebral column
qa.e: The vertebral column replaces the embryonic notochord.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates
qa.e: Urochordates and cephalochordates are chordates without a vertebral column.

qa.q: Jawless vertebrates belong to:
qa.e: A- means without, gnathos means jaw.

qa.q: In chordates, the heart is:
qa.e: Chordate heart is ventral; non-chordate heart, if present, is dorsal.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ascidia is a non-chordate because the adult has no notochord. Reason (R): Ascidia has a notochord in its larval tail.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: Ascidia is a chordate (subphylum Urochordata). R is true: its larva has a notochord in the tail, and having a notochord at any stage is enough to make it a chordate.

qa.q: Cyclostomes have how many pairs of gill slits?
qa.e: Cyclostomes have 6 to 15 pairs of gill slits.

qa.q: Why must cartilaginous fishes swim constantly?
qa.e: Without an air bladder they cannot stay buoyant at rest.

qa.q: Which fish has electric organs?
qa.e: Torpedo (electric ray) has electric organs; Trygon has a poison sting.

qa.q: The gill cover in bony fishes is called the:
qa.e: Osteichthyes have an operculum on each side.

qa.q: Scales of bony fishes are:
qa.e: Placoid scales are in cartilaginous fish; bony fish have cycloid/ctenoid scales.

qa.q: How many chambers does a fish heart have?
qa.e: Fish hearts have one auricle and one ventricle.

qa.q: Cyclostomes live in the sea but:
qa.a: Migrate to fresh water to spawn
qa.e: They migrate to fresh water for spawning and die soon after.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Teeth of sharks are modified placoid scales. Reason (R): Sharks have a bony endoskeleton.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Shark teeth are modified placoid scales (A true), but sharks have a cartilaginous endoskeleton, so R is false.

qa.q: The heart of an amphibian has:
qa.e: Amphibians have a three-chambered heart.

qa.q: The common chamber into which gut, urinary and reproductive tracts open in amphibians is the:
qa.e: The cloaca opens to the outside.

qa.q: Which reptile has a four-chambered heart?
qa.e: Crocodiles are the exception with four chambers.

qa.q: Ichthyophis is a:
qa.e: Ichthyophis is a limbless amphibian, not a snake.

qa.q: In amphibians, respiration occurs through:
qa.e: Amphibians use gills (larvae), lungs and moist skin.

qa.q: The skin of reptiles is:
qa.a: Dry and cornified with epidermal scales
qa.e: Reptile skin is dry with scales or scutes.

qa.q: Which is a poisonous snake?
qa.e: Vipera (viper) is venomous; the others are a lizard, tortoise and turtle.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Snakes and lizards shed their scales as skin cast. Reason (R): Reptiles are warm-blooded animals.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Shedding skin cast is true, but reptiles are poikilotherms (cold-blooded), so R is false.

qa.q: Pneumatic bones are found in:
qa.e: Birds have hollow long bones with air cavities.

qa.q: The most unique feature of mammals is:
qa.e: Birds also have four chambers and lungs; mammary glands are found only in mammals.

qa.q: Which mammal lays eggs?
qa.e: The platypus is an oviparous mammal.

qa.q: The skin of birds has only one gland, the:
qa.a: Oil gland at the base of the tail
qa.e: Bird skin is dry with only an oil gland near the tail.

qa.q: Additional chambers in the bird digestive tract are:
qa.e: The crop stores food and the gizzard grinds it.

qa.q: Which bird is flightless?
qa.e: Struthio (ostrich) cannot fly.

qa.q: Pteropus is a:
qa.e: Pteropus is a bat, a mammal adapted for flight.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Birds and mammals can live in very cold and very hot places. Reason (R): Birds and mammals are homoiothermous and keep a constant body temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; a constant body temperature lets them stay active in extreme climates.

qa.q: An animal is bilateral, triploblastic, has no body cavity and a gut with one opening. It belongs to:
qa.e: Acoelomate with an incomplete gut fits flatworms.

qa.q: Which pair both have open circulation?
qa.e: Arthropods and molluscs have open circulation; annelids and chordates have closed.

qa.q: Which phylum has radial symmetry in adults and is coelomate?
qa.e: Coelenterates and ctenophores are radial but not coelomate.

qa.q: Indirect development means:
qa.a: There is a larval stage that differs from the adult
qa.e: A distinct larva shows indirect development.

qa.q: Which phylum is segmented and coelomate but has closed circulation?
qa.e: Annelids are segmented coelomates with closed circulation.

qa.q: A marine animal is diploblastic with eight rows of comb plates. Its phylum is:
qa.e: Comb plates are diagnostic of ctenophores.

qa.q: Which group shows direct development?
qa.e: Birds hatch as miniature adults; the others have larvae.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Molluscs and arthropods both have open circulation. Reason (R): Molluscs and arthropods are both segmented.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Both do have open circulation, but molluscs are unsegmented, so R is false.

qa.q: The tap root system develops from the:
qa.e: The radicle elongates directly into the primary root.

qa.q: Wheat has which type of root system?
qa.e: Monocots like wheat have fibrous roots from the stem base.

qa.q: Roots arising from any part of the plant other than the radicle are called:
qa.e: Adventitious roots arise from stem, branches or nodes.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of roots?
qa.a: Photosynthesis as the main food-making organ
qa.e: Leaves are the main photosynthetic organs; roots absorb, anchor, store and make growth regulators.

qa.q: Morphology is the study of:
qa.e: Anatomy studies internal structure; morphology studies external form.

qa.q: In monocots, the primary root is:
qa.a: Short-lived and replaced by many roots from the stem base
qa.e: This replacement forms the fibrous root system.

qa.q: Mustard is an example of a plant with:
qa.e: Mustard is a dicot with a tap root.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Banyan has adventitious roots. Reason (R): In the banyan, roots grow down from the branches.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; roots from branches arise from a part other than the radicle, so they are adventitious.

qa.q: Which part protects the tender root apex?
qa.e: The thimble-like root cap shields the apex.

qa.q: Root hairs develop from the region of:
qa.e: Epidermal cells in the maturation region form root hairs.

qa.q: Cells that divide repeatedly in a root lie in the:
qa.e: Small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm divide repeatedly there.

qa.q: The portion of a stem between two nodes is the:
qa.e: Nodes bear leaves; internodes lie between nodes.

qa.q: Which is a function of the stem?
qa.e: Stems conduct materials and spread branches.

qa.q: The stem develops from the:
qa.e: The plumule gives the shoot; the radicle gives the root.

qa.q: Root hairs mainly:
qa.e: Their large surface area aids absorption.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A root grows in length mainly because of the root cap. Reason (R): Cells in the region of elongation enlarge and elongate rapidly.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the root cap only protects the tip. R is true: rapid enlargement and elongation of cells in the region of elongation is what increases root length.

qa.q: A swollen leaf base in some leguminous plants is called the:
qa.e: The pulvinus is a swollen leaf base.

qa.q: Venation in which veinlets form a network is:
qa.e: A network of veinlets is reticulate venation.

qa.q: Parallel venation is typical of:
qa.e: Monocots generally have parallel venation.

qa.q: How does a long flexible petiole help a leaf?
qa.a: Lets the blade flutter, cooling it and bringing fresh air
qa.e: Fluttering cools the leaf and refreshes air at its surface.

qa.q: The three main parts of a typical leaf are:
qa.e: Leaf base, petiole and lamina make a typical leaf.

qa.q: In monocots, the leaf base usually:
qa.a: Expands into a sheath that covers the stem
qa.e: The sheathing leaf base is a monocot feature.

qa.q: Veins in the lamina:
qa.a: Provide rigidity and transport water, minerals and food
qa.e: Veins support the blade and act as channels of transport.

qa.q: Stipules are:
qa.a: Two small leaf-like structures that may be borne at the leaf base
qa.e: Stipules are lateral outgrowths of the leaf base.

qa.q: Neem has which type of leaf?
qa.e: Neem leaflets are on a common rachis.

qa.q: In a palmately compound leaf, leaflets are attached:
qa.a: At a common point at the tip of the petiole
qa.e: Palmate leaflets radiate from the petiole tip, as in silk cotton.

qa.q: Guava shows which phyllotaxy?
qa.e: Guava and Calotropis have a pair of leaves at each node.

qa.q: Alstonia shows:
qa.e: More than two leaves arise at each node of Alstonia.

qa.q: A leaf is compound when:
qa.a: Incisions of the lamina reach the midrib, forming leaflets
qa.e: Incisions reaching the midrib break the lamina into leaflets.

qa.q: Phyllotaxy refers to:
qa.a: The arrangement of leaves on a stem
qa.e: Phyllotaxy is leaf arrangement; venation is vein arrangement.

qa.q: China rose shows which phyllotaxy?
qa.e: A single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A leaflet of a compound leaf has no axillary bud. Reason (R): In a compound leaf, the axillary bud is found only in the axil of the petiole.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains why the leaflets themselves lack buds.

qa.q: In a racemose inflorescence, the flowers are arranged in:
qa.e: Older flowers below, younger above: acropetal.

qa.q: In a cymose inflorescence, the main axis:
qa.e: The apex becomes a flower, limiting growth.

qa.q: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called:
qa.e: Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers.

qa.q: A flower is regarded as a modified:
qa.e: The shoot apical meristem changes into a floral meristem.

qa.q: Basipetal order means:
qa.a: Older flowers at the top, younger towards the base
qa.e: Basipetal is typical of cymose inflorescences.

qa.q: Which is the key difference between racemose and cymose inflorescences?
qa.a: Whether the main axis continues to grow or ends in a flower
qa.e: Racemose axes keep growing; cymose axes end in a flower.

qa.q: When a flower is formed, the internodes of the floral axis:
qa.a: Do not elongate, so the axis condenses
qa.e: Condensed internodes allow floral whorls to form close together.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Growth of the main axis is limited in a racemose inflorescence. Reason (R): In a racemose inflorescence, the apex does not turn into a flower.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: in racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing; limited growth is a cymose feature. R is true: the apex never becomes a flower, which is why growth is unlimited.

qa.q: The swollen end of the pedicel on which floral whorls are borne is the:
qa.e: The thalamus (receptacle) carries all four whorls.

qa.q: A flower that can be divided into two similar halves only in one vertical plane is:
qa.e: Pea and gulmohur flowers are zygomorphic.

qa.q: Canna has which type of flower symmetry?
qa.e: No vertical plane divides a canna flower into similar halves.

qa.q: When calyx and corolla cannot be told apart, as in lily, they are called:
qa.e: The undifferentiated outer whorls form the perianth.

qa.q: Which are the reproductive whorls of a flower?
qa.e: Stamens and carpels are reproductive; sepals and petals are accessory.

qa.q: A flower with floral parts in multiples of four is:
qa.e: Tetra- means four.

qa.q: A flower lacking bracts is described as:
qa.e: Ebracteate means without bracts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A unisexual flower has only stamens or only carpels. Reason (R): In a unisexual flower, the calyx and corolla are always absent.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is the definition of unisexual. R is false: unisexual flowers can have sepals and petals.

qa.q: In which flower is the ovary inferior?
qa.e: Guava is epigynous with an inferior ovary.

qa.q: Perigynous flowers have an ovary that is:
qa.e: Other parts are on the thalamus rim at about the ovary's level.

qa.q: Twisted aestivation is found in:
qa.a: China rose, lady's finger and cotton
qa.e: Each petal overlaps the next in one direction.

qa.q: In valvate aestivation, the sepals or petals:
qa.a: Just touch at the margins without overlapping
qa.e: Valvate means edge-to-edge contact, as in Calotropis.

qa.q: In vexillary aestivation, the two smallest anterior petals are called the:
qa.e: Standard is largest, wings are lateral, keel is smallest and anterior.

qa.q: A calyx with united sepals is:
qa.e: Gamo- means united.

qa.q: Brinjal flowers are:
qa.e: Brinjal has a superior ovary.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Petals are usually brightly coloured. Reason (R): Bright petals attract insects for pollination.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; attracting pollinators is the reason for bright colours.

qa.q: A stamen consists of:
qa.e: Filament is the stalk; the anther makes pollen.

qa.q: A sterile stamen is called a:
qa.e: Staminode is a stamen that does not produce fertile pollen.

qa.q: Stamens united in two bundles are:
qa.e: Di- means two, as in pea.

qa.q: Stamens attached to the perianth, as in lily, are:
qa.e: Epiphyllous means on the perianth.

qa.q: How many pollen sacs are present in a typical bilobed anther?
qa.e: Two lobes, each with two pollen sacs: 2 × 2 = 4.

qa.q: China rose has which type of stamens?
qa.e: All stamens of china rose are united in one bundle around the style.

qa.q: Citrus has stamens that are:
qa.e: Citrus stamens form more than two bundles.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Brinjal has epipetalous stamens. Reason (R): In brinjal, stamens are fused with the gynoecium.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Brinjal stamens are attached to the petals (A true). R is false: they are not fused with the gynoecium.

qa.q: Placentation in pea is:
qa.e: Ovules lie in two rows on a ridge along the ventral suture.

qa.q: Axile placentation is found in:
qa.e: Ovules are on a central axis in a multilocular ovary.

qa.q: In which placentation does a false septum make a one-chambered ovary two-chambered?
qa.e: Mustard and Argemone show parietal placentation with a false septum.

qa.q: Free central placentation is seen in:
qa.e: Ovules are on a central axis without septa.

qa.q: A gynoecium with free carpels is called:
qa.e: Lotus and rose have free carpels.

qa.q: The receptive surface for pollen grains is the:
qa.e: Pollen lands on the stigma.

qa.q: In sunflower and marigold, placentation is:
qa.e: The placenta is at the base with a single ovule.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A ripened ovary forms the fruit. Reason (R): After fertilisation, ovules develop into seeds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true statements about events after fertilisation, but seed formation from ovules does not explain how the ovary becomes the fruit.

qa.q: A fruit that develops without fertilisation is called:
qa.e: Parthenocarpy means fruit formation without fertilisation.

qa.q: The edible part of mango is the:
qa.e: The fleshy mesocarp is eaten.

qa.q: In coconut, the mesocarp is:
qa.e: The fibrous mesocarp gives coir.

qa.q: Drupes develop from:
qa.a: Monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded
qa.e: Mango and coconut are one-seeded drupes from monocarpellary superior ovaries.

qa.q: The three layers of a fleshy pericarp, from outside, are:
qa.e: Epi = outer, meso = middle, endo = inner.

qa.q: A seed is made up of:
qa.a: A seed coat and an embryo
qa.e: The embryo inside has a radicle, embryonal axis and cotyledons.

qa.q: Which plants have embryos with two cotyledons?
qa.e: Gram and pea are dicots.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mango is called a drupe. Reason (R): Mango develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and has a single seed with a stony endocarp.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R lists the features that define a drupe.

qa.q: The scar on a seed coat where the seed was attached to the fruit is the:
qa.e: The hilum marks the point of attachment.

qa.q: Which is an endospermic dicot seed?
qa.e: Castor keeps its endosperm; gram, pea and bean do not.

qa.q: The single shield-shaped cotyledon of maize is the:
qa.e: Scutellum is the maize cotyledon.

qa.q: The coleoptile encloses the:
qa.e: Coleoptile covers the plumule; coleorhiza covers the radicle.

qa.q: The proteinous layer separating the endosperm from the embryo in maize is the:
qa.e: The aleurone layer is the outer covering of the endosperm.

qa.q: The inner layer of the dicot seed coat is the:
qa.e: Outer testa, inner tegmen.

qa.q: Which monocot seeds are non-endospermic?
qa.e: Most monocot seeds are endospermic; orchids are an exception.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In maize, the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall. Reason (R): In maize, the seed coat is membranous.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true features of maize grain, but being membranous does not explain why the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall.

qa.q: In a floral formula, C(5) means:
qa.e: Brackets show cohesion (fusion) within a whorl.

qa.q: The symbol % in a floral formula stands for:
qa.e: % shows a zygomorphic flower; ⊕ is actinomorphic.

qa.q: A line drawn below G in a floral formula indicates:
qa.e: G̲ means superior; Ḡ means inferior.

qa.q: In a floral diagram, the dot at the top represents the:
qa.e: The dot shows the position of the mother axis relative to the flower.

qa.q: Adhesion between two whorls in a floral formula is shown by:
qa.a: A line drawn above the symbols of those whorls
qa.e: A line above the symbols joins the adhering whorls, e.g. C and A.

qa.q: In a floral diagram, which whorl is drawn at the centre?
qa.e: Calyx is outermost; gynoecium is in the centre.

qa.q: In a semi-technical description, which is described first?
qa.e: Description starts with habit, then vegetative and floral characters.

qa.q: In the formula ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), how many floral parts (sepals + petals + stamens) are there outside the gynoecium?
qa.e: Sepals 5 + petals 5 + stamens 5 = 15.

qa.q: Placentation in Solanaceae is:
qa.e: A swollen placenta with many ovules on the axis of a bilocular ovary.

qa.q: How many stamens does a Solanaceae flower usually have?
qa.e: Five epipetalous stamens.

qa.q: Which Solanaceae plant is used as a medicine?
qa.e: Belladonna and ashwagandha are medicinal.

qa.q: The fruit of Solanaceae is a:
qa.e: Fruits are berries (tomato, brinjal) or capsules.

qa.q: The ovary in Solanaceae is:
qa.e: Ovary is superior, made of two fused carpels.

qa.q: Tobacco is used as a:
qa.e: NCERT lists tobacco as a fumigatory.

qa.q: Aestivation of the calyx and corolla in Solanaceae is:
qa.e: Both sepals and petals are valvate.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Potato is placed in Solanaceae. Reason (R): The potato tuber is an underground stem.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but having an underground stem is not why potato belongs to Solanaceae; its floral characters place it there.

qa.q: The three tissue systems are classified on the basis of their:
qa.e: Epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems are defined by where they lie.

qa.q: Which is a complex permanent tissue?
qa.e: Phloem has several kinds of cells working together.

qa.q: Anatomy is the study of:
qa.e: Morphology deals with external form; anatomy with internal structure.

qa.q: Collenchyma provides:
qa.e: Its corner-thickened living cells support growing parts.

qa.q: Which tissue conducts water and minerals?
qa.e: Xylem moves water and minerals; phloem moves food.

qa.q: Sclerenchyma cells are usually:
qa.e: Sclerenchyma fibres and sclereids are dead, lignified cells.

qa.q: Tissues that keep dividing are:
qa.e: Meristems are regions of active cell division.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Xylem is called a complex tissue. Reason (R): Xylem is made of more than one type of cell.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; having several cell types is exactly what makes a tissue complex.

qa.q: Guard cells in grasses are:
qa.e: Grasses have dumb-bell shaped guard cells; dicots have bean-shaped ones.

qa.q: The stomatal apparatus consists of:
qa.a: Stomatal aperture, guard cells and subsidiary cells
qa.e: All three parts together form the stomatal apparatus.

qa.q: Which wall of a guard cell is highly thickened?
qa.e: Thick inner and thin outer walls help the pore open as guard cells swell.

qa.q: Cuticle is absent in:
qa.e: Roots absorb water, so they lack cuticle.

qa.q: Root hairs are:
qa.e: Each root hair is an extension of one epidermal cell.

qa.q: Trichomes help the plant by:
qa.a: Preventing water loss due to transpiration
qa.e: Trichomes reduce transpiration losses.

qa.q: The main functions of stomata are:
qa.e: Stomata regulate water vapour loss and gas exchange.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The epidermis of roots is covered by a thick cuticle. Reason (R): The cuticle reduces loss of water from the plant surface.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: the cuticle is absent in roots, which must absorb water. R is true: on leaves and stems the waxy cuticle cuts water loss.

qa.q: Vascular bundles with cambium are called:
qa.e: Cambium allows secondary growth, making bundles open.

qa.q: In roots, vascular bundles are:
qa.e: Xylem and phloem alternate on different radii in roots.

qa.q: Protoxylem lying towards the centre and metaxylem towards the periphery is:
qa.e: Endarch condition is typical of stems.

qa.q: In leaves, the ground tissue is called the:
qa.e: Leaf ground tissue is chloroplast-rich mesophyll.

qa.q: Monocot vascular bundles are closed because they:
qa.e: No cambium means no secondary tissues.

qa.q: In conjoint vascular bundles, phloem usually lies:
qa.a: On the outer side of xylem
qa.e: Conjoint bundles are usually collateral, with phloem outside.

qa.q: Which tissues are part of the ground tissue system?
qa.a: Cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays
qa.e: Ground tissue is everything except epidermis and vascular bundles.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Dicot stems can undergo secondary growth. Reason (R): Dicot stem vascular bundles are open, with cambium between xylem and phloem.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; cambium in open bundles produces secondary xylem and phloem.

qa.q: Casparian strips are made of:
qa.e: Waxy, water-impermeable suberin forms the Casparian strips.

qa.q: Lateral roots originate from the:
qa.e: Pericycle cells initiate lateral roots and vascular cambium.

qa.q: The outermost layer of a root is the:
qa.e: Root epidermis is called epiblema and has no cuticle.

qa.q: Monocot roots usually have:
qa.e: Monocot roots are polyarch.

qa.q: Parenchyma lying between xylem and phloem in a root is the:
qa.e: Conjunctive tissue lies between xylem and phloem patches.

qa.q: All tissues inside the endodermis together form the:
qa.e: Pericycle, vascular bundles and pith make up the stele.

qa.q: The endodermis of a root is made of:
qa.a: One layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces
qa.e: Its compact barrel-shaped cells bear Casparian strips.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Monocot roots do not show secondary growth. Reason (R): Monocot roots have a large, well-developed pith.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, but a large pith is not the reason; the absence of a vascular cambium is.

qa.q: In a dicot stem, the hypodermis is made of:
qa.e: Dicot stem hypodermis is collenchymatous; monocot stem hypodermis is sclerenchymatous.

qa.q: The endodermis of a dicot stem is also called the:
qa.e: Its cells are rich in starch grains.

qa.q: Vascular bundles in a dicot stem are:
qa.a: Conjoint, open and endarch, arranged in a ring
qa.e: Ring arrangement of open, endarch bundles is the dicot stem signature.

qa.q: Water-containing cavities in vascular bundles are seen in:
qa.e: They are a feature of monocot stem bundles.

qa.q: In a monocot stem, the peripheral vascular bundles are generally:
qa.e: Peripheral bundles are smaller.

qa.q: Phloem parenchyma is absent in:
qa.e: Monocot stem bundles lack phloem parenchyma.

qa.q: In a dicot stem, the pericycle occurs as:
qa.a: Semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma above the phloem
qa.e: Pericycle forms sclerenchyma caps over the phloem.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A monocot stem has no distinct pith. Reason (R): Vascular bundles in a monocot stem are scattered throughout the ground tissue.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because bundles are scattered, there is no clear central pith zone.

qa.q: Bulliform cells are found in:
qa.e: Bulliform cells are modified adaxial epidermal cells of grasses.

qa.q: In a dorsiventral leaf, the palisade parenchyma is:
qa.a: Elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel, towards the upper side
qa.e: Palisade cells are adaxial, elongated and parallel.

qa.q: Which surface of a dicot leaf usually has more stomata?
qa.e: The abaxial epidermis generally bears more stomata.

qa.q: In an isobilateral leaf, the mesophyll is:
qa.a: Not differentiated into palisade and spongy
qa.e: Monocot leaves lack the palisade-spongy distinction.

qa.q: When bulliform cells become flaccid, the leaf:
qa.a: Curls inwards to reduce water loss
qa.e: Flaccid bulliform cells roll the leaf to cut transpiration.

qa.q: Bundle sheath cells in leaves are:
qa.e: They form a layer around each vascular bundle.

qa.q: Spongy parenchyma has:
qa.a: Loosely arranged cells with large air spaces
qa.e: Its loose cells and air cavities aid gas exchange.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In monocot leaves, vascular bundles are of nearly similar size except in main veins. Reason (R): Monocot leaves have parallel venation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; parallel venation is reflected in the near-similar sizes of the bundles.

qa.q: A section shows conjoint, closed bundles scattered in ground tissue with a sclerenchymatous hypodermis. It is a:
qa.e: Scattered closed bundles and sclerenchymatous hypodermis mean monocot stem.

qa.q: Which feature tells a root from a stem in a T.S.?
