qa.a: Radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem
qa.e: Radial, exarch bundles are typical of roots.

qa.q: A leaf section shows stomata on both surfaces and undifferentiated mesophyll. It is:
qa.e: These are features of an isobilateral leaf.

qa.q: Which feature is common to dicot root, monocot root, dicot stem and monocot stem?
qa.e: All have vascular tissue; the others are specific to one organ.

qa.q: A T.S. shows a ring of bundles, each with cambium between xylem and phloem. It is a:
qa.e: Ring arrangement with open bundles identifies dicot stem.

qa.q: Which structure must be labelled in a T.S. of a dorsiventral leaf?
qa.e: Palisade and spongy mesophyll are key leaf labels.

qa.q: A root T.S. with more than six xylem bundles is most likely from:
qa.e: Polyarch roots are typical of monocots.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A T.S. showing radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem is from a root. Reason (R): Stems also have radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: radial bundles with exarch xylem are the signature of roots. R is false: stems have conjoint bundles with endarch xylem.

qa.q: How many basic types of tissues are found in animals?
qa.e: Epithelial, connective, muscular and neural.

qa.q: A group of similar cells with intercellular material performing a common function is a:
qa.e: That is the definition of a tissue.

qa.q: The heart, lungs and kidneys are examples of:
qa.e: Each is made of several tissues working together.

qa.q: Which tissue type is mainly responsible for control and coordination?
qa.e: Neural tissue controls the body's responses.

qa.q: In animals, anatomy refers to the study of:
qa.e: Anatomy deals with internal organs; morphology with external form.

qa.q: Division of labour in a multicellular animal means:
qa.a: Different cells, tissues and organs perform different functions for the whole body
qa.e: Specialisation of parts allows efficient functioning.

qa.q: Organs working together to perform a common function form:
qa.e: For example, the digestive system.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The complexity of organ systems in animals shows an evolutionary trend. Reason (R): All animals have the same number of organ systems.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Complexity does show an evolutionary trend (A true), but animals differ in their organ systems, so R is false.

qa.q: The most common Indian frog is:
qa.e: NCERT names Rana tigrina as the common Indian frog.

qa.q: Summer sleep in frogs is called:
qa.e: Aestivation is summer sleep; hibernation is winter sleep.

qa.q: How does a frog take in water?
qa.e: A frog never drinks; water is absorbed through the moist skin.

qa.q: Which structure protects a frog's eyes under water?
qa.e: The nictitating membrane covers the eye.

qa.q: Which feature is present only in male frogs?
qa.a: Copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimb
qa.e: Copulatory pads and vocal sacs are male features.

qa.q: Frogs are called poikilotherms because they:
qa.a: Do not have a constant body temperature
qa.e: Their body temperature varies with the environment.

qa.q: The colour of the frog's ventral skin is:
qa.e: Dorsal is olive green with spots; ventral is pale yellow.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Frogs can change colour. Reason (R): Colour change helps frogs hide from their enemies.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; camouflage from enemies is the purpose of colour change.

qa.q: Why is the frog's alimentary canal short?
qa.e: Carnivores have shorter intestines.

qa.q: Food is captured by the frog's:
qa.e: The sticky bilobed tongue catches prey.

qa.q: Respiration through the skin is called:
qa.e: Cutaneous means 'of the skin'.

qa.q: Bile in frogs is secreted by the:
qa.e: The liver secretes bile; the gall bladder stores it.

qa.q: During hibernation, frogs exchange gases through the:
qa.e: Gas exchange during aestivation and hibernation is cutaneous.

qa.q: The partly digested food that passes from the stomach to the duodenum is:
qa.e: Chyme moves to the duodenum for further digestion.

qa.q: In frogs, digested food is absorbed by:
qa.a: Villi and microvilli of the intestine
qa.e: Finger-like folds in the intestinal wall absorb nutrients.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Frogs can stay under water for a long time. Reason (R): In water, a frog's moist skin exchanges dissolved oxygen by diffusion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; cutaneous respiration lets frogs get oxygen under water.

qa.q: Which feature is NOT an adaptation of the frog to its amphibious life?
qa.a: A body covered with dry scales
qa.e: Moist skin (breathing in water), webbed hind feet (swimming), lungs (air) and the nictitating membrane (eye protection in water) all suit life in water and on land. Frog skin has no scales.

qa.q: The frog heart has:
qa.e: A three-chambered heart.

qa.q: The triangular structure joining the right atrium of the frog heart is the:
qa.e: The sinus venosus receives blood from the venae cavae.

qa.q: The venous connection between the intestine and the liver in frogs is the:
qa.e: Hepatic refers to the liver.

qa.q: Frog red blood cells are:
qa.e: Frog RBCs keep their nuclei.

qa.q: Frogs excrete mainly:
qa.e: Frogs are ureotelic.

qa.q: The structural and functional units of frog kidneys are:
qa.e: Each kidney has many uriniferous tubules.

qa.q: In male frogs, the ureters also carry sperms and act as:
qa.e: Male ureters are urinogenital ducts opening into the cloaca.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Lymph differs from blood. Reason (R): Lymph lacks a few proteins and red blood cells.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R states how lymph differs from blood.

qa.q: How many pairs of cranial nerves arise from the frog's brain?
qa.e: Frogs have ten pairs of cranial nerves.

qa.q: The mid-brain of a frog is characterised by:
qa.e: Optic lobes form the mid-brain.

qa.q: The medulla oblongata leaves the cranium through the:
qa.e: It continues as the spinal cord through the foramen magnum.

qa.q: Which is NOT an endocrine gland of the frog?
qa.e: The gall bladder stores bile and is not endocrine.

qa.q: The organ of smell in the frog is the:
qa.e: Smell is sensed by the nasal epithelium.

qa.q: Which frog sense organs are well-organised structures?
qa.e: Other senses are cellular aggregations around nerve endings.

qa.q: The autonomic nervous system of the frog consists of:
qa.e: The ANS has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Frogs have a prominent external ear (pinna). Reason (R): In frogs, only the tympanum is seen externally.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: frogs have no external ear. R is true: only the membranous tympanum is visible on each side of the head.

qa.q: Testes of a frog are attached to the kidneys by the:
qa.e: The mesorchium is a double fold of peritoneum.

qa.q: How many vasa efferentia arise from each testis of a frog?
qa.e: NCERT gives 10 to 12 vasa efferentia.

qa.q: Fertilisation in frogs is:
qa.e: Eggs and sperms meet in water outside the body.

qa.q: The larval stage of a frog is the:
qa.e: Tadpoles undergo metamorphosis.

qa.q: The common chamber that passes faeces, urine and sperms to the outside is the:
qa.e: The cloaca is shared by digestive, excretory and reproductive tracts.

qa.q: Frogs maintain ecological balance mainly because they:
qa.a: Are an important link in food chains and food webs
qa.e: They eat insects and are eaten by larger animals.

qa.q: A mature female frog can lay about how many ova at a time?
qa.e: NCERT states 2500 to 3000 ova.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Frog development is called indirect. Reason (R): Frogs pass through a tadpole larva that undergoes metamorphosis.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; a distinct larval stage is what makes development indirect.

qa.q: Who first saw and described a live cell?
qa.e: Leeuwenhoek observed live cells with his microscopes.

qa.q: 'Omnis cellula-e cellula' was given by:
qa.e: Virchow (1855) said all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

qa.q: Schwann concluded that a unique feature of plant cells is the:
qa.e: He found the cell wall present only in plant cells.

qa.q: Which statement belongs to the modern cell theory?
qa.a: All cells arise from pre-existing cells
qa.e: Modern cell theory includes Virchow's idea.

qa.q: The nucleus was discovered by:
qa.e: Robert Brown discovered the nucleus.

qa.q: The main gap in Schleiden and Schwann's cell theory was that it did not explain:
qa.e: Virchow later filled this gap.

qa.q: A unicellular organism is one that:
qa.a: Carries out all life functions within a single cell
qa.e: One cell performs all activities and lives independently.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The cell is called the structural and functional unit of life. Reason (R): Anything less than a complete cell does not ensure independent living.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since nothing smaller than a cell can live independently, the cell is the basic unit of life.

qa.q: The smallest cells known are:
qa.e: Mycoplasma are only about 0.3 µm long.

qa.q: The largest isolated single cell is the:
qa.e: The ostrich egg is the largest single cell.

qa.q: About how many micrometres is the diameter of a human red blood cell?
qa.e: Human RBCs are about 7.0 µm across.

qa.q: Which organelle is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
qa.e: Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound and present in all cells.

qa.q: The main arena of cellular activities is the:
qa.e: Most chemical reactions occur in the cytoplasm.

qa.q: Which cells are among the longest in the body?
qa.e: Nerve cells can be very long.

qa.q: A 3 µm long bacterium is how many times longer than a 0.3 µm Mycoplasma?
Assertion (A): Ribosomes are found inside mitochondria and chloroplasts. Reason (R): Ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Ribosomes do occur in mitochondria and chloroplasts (A true), but they are not membrane-bound (R false).

qa.q: Small circular DNA molecules outside the genomic DNA of bacteria are:
qa.e: Plasmids carry extra genes such as antibiotic resistance.

qa.q: The outermost layer of the bacterial cell envelope is the:
qa.e: Glycocalyx lies outside the cell wall.

qa.q: A thick and tough glycocalyx is called a:
qa.e: A loose sheath is a slime layer; a thick tough one is a capsule.

qa.q: Bacteria are classified as Gram-positive or Gram-negative based on:
qa.a: Their cell envelope and response to Gram staining
qa.e: Gram staining reflects differences in the cell envelope.

qa.q: Which prokaryote lacks a cell wall?
qa.e: Mycoplasma is the exception.

qa.q: The genomic DNA of a bacterium is:
qa.e: It is a single circular DNA in the nucleoid.

qa.q: The bacterial cell wall:
qa.a: Gives shape and prevents the cell from bursting or collapsing
qa.e: Structural support is the wall's role; the plasma membrane is semi-permeable.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Some bacteria survive antibiotic treatment. Reason (R): Plasmids in some bacteria carry genes for antibiotic resistance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; plasmid-borne resistance explains survival.

qa.q: Infoldings of the bacterial plasma membrane are called:
qa.e: Mesosomes are membrane extensions into the cell.

qa.q: The three parts of a bacterial flagellum are:
qa.e: Bacterial flagella differ from the 9+2 eukaryotic flagella.

qa.q: Which surface structures of bacteria do NOT help in motility?
qa.e: Pili and fimbriae are for attachment and other roles, not movement.

qa.q: Prokaryotic ribosomes are:
qa.e: 70S with 50S + 30S subunits.

qa.q: A chain of ribosomes attached to a single mRNA is a:
qa.e: Polysomes translate one mRNA many times at once.

qa.q: Which is NOT an inclusion body in prokaryotes?
qa.e: Mitochondria are absent in prokaryotes; the others are inclusions.

qa.q: Pigment-containing membranous extensions in cyanobacteria are:
qa.e: Chromatophores hold pigments for photosynthesis.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Inclusion bodies in prokaryotes lie free in the cytoplasm. Reason (R): Inclusion bodies are not bounded by any membrane system.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; lacking a membrane is why they lie free in the cytoplasm.

qa.q: Which structure is found in animal cells but absent in almost all plant cells?
qa.e: Centrioles are typical of animal cells.

qa.q: Which organisms are eukaryotes?
qa.e: All except Monera are eukaryotic.

qa.q: Which feature is present in plant cells but not in animal cells?
qa.e: Plant cells have cell walls; both have mitochondria, ribosomes and Golgi.

qa.q: Eukaryotic cells differ from prokaryotic cells in having:
qa.a: Membrane-bound organelles and an organised nucleus
qa.e: Ribosomes, cytoplasm and membrane are found in both.

qa.q: The cytoplasmic ribosomes of eukaryotic cells are:
qa.e: Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S.

qa.q: A cell has no nuclear membrane and no mitochondria but has 70S ribosomes. It is:
qa.e: These are prokaryotic features.

qa.q: A large central vacuole is characteristic of:
qa.e: Plant vacuoles can occupy most of the cell volume.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fungi are prokaryotes. Reason (R): Fungal cells have an organised nucleus with a nuclear envelope.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: fungi are eukaryotes. R is true: an organised nucleus with a nuclear envelope is exactly the feature that makes them eukaryotic.

qa.q: The fluid mosaic model was proposed by:
qa.e: Singer and Nicolson proposed it in 1972.

qa.q: In the lipid bilayer, the hydrophobic tails face:
qa.a: The inner part of the membrane
qa.e: Tails are tucked inside, away from water.

qa.q: The human RBC membrane has approximately what percentage of protein?
qa.e: About 52% protein and 40% lipids.

qa.q: Proteins that are partially or totally buried in the membrane are:
qa.e: Integral proteins are embedded; peripheral ones sit on the surface.

qa.q: Movement of molecules against a concentration gradient using ATP is:
qa.e: Active transport, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

qa.q: Why do polar molecules need carrier proteins to cross the membrane?
qa.a: They cannot pass through the non-polar lipid bilayer
qa.e: The hydrophobic core blocks polar molecules.

qa.q: If a membrane has 52% protein and 40% lipid, the remaining share is:
Assertion (A): Proteins are held rigidly in fixed positions within the cell membrane. Reason (R): The lipid of the membrane is in a quasi-fluid state.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: membrane proteins can move sideways. R is true: the quasi-fluid lipid bilayer is what allows this lateral movement (fluid mosaic model).

qa.q: The middle lamella is mainly made of:
qa.e: Calcium pectate glues neighbouring cells together.

qa.q: Plasmodesmata connect:
qa.e: They pass through the wall and middle lamella.

qa.q: The secondary wall is formed:
qa.a: On the inner side of the primary wall, towards the membrane
qa.e: It is laid down inside as the cell matures.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of the cell wall?
qa.e: ATP is made in mitochondria and chloroplasts, not the wall.

qa.q: Algal cell walls contain:
qa.a: Cellulose, galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate
qa.e: This is the NCERT composition of algal walls.

qa.q: The primary wall of a young plant cell:
qa.e: Its growth capacity reduces as the cell matures.

qa.q: A cell wall is found in:
qa.e: Plants and fungi (and most prokaryotes) have walls.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The cell wall is described as non-living. Reason (R): The cell wall has no metabolism of its own; it is secreted by the cell.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; it is a secreted, non-metabolising structure, hence non-living.

qa.q: Which organelle is NOT part of the endomembrane system?
qa.e: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes work independently of the system.

qa.q: Steroidal hormones in animal cells are synthesised in the:
qa.e: SER makes lipids and steroids.

qa.q: The forming face of the Golgi apparatus is the:
qa.e: Cis is forming (convex); trans is maturing (concave).

qa.q: The Golgi apparatus was first observed by:
qa.e: Camillo Golgi described it in 1898.

qa.q: An important site for formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids is the:
qa.e: Golgi modifies proteins and lipids by adding sugars.

qa.q: Rough ER is abundant in cells that are:
qa.e: Its ribosomes make proteins for secretion.

qa.q: The ER divides the intracellular space into:
qa.e: Inside the ER is luminal; the cytoplasm is extra-luminal.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Golgi apparatus remains closely associated with the ER. Reason (R): Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; materials flowing from the ER to the Golgi explain why they stay close.

qa.q: Lysosomal enzymes are optimally active at:
qa.e: Lysosomal hydrolases work best in acidic conditions.

qa.q: The membrane of the vacuole is called the:
qa.e: The tonoplast is the single membrane around the vacuole.

qa.q: The contractile vacuole of Amoeba is important for:
qa.e: It expels excess water and wastes.

qa.q: Lysosomes are formed by packaging in the:
qa.e: The Golgi packages lysosomal enzymes into vesicles.

qa.q: Up to what percentage of a plant cell's volume can the vacuole occupy?
qa.e: Vacuoles can take up to 90% of the volume.

qa.q: Lysosomes can digest:
qa.a: Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids
qa.e: They contain almost all types of hydrolytic enzymes.

qa.q: Food vacuoles in protists are formed by:
qa.e: Food is enclosed when engulfed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ions are more concentrated in the plant vacuole than in the cytoplasm. Reason (R): The tonoplast transports ions into the vacuole against their concentration gradient.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; active transport across the tonoplast builds up ions in the vacuole.

qa.q: Infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane are called:
qa.e: Cristae increase surface area for respiration.

qa.q: Mitochondria are called power houses of the cell because they:
qa.e: They are sites of aerobic respiration that release energy as ATP.

qa.q: Amyloplasts store:
qa.e: Amyloplasts store starch; elaioplasts oils; aleuroplasts proteins.

qa.q: Stacks of thylakoids in a chloroplast are called:
qa.e: Thylakoids stack like piles of coins into grana.

qa.q: Ribosomes of chloroplasts and mitochondria are:
qa.e: They are 70S, smaller than the 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes.

qa.q: Chlorophyll pigments in the chloroplast are located in the:
qa.e: Chlorophyll is in the thylakoid membranes.

qa.q: How do mitochondria multiply?
qa.e: Mitochondria divide by fission.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mitochondria are called semi-autonomous organelles. Reason (R): Mitochondria contain 80S ribosomes identical to those in the cytoplasm.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: with their own circular DNA and ribosomes, mitochondria make some of their own proteins. R is false: mitochondrial ribosomes are 70S, not 80S.

qa.q: Ribosomes were first observed by:
qa.e: Palade saw them as dense particles under the electron microscope in 1953.

qa.q: The 80S ribosome is made of:
qa.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes have 60S and 40S subunits.

qa.q: The 'S' in 70S and 80S stands for:
qa.e: S is the sedimentation coefficient, related to density and size.

qa.q: The arrangement of microtubules in the axoneme of a cilium is:
qa.e: Nine peripheral doublets and a central pair.

qa.q: A centriole is made of nine peripheral:
qa.e: Centrioles have nine triplets in a cartwheel pattern.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of the cytoskeleton?
qa.e: Protein synthesis happens on ribosomes.

qa.q: How many microtubules in total are there in a 9+2 axoneme?
qa.e: 9 doublets × 2 + 2 central = 20.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Centrioles help in cell division in animal cells. Reason (R): Centrioles give rise to spindle fibres that form the spindle apparatus.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; forming the spindle apparatus is how centrioles help in division.

qa.q: The site of active ribosomal RNA synthesis is the:
qa.e: The nucleolus synthesises rRNA.

qa.q: A chromosome with a terminal centromere is:
qa.e: Telo- means end; the centromere is at the tip.

qa.q: A chromosome with the centromere in the middle forming two equal arms is:
qa.e: Meta- here means middle.

qa.q: The space between the two membranes of the nuclear envelope is the:
qa.e: It is 10 to 50 nm wide.

qa.q: Disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere are:
qa.e: Kinetochores lie on the centromere.

qa.q: Which cells lack a nucleus when mature?
qa.a: Mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells
qa.e: These are NCERT's examples of enucleate cells.

qa.q: The non-staining secondary constriction gives some chromosomes a small fragment called a:
qa.e: A satellite appears beyond the secondary constriction.

qa.q: A human cell contains about 2 m of DNA in 46 chromosomes. What is the average DNA length per chromosome, in centimetres?
Living tissue is ground in which acid to separate acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions?
qa.e: Trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) is used.

qa.q: After straining, the filtrate is called the:
qa.e: Filtrate = acid-soluble; retentate = acid-insoluble.

qa.q: Ash obtained after burning a tissue contains:
qa.a: Inorganic elements such as calcium and magnesium
qa.e: Carbon compounds burn off; inorganic elements remain.

qa.q: All carbon compounds obtained from living tissues are called:
qa.e: This is the NCERT definition of biomolecules.

qa.q: Which element is much more abundant in the Earth's crust than in the human body?
qa.e: Silicon is 27.7% of the crust but negligible in the body.

qa.q: By weight, carbon makes up about what percentage of the human body?
qa.e: Carbon is about 18.5% of the body versus 0.03% of the crust.

qa.q: A 50 g tissue sample dries to 10 g. What percentage of the fresh tissue was water?
Assertion (A): When a tissue is burnt, its carbon compounds are lost. Reason (R): On burning, carbon compounds are converted into inorganic ash that remains behind.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: carbon compounds disappear on burning. R is false: they are oxidised to gases such as CO₂ and water vapour; the ash that remains holds only inorganic elements.

qa.q: In glycine, the R group is:
qa.e: Glycine has H; alanine has methyl; serine has hydroxymethyl.

qa.q: Which is a basic amino acid?
qa.e: Lysine is basic; glutamic acid is acidic; valine is neutral.

qa.q: Which is an aromatic amino acid?
qa.e: Tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan are aromatic.

qa.q: A nitrogen base attached to a sugar is called a:
qa.e: Base + sugar = nucleoside; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide.

qa.q: Uridylic acid is a:
qa.e: Names ending in -ylic acid are nucleotides.

qa.q: Why does the structure of an amino acid change in solutions of different pH?
qa.a: Its amino and carboxyl groups are ionisable
qa.e: Ionisation of –NH₂ and –COOH depends on pH, giving forms such as the zwitterion.

qa.q: How many types of amino acids occur in proteins?
qa.e: Twenty types of amino acids make up proteins.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Alanine is an α-amino acid. Reason (R): In alanine, the amino and carboxyl groups are attached to the same α-carbon.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; attachment to the α-carbon is what defines an α-amino acid.

qa.q: Palmitic acid has how many carbon atoms, including the carboxyl carbon?
qa.e: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons; arachidonic acid has 20.

qa.q: Glycerol is chemically:
qa.e: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups on a propane backbone.

qa.q: Lecithin is an example of a:
qa.e: Lecithin contains phosphorus and is found in membranes.

qa.q: A fatty acid with one or more C=C double bonds is:
qa.e: Double bonds make a fatty acid unsaturated.

qa.q: Why do lipids appear in the acid-insoluble fraction even though they are small?
qa.a: Membranes break into water-insoluble vesicles during grinding
qa.e: Membrane fragments form vesicles that separate with the macromolecules.

qa.q: Oils differ from fats mainly in having:
qa.e: Oils stay liquid at lower temperatures.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms does arachidonic acid have?
qa.e: Arachidonic acid has 20 carbons including the carboxyl carbon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Lipids are not strictly macromolecules. Reason (R): The molecular weight of lipids does not exceed about 800 Da.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their small size means they are not true macromolecules.

qa.q: Morphine and codeine are examples of:
qa.e: They are alkaloids.

qa.q: Concanavalin A is a:
qa.e: NCERT lists concanavalin A as a lectin.

qa.q: Which is a primary metabolite?
qa.e: Amino acids have known roles in normal physiology.

qa.q: Abrin and ricin are:
qa.e: They are poisonous secondary metabolites.

qa.q: Carotenoids and anthocyanins are:
qa.e: They give colour.

qa.q: Which statement about secondary metabolites is correct?
qa.a: Many are useful to humans, though the role of all of them in their hosts is not yet understood
qa.e: Secondary metabolites have many human uses; their host roles are not all known.

qa.q: Vinblastine and curcumin are classed as:
qa.e: NCERT lists them under drugs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rubber is a secondary metabolite. Reason (R): Rubber has a clearly known role in the normal physiological processes of every plant.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Rubber is a secondary (polymeric) metabolite (A true). R is false: secondary metabolites do not have such a clearly known role in normal physiology.

qa.q: Which is the most abundant chemical in living organisms?
qa.e: Water makes up 70 to 90% of cells.

qa.q: Which compounds of the acid-insoluble fraction are NOT true macromolecules?
qa.e: Lipids are small but appear there because of membrane vesicles.

qa.q: Micromolecules have molecular weights below about:
qa.e: Micromolecules are below 1000 daltons.

qa.q: What percentage of a cell is protein on average?
qa.e: Proteins are 10 to 15% of the cell.

qa.q: The acid-soluble pool contains molecules of molecular weight from about:
qa.e: Small molecules such as water (18 Da) to about 800 Da.

qa.q: Carbohydrates make up what percentage of a cell, on average?
qa.e: NCERT gives 3% carbohydrates.

qa.q: Which is a true biomacromolecule?
qa.e: DNA is a polymer with very high molecular weight.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are found in the acid-soluble pool. Reason (R): These compounds have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: these macromolecules are in the acid-insoluble fraction; the acid-soluble pool has molecules of about 18 to 800 Da. R is true: their very high molecular weight is why they stay in the acid-insoluble fraction.

qa.q: The most abundant protein in the whole biosphere is:
qa.e: RuBisCO is in all photosynthetic organisms.

qa.q: The most abundant protein in the animal world is:
qa.e: Collagen is the most abundant animal protein.

qa.q: Amino acids that must be supplied through the diet are called:
qa.e: Essential ones cannot be made by the body.

qa.q: A protein is a heteropolymer because:
qa.a: It is made of different types of amino acids
qa.e: Up to 20 types of amino acids make a protein.

qa.q: Which protein enables glucose transport into cells?
qa.e: GLUT-4 is a glucose transporter.

qa.q: Trypsin is an example of a protein that acts as a(n):
qa.e: Trypsin digests proteins.

qa.q: The bonds joining amino acids in a protein are:
qa.e: Peptide bonds link amino acids.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Insulin is a protein. Reason (R): Insulin acts as a hormone.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but acting as a hormone is not why insulin is a protein; it is a protein because it is a polypeptide.

qa.q: Inulin is a polymer of:
qa.e: Inulin is made of fructose units.

qa.q: The storage polysaccharide of animals is:
qa.e: Animals store glycogen; plants store starch.

qa.q: Why does cellulose not give a blue colour with iodine?
qa.a: It lacks the complex helices that hold iodine
qa.e: Iodine fits only into starch helices.

qa.q: Chitin, found in arthropod exoskeletons, is built from:
qa.e: Chitin is a complex polysaccharide with amino sugars.

qa.q: In a glycogen chain, the right end is the:
qa.e: Right end is reducing; left end is non-reducing.

qa.q: Cellulose is described as a:
qa.e: It contains only glucose.

qa.q: Paper and cotton fibre are made mainly of:
qa.e: Both are cellulosic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Starch can hold iodine molecules. Reason (R): Starch is a polymer of fructose.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: starch holds I₂ in its helices and turns blue. R is false: starch is a polymer of glucose; inulin is the fructose polymer.

qa.q: Which bases are purines?
qa.e: A and G are purines; C, T and U are pyrimidines.

qa.q: The sugar present in DNA is:
qa.e: DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose.

qa.q: A nucleotide is made of:
qa.a: A nitrogen base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate
qa.e: These three parts make a nucleotide.

qa.q: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
qa.e: RNA has uracil in place of thymine.

qa.q: Nucleic acids are polymers of:
qa.e: Nucleic acids are polynucleotides.

qa.q: Cytosine is a:
qa.e: Cytosine is a pyrimidine.

qa.q: How many types of nitrogen bases occur in nucleic acids in total (DNA and RNA together)?
qa.e: A, G, C, T and U.

qa.q: Assertion (A): RNA contains ribose sugar. Reason (R): In RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true facts about RNA, but having uracil does not explain why its sugar is ribose.

qa.q: The sequence of amino acids in a protein is its:
qa.e: Primary structure is the positional information of amino acids.

qa.q: In proteins, the helices observed are:
qa.e: NCERT states only right-handed helices are observed.

qa.q: The first amino acid of a polypeptide is called the:
qa.e: The chain starts at the N-terminus.

qa.q: Adult human haemoglobin consists of:
qa.a: Two α and two β subunits
qa.e: Adult Hb has 2 α + 2 β.

qa.q: Folding of a protein chain upon itself like a hollow woollen ball gives the:
qa.e: Tertiary structure is the 3-D folding.

qa.q: Which structure is absolutely necessary for many biological activities of proteins?
qa.e: Function depends on the 3-D shape.

qa.q: How many polypeptide subunits does adult human haemoglobin have?
qa.e: 2 α + 2 β = 4 subunits.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Haemoglobin shows quaternary structure. Reason (R): Haemoglobin is made of more than one polypeptide subunit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; quaternary structure exists only when several subunits assemble.

qa.q: Nucleic acids that act as enzymes are called:
qa.e: Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules.

qa.q: The pocket in an enzyme into which the substrate fits is the:
qa.e: The active site is a crevice formed by tertiary folding.

qa.q: Enzymes from thermophilic organisms are special because they:
qa.a: Stay stable and active even at 80 to 90°C
qa.e: Thermal stability is their key quality.

qa.q: Carbonic anhydrase increases the rate of CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ by about:
qa.e: From about 200 per hour to about 600,000 per second, roughly 10⁷ times.

qa.q: In yeast, during fermentation, the glucose-to-pyruvate pathway leads to:
qa.e: Yeast makes ethanol; muscle under anaerobic conditions makes lactic acid.

qa.q: Using the rule of thumb, if a reaction rate is 60 units at 30°C, what is it at 20°C?
qa.e: A 10°C fall roughly halves the rate: 60 ÷ 2 = 30.

qa.q: Which is a physical change rather than a chemical reaction?
qa.e: Melting changes state without breaking or forming bonds.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Glucose can give different end products in different cells. Reason (R): In skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions lactic acid forms, while yeast produces ethanol by fermentation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R gives the examples that show why the end product differs.

qa.q: Enzymes speed up reactions by:
qa.e: They lower the energy barrier to the transition state.

qa.q: Activation energy is the energy difference between the:
qa.e: It is the barrier from S to the transition state.

qa.q: A reaction in which the product has less energy than the substrate is:
qa.e: Energy is released, so it is exothermic.

qa.q: Which correctly represents enzyme action?
qa.a: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P
qa.e: ES and EP complexes form before the free enzyme is released.

qa.q: The change in enzyme shape after substrate binding, to fit more tightly, is called:
qa.e: Binding induces the enzyme to alter its shape.

qa.q: A substrate is at 30 units of energy and the transition state at 110 units. What is the activation energy?
At the end of the catalytic cycle, the enzyme:
qa.a: Is released unchanged and can bind another substrate
qa.e: Enzymes are not consumed in the reaction.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Even an exothermic reaction may need an enzyme to proceed quickly. Reason (R): In both exothermic and endothermic reactions, the substrate must pass through a higher-energy transition state.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the activation energy barrier exists even for exothermic reactions, so enzymes help.

qa.q: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it:
qa.e: It competes with succinate for the active site.

qa.q: High temperature destroys enzyme activity because:
qa.e: Heat disrupts the enzyme's structure.

qa.q: When all enzyme molecules are saturated with substrate, the reaction velocity:
qa.e: No free enzyme remains to bind more substrate.

qa.q: Low temperature affects enzymes by:
qa.e: Cooling preserves enzymes in an inactive state.

qa.q: A competitive inhibitor:
qa.a: Competes with the substrate for the substrate-binding site
qa.e: It resembles the substrate and blocks the active site.

qa.q: An enzyme reaches 120 units of velocity at 10 mM substrate and stays at 120 units at 20 mM and 40 mM. What is its Vmax?
qa.e: The velocity levels off at 120 units, which is Vmax.

qa.q: Competitive inhibitors are often used to:
qa.e: They can block key bacterial enzymes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Enzyme velocity does not exceed Vmax. Reason (R): At high substrate concentration, all enzyme molecules are occupied, leaving none free for additional substrate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; saturation of enzyme molecules is why velocity levels off at Vmax.

qa.q: Enzymes that catalyse the transfer of a group G (other than hydrogen) between two substrates are:
qa.e: S–G + S' → S + S'–G is transfer.

qa.q: Which enzyme class removes groups from substrates by non-hydrolytic mechanisms, leaving double bonds?
qa.e: Lyases remove groups and leave double bonds.

qa.q: The protein part of an enzyme that needs a co-factor is the:
qa.e: Apoenzyme + co-factor gives the active enzyme.

qa.q: Haem in peroxidase and catalase is a:
qa.e: It is an organic co-factor tightly bound to the enzyme.

qa.q: The coenzymes NAD and NADP contain the vitamin:
qa.e: Niacin is an essential part of NAD and NADP.

qa.q: Zinc is a co-factor for:
qa.e: Zinc is the metal-ion co-factor of carboxypeptidase.

qa.q: An enzyme converts glucose-6-phosphate into its isomer fructose-6-phosphate. Its class is:
qa.e: Interconversion of isomers is done by isomerases.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Coenzymes differ from prosthetic groups. Reason (R): Coenzymes bind to the apoenzyme only transiently, while prosthetic groups are tightly bound.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the strength of binding is the stated difference.

qa.q: Human cells in culture divide approximately once every:
qa.e: About 24 hours; yeast takes about 90 minutes.

qa.q: Division of the nucleus is called:
qa.e: Karyo- refers to the nucleus.

qa.q: The phase between two successive M phases is the:
qa.e: Interphase lies between divisions.

qa.q: Interphase is divided into:
qa.e: G1, S and G2 make up interphase.

qa.q: In a 24-hour human cell cycle, M phase lasts about:
qa.e: Division proper takes only about an hour.

qa.q: A cell cycle lasts 20 hours and interphase takes 19 hours. What percentage of the cycle is M phase?
qa.e: M phase = 1 hour; 1 ÷ 20 × 100 = 5%.

qa.q: Why is interphase not truly a 'resting' phase?
qa.a: The cell grows and replicates its DNA during it
qa.e: Interphase prepares the cell for division.

qa.q: Assertion (A): DNA replication does not occur throughout the cell cycle. Reason (R): DNA synthesis takes place only during the S phase.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; DNA is replicated only in S phase, so not throughout the cycle.

qa.q: During S phase, the DNA content of a cell changes from:
qa.e: DNA doubles during replication.

qa.q: If a cell has 2n = 14 in G1, how many chromosomes does it have after S phase?
qa.e: DNA doubles but chromosome number stays 2n = 14.

qa.q: Cells that exit G1 and stop dividing enter the:
qa.e: G0 cells stay active but do not proliferate.

qa.q: In animal cells, centrioles duplicate during the:
qa.e: Centriole duplication happens in the cytoplasm during S phase.

qa.q: Proteins needed for mitosis are synthesised mainly in:
qa.e: G2 prepares the cell for mitosis.

qa.q: Which cells usually do not divide in adult animals?
qa.e: Heart cells are a classic example of non-dividing (G0) cells.

qa.q: A cell with 4C DNA in G2 divides by mitosis. What is the DNA content of each daughter cell?
qa.e: Mitosis shares the replicated DNA equally: 4C ÷ 2 = 2C.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Plants can show mitotic division in haploid cells. Reason (R): In animals, mitosis is seen only in diploid somatic cells.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the animal pattern does not explain why plants can divide haploid cells by mitosis.

qa.q: Mitosis is called equational division because:
qa.a: Daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent
qa.e: Chromosome number stays equal.

qa.q: Which stage is best for studying chromosome morphology?
qa.e: Chromosomes are fully condensed at metaphase.

qa.q: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes at the:
qa.e: Kinetochores on the centromere are attachment sites.

qa.q: Which structures are NOT seen at the end of prophase?
qa.a: Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope
qa.e: These disappear by the end of prophase.

qa.q: The start of metaphase is marked by:
qa.a: Complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope
qa.e: Metaphase begins when the nuclear envelope has fully broken down.

qa.q: Asters and spindle fibres together form the:
qa.e: Together they make the mitotic apparatus.

qa.q: A metaphase chromosome consists of:
qa.a: Two sister chromatids held together at the centromere
qa.e: Replication in S phase gave each chromosome two chromatids.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chromosomes are clearly visible under the microscope at metaphase. Reason (R): The nuclear envelope reforms around the chromosomes at metaphase.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: condensation is complete by metaphase, so chromosomes are clearest then. R is false: metaphase begins with complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope; it reforms only in telophase.

qa.q: Centromeres split and chromatids separate during:
qa.e: Splitting of centromeres marks anaphase.

qa.q: In anaphase, the part of each chromosome leading towards the pole is the:
qa.e: The centromere leads; arms trail behind.

qa.q: Reformation of the nuclear envelope and nucleolus occurs in:
qa.e: Telophase rebuilds two daughter nuclei.

qa.q: Cytokinesis in plant cells begins with the formation of a:
qa.e: The cell plate forms at the centre and grows outward.

qa.q: The cell plate represents the:
qa.a: Middle lamella between the two new cells
qa.e: It becomes the middle lamella.

qa.q: The liquid endosperm of coconut is an example of a:
qa.e: Nuclear divisions without cytokinesis give a multinucleate syncytium.

qa.q: In which stage do chromosomes decondense and lose their individuality?
qa.e: At the poles, chromosomes decondense into chromatin.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Plant cells cannot divide their cytoplasm by forming a furrow. Reason (R): Plant cells are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the rigid wall is the reason a furrow cannot form.

qa.q: Mitosis usually produces daughter cells that are:
qa.e: Mitosis copies the genetic material exactly.

qa.q: Why must a growing cell divide?
qa.e: Growth disturbs the ratio between nucleus and cytoplasm.

qa.q: Which cells are constantly replaced by mitosis?
qa.e: Gut lining, epidermis and blood cells are replaced continuously.

qa.q: Continuous growth of plants throughout life is due to mitosis in:
qa.e: Meristems keep dividing.

qa.q: Starting with one cell, how many cells result after 6 rounds of mitosis (all cells dividing each time)?
Healing of a cut on the skin depends mainly on:
qa.e: New skin cells form by mitosis.

qa.q: Mitosis in some lower plants and social insects can occur in:
qa.e: Mitosis is usually in diploid cells, but haploid cells also divide by mitosis in some lower plants and social insects.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mitosis is important for growth of multicellular organisms. Reason (R): Mitosis increases the number of cells.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; adding cells by mitosis is how multicellular bodies grow.

qa.q: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes occurs during:
qa.e: Pairing begins in zygotene.

qa.q: Crossing over occurs during:
qa.e: Recombination nodules and crossing over mark pachytene.

qa.q: Crossing over takes place between:
qa.e: Exchange is between non-sister chromatids of homologues.

qa.q: The enzyme involved in crossing over is:
qa.e: Recombinase mediates crossing over.

qa.q: Meiosis involves how many rounds of DNA replication?
qa.e: Two divisions, but only one replication.

qa.q: A cell with 2n = 20 enters meiosis. How many bivalents form in zygotene?
qa.e: Bivalents = 2n ÷ 2 = 10.

qa.q: The complex structure formed during synapsis is the:
qa.e: It accompanies chromosome pairing in zygotene.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Meiosis produces haploid cells from a diploid cell. Reason (R): In meiosis, there are two divisions but only one round of DNA replication.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; one replication followed by two divisions halves the chromosome number.

qa.q: X-shaped structures seen in diplotene are called:
qa.e: Chiasmata mark sites of crossing over.

qa.q: Terminalisation of chiasmata occurs during:
qa.e: It is the hallmark of diakinesis.

qa.q: During anaphase I:
qa.a: Homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay together
qa.e: Reduction happens because whole homologues move apart.

qa.q: The short stage between meiosis I and meiosis II is:
qa.e: Interkinesis has no DNA replication.

qa.q: Dissolution of the synaptonemal complex marks the beginning of:
qa.e: Diplotene begins as the complex dissolves.

qa.q: A cell with 2n = 12 completes meiosis I. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell have?
qa.e: Homologues separate, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

qa.q: In oocytes of some vertebrates, which stage can last for months or years?
qa.e: Diplotene can be prolonged in oocytes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Meiosis I is called the equational division. Reason (R): In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: meiosis I is the reductional division; meiosis II is equational. R is true: separation of homologues in anaphase I is what halves the chromosome number.

qa.q: Splitting of centromeres in meiosis occurs during:
qa.e: Sister chromatids separate only in anaphase II.

qa.q: At the end of meiosis II, one diploid cell has produced:
qa.e: A tetrad of four haploid cells forms.

qa.q: Meiosis II is described as equational because:
qa.a: The chromosome number does not change during it
qa.e: Only sister chromatids separate.

qa.q: Which statement about the significance of meiosis is correct?
qa.a: It conserves the species' chromosome number across generations and increases variability
qa.e: Halving in gametes and restoration at fertilisation keep the number constant.

qa.q: A plant with 2n = 24 forms gametes by meiosis. How many chromosomes does each gamete have?
qa.e: Gametes are haploid: 24 ÷ 2 = 12.

qa.q: Genetic variation from meiosis is important because it:
qa.e: Variations are very important for evolution.

qa.q: Meiosis II begins:
qa.a: Immediately after cytokinesis of meiosis I, usually before chromosomes fully elongate
qa.e: There is no DNA replication before meiosis II.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chromosome number of a species stays constant from one generation to the next. Reason (R): Meiosis halves the chromosome number in gametes, and fertilisation restores it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; halving then restoring keeps the number constant.

qa.q: Which occurs in meiosis but not in mitosis?
qa.e: Crossing over between homologues happens only in meiosis I.

qa.q: A cell shows bivalents arranged on the equator. The stage is:
qa.e: Only metaphase I has paired homologues at the equator.

qa.q: A 2n cell has 4C DNA in G2. After meiosis I, each cell has DNA content:
qa.e: Meiosis I halves the DNA: 4C → 2C.

qa.q: What is the DNA content of each cell at the end of meiosis II, if the G1 cell had 2C?
qa.e: 2C → 4C after S → 2C after meiosis I → 1C after meiosis II.

qa.q: How many daughter cells are produced from one cell by mitosis and by meiosis respectively?
qa.e: Mitosis gives 2; meiosis gives 4.

qa.q: Daughter cells of meiosis are genetically different from each other mainly because of:
qa.e: Recombination and random arrangement of homologues create variety.

qa.q: A cell with 2n = 46 divides. Daughter cells each have 46 chromosomes. The division was:
qa.e: Same chromosome number as the parent means mitosis.

qa.q: In a cell with 2n = 10, how many chromatids are present at metaphase of mitosis?
qa.e: 10 chromosomes × 2 chromatids = 20.

qa.q: Why is KOH used in the half-leaf experiment?
qa.e: KOH removes CO₂ from the enclosed air.

qa.q: A variegated leaf kept in sunlight and tested with iodine shows starch only in the:
qa.e: Chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

qa.q: The half-covered leaf experiment demonstrates the need for:
qa.e: Covered parts receive no light and make no starch.

qa.q: Photosynthesis is described as a physico-chemical process because it:
qa.a: Uses light energy to drive chemical synthesis of organic compounds
qa.e: Light (physical) drives chemical reactions.

qa.q: Which reagent is used to test a leaf for starch?
qa.e: Starch turns blue-black with iodine.

qa.q: Two importance of photosynthesis are:
qa.a: It is the primary source of food and releases oxygen
qa.e: Food and oxygen both come from photosynthesis.

qa.q: In the starch test, why is alcohol heated in a water bath and not over an open flame?
qa.e: Alcohol vapour catches fire easily, so a water bath is the safe method.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The part of a leaf enclosed with KOH does not form starch. Reason (R): KOH absorbs CO₂, so that part cannot photosynthesise.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; lack of CO₂ stops photosynthesis and thus starch formation.

qa.q: Who showed that only the green parts of plants release oxygen, and only in light?
qa.e: Ingenhousz observed oxygen bubbles around green parts in sunlight.

qa.q: Engelmann used which alga in his action spectrum experiment?
qa.e: He illuminated Cladophora with split light.

qa.q: In Engelmann's experiment, aerobic bacteria accumulated mainly in:
qa.e: Photosynthesis and O₂ release were highest in blue and red regions.

qa.q: Van Niel concluded that the oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from:
qa.e: Comparison with H₂S-using bacteria showed water is the hydrogen donor and O₂ source.

qa.q: When purple and green sulphur bacteria use H₂S as the hydrogen donor, the oxidation product is:
qa.e: They do not release O₂.

qa.q: Who provided evidence that glucose is made in green parts and stored as starch?
qa.e: Von Sachs (1854) showed this.

qa.q: In the equation 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂, how many molecules of water are consumed in total?
qa.e: Twelve water molecules appear on the reactant side.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Priestley's mouse survived in a closed bell jar containing a mint plant. Reason (R): Plants restore to the air what breathing animals remove.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R is Priestley's explanation of why the mouse survived.

qa.q: Light reactions take place in the:
qa.e: The membrane system traps light and makes ATP and NADPH.

qa.q: Sugar synthesis in the chloroplast occurs in the:
qa.e: Enzymatic carbon reactions are in the stroma.

qa.q: The dark reactions are called so because they:
qa.e: They depend on light indirectly through ATP and NADPH.

qa.q: Chloroplasts align along the walls of mesophyll cells to:
qa.e: Positioning maximises light capture.

qa.q: The products of the light reaction used in the carbon reactions are:
qa.e: ATP and NADPH drive sugar synthesis.

qa.q: Which cells in a leaf have the most chloroplasts?
qa.e: Mesophyll is the main photosynthetic tissue.

qa.q: The carbon reactions are also called:
qa.e: By convention they are called dark reactions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The dark reactions continue at the same rate for many hours after the light is switched off. Reason (R): Dark reactions depend on ATP and NADPH produced by the light reactions.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: carbon fixation continues only briefly and then stops once light is off. R is true: it needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and these run out in darkness.

qa.q: The chief pigment associated with photosynthesis is:
qa.e: Chlorophyll a forms the reaction centres.

qa.q: A graph showing the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths of light is the:
qa.e: Action spectrum = rate of the process against wavelength.

qa.q: On a paper chromatogram, chlorophyll b appears:
qa.e: Chlorophyll a is blue-green; b is yellow-green.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of accessory pigments?
qa.a: Acting as the reaction centre of photosystems
qa.e: Reaction centres are chlorophyll a molecules.

qa.q: Maximum absorption by chlorophyll a occurs in the:
qa.e: Blue and red light are absorbed most.

qa.q: How many pigments are separated in a typical paper chromatogram of leaf pigments?
qa.e: Chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids.

qa.q: There is a close correlation between the absorption spectrum of chlorophylls and the:
qa.e: Light absorbed by chlorophyll drives photosynthesis.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Leaves appear green. Reason (R): Chlorophyll absorbs green light most strongly.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Leaves do look green (A true), but that is because chlorophyll absorbs little green light and reflects it, so R is false.

qa.q: The reaction centre of PS I is:
qa.e: PS I absorbs maximally at 700 nm.

qa.q: Photosystems I and II are named according to:
qa.e: PS II acts first but was discovered after PS I.

qa.q: Water splitting is associated with:
qa.e: It supplies electrons to PS II.

qa.q: The products of splitting 2H₂O are:
qa.e: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻.

qa.q: In the Z scheme, the final electron acceptor is:
qa.e: Electrons end up reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH + H⁺.

qa.q: The antenna of a light harvesting complex consists of:
qa.a: Hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins
qa.e: All pigments except the reaction-centre chlorophyll a form the antennae.

qa.q: How many molecules of water are split to release 4 molecules of O₂?
qa.e: 2 H₂O per O₂, so 4 × 2 = 8.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Protons accumulate in the lumen of the thylakoid during the light reaction. Reason (R): Water splitting occurs on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because water is split on the lumen side, its protons are released into the lumen.

qa.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation produces:
qa.e: Electrons return to PS I, so NADP⁺ is not reduced.

qa.q: Stroma lamellae lack:
qa.e: That is why only cyclic flow occurs there.

qa.q: In the chloroplast, protons accumulate in the:
qa.e: The lumen becomes acidic as protons build up.

qa.q: The part of ATP synthase that forms the transmembrane proton channel is:
qa.e: F₀ is embedded in the membrane; F₁ makes ATP.

qa.q: Which is NOT required for chemiosmosis?
qa.e: RuBisCO is a Calvin cycle enzyme, not part of chemiosmosis.

qa.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation takes place when only light of wavelength:
qa.e: PS II cannot be excited by such light, so only PS I works.

qa.q: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation involves:
qa.a: PS II and PS I working in series
qa.e: Both photosystems are linked by an ETC.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The pH of the thylakoid lumen falls during the light reaction. Reason (R): NADP reductase on the lumen side pumps protons into the lumen.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: protons build up in the lumen, lowering its pH. R is false: NADP reductase sits on the stroma side and removes protons from the stroma; protons enter the lumen from water splitting and from the proton-carrying electron carrier.

qa.q: The primary CO₂ acceptor in C3 plants is:
qa.e: Ribulose bisphosphate, a 5-carbon sugar, accepts CO₂.

qa.q: The first stable product of CO₂ fixation in C3 plants is:
qa.e: Calvin found the 3-carbon PGA first.

qa.q: How many ATP molecules are needed to fix one molecule of CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
qa.e: 2 ATP for reduction + 1 ATP for regeneration = 3.

qa.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle produce one molecule of glucose?
qa.e: Six CO₂, one per turn, make one glucose.

qa.q: How many NADPH molecules are needed to make one glucose molecule?
qa.e: 2 NADPH per CO₂ × 6 = 12.

qa.q: Which enzyme catalyses carboxylation of RuBP?
qa.e: RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase fixes CO₂.

qa.q: Melvin Calvin traced the path of carbon using:
qa.e: ¹⁴C labelling revealed PGA as the first product.

qa.q: How many ATP are needed to make 3 molecules of glucose through the Calvin cycle?
qa.e: 18 ATP per glucose × 3 = 54.

qa.q: The primary CO₂ acceptor in C4 plants is:
qa.e: PEP is the 3-carbon acceptor in mesophyll cells.

qa.q: The first stable product in C4 plants is:
qa.e: OAA is the 4-carbon first product.

qa.q: 'Kranz' means:
qa.e: It describes the wreath-like ring of bundle sheath cells.

qa.q: In C4 plants, the Calvin cycle occurs in:
qa.e: RuBisCO is in bundle sheath cells.

qa.q: Mesophyll cells of C4 plants lack:
qa.e: Mesophyll cells have PEPcase but no RuBisCO.

qa.q: Bundle sheath cells of C4 plants have:
qa.a: Many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gases, no intercellular spaces
qa.e: These features help concentrate CO₂.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms are in the primary CO₂ acceptor of C4 plants?
qa.e: PEP has 3 carbons; OAA has 4; RuBP has 5.

qa.q: Assertion (A): C4 plants use the Calvin cycle for sugar synthesis. Reason (R): The CO₂ released in bundle sheath cells enters the C3 (Calvin) pathway.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains how C4 plants feed CO₂ into the Calvin cycle.

qa.q: When RuBisCO binds O₂, RuBP forms:
qa.e: Oxygenation gives one PGA and phosphoglycolate.

qa.q: Photorespiration does NOT occur in C4 plants because:
qa.a: CO₂ concentration is raised at the RuBisCO site
qa.e: High CO₂ keeps RuBisCO working as a carboxylase.

qa.q: Which is the most abundant enzyme in the world?
qa.e: RuBisCO is found in all photosynthetic organisms.

qa.q: Photorespiration is considered wasteful because:
qa.a: No sugar, ATP or NADPH is made, and CO₂ is released
qa.e: Energy is used and fixed carbon is lost.

qa.q: Which factor favours photorespiration in C3 plants?
qa.a: High O₂ and low CO₂ concentration
qa.e: Relative concentrations decide whether O₂ or CO₂ binds.

qa.q: In C3 plants, the Calvin cycle occurs in:
qa.e: C3 plants carry out the whole process in mesophyll cells.

qa.q: Which feature is found in C4 plants but not in C3 plants?
qa.e: Both have RuBisCO, the Calvin cycle and chloroplasts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): C4 plants show higher productivity than C3 plants in hot conditions. Reason (R): C4 plants lack photorespiration.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; avoiding the wasteful photorespiration is a major reason for their higher productivity.

qa.q: Blackman's law of limiting factors was given in:
qa.e: F.F. Blackman stated it in 1905.

qa.q: According to Blackman's law, the rate of a process is determined by the factor:
qa.e: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate.

qa.q: Light saturation for photosynthesis occurs at about what percentage of full sunlight?
qa.e: Beyond about 10% of full sunlight, other factors limit.

qa.q: Why do greenhouse tomatoes give higher yields in CO₂-enriched air?
qa.a: They are C3 plants that respond to higher CO₂ with faster photosynthesis
qa.e: C3 plants are limited by current CO₂ levels.

qa.q: Water stress reduces photosynthesis mainly by:
qa.e: Closed stomata cut CO₂ entry and wilted leaves have less area.

qa.q: C4 plants show CO₂ saturation at about:
qa.e: C4 saturate at about 360; C3 only beyond 450.

qa.q: Which reactions of photosynthesis are more strongly controlled by temperature?
qa.e: Enzymatic carbon reactions are temperature-sensitive.

qa.q: On a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity, the curve is linear at first and then flattens. The flat part shows that:
qa.a: Some other factor has become limiting
qa.e: Beyond saturation, factors such as CO₂ or temperature limit the rate.

qa.q: Gas exchange in a woody stem occurs mainly through:
qa.e: Lenticels in bark allow gas exchange.

qa.q: The most common respiratory substrate is:
qa.e: Carbohydrates are usually oxidised first.

qa.q: Why can plants manage without specialised respiratory organs?
qa.a: Each part handles its own gas exchange and living cells are close to the surface
qa.e: Low demand, short diffusion paths and local gas exchange are enough.

qa.q: In the complete combustion of glucose, how many molecules of water are formed per molecule of glucose?
qa.e: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

qa.q: If a cell burned glucose in a single step, most energy would be lost as:
qa.e: Combustion releases energy mostly as heat; step-wise oxidation traps it as ATP.

qa.q: During photosynthesis, why is O₂ supply not a problem for leaf cells?
qa.a: O₂ is released within the cells themselves
qa.e: Photosynthesis produces O₂ inside the cell.

qa.q: All living organisms can partly oxidise glucose without oxygen. This process is:
qa.e: Glycolysis is universal and anaerobic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Energy in respiratory substrates is released step by step in cells. Reason (R): Releasing it step by step allows energy to be trapped as ATP instead of being lost as heat.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; stepwise release lets the cell capture energy in ATP.

qa.q: Glycolysis takes place in the:
qa.e: It is cytoplasmic in all organisms.

qa.q: The enzyme that phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate is:
qa.e: Hexokinase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose.

qa.q: NADH + H⁺ is formed in glycolysis when:
qa.e: PGAL is oxidised, reducing NAD⁺.

qa.q: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into:
qa.e: It splits into two 3-carbon sugar phosphates.

qa.q: The EMP pathway is named after:
qa.e: They worked out glycolysis.

qa.q: Substrate-level ATP synthesis in glycolysis occurs at:
qa.a: BPGA → PGA and PEP → pyruvic acid
qa.e: These two steps directly make ATP.

qa.q: How many enzyme-controlled reactions make up glycolysis?
qa.e: Glycolysis is a chain of ten reactions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Glycolysis is found in all living organisms. Reason (R): Glycolysis requires a mitochondrion.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Glycolysis is universal (A true), but it occurs in the cytoplasm and needs no mitochondrion (R false).

qa.q: The net gain of ATP in glycolysis per glucose molecule is:
qa.e: 4 formed - 2 used = 2.

qa.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from one glucose?
qa.e: One 6-carbon glucose gives two 3-carbon pyruvates.

qa.q: The enzyme that converts sucrose into glucose and fructose is:
qa.e: Invertase hydrolyses sucrose.

qa.q: How many NADH + H⁺ are produced in glycolysis per glucose?
qa.e: One per PGAL, and there are two PGAL per glucose.

qa.q: Which is NOT a fate of pyruvic acid?
qa.e: The three fates are lactic acid, ethanol, or Krebs cycle.

qa.q: What is the net ATP gain when 5 molecules of glucose go through glycolysis?
qa.e: 2 per glucose × 5 = 10.

qa.q: Complete oxidation of pyruvate to CO₂ and H₂O requires:
qa.e: Aerobic respiration needs O₂.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Glycolysis produces 4 ATP but the net gain is only 2. Reason (R): Two ATP are used up in the early steps of glycolysis.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; subtracting the 2 ATP used gives a net gain of 2.

qa.q: Enzymes converting pyruvic acid into ethanol and CO₂ are:
qa.a: Pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase
qa.e: These two enzymes act in yeast.

qa.q: In muscles during heavy exercise, pyruvic acid is converted to:
qa.e: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate when O₂ is short.

qa.q: Yeasts die when the alcohol concentration reaches about:
qa.e: They poison themselves at about 13% alcohol.

qa.q: Fermentation releases what fraction of the energy in glucose?
qa.e: Most energy stays locked in lactic acid or ethanol.

qa.q: The net ATP produced when one glucose is fermented to ethanol is:
qa.e: Only glycolysis yields ATP: net 2.

qa.q: The main purpose of converting pyruvate to lactic acid in muscles is to:
qa.a: Regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue
qa.e: Reoxidising NADH allows glycolysis to keep producing ATP.

qa.q: Why are fermentation products called hazardous?
qa.a: They are acids or alcohols that can harm cells
qa.e: Acid or alcohol build-up is harmful.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fermentation yields more energy per glucose than aerobic respiration. Reason (R): In fermentation, glucose is only partially oxidised.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: fermentation gives a net 2 ATP, far less than aerobic respiration. R is true: glucose is only partly broken down, so most of its energy stays locked in ethanol or lactic acid.

qa.q: The link reaction converts pyruvate into:
qa.e: Pyruvic dehydrogenase forms acetyl CoA, CO₂ and NADH.

qa.q: The enzyme catalysing the link reaction is:
qa.e: Pyruvic dehydrogenase carries out oxidative decarboxylation.

qa.q: The first product of the Krebs cycle formed from acetyl CoA and OAA is:
qa.e: Citrate synthase forms citric acid.

qa.q: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle occurs during conversion of:
qa.e: A GTP forms here, which gives ATP.

qa.q: Per pyruvate, the Krebs cycle itself produces how many NADH?
qa.e: Three NAD⁺ reduction points in the cycle; the 4th NADH comes from the link reaction.

qa.q: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?
qa.e: The TCA cycle runs in the matrix.

qa.q: How many CO₂ molecules are released in the complete oxidation of one glucose (link reaction plus Krebs cycle)?
qa.e: 3 per pyruvate × 2 pyruvate = 6.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Krebs cycle needs a continuous supply of oxaloacetic acid. Reason (R): OAA is the first member of the cycle and condenses with acetyl CoA to form citric acid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since OAA is needed to accept each acetyl group, it must be continually replenished.

qa.q: The final acceptor of electrons in the ETS is:
qa.e: O₂ accepts electrons and hydrogen to form water.

qa.q: Complex IV of the ETS is:
qa.e: It contains cytochromes a, a₃ and copper centres.

qa.q: How many ATP are formed from oxidation of one NADH in the ETS?
qa.e: NADH gives 3 ATP; FADH₂ gives 2.

qa.q: The mobile carrier that transfers electrons between complex III and complex IV is:
qa.e: Cytochrome c is attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane.

qa.q: ATP synthesis using energy from oxidation-reduction in mitochondria is called:
qa.e: Redox energy builds the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase.

qa.q: How many ATP are produced in the ETS from 2 NADH and 2 FADH₂?
In ATP synthase, the part that forms the proton channel across the inner membrane is:
qa.e: F₀ is the integral channel; F₁ makes ATP.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Oxygen is vital for aerobic respiration even though it acts only at the last step. Reason (R): Oxygen drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system as water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; without O₂ accepting electrons, the chain backs up and stops.

qa.q: The theoretical net gain of ATP from aerobic respiration of one glucose is:
qa.e: Based on the balance-sheet assumptions.

qa.q: Which is NOT an assumption of the respiratory balance sheet?
qa.a: Intermediates are withdrawn to make other compounds
qa.e: The sheet assumes no intermediates are withdrawn.

qa.q: How many NADH are produced in total from one glucose in aerobic respiration?
qa.e: Glycolysis 2 + link 2 + Krebs 6 = 10.

qa.q: Fermentation differs from aerobic respiration in that fermentation:
qa.e: Fermentation is partial breakdown with only 2 ATP.

qa.q: How many ATP come from FADH₂ in the complete oxidation of one glucose?
qa.e: 2 FADH₂ × 2 ATP = 4.

qa.q: Why is the 38 ATP figure called theoretical?
qa.a: In real cells, pathways work simultaneously and intermediates are withdrawn
qa.e: The assumptions do not fully hold in living systems.

qa.q: Respiration differs from combustion because respiration:
qa.a: Releases energy in small enzyme-controlled steps and traps it as ATP
qa.e: Stepwise oxidation allows energy capture.

qa.q: How many times more ATP does aerobic respiration give per glucose than fermentation (using 38 and 2)?
The respiratory pathway is called amphibolic because it is involved in:
qa.e: Its intermediates are used for both breakdown and synthesis.

qa.q: Fatty acids enter the respiratory pathway as:
qa.e: They are degraded to acetyl CoA.

qa.q: Glycerol enters the respiratory pathway after conversion to:
qa.e: Glycerol becomes PGAL, a glycolytic intermediate.

qa.q: Before entering respiration, amino acids undergo:
qa.e: Amino groups are removed first.

qa.q: Synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones is:
qa.e: Anabolism builds; catabolism breaks down.

qa.q: Proteins are broken into amino acids by:
qa.e: Proteases digest proteins.

qa.q: When an organism needs to synthesise fatty acids, which intermediate is withdrawn from the respiratory pathway?
qa.e: Acetyl CoA is the building block for fatty acids.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The respiratory pathway is better described as amphibolic than catabolic. Reason (R): Respiratory intermediates such as acetyl CoA are also withdrawn for synthesis of compounds like fatty acids.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; use of intermediates for synthesis shows the pathway is anabolic as well as catabolic.

qa.q: RQ is defined as:
qa.a: Volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed
qa.e: RQ = CO₂ out / O₂ in.

qa.q: What is the RQ when glucose is completely oxidised?
qa.e: 6 CO₂ ÷ 6 O₂ = 1.

qa.q: The RQ of tripalmitin, 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O, is about:
The RQ for proteins is about:
qa.e: Proteins give an RQ of about 0.9.

qa.q: A germinating seed evolves 14 mL CO₂ while consuming 20 mL O₂. Its RQ is:
qa.e: 14 ÷ 20 = 0.7, suggesting fats are being respired.

qa.q: Why is the RQ of fats less than 1?
qa.a: Fats are poor in oxygen, so more O₂ is needed than CO₂ released
qa.e: Oxygen-poor fats consume relatively more O₂.

qa.q: For malic acid (C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O), the RQ is:
qa.e: 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.33; organic acids give RQ above 1.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The RQ of carbohydrates is 1. Reason (R): Carbohydrates contain no oxygen atoms in their molecules.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: on complete oxidation, equal volumes of CO₂ are evolved and O₂ consumed, so RQ = 1. R is false: carbohydrates such as glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) are rich in oxygen.

qa.q: Growth is best defined as:
qa.a: An irreversible permanent increase in size
qa.e: Growth is permanent and irreversible.

qa.q: The open form of growth in plants is due to:
qa.a: Meristems that keep adding new cells
qa.e: Meristem cells divide and self-perpetuate.

qa.q: Secondary growth in dicots is caused by:
qa.e: Lateral meristems increase girth.

qa.q: Which is an intrinsic factor controlling plant development?
qa.e: PGRs and genetic factors are intrinsic.

qa.q: Primary growth results in:
qa.a: Elongation of the plant along its axis
qa.e: Apical meristems make roots and shoots longer.

qa.q: Development in plants runs from:
qa.a: Germination of the seed (from the zygote) to senescence
qa.e: Development covers the whole life cycle.

qa.q: Expansion of a leaf is an example of:
qa.e: It is an irreversible increase in size.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Plants can grow throughout their life. Reason (R): Plants have meristems whose cells retain the capacity to divide and self-perpetuate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; meristems explain lifelong, indeterminate growth.

qa.q: Growth of a pollen tube is measured in terms of its:
qa.e: A pollen tube grows longer.

qa.q: Cells of the meristematic phase have:
qa.a: Dense protoplasm, large nuclei and thin primary cellulose walls
qa.e: These are features of actively dividing cells.

qa.q: Increased vacuolation and cell enlargement occur in the:
qa.e: Elongation zone cells enlarge and vacuolate.

qa.q: Watermelon cells may increase in size by up to:
qa.e: NCERT gives 3,50,000 times.

qa.q: At the cellular level, growth is mainly an increase in:
qa.e: Growth is principally an increase in protoplasm.

qa.q: A maize root meristem forms 17,500 cells per hour. How many cells form in 2 hours?
Cells reach maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasmic modification in the:
qa.e: Maturation phase is furthest from the apex.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Growth is usually measured indirectly. Reason (R): Increase in protoplasm is difficult to measure directly.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; so we measure proportional quantities such as weight, length or area.

qa.q: In arithmetic growth, after mitosis:
qa.a: Only one daughter cell continues to divide
qa.e: The other daughter differentiates and matures.

qa.q: A sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve has which phases in order?
qa.e: Slow start, rapid exponential growth, then levelling off.

qa.q: In W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ, r stands for:
qa.e: r is the relative growth rate, also called the efficiency index.

qa.q: A root 3 cm long grows arithmetically at 2 cm per day. What is its length after 4 days?
Leaf A grows from 5 cm² to 10 cm²; leaf B from 50 cm² to 55 cm². Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Same absolute growth, but A has a higher relative growth rate
qa.e: Both grew 5 cm², but A doubled (100%) while B grew 10%.

qa.q: A leaf grows from 20 cm² to 30 cm² in a week. Its relative growth rate for the week, in percent, is:
Arithmetic growth gives which kind of curve when length is plotted against time?
qa.e: Constant rate gives a straight line.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Growth slows down in the stationary phase of a sigmoid curve. Reason (R): In the stationary phase, cells divide faster than in any other phase.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true: the curve flattens in the stationary phase. R is false: division is fastest in the log (exponential) phase; growth slows in the stationary phase because nutrient supply becomes limited.

qa.q: Regaining the capacity to divide by living differentiated cells is:
qa.e: Example: parenchyma forming cork cambium.

qa.q: Formation of interfascicular cambium from parenchyma is an example of:
qa.e: Mature parenchyma regains the ability to divide.

qa.q: During differentiation into tracheary elements, cells:
qa.a: Lose their protoplasm and form lignocellulosic secondary walls
qa.e: They become dead, strong water-conducting tubes.

qa.q: Differentiation in plants is called 'open' because:
qa.a: The final structure of a cell depends on its location
qa.e: Cells from the same meristem mature differently by position.

qa.q: Water is needed for growth because it:
qa.a: Helps cell enlargement through turgidity and is a medium for enzymes
qa.e: Turgid cells expand, and enzymes work in water.

qa.q: Secondary xylem formed by the activity of vascular cambium is a product of:
qa.e: Cambium-derived cells mature again to perform specific functions.

qa.q: Oxygen is needed for growth because it:
qa.e: Aerobic respiration releases energy for growth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cells positioned away from the root apical meristem become root-cap cells. Reason (R): In plants, the final structure of a cell is influenced by its location.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; location determines fate, which is why these cells become root-cap cells.

qa.q: The ability of plants to follow different pathways to form different structures is:
qa.e: Plasticity gives heterophylly, for example.

qa.q: Heterophylly in buttercup is caused by:
qa.a: Environment (leaves in air vs in water)
qa.e: Leaves formed in water and in air differ.

qa.q: Which plant shows heterophylly due to life phase?
qa.e: Cotton, coriander and larkspur show it.

qa.q: Development in plants is the sum of:
qa.e: Both together make development.

qa.q: Development covers changes from:
qa.e: Development is the whole life history.

qa.q: Larkspur's juvenile and mature leaves differ in shape. This is:
qa.e: Leaf shape changes with life phase.

qa.q: Which pair are both intrinsic controls of development?
qa.e: Genetic and hormonal controls are intrinsic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Heterophylly is an example of plasticity. Reason (R): In heterophylly, a plant forms differently shaped leaves in different phases or environments.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; producing different structures in response to conditions is what plasticity means.

qa.q: Auxin was first isolated from coleoptile tips of oat seedlings by:
qa.e: Went isolated auxin; the Darwins showed the tip was involved.

qa.q: 'Bakanae' disease of rice is caused by:
qa.e: This fungus produces gibberellins.

qa.q: Kinetin was discovered from:
qa.e: Zeatin came from corn kernels and coconut milk.

qa.q: Abscisic acid is chemically a derivative of:
qa.e: ABA is a carotenoid derivative.

qa.q: Inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin were later shown to be:
qa.e: All three are chemically identical: ABA.

qa.q: Which PGR is a growth inhibitor?
qa.e: ABA is the main growth inhibitor.

qa.q: The volatile substance from ripened oranges that hastened banana ripening was:
qa.e: Cousins showed it was ethylene.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Darwins concluded that the coleoptile tip was involved in phototropism. Reason (R): Canary grass coleoptiles bent towards unilateral light, and the tip was the site of a transmittable influence.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their experiments located the influence in the tip.

qa.q: Inhibition of lateral buds by the growing apical bud is called:
qa.e: Auxin from the apex suppresses lateral buds.

qa.q: Which is a synthetic auxin used as a weedicide?
qa.e: 2,4-D kills dicot weeds.

qa.q: Decapitation in tea plantations helps because it:
qa.a: Removes apical dominance so lateral branches grow
qa.e: Lateral buds grow when the tip is removed.

qa.q: Auxins were first isolated from:
qa.e: NCERT notes auxins were first isolated from human urine.

qa.q: Which is a natural auxin?
qa.e: IAA and IBA are natural auxins.

qa.q: Seedless tomatoes can be produced by applying:
qa.e: Auxins induce parthenocarpy.

qa.q: Auxins promote abscission of:
qa.e: They prevent early drop but promote abscission of older parts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): 2,4-D sprayed on a lawn kills the mature grass along with the weeds. Reason (R): 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin used as a herbicide against dicot weeds.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: 2,4-D does not affect mature monocots such as lawn grass. R is true: it is a synthetic auxin that kills dicotyledonous weeds, which is why it is used for weed-free lawns.

qa.q: Bolting in beet and cabbage is promoted by:
qa.e: GAs cause internode elongation before flowering.

qa.q: Malting in the brewing industry is speeded up by:
qa.e: Gibberellic acid hastens malting.

qa.q: Spraying sugarcane with gibberellins increases yield by as much as:
qa.e: Longer stems store more sugar.

qa.q: A natural cytokinin isolated from corn kernels and coconut milk is:
qa.e: Kinetin is not natural in plants; zeatin is.

qa.q: Cytokinins delay leaf senescence by:
qa.e: Nutrients are moved into the leaf, keeping it active.

qa.q: Natural cytokinins are synthesised in:
qa.a: Regions of rapid cell division such as root apices and young fruits
qa.e: They form where cells divide rapidly.

qa.q: Which PGR helps overcome apical dominance?
qa.e: Cytokinins promote lateral shoot growth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gibberellins promote bolting in cabbage and beet. Reason (R): Gibberellins are used to speed up malting in the brewing industry.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true uses of gibberellins, but malting in brewing has nothing to do with why cabbage bolts; bolting is due to GA-induced internode elongation just before flowering.

qa.q: The rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening caused by ethylene is called:
qa.e: Ethylene enhances respiration in ripening fruits.

qa.q: ABA is called the stress hormone because it:
qa.a: Closes stomata and increases tolerance to stresses
qa.e: It helps plants cope with drought and other stresses.

qa.q: The most widely used source of ethylene in agriculture is:
qa.e: Ethephon releases ethylene in the plant.

qa.q: Which PGR induces flowering in mango?
qa.e: Ethylene induces flowering in mango and pineapple.

qa.q: ABA in most situations acts as an antagonist to:
qa.e: ABA opposes GA effects, e.g. in germination.

qa.q: Ethylene promotes rapid internode elongation in:
qa.e: This keeps leaves above water.

qa.q: Horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings are effects of:
qa.e: Together these are the triple response to ethylene.

qa.q: Assertion (A): ABA helps seeds survive desiccation. Reason (R): ABA induces seed dormancy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; by inducing dormancy, ABA helps seeds withstand desiccation.
